name: fast-strlen.c (bjourne gist): multi-threaded memchr-based strlen
baseline: libc strlen (labelled 'strlen' in the gist's printed output; libc implementation and version not stated, glibc presumed on Linux)
workload: strlen of one posix_memalign'd 2e9-byte buffer filled with 'A' and NUL-terminated at the last byte (length 1999999999), scanned 10 times per variant, with each call's result asserted equal to the first. The E5-2650 v4 block in the header reports a 4.00GB scan with length 4000007776, which does not match N_BUF in either gist revision.
claimed_speedup: Xeon W-2245 @ 3.90GHz, gcc 13.1.1, 2.00GB buffer scanned 10 times: threaded_strlen 43.56 GB/s (0.46 s) vs libc strlen 16.84 GB/s (1.19 s), about 2.6x (derived from page data). Xeon E5-2650 v4 @ 2.20GHz, gcc 9.4.0, 4.00GB header: 34.09 GB/s (1.17 s) vs 8.76 GB/s (4.56 s), about 3.9x (derived from page data), measured on an unpublished variant of the code. threaded_strlen uses sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN) threads, against single-threaded libc strlen.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -march=native fast-strlen.c -lpthread -o fast-strlen (gcc 9.4.0 and gcc 13.1.1); gist says to use gcc because clang optimizes away parts of the benchmark
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2650 v4 @ 2.20GHz; Intel Xeon W-2245 @ 3.90GHz
tradeoffs: Not a usable strlen replacement. The fast path deliberately triggers SIGSEGV to find the end of mapped memory, then fans memchr out over all online CPUs; the author says it 'heavily relies on undefined behavior' and exists to beat benchmarks. It only pays off for multi-gigabyte strings and occupies every core. No license.
caveats: Written for fun to beat the '{n} times faster' benchmark. The author says the technique 'heavily relies on undefined behavior' and 'shouldn't be used for anything other than beating benchmarks'. A helper thread probes past the string in 4 MB steps until it hits SIGSEGV, then memchr runs in parallel over chunks up to the faulting address, so on a real heap with mapped memory after a short string it can scan far beyond the string. The speedup comes from using every online CPU (sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)) against single-threaded libc strlen, not from a better single-thread algorithm. On the same pages the single-thread vector versions do not beat libc: strlen_avx2 7.86 vs 8.76 GB/s on the E5-2650 v4, and strlen_avx2 15.36 and strlen_avx512 16.36 vs 16.84 GB/s on the W-2245. On the W-2245 the byte-loop slow_strlen (while (s[i++] != '\0');) also prints 16.87 GB/s, level with libc, which fits GCC 12+ loop distribution turning the loop into a strlen call or a memory-bandwidth limit (inference, not confirmed). The E5-2650 v4 numbers came from a code version not in the gist (4.00GB, length 4000007776, while both revisions use N_BUF = 2e9). Both gist revisions are dated 2023-07-13; the 2025-12-27 'last active' date does not reflect a code change. The libc and glibc version are not named. No license.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'SWAR OR SIMD strlen strnlen strcpy faster than libc benchmark repository C header-only' returned the gist 'fast-strlen.c'; gist opened twice on gist.github.com

verification.tier_reason: The gist itself (fast-strlen.c) is the public benchmark, timing libc strlen next to threaded_strlen with the build command (gcc -O3 -march=native ... -lpthread), the compiler version (gcc 13.1.1) and the CPU (Xeon W-2245 @ 3.90GHz) all stated: 43.56 vs 16.84 GB/s, with every variant's returned length asserted equal and printed. The earlier E5-2650 v4 / gcc 9.4.0 block was produced by a version of the code that is not in the gist (it scanned 4.00GB and found length 4000007776, while both revisions set N_BUF to 2e9), so only the W-2245 run is reproducible from published code.
verification.notes: Numbers and the libc strlen baseline are as recorded and the code is public, so tier A holds on the W-2245 run (2.6x, derived from page data). Shortcomings to record: multi-threaded vs single-threaded baseline, UB-based SIGSEGV probing that the author says is for benchmarks only, E5-2650 v4 run from unpublished code, and single-thread AVX2/AVX-512 variants not faster than libc. last_commit corrected to 2023-07-13 (both revisions), which makes it abandoned under the 3-year rule.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: threaded_strlen 34.09 GB/s versus libc strlen 8.76 GB/s on Xeon E5-2650 v4 @ 2.20GHz with gcc 9.4.0; 43.56 GB/s versus 16.84 GB/s on Xeon W-2245 @ 3.90GHz with gcc 13.1.1 (about 3.9x and 2.6x, derived from page data).
corrected_fields.workload: strlen of a single multi-gigabyte buffer of 'A' bytes (printed lengths 4000007776 and 1999999999), scanned 10 times per variant.
corrected_fields.caveats: Author wrote it for fun after a '{n} times faster' benchmark post. Tier A only in the narrow sense that code, flags and CPU models are public; the workload is artificial. In the same output the single-thread vectorised versions do not beat libc: strlen_avx2 7.86 versus libc 8.76 GB/s on the E5-2650 v4, strlen_avx2 15.36 and strlen_avx512 16.36 versus libc 16.84 GB/s on the W-2245. On the W-2245 the byte-by-byte slow_strlen also prints 16.87 GB/s, level with libc, which suggests memory-bandwidth limits and possibly a compiler builtin (inference, not confirmed). The first run header says 4.00GB, the second 2.00GB. Date is the gist's 'last active' date, not a commit date.

name: Memset by memcpy doubling (riteme gist: 'Memcpy is faster than memset on Intel i7 12700 with glibc 2.36')
baseline: glibc 2.36 memset()
workload: Fill a 1 GiB char buffer (1 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024) 100 times with either glibc memset or my_memset. Above a threshold constant written as 2 * 2048 * 2048 (8 MiB, although the code comment says 2 MiB), my_memset memsets the first chunk once. It then copies that same chunk with memcpy(s + i, s, threshold) to each later chunk-sized slot (the ranges do not overlap) and memsets any tail. The test prints a[0] so the fills are not optimised away.
claimed_speedup: glibc memset 6.23 s user / 6.34 s elapsed versus my_memset 2.47 s user / 2.57 s elapsed for 100 fills of 1 GiB on an i7-12700 with glibc 2.36 (single /usr/bin/time run each). The author calls this about 60 percent faster. That means about 60 percent less time, a 2.47x speedup (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: g++ memset_test.cpp -O3 -march=native (g++ version not stated); -DUSE_MY_MEMSET selects the custom version
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700 (12 cores, 20 threads), 15 GiB RAM, Manjaro Linux kernel 6.1.0-1, glibc 2.36-6
stars_or_usage: Gist with 1 star, 12 revisions and 3 comments (January 1-5, 2023); last active 2025-12-27.
tradeoffs: A technique snippet, not a library. It only makes sense for very large fills (the first block is memset, the rest is doubled with memcpy), and it needs a correct handling of the final partial block. No licence on the gist.
caveats: This is a single wall-clock run per variant with no repetitions or variance, and the g++ version is not stated. The chunk is 8 MiB (2 * 2048 * 2048), not the 2 MiB the comment says. The source chunk is always the first chunk, so it likely stays in the i7-12700's 25 MB L3 while the destination streams to DRAM. The 'contradiction' in the comments is a different regime: perf bench mem (author's i7-12700: memset default 72.70 GB/s vs memcpy default 31.20 GB/s; Ristovski's Ryzen 5700G: memcpy default 51.79 vs memset default 37.38 GB/s) ran on 1 MB cache-resident buffers, not on 1 GiB fills. Neither commenter ran memset_test.cpp, and sada-amd only guessed rep stosb vs vector moves without a disassembly. The baseline is probably outdated (WebSearch snippet only, patchwork and Phoronix not opened): glibc before May 2024 used rep stosb for all large memsets. Noah Goldstein's 'x86: Improve large memset perf with non-temporal stores' (glibc 2.40, Intel only, disabled on Skylake Server) added the non-temporal path that memcpy already had, so the gap this gist exploits is likely closed on glibc 2.40+. The gist has no licence.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch '"faster than glibc" memcpy OR memset OR strlen OR memcmp own implementation blog post github' (gist.github.com/riteme result); then opened the gist.

verification.tier_reason: The gist has the full benchmark (memset_test.cpp, with my_memset selected by -DUSE_MY_MEMSET), the compile command (g++ -O3 -march=native; the g++ version is not stated), the CPU (Intel Core i7-12700) and glibc 2.36-6. Its /usr/bin/time output gives 6.23 s user / 6.34 s elapsed for glibc memset and 2.47 s user / 2.57 s elapsed for my_memset. That is enough for tier A, but it is a single run with no repetitions.
verification.notes: The measurement is valid and crude: both variants produce the same fill, and the memcpy ranges do not overlap. Tier A stands on code + flags + CPU + glibc version, but the result is one run on glibc 2.36. glibc 2.40's non-temporal large memset probably removes the advantage (snippet only). Record shortcomings: single run, unstated g++ version, the code comment says 2 MiB but the chunk is 8 MiB, the baseline is superseded, and there is no licence.

corrected_fields.workload: Fill a 1 GiB char buffer 100 times with either glibc memset or my_memset, which memsets the first 2 MiB once and then fills the rest by repeatedly memcpy-ing the already-filled block forward.
corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: glibc memset 6.34 s elapsed (6.23 s user) versus my_memset 2.57 s elapsed (2.47 s user); the author calls it about 60 percent faster (2.5x, derived from page data).
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: gist with a few comments dated January 2023; last activity 2025-12-27

In the gist comments the author's own 'perf bench mem' run on the same i7-12700 shows glibc memset at about 72.7 GB/s versus memcpy at about 31.2 GB/s, which the author calls contrary to the wall-clock test; a commenter on a Ryzen 5700G saw memset and memcpy variants performing similarly; another commenter guesses glibc uses rep stosb for memset and vector moves for memcpy (no disassembly posted). name: memx-cdy (C ABI of the Rust memx crate: memchr, memmem, memcmp, memcpy, memset)
language: Rust (C ABI shared and static library, LD_PRELOAD capable)
baseline: glibc and musl libc memchr, memmem, memcmp, memcpy and memset (called from Rust through FFI as libc_* rows), alongside Rust std and the memchr crate
workload: Criterion time per pass (200 samples, 100 ms warm-up, 1 s measurement; cache lines flushed before each function's run) over a fixed set of text lines, each pass making many calls, not time per single call: memmem searches the 48-byte needle 'just before we went into the very simple problem' in 21 alternating English lines (en, 10 matches) or a 39-byte Japanese needle in 21 Japanese lines (ja); memchr scans for 'r' (768 matches on en); memcpy copies a 15-byte (en) or 144-byte (ja) source into successive slices of the lines. Built for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and x86_64-unknown-linux-musl from memx xbench/benches/*.rs; the libc_* rows call the C library through Rust FFI.
claimed_speedup: memx-cdy README: 'Faster os libc and musl libc'. Derived from page data (memx docs tables, Intel i5-4570, rustc 1.69.0, Criterion time per pass, libc divided by memx): memmem gnu:en 2.173 vs 0.798 us (2.7x), gnu:ja 3.828 vs 1.230 us (3.1x), musl:en 3.948 vs 0.794 us (5.0x), musl:ja 7.010 vs 1.197 us (5.9x); memchr gnu 1.09x and 1.07x (4.849 vs 4.451, 5.764 vs 5.402 us), musl 2.0x and 1.9x (8.757 vs 4.426, 10.205 vs 5.322 us); memcmp musl:en 1.14x and musl:ja 3.8x (8.653 vs 2.293 us) but slower on glibc (gnu:en 1.584 vs 2.828 us, 0.56x; gnu:ja 1.582 vs 2.022 us, 0.78x); memset gnu:ja 1.14x and musl:ja 1.50x but slower on the short en case (gnu:en 2.003 vs 3.388 us, 0.59x; musl:en 2.139 vs 3.515 us, 0.61x). memcpy: memx is 3.1x faster than musl on en (20.289 vs 6.527 us) and 1.55x on ja, but 0.50x of glibc on en (3.483 vs 7.016 us) and 0.96x on ja; memx-cdy does not deliver the musl memcpy win, because its memcpy export is compiled out on musl targets and by the default 'no_memcpy' feature.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.69.0 (84c898d65 2023-04-16); cargo bench profile opt-level = 3, codegen-units = 1, lto = true (memx Cargo.toml); glibc and musl versions not stated
hardware: Intel i5-4570 @ 3.2 GHz for the quoted figures (AVX2 build); Intel Q6600 @ 2.4 GHz and an armv7 1.5 GHz device are also tabulated
stars_or_usage: 4 stars (memx-cdy), 26 stars (memx), memx has about 472k crates.io downloads
tradeoffs: Rust implementation with SSE2/AVX2 paths selected at run time (cpufeatures) plus a basic fallback; usable from C or C++ by linking libmemx_cdy.a/.so or LD_PRELOAD, but it needs a Rust toolchain to build and the Rust side must call memx_init(). Substantially slower than glibc for memcmp, memcpy and memset on the same CPU, so only the search functions (memmem, memchr on musl) are wins.
caveats: First-party benchmarks on a 2013-era desktop CPU with rustc 1.69 (2023); memx is now 0.2.2 (2026) and the tables were not regenerated with a date, so they may not reflect current code. glibc and musl versions are not stated. The benchmark times the memx Rust functions directly, not memx-cdy's C ABI exports or the LD_PRELOAD path; the wrappers add slice construction and memcmp switches to a byte loop for n < 4. memx-cdy's memcpy is exported only on non-musl targets and only when the default 'no_memcpy' feature is disabled (src/lib.rs notes a duplicate-symbol link error on musl), so the memcpy musl rows do not apply to it, and on glibc memx's memcpy is slower on short copies. Timings are per pass over 21 text lines with many short calls each, so per-call overhead (FFI and PLT for libc_*) weighs heavily; musl's memchr, memmem and memcpy are simple C, so the musl gaps largely reflect musl's weakness. memx's own harness calls memchr::memmem::find per call (building a searcher each time), which is why the memchr crate's memmem row is about 4x slower than glibc; treat the memmem comparison with care. One Criterion table per function, no confidence intervals reported. Benchmark code and docs live in the memx repository, not memx-cdy.
found_via: crates.io API query 'libc replacement' and 'memx' surfaced memx-cdy and memx; then README of memx-cdy and docs/README.{memchr,memcmp,memcpy,memset,memmem}.md of aki-akaguma/memx

verification.tier_reason: The memx docs tables (docs/README.memmem.md and siblings) compare memx against libc_* rows for glibc and musl, the harness is public (memx xbench/benches/bench-memmem.rs, bench-memcpy.rs, create_data.rs, driven by makefile.build), the compiler is stated (rustc 1.69.0), the bench profile flags are in memx Cargo.toml (opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, lto) and the CPU is named (i5-4570), so tier A stands; the downgrade is for the overstated claim, not the tier.
verification.notes: Tier A kept; downgraded for overstatement: the memcpy musl 3.1x figure cannot be obtained through memx-cdy (memcpy export compiled out on musl and by the default no_memcpy feature), timings are per pass not per call, and memset/memcmp are slower than glibc on the short case. Real wins are memmem (2.7-5.9x over glibc and musl) and memchr/memcmp over musl; versus glibc only memmem is clearly faster. memx itself was already folded into this entry as a duplicate.

corrected_fields.workload: Time per call of each function on a short English haystack (:en) and a long Japanese haystack (:ja), built for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, from the memx xbench micro-benchmarks.
corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: memx-cdy README: 'Faster os libc and musl libc'. Derived from the memx docs tables (Intel i5-4570, rustc 1.69.0, time per call, libc divided by memx): memmem gnu:en 2.173 vs 0.798 us (2.7x), gnu:ja 3.828 vs 1.230 us (3.1x), musl:en 3.948 vs 0.794 us (5.0x), musl:ja 7.010 vs 1.197 us (5.9x); memchr musl:en 8.757 vs 4.426 us (2.0x), musl:ja 10.205 vs 5.322 us (1.9x) but only 1.09x and 1.07x on glibc (4.849 vs 4.451 us, 5.764 vs 5.402 us); memcpy musl:en 20.289 vs 6.527 us (3.1x). On glibc memcmp (1.584 vs 2.828 us), memcpy gnu:en (3.483 vs 7.016 us) and memset (2.003 vs 3.388 us) memx is slower.
corrected_fields.caveats: First-party benchmarks on a 2013-era desktop CPU with rustc 1.69; the libc_* rows are libc functions called through Rust FFI. memx's own harness shows the memchr crate's memmem about 4x slower than glibc memmem (9.127 vs 2.173 us), which contradicts the memchr author's rebar results, so the harness probably builds a searcher on every call and the memmem gap should be treated with care. Single table per function, no repeat statistics. The benchmark code and docs live in the memx repository, not memx-cdy.

name: optimization-detective (SWAR memcasecmp, common suffix and whitespace patches for Abseil)
baseline: Abseil absl::strings_internal::memcasecmp, FindLongestCommonSuffix and RemoveExtraAsciiWhitespace (verbatim upstream code from abseil-cpp@7e706921, byte-at-a-time loops)
workload: Standalone microbenchmarks (median of 25 reps, autotuned iteration count) of each function on 256 B to 4096 B strings: full match, half match, byte-identical and case-flipped equality.
claimed_speedup: FindLongestCommonSuffix 6.87x headline (the half_match/256 row of results/absl_lcp_lcs_bench.txt: 55.84 to 8.13 ns); FINDINGS.md table: full match 4096 B 1524 to 233 ns (6.5x), 256 B 100 to 15 ns (6.9x), half match 4096 B 754 to 121 ns (6.2x); regresses to about 0.5x (0.55 to about 1.05 ns) when the last bytes differ. memcasecmp 5.98x headline (FINDINGS.md: eq_case 256 B 229 to 38 ns; 4096 B eq_exact 1227 to 246 ns 4.99x, eq_case 3557 to 612 ns 5.82x; the checked-in results file is a slightly different run: eq_case/256 6.29x, eq_case/4096 5.97x, eq_exact/4096 4.96x); 4.1-4.3x at 16 B; mismatch at byte 0 is 0.47x (0.90 to 1.91 ns). RemoveExtraAsciiWhitespace 1.40x on already-clean 4096 B input (2460 to 1758 ns; results file 1.38x), 1.27-1.46x on clean input across sizes, but 0.78-0.84x on input with one internal double space (64-4096 B).
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 14, -std=c++17 -O3
hardware: Apple M2, macOS 24.5
tradeoffs: Header-only drop-in replacements (original.h, optimized.h, test.cc, bench.cc per function, no build system); the SWAR 8-byte loads assume little-endian and ASCII-only case folding; the suffix and case-compare versions pay about 0.5-1 ns extra when the mismatch is in the first or last byte.
caveats: Baseline is Abseil's scalar loop copied verbatim into original.h (abseil-cpp@7e706921) and compiled in the same file as the patch, not glibc strncasecmp or memcmp, so the ratios say nothing about libc; one machine (Apple M2) and one compiler (Apple clang 14; 'macOS 24.5' is probably the Darwin version, i.e. macOS 15.5). Each benchmark re-runs one fixed input pair in a hot loop (cache-resident, perfectly predicted), and the eq_case workload flips every letter, the worst case for the original's per-byte branch. Raw outputs in results/ (absl_lcp_lcs_bench.txt, absl_memcasecmp_bench.txt, absl_remove_ws_bench.txt) come from a slightly different run than the FINDINGS.md tables (within a few percent). The patches regress on early mismatches (about 2x slower at 1-2 ns absolute) and RemoveExtraAsciiWhitespace is 16-28% slower when a rewrite is needed. The patches are not upstreamed to Abseil (no PR linked); the author notes FindLongestCommonSuffix has no call sites in the codebases checked. The repo's dollar and CO2 fleet estimates are heuristics, not evidence. Two more patches in the repo (nlohmann/json dump_escaped 4.62x, cpp-httplib header hash 1.44x) belong to JSON and HTTP categories and are not recorded here. Optimized code lives alongside verbatim Apache-2.0 Abseil source (original.h); the author's additions are MIT.
found_via: github.com/topics/swar listing (C++ entry 'drop-in performance patches for Abseil, nlohmann/json, and cpp-httplib'); repo README, FINDINGS.md and commits page opened

verification.tier_reason: Public standalone benchmark code (src/absl_lcp_lcs/bench.cc, src/absl_memcasecmp/bench.cc, src/absl_remove_ws/bench.cc on the bench/bench.h harness, driven by run_all.sh) times verbatim Abseil code (original.h) against the patch; compiler (Apple clang 14), flags (-std=c++17 -O3) and CPU (Apple M2) are stated, and raw outputs are checked in under results/.
verification.notes: Numbers check out against FINDINGS.md and the checked-in results files; code is correct on inspection (SWAR tolower masks to 7 bits, clz/ctz guarded against zero). Shortcomings to record: Abseil scalar loops as baseline (not libc), single Apple M2 machine, fixed hot-cache inputs, regressions on early-mismatch and needs-rewrite inputs, patches not upstreamed, 0-star repo from 2026-08.

The repo's dollar and CO2 fleet estimates are heuristics, not evidence. Optimized code lives alongside verbatim Apache-2.0 Abseil source (original.h); the author's additions are MIT. name: rvv-bench (RISC-V Vector memcpy, memset and strlen assembly)
language: Assembly (RISC-V Vector 1.0) with a C harness
baseline: libc memcpy, memset and strlen of the benchmarked RISC-V board (hosted libc, version not stated); the same harness also times musl's C memcpy/strlen, a byte-wise scalar loop and a compiler auto-vectorized scalar loop
workload: Bytes per cycle (hardware cycle counter) of memcpy (random misalignment and aligned), memset and strlen for sizes from 1 byte to tens of MB, comparing hand-written RVV assembly variants (LMUL m1 to m8, aligned, tail-handling and vlmax strategies) with libc, musl and scalar code.
claimed_speedup: No headline number in the README; the numbers are in the per-board results pages. Derived from page data (SpacemiT X60 results, fixed variant rvv_m4 against the libc row, bytes/cycle at the nearest recorded size): memcpy 4.73x at 66 B (1.941 vs 0.410), 2.71x at about 1 KB (4.298 vs 1.585), 2.71x at about 16 KB (5.040 vs 1.860), 2.05x at about 265 KB (3.438 vs 1.674), 1.07-1.11x at 8-64 MB; never below libc over all 233 sizes (geomean 2.0x). memset 3.55x at 66 B, 1.64x at about 1 KB, 1.72x at about 16 KB, 1.79x at about 265 KB, parity (1.00-1.02x) from 8 MB up (geomean 1.5x over 245 sizes). strlen is noisy and mixed: 1.36x at 61 B (but 0.72x at 55 B and 1.15x at 67 B), 1.81x at about 1 KB, 2.44x at about 16 KB; the 2.89x at about 260 KB is an isolated spike (0.65x at 245 KB, 0.95x at 275 KB), and above about 280 KB rvv_m4 is slower than libc (about 0.30 vs 0.45 B/cycle, 0.65-0.7x); rvv_m4 is slower than libc at 135 of 262 strlen sizes (geomean 1.15x). Other strlen variants do better: rvv_m1 stays about 2x libc at multi-MB sizes (0.98 vs 0.46 B/cycle at 3.6 MB) and rvv_page_aligned_m8 reaches 4.9x at 16 KB (6.388 vs 1.308 B/cycle), a best-variant selection.
compiler_and_flags: config.mk default: cc -march=rv64gcv -O3 -Wall -Wextra -DUSE_PERF_EVENT (native build; the compiler name and version are not stated in the files opened; the results page labels the compiler auto-vectorized scalar row 'scalar_autovec_clang18')
hardware: SpacemiT X60 cores of the SpacemiT K1 (Banana Pi BPI-F3), 1.6 GHz, RVV 1.0 with VLEN 256, for the figures quoted; the results repository also has folders for SiFive P870, XuanTie C920V2, SpacemiT A100 and X100, Tenstorrent X280 and others, Sipeed Lichee Pi 4A, CanMV K230 and more
tradeoffs: RISC-V Vector 1.0 hardware only (rv64gcv); an XTheadVector instruction-timing directory exists but the README says it is no longer maintained. The kernels are benchmark implementations in bench/*.S, meant to be studied or copied rather than a drop-in libc; the best variant (LMUL, alignment strategy) differs per core, and the page-aligned strlen needs the page size to be known.
caveats: The baseline is whatever libc the board ran (distribution and version not recorded; most likely a scalar glibc without an RVV string path), so much of the gap is the absence of RVV code in that libc, not a better algorithm; the author's own observations on the X60 index page compare against musl's SWAR code. Ratios are derived from the chart data embedded in the results HTML at the nearest recorded size, for one fixed variant; best-variant figures are selections. Each point is the median of 10 to 64 repeats (bench/config.h MIN_REPEATS 10, MAX_REPEATS 64) with output validated against a reference on the first repetition, but no spread is shown, and strlen in the 30-400 KB range swings between 0.33x and 3.5x of libc from one size to the next. memcpy and memset gains shrink to parity once data leaves the caches (8 MB and up). The compiler is only identified by the 'scalar_autovec_clang18' label; config.mk's default is CC=cc. The rendered results site is on github.io (blocked here), so the HTML in the rvv-bench-results repository was parsed. Other kernels in the repo (utf8_count, memreverse, mergelines, byteswap, base64) have no libc counterpart and are not part of this claim. The routines are benchmark kernels in bench/*.S, not a packaged library.

name: sve-string-routines-benchmarks (Arm SVE strcpy, strncpy, strcmp, strncmp)
language: Assembly (AArch64 SVE) with a C harness
baseline: GNU libc 2.39 string routines (strcpy, strncpy, strcmp, strncmp, strlen, memcpy as selected on Graviton3E) and the Arm Optimized Routines 23.01 SVE versions

claimed_speedup: README: the proposed SVE implementations 'never' regress against Arm optimized-routines and 'are competitive with their GNU libc counterparts, namely: strcpy, strncpy, strcmp and strncmp'. Derived from page data (raw .dat median runtimes, glibc time divided by proposed time, geometric mean over buffer sizes, aligned/unaligned): 64 B to 512 MiB strcpy 1.64x/1.61x, strncpy 1.40x/1.39x, strcmp 1.37x/1.32x, strncmp 1.45x/1.43x; 1 to 128 B strncpy 1.63x/1.58x, strcpy 1.32x/1.13x (unaligned dips to 0.37x at some lengths), strncmp 1.19x/1.18x, strcmp 1.13x/1.13x (as low as 0.55x at some short lengths). Against Arm optimized-routines 23.01 at 64 B to 512 MiB (derived): strcpy 2.8x, strlen 3.0x, strcmp 1.8x. compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.3.0 on kernel 6.2.0-1018-aws; CMake C11 build with target_compile_options -march=armv8.4-a+sve and no optimization level (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release is commented out, so the C harness builds at GCC's default -O0); the measured routines are hand-written .S files, so the driver flags matter little; -DSHORT_STRS, -DFULL_SIZE_RANGE, -DALIGNED_ALLOCS and -DCMP_LIBC select the modes
hardware: AWS Graviton3E (hpc7g.16xlarge, Neoverse V1 with SVE); the latest commit message says NVIDIA Grace results were added (results/raw/Grace folder exists, not read)

tradeoffs: AArch64 with SVE only (Neoverse V1/V2, A64FX, Grace). name: WojciechMula/toys avx512-string (AVX512F strlen, strchr, strrchr, strcmp)
baseline: libc strlen/strchr/strrchr/strcmp via <cstring> (labelled 'std' in the harness; libc version not stated)
workload: strlen/strchr/strrchr/strcmp over 10 kB strings on a Knights Landing CPU, AVX512F kernels (SWAR tricks since AVX512F has no byte ops) versus the stdlib routine.
tradeoffs: Requires AVX512F (Xeon Phi KNL, Skylake-X and later). The strlen kernel uses unaligned 64-byte loads that can read past the terminator and across a page boundary, so it is only safe on padded buffers (the harness pads by 64 bytes). Only four functions (strlen, strchr, strrchr, strcmp); no memcpy/memchr.
caveats: Author says the tests 'aren't very good' and do not cover a range of string lengths: one 10 KiB buffer filled with '?', the terminator (or target char) moved through every position, 5 iterations, gettimeofday timing, no repetitions or variance. Measured once in October 2016 on one old CPU with GCC 5.4.3 (not an official GCC release number; 5.4.0 and 5.5.0 exist); the glibc version and which of its ifunc variants ran on KNL are not stated, so the baseline may be a weak SSE2 path (the 16x strrchr gain points that way). The AVX512F kernels use unaligned 64-byte loads with no page-boundary handling (avx512f_strlen does _mm512_loadu_si512(s + len) in a loop), so they can read up to 63 bytes past the terminator and fault at the end of a mapped page; the benchmark pads every buffer by 64 bytes, so they are not drop-in libc replacements without aligned or masked loads. speed_strlen discards the strlen result (the other three harnesses accumulate into a volatile counter); the measured times look like real work. avx512f-strcmp.cpp was simplified by KWillets on 2020-04-06 (commit 8759381, removes a redundant zero2 mask, not a correctness fix), after the README numbers were taken. The README lists custom scalar versions too but reports only std vs AVX512F. Date shown is the last commit touching avx512-string; the toys repo itself was last pushed 2026-04-08. An SSE2 version of the same four functions lives in WojciechMula/sse2string, whose README gives no numbers.

name: tinymembench (NEON, prefetching and SSE2 copy and fill kernels against libc memcpy and memset)
language: C and assembly (ARM, AArch64, x86 SSE2, MIPS)
baseline: the libc memcpy and memset ('standard memcpy', 'standard memset') of each tested board's OS image
workload: Sequential copy and fill bandwidth on large aligned blocks, reporting MB/s for libc memcpy and memset next to C, NEON, VFP, ARM LDM/STM, SSE2 and non-temporal copy and fill kernels with different prefetch strategies; the wiki holds 68 community-submitted boards and PCs.
claimed_speedup: No headline claim; results are per-board wiki tables (ratios derived from page data). BeagleBone Black (Cortex-A8 AM3358 r2.1 at 1 GHz, tinymembench v0.4.9): standard memcpy 258.3 MB/s vs 'C copy prefetched (32 bytes step)' 505.1 MB/s (1.96x), 'ARM copy prefetched (wrap pld)' 508.4 MB/s (1.97x) and 'NEON copy prefetched (32 bytes step)' 563.5 MB/s (2.18x); standard memset 1511.9 MB/s is level with every custom fill (1510.6 to 1512.0 MB/s). Allwinner A13 (v0.2.9): standard memcpy 249.8 vs 'C copy prefetched (32 bytes step)' 406.5 MB/s (1.63x) and 'NEON unrolled copy' 499.9 MB/s (2.00x). Intel Core i7-8700T (v0.4.9): standard memcpy 16647.8 vs 'SSE2 nontemporal copy' 17273.1 MB/s (1.04x); standard memset 32815.6 vs 'SSE2 nontemporal fill' 41097.4 MB/s (1.25x). Raspberry Pi BCM2835 at stock 700 MHz with Raspbian 2015-01-31: libc memcpy 387.6 MB/s is level with the best custom copy (392.6 MB/s) and libc memset 1458.5 MB/s ties 'ARM fill (STM with 4 registers)' 1458.4 MB/s; on the same page's overclocked run with a custom 4.1.15 kernel, standard memcpy 307.9 vs 'C copy prefetched' 543.5 MB/s (1.77x). AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D: standard memcpy 81381.2 vs best custom 'SSE2 copy prefetched (64 bytes step)' 81804.8 MB/s (1.005x, a tie), standard memset 156460.7 vs 'SSE2 fill' 162148.8 MB/s (1.04x), and the SSE2 nontemporal copy (32028.6 MB/s) is 2.5x slower than libc.
compiler_and_flags: Not recorded on the wiki pages; the readme.txt build examples use CFLAGS=-O2 with a per-board -mcpu (for example -mcpu=cortex-a9, -mcpu=cortex-a8 -static)
hardware: Per wiki page: ARM Cortex-A8 AM3358 at 1 GHz (BeagleBone Black), Allwinner A13, Intel Core i7-8700T (6 cores, DDR4-2666), Raspberry Pi BCM2835 and 60+ other boards and PCs
stars_or_usage: 418 stars; a sibling report says amd/aocl-libmem bundles it in its benchmark tooling
tradeoffs: A benchmark program rather than a library: the kernels (arm-neon.S, aarch64-asm.S, x86-sse2.S, mips-32.S) are bandwidth tests on aligned blocks, not memcpy replacements (no small-size, misalignment or overlap handling). Prefetch distance is tuned per core, and non-temporal stores avoid cache pollution at the price of making later reads of the copy slow.
caveats: The harness is the project's own benchmark program, and the wiki pages (68 pages, community-submitted; the BeagleBone Black page came from a third-party contributor in March 2017) record neither compiler, flags nor libc version, so the baseline is whatever libc memcpy each OS image shipped. The ARM wins come from 2012 to 2017 era boards (Cortex-A8, Allwinner A13) whose glibc memcpy lacked prefetching or NEON loops; they may not hold for current glibc, Bionic or Arm optimized-routines, and stock Raspbian (which preloads its own copy routines) already matches the best kernel. On modern x86 libc memcpy ties or beats every custom copy (Ryzen 9800X3D 81381.2 vs 81804.8 MB/s; nontemporal copies 2.5x slower there), and the only x86 wins are 4 to 25 percent from nontemporal stores on an i7-8700T. Libc memset is level with the custom fills on BeagleBone Black and Raspberry Pi. Runs span tinymembench v0.2.9 to v0.4.9 and many contributors. Results are large-block bandwidth with aligned buffers, not small-copy latency or correctness-checked memcpy replacements: the kernels are benchmark loops inside a test program (MIT), not a packaged memcpy library. The code repository has had no commit since 2017-02-14, though the wiki still receives runs (Ryzen 9800X3D, Core i9-13900K pages).

Intel Core i7-8700T: standard memcpy 16647.8 vs 'SSE2 nontemporal copy' 17273.1 MB/s (1.04x), standard memset 32815.6 vs 'SSE2 nontemporal fill' 41097.4 MB/s (1.25x). corrected_fields.caveats: The ARM wins come from 2013 to 2017 era boards and are measured against whatever libc memcpy those OS images shipped (likely older glibc builds without NEON or prefetching copy loops, but the wiki records neither libc versions nor compiler flags), so they may not hold for current glibc, Bionic or Arm optimized-routines. name: asmlib (Agner Fog): assembly memcpy, memmove, memset, strlen, strcpy and related replacements
baseline: glibc 2.7/2.8 memcpy and strlen (32-bit and 64-bit builds), plus MSVC 2008, CodeGear, Intel C++ 10.1 and Mac Darwin8 libraries
workload: Fog's comparison table in the asmlib manual: memcpy of 16 kB with aligned and unaligned operands, and strlen of 128-byte strings, measured in core clock cycles per byte. The libraries compared are MSVC 2008 (9.0), CodeGear bcc 5.5, Intel C++ 10.1.020 (_intel_fast_memcpy, __intel_new_strlen), Mac Darwin8 g++ 4.0.1, glibc 2.7/2.8 (32-bit with and without -fno-builtin, 64-bit with -fno-builtin) and asmlib 2.10.
claimed_speedup:
asmlib-instructions.pdf section 1.5 (core clock cycles per byte, lower is better; asmlib v2.10 vs glibc 2.7/2.8):
- memcpy 16 kB unaligned, Core 2: asmlib 0.12 vs Gnu 64-bit -fno-builtin 0.44 (3.7x), Gnu 32-bit -fno-builtin 0.57 (4.75x) and Gnu 32-bit builtin 1.21 (10x).
- memcpy 16 kB aligned, Core 2: 0.11 vs 0.18 (1.6x).
- strlen of 128 bytes, Core 2: 0.27 vs Gnu 64-bit 0.59 (2.2x).
- Opteron K8: memcpy aligned 0.22 vs 0.28 (1.27x), unaligned 0.28 vs 0.29 (a tie), and strlen 1.19 vs Gnu 64-bit 0.6 (asmlib about 2x slower).
All ratios are derived from page data. Fog's 2008 gcc and libc-help posts (search snippets only) state the matching 'factor 4-5 for unaligned data on a Core 2' and '3-4 times slower' for 64-bit libc.
hardware: Intel Core 2 and AMD Opteron K8 (exact models not stated)
license: GPL-3.0-or-later (commercial licences available on request from the author)
stars_or_usage: classic reference library for CPU-dispatched x86 string routines, cited in mailing-list threads and forums
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 only; functions carry an A_ prefix (for example A_memcpy, A_memmove per a PureBasic forum snippet) and the library dispatches on instruction-set level (SSE2 and later), so it is linked or wrapped rather than a transparent libc replacement. Search snippets describe the licence as GPL; the licence file in the zip was not read, so usability is left as reference.
caveats: First-party numbers from 2008-era libraries; the manual itself calls them 'not up to date'. No benchmark code was published for the table, and the CPUs are named only by family (Core 2, Opteron K8). The tests are memcpy at one size (16 kB) and strlen at one size (128 bytes). On Opteron K8, asmlib's strlen (1.19 c/B) is about 2x slower than 64-bit glibc (0.6 c/B), and unaligned memcpy is a tie (0.28 vs 0.29). The largest Core 2 gaps are against 32-bit glibc with GCC's builtin inline string code; against 64-bit glibc the unaligned memcpy gain is 3.7x and the aligned one 1.6x. The numbers predate glibc's SSE2/SSSE3/AVX2/EVEX ifunc string routines, and no current asmlib-vs-glibc benchmark was found. A glibc-side reply in the 2008 gcc thread said glibc 2.6.1 x86-64 routines were already much faster (search snippet only). www.agner.org, gcc.gnu.org and sourceware.org all fail with getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND here. The manual was read from the third-party mirror github.com/tpn/agner (asmlib v2.51, 2016-11-16, mirrored 2018-04-11), so the latest release on agner.org could not be checked. The licence is GPL-3.0-or-later per the manual's section 9 and license.txt (copyleft).

name: copies-and-fills (libcofi_rpi.so)
baseline: generic libc memcpy and memset on Raspberry Pi (ARM)
workload: Modified ssvb-membench with random numbers, iterating over sizes and source/destination alignments; memcpy and memset on a Raspberry Pi.
claimed_speedup: memcpy reaches performance parity with generic libc at around ~150 byte copies and 'eventually gains 2-3x throughput, especially when the source buffer is uncached' (up to 680 MB/s, effective 339 MB/s copy); memset reaches parity at around 100 bytes and peaks at 1390 MB/s, '~7x faster than the libc version'
hardware: Raspberry Pi (model and CPU not stated in the README; the notes mention a single-issue core)
stars_or_usage: 72 stars, 9 forks; packaged as libcofi (libcofi_rpi.so) in Buildroot (package/libcofi, e.g. 2017.08) and Exherbo (sys-rpi/copies-and-fills), and shipped by Arch Linux ARM until arm-mem replaced it (search snippets only)
tradeoffs: Hand-written ARM assembly (memcpy.s, memset.s) tuned for the original single-issue Raspberry Pi core; used by setting LD_PRELOAD=/full/path/to/libcofi_rpi.so. The misaligned-copy inner loop is derived from the GNU libc ARM port, hence LGPL. Not portable to other ARM cores or to 64-bit.
caveats: First-party claim in a 2012 README with no CPU model, compiler, flags, libc version or result tables; the benchmark harness is a modified copy of ssvb-membench that is not in this repo. name: fancy-memset (fm): SSE2 and AVX2 memset in x86-64 assembly
language: x86-64 assembly (GNU as) with a C benchmark harness
baseline: glibc memset (the harness's 'sys' row calls the system libc memset; glibc version not stated); the harness also times FreeBSD, Bionic and Solaris memset, a naive rep stos and a naive -O3 loop
workload: bench.c: for each size, 16 warm-up calls, then 100000 calls at each of 64 destination offsets (base malloc+1 plus 0-63), timed with rdtsc/rdtscp around cpuid, fill value 0. main() calls test(64..4100) and bench() subtracts 63, so the measured lengths run from 1 to 4037 bytes, all cache-resident. The output prints each column's time as a ratio to the SSE2 version; no results are committed.
claimed_speedup: AVX2 version: '10-370% faster than glibc memset', '300-400% faster than a naive loop compiled with -O3 by gcc/icc/clang', '50-470% faster than freebsd memset, for sizes larger than 64 bytes'. SSE2 version: '20-150% faster than freebsd memset', '5-100% faster than bionic memset'; no glibc figure for SSE2 ('don't know about glibc, idk how to force it to use sse2'). README says numbers 'are variable and depend heavily on sizes'.
compiler_and_flags: bench.c built with CFLAGS -O3 -g -fno-builtin (makefile); compiler name and version not stated; assembly files assembled with as or cc -x assembler-with-cpp; 'make erms=' builds the variant for CPUs without ERMS
hardware: CPU model not stated; x86-64 only (SSE2 or AVX2 versions); README discusses Intel CPUs with ERMS and AMD CPUs without ERMS
tradeoffs: x86-64 only. The AVX2 version needs AVX2 and the SSE2 version SSE2; selection is by which object you link (no runtime dispatch seen in the makefile). ERMS use is chosen at assembly time (makefile --defsym erms), so the build must match the CPU. Author notes that very small and constant-size memsets are better inlined by the compiler, so the benchmark does not cover them. No LICENSE file in the repo root, so the code cannot be assumed copyable.
caveats: Public benchmark code and flags, but no CPU model, compiler version or glibc version, so it falls short of tier A. The 'sys' row is the libc memset reached through -fno-builtin; on glibc the ifunc picks a different variant per CPU, so 'glibc' means different code on different machines. The glibc figure (10-370% for AVX2) has no per-size table, and the author could not force glibc onto its SSE2 path, so the SSE2 version has no glibc figure. The committed bench covers lengths of 1-4037 bytes only, so the README's large-size claims (erms, up to 2x over bionic) are not exercised by it. Ratios are printed relative to the SSE2 version, so AVX2-vs-glibc must be derived. Fill value is always 0, buffers are warm and the same region is hit 100000 times. The README notes that the compiler inlines small constant memsets in real code. The repo describes itself as 'based on microsoft's design'. The competition/ folder vendors bionic, FreeBSD and Solaris memsets. No license file. Last commit 2022-04-05.

name: go-memset (tmthrgd): Go amd64 assembly memset
baseline: Go's own fill loop (README benchmarks BenchmarkGoSet for non-zero fill and BenchmarkGoZero for the zeroing loop idiom)
workload: memset of 32 B to 512 MB buffers; README lists Memset/GoZero/GoSet benchmark outputs and a benchcmp-style old-vs-new table.
claimed_speedup: README benchcmp table, non-zero fill (BenchmarkSet, Go fill loop vs Memset): 2.75x at 32 B, 11.13x at 128 B, 23.84x at 1k (545 ns vs 22.9 ns), peak 31.04x at 16k, 18.54x at 128k, 13.74x at 1M, 7.92x to 8.11x at 16M-512M (-63.68% to -96.78% ns/op). Zeroing (BenchmarkZero, Go's memclr-optimised loop vs Memset): slower at small sizes (0.54x at 32 B, 0.69x at 128 B, 0.84x at 1k), parity at 16k-1M, 1.18x to 1.22x faster at 16M-512M where the AVX path switches to non-temporal stores.
compiler_and_flags: Go version and flags not stated (go test -bench; test file memset_test.go).
hardware: Not stated; benchmark names carry the -8 suffix (8 threads).
tradeoffs: Go package with a pure-Go fallback (memset_other.go); only the amd64 build uses assembly. Archived read-only by the owner on 2024-12-14 and marked 'Not maintained' in the README.
caveats: Baseline is a plain Go loop, not libc memset; for zeroing the Go compiler already lowers the loop to runtime memclr, and Memset is slower than it below 16k. The README benchmark output was last updated on 2016-11-11 (README commit history), before the April 2018 commits that rewrote the assembly for go1.10 and moved CPU detection to x/sys/cpu, so the published numbers were measured on an older version of the code with a 2016 Go toolchain (sub-benchmarks imply Go 1.7+); no Go version, CPU model or flags are given (the -8 suffix is GOMAXPROCS=8). The amd64 assembly uses PSHUFB (SSSE3) for buffers of 16 bytes or more without checking for SSSE3; only AVX is detected. Large fills (16 MB and up) use VMOVNTDQ non-temporal stores, which bypass cache and can hurt a consumer that reads the buffer right after. The repository was archived by its owner on 2024-12-14 and the description says 'Not maintained'. Later Go toolchains may behave differently.

name: gofiber/utils v2 simd package (AVX2 Memchr2, Memchr3, Memmem, IsASCII for Go)
baseline: Go standard library, per simd/bench_test.go: bytes.Contains (bytes.Index) for Memmem; bytes.ContainsAny(data, "zy") and bytes.ContainsAny(data, "zyx") for Memchr2 and Memchr3 (a per-byte ASCII-set loop, not a vectorised search); the package's own scalar loops (memchr2Generic, memchr3Generic) and SWAR fallbacks as second baselines. bytes.IndexByte is deliberately not wrapped because the Go runtime already vectorises it.
workload: simd/bench_test.go: synthetic haystacks of 8-4096 B filled with the repeating bytes 'a'..'w', worst-case misses so every variant scans the whole input; Memchr2/Memchr3 search for 'z','y'(,'x'); Memmem searches for the needle "q7z" (8-4096 B); IsASCII, FirstNonASCII, CountNonASCII, MemchrPair, MemchrDigit, MemchrWord scans; each reported as simd, scalar/swar and default (stdlib) rows in ns/op.
claimed_speedup: README amd64 table (go test ./simd/ -count=1): Memmem 4096 B 38.44 ns (simd) vs 921.5 ns (bytes.Contains), about 24x; 512 B 10.22 vs 119.8 ns, about 11.7x; 96 B 8.323 vs 20.11 ns, about 2.4x; slower up to 64 B (8 B 4.450 vs 3.551 ns). Memchr2 4096 B 26.22 ns vs 1572 ns for bytes.ContainsAny (about 60x) but vs 422.0 ns for the package's own scalar loop (about 16x); Memchr3 4096 B 35.38 vs 1620 ns ContainsAny (about 46x), vs 506.4 ns scalar (about 14x); IsASCII 4096 B 14.17 vs 46.72 ns SWAR (about 3.3x). All ratios derived from page data. README text also quotes benchstat -count=10 gains of -35% to -88% ns/op against the SWAR paths at 32-512 B.
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain version not stated (go.mod requires go 1.26.0, so 1.26 or later); go test ./simd/ -benchmem -run=^$ -bench=Benchmark_ -count=1
hardware: linux/amd64, cpu: AMD EPYC (exact model not stated), 4 threads (-4 suffix); arm64 catalog on Apple M2 Pro for the non-SIMD helpers.
stars_or_usage: 57 stars; used by the Fiber web framework
tradeoffs: AVX2 kernels engage only on amd64 for inputs of 32 bytes or more (simd.MinLen); portable SWAR fallbacks elsewhere; []byte only; no single-byte Memchr because bytes.IndexByte is already vectorised; Memmem delegates to bytes.Index up to 64 bytes and bails to it after a bounded number of failed candidates.
caveats: Baseline is the Go standard library, not glibc or musl. The 60x Memchr2 and 46x Memchr3 ratios are against bytes.ContainsAny, a per-byte ASCII-set loop with setup overhead (15.47 ns even at 8 B), not against a vectorised stdlib path; against the package's own scalar loop the gain is about 16x and 14x at 4096 B. The Memmem benchmark is favourable to the paired prefilter: two of the needle's three bytes ('7', 'z') never occur in the 'a'..'w' haystack, so the prefilter never produces a candidate while bytes.Index anchors on 'q' every 23 bytes; when the anchor byte is common the single-rare-byte path tracks or trails bytes.Index (Benchmark_Memmem_Prefilter 4096 B single 922.7 ns vs 863.5 ns stdlib), and the adversarial case is at parity. Numbers are one run (-count=1) on an unspecified EPYC model with an unstated Go 1.26+ toolchain and GOMAXPROCS=4; the README itself warns that small-input rows drifted up to 17% between runs. Per-commit benchmark charts live on gofiber.github.io (blocked here). The kernels are adapted from the coregx/coregex simd package (MIT, simd/LICENSE), so part of the design is upstream. Inputs under 32 bytes never reach the AVX2 kernels, and Memmem delegates to bytes.Index up to 64 bytes. AVX2 path is amd64-only.

name: hglm ARM memcpy, memset, memzero and copy_page kernel patches (test-arm-kernel-memcpy)
baseline: original Linux kernel ARM memcpy, memset, memzero and copy_page (the benchmark harness also runs libc memcpy/memset alongside)
workload: bench.script drives benchmark.c over a set of tests (mixed power-of-2 sizes, unaligned mixed sizes, copy_page) for the original kernel routines, libc and the optimized routines on ARMv6 and ARMv7.
claimed_speedup: The hglm/patches README says copy_page and larger memcpy gain 'on the order of 70%' on the armv6 Raspberry Pi, with a smaller benefit on armv7. The commit message of arm-mem-funcs/0002-Optimize-copy_page-for-modern-ARM-platforms.patch (2013-07-12) gives copy_page speed-ups from 10% (Cortex A8) to 80% (armv6 in the Raspberry Pi) over the existing kernel copy_page. No results table is checked in.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: $(CC) with -std=gnu99 -Ofast -Wall -DARMV7 by default (-DARMV6 for armv6, optional Thumb2 flags); compiler version and the flags used for the quoted speedups not stated
hardware: ARMv6 Raspberry Pi (32-byte cache line) and ARMv7 including a Cortex-A8 (64-byte cache line); exact SoCs and clocks not stated
license: Per-file headers: MIT/X11 (benchmark.c, memcpy_armv6v7.S, new_arm.S, Copyright 2013 Harm Hanemaaijer) and GPL-2.0-only (kernel-derived memset.S, memzero.S, copy_page.S, copy templates, user-copy variants and the *_orig.S baselines); asm.h, new_arm.h and kernel_defines*.h have no header; no repo-level LICENSE file
tradeoffs: 32-bit ARM only (ARMv6/ARMv7); the optimized memcpy, copy_from_user and copy_to_user use PLD unconditionally so they do not work on ARMv4; NEON paths were experimental and later removed from copy_page, memset and memzero; patches no longer applied cleanly to upstream kernels by February 2015.
caveats: First-party, loosely worded speedups ('order of 70%', '10% to 80%') with no published run output, no compiler version, and no exact SoC or clock. The baseline is the 2013 in-kernel ARM routines rather than glibc, although the harness also runs libc memcpy/memset and no libc numbers are quoted. The work is unfinished per the patches README: copy_page, memset and memzero are done, while memcpy and the user-copy variants are still in progress. As of February 2015 the patches no longer applied cleanly to upstream kernels. Licensing is per-file (MIT for the new memcpy, GPL-2.0-only for kernel-derived files), and a few small headers have no licence. NEON paths were removed from copy_page, memset and memzero; the last commit was 2013-08-28.

name: ImGui SIMD ImStrlen/ImMemchr (PR #8421, Kraionix/ImGuiMemchrBench)
baseline: C runtime strlen and memchr (labelled CSTD; ImMemchrCSTD is a plain memchr call). The bench repo is a Visual Studio 2022 project (v143 toolset, Release|x64, static CRT /MT), so CSTD is the MSVC CRT implementation, not glibc
workload: Google Benchmark on std::string buffers of random ASCII from 1 MB to 1 GB: strlen scans for the terminator; memchr scans for 131-character lines ending in a newline; SSE, SSE+prefetch, AVX2 and AVX2+prefetch variants.
claimed_speedup: 1 GB buffer: ImStrlen AVX2_PREFETCH 56.6 ms (17.6 Gi/s) vs CSTD 79.9 ms (12.5 Gi/s), 1.41x; ImMemchr AVX2_PREFETCH 58.2 ms (17.17 Gi/s) vs CSTD 89.9 ms (10.93 Gi/s), 1.54x, which is the '55%' in the PR title; plain AVX2 ImMemchr without prefetch 79.8 ms, only 1.13x; 16 MB ImMemchr 0.799 vs 1.17 ms (1.46x); 1 MB ImStrlen 0.010 vs 0.059 ms (about 5.9x, 93.3 vs 16.4 Gi/s) (ratios derived from page data). A later comment says AVX2 ImMemchr gave 'about 60%' more performance on a 16 MB buffer and ImGui::TextUnformatted dropped from 1.6 ms to 0.98 ms per frame
compiler_and_flags: MSVC, Visual Studio 2022 v143 toolset (exact version not stated); ImMemchrBench.vcxproj Release|x64: /Oi, /GL whole-program optimization, /Ob2, /arch:AVX2, /MT, /std:c++latest (no Optimization element, so the MSBuild Release default /O2 applies); the README says only 'Compiled benchmark in release'
hardware: Intel Core i9-10980XE (18 cores / 36 threads, all cores 4600 MHz, uncore 3200 MHz), 128 GB quad-channel at 4000 MHz, power saving disabled, AVX offset 400 MHz
stars_or_usage: 4 stars on the bench repo; proposed for Dear ImGui (PR open, not merged)
tradeoffs: x86-64 only (SSE and AVX2 variants; the bench repo's run_benchmark.ps1 exists 'to avoid crashes when avx512 is not supported'); the PR adds compile-time SIMD config macros (IMGUI_ENABLE_SSE, SSE4_2, AVX, AVX2). The maintainer rebased the PR and added ImStrlen/ImMemchr hooks (commit 1ec99f4, 2025-03-07) but the SIMD versions were not shown as merged; a reviewer argued libc should be optimized instead.
caveats: Numbers are from a PR thread (ocornut/imgui #8421, still open, not merged); the bench repo README has no results table, no compiler or flags, and no LICENSE file (so reference only; the PR code would carry ImGui's licence if merged). The bench repo only benchmarks memchr: the ImStrlen code was added to the PR on 2025-03-01, after the repo's last commit, so the strlen numbers have no public harness. The posted table omits the AVX-512, UNROLL and SSE4.2 variants the harness also runs, run_benchmark.ps1 named in the README is not in the repo, and TestData::set_lines wrote past the end of the test buffer until a fix on 2025-02-23 (harness only; newline pattern unchanged). Buffers of 1 MB to 1 GB are far from typical ImGui string lengths and the 1 GB gain comes mostly from software prefetch (AVX2 without prefetch is 1.13x); the 60% figure is for one text-rendering workload. Baseline is the MSVC CRT on Windows, so gains over glibc's AVX2 strlen/memchr may be smaller. Google Benchmark's header reports 36 x 3000 MHz although the PR states a 4600 MHz all-core overclock. The maintainer only added ImStrlen/ImMemchr #define hooks to master (commit 1ec99f4, 2025-03-07) so such variants can be supplied externally, and a commenter argued these belong in the C library.

name: jnettlet/cortex_a72_memcpy (Cortex-A72 tuned AArch64 memcpy/memset)
baseline: glibc memcpy (the 'memcpy' row) and Arm Optimized Routines memcpy (__memcpy_aarch64, __memcpy_aarch64_simd)
workload: Arm optimized-routines memcpy benchmark (string/bench/memcpy.c) on a Cortex-A72: random copies (16384 copies with lengths from a SPEC2017-derived size distribution under 4 KB) over 32K to 1024K working sets, aligned and unaligned medium copies 8 B to 512 B, large copies 1K to 64K, and forwards/backwards unaligned memmove 1K to 64K, in bytes per ns.
claimed_speedup: README: 'We are now pretty equivalent or faster than glibc's memcpy and Arm's optimized library memcpy on the optimized library's memcpy benchmark.' Aligned medium memcpy (bytes/ns): 16 B __memcpy_a72 4.40 vs memcpy 2.51; 32 B 8.79 vs 5.03; 64 B 12.80 vs 9.38 (about 1.75x, 1.75x, 1.36x, derived from page data). Random memcpy average 2.01 vs 1.97; large copies equal within 1-2%; unaligned backwards memmove 64K 11.69 vs 6.54.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark. The library's Makefile builds the assembly with CPPFLAGS -fPIC -g -fno-inline -fno-builtin-inline -fno-inline-functions -fno-builtin and LDFLAGS -shared; compiler version unstated.
hardware: Cortex-A72 (board, SoC and clock not stated)
tradeoffs: AArch64 Cortex-A72 only; built as libmemcpy.so for LD_PRELOAD or /etc/ld.so.preload; the stated purpose is fixing copies to memory-mapped device memory (framebuffers, SPDK) by reordering two stores in the 96-byte path, not general speed.
caveats: The repo's stated purpose is a device-memory fix (re-ordered stores in the 96-byte path for framebuffers/SPDK); the code is an initial import of Arm optimized-routines memcpy (Arm MIT header; memset.S is MIT OR Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception; COPYING is MIT, Solidrun Ltd 2021), loaded via LD_PRELOAD. README tables (added July 2022) give no compiler, flags, board, SoC or clock, and the code was reworked again in January 2024 after the numbers were published. The 'memcpy' row is the system libc (presumably glibc). Gains are mostly small aligned sizes (8-64 B: 1.36-1.75x over libc, 1.18-1.50x over __memcpy_aarch64); random and large copies are within 1-2%; the backwards-memmove 64K win (11.69 vs 6.54) is shared by Arm's __memcpy_aarch64 (11.67); unaligned 64 B (8.46 vs 9.35) and backwards memmove 1K-8K (e.g. 16.48 vs 16.70 at 4K) are slightly slower than libc.

name: KmStrSearch (Windows kernel UTF-8 and UTF-16 substring search)
baseline: Windows kernel CRT strstr and wcsstr (MSVC runtime; not glibc or musl)
workload: Three throughput inputs whose pattern's last character ('k', 'b', 'K') never occurs in the text, so each search degenerates to a one-byte memchr; alternate calls shifted by 32 characters but credited the full buffer; one 2 s run per cell
claimed_speedup: i7-1165G7, 8-bit, GB/s (CRT baseline vs Smart Auto): 10 KB 22.38 vs 45.71, 1 MB 22.66 vs 85.93; 16-bit 20 KB 26.67 vs 68.43. Worse on small buffers: 40 B 3.61 vs 1.95, 256 B 15.03 vs 4.88. README: on mismatched dense text CRT collapses to 0.21-0.37 GB/s while the hybrid delivers 49-81 GB/s, 'up to 385x faster'.
tradeoffs: Windows kernel-mode (WDK driver) code: routes small buffers to a SWAR path to avoid the KeSaveExtendedProcessorState cost of entering vector mode, and uses AVX2/AVX-512BW or ARM64 NEON for larger buffers. Uses 8 KB (UTF-16) skip tables allocated from paged pool. Not a user-mode library; the README says user-mode (TestUm) timings cannot be trusted.
caveats: Very new, single-author exploration with 0 stars and 4 commits ('not strictly benchmark-driven during its design'); no repetition counts or variance; MSVC version and build configuration unstated. The README calls the harness multi-threaded and memory-bus saturating, but RunPerformanceSuiteT calls StartThreads(pMgr, 1, ...), so each figure is single-thread throughput. Throughput counts the whole buffer per call even though BMH skips most bytes, so the 80-105 GB/s figures at 1 MB are not memory bandwidth; the 'standard' input is the best case for BMH (text all 'A', pattern contains no 'A'). The 'up to 385x' dense-text figure comes from a pattern whose last character never occurs in the text, so the hybrid reduces to a vectorized memchr while the CRT's naive strstr does O(N*M) work; glibc's two-way strstr would not collapse this way. The baseline is the Windows kernel CRT strstr/wcsstr, not glibc or musl; on the VMware guest it measures only 1.35-1.67 GB/s on 256 B to 1 MB inputs (about 15x below the same CRT on bare metal). Loses to CRT on tiny and small buffers on bare metal (40 B 3.61 vs 1.95 GB/s, 256 B 15.03 vs 4.88 GB/s for 8-bit Smart Auto). User-mode build is declared untrustworthy for timing. Kernel driver telemetry only; no independent reproduction.

No invalid evidence found: the CRT and hybrid run the same buffers and the hybrid has correctness tests.

All three throughput inputs reduce to a one-byte memchr because the pattern's last character never occurs in the text, so the candidate-verification and skip-table paths that define the algorithm never execute; every second call is shifted 32 characters but credited the full buffer, and the 40 B cell returns -1 without searching. ThreadPool degenerate-benchmark precedent.

name: LibC-String-Optimisations (XEOS x86 and x86-64 string functions)
baseline: OS X 10.9 libc strlen, memset, memchr, memcpy, strcat (the README notes it is also heavily optimised); not glibc or musl
workload: 10,000,000 calls per function: strlen on 1000 chars, memset 4096 B, memchr 1000 B searching last char, memcpy 4096 B (aligned and misaligned), strcat on 1000 chars; 32-bit and 64-bit builds.
claimed_speedup: 64-bit: strlen 0.527532 s vs 0.531318 s OS X; memset 0.778556 s vs 0.906685 s; memchr 0.476380 s vs 0.516240 s; memcpy 0.858043 s vs 0.928405 s; strcat 1.269549 s vs 1.314561 s, misaligned 1.423539 s vs 3.920867 s. 32-bit: memchr 0.532130 s vs 6.374186 s; strcat misaligned 1.515425 s vs 4.644904 s. Loses: misaligned memcpy 1.408296 s vs OS X 1.218205 s (64-bit) and 1.457572 s vs 1.446217 s (32-bit).
license: XEOS Software License 1.0 (custom BSD-style licence with an advertising clause and a clause forbidding combination or linking with GPL/LGPL software; not OSI-approved)
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 assembly only; SSE2 versions used when the CPU supports them, slower fallbacks otherwise. Developed for the XEOS operating system; README status badge says prototype. caveats: First-party numbers from the README only; the CPU, compiler versions and run count are not stated, and the baseline is the 2013-era OS X 10.9 libc rather than glibc. Each test harness runs the loop twice (SSE2 path, then the non-SSE2 path with _SSE2Status = 0) and the README does not say which pass it quotes. Harness C files are built without an -O flag, so loop overhead is unoptimised (it applies equally to both sides). Wins on most rows are 1-15%; the 12x memchr gain is against OS X's 32-bit memchr and the 2.8-3x strcat gains only on misaligned input. XEOS loses on misaligned memcpy in both 32-bit and 64-bit builds. The strlen margin is under 1% (0.527532 s vs 0.531318 s). name: memcpy_fast (gamesun): Cortex-M4 word and doubleword memcpy
baseline: the toolchain's standard memcpy on Cortex-M4 (C library not stated)
workload: memcpy_test() in memcpy_fast.c: for each destination offset a, source offset b and length offset c in 0-7, copy TEST_BUFF_SIZE (10240) + c bytes from an 8-byte-aligned static source to an 8-byte-aligned static destination with memcpy_fast and then with memcpy, timing each with TIM5 (1 us resolution) with interrupts disabled; memcpy_fast's result is checked with memcmp. The published table collapses c = 0-7 into one row per (a, b) pair.
claimed_speedup: Results table (memcpy_fast_vs_memcpy.png, linked from the README), 10240-byte copies, times in microseconds: same alignment mod 8 but not 8-aligned (a=b=1,2,3,5,6,7) 121-122 us vs 640-641 us for memcpy, 5.25x-5.29x; both 8-aligned or 4-offset pairs (0,0 and 4,4) 121-122 vs 213 us, 1.75x-1.76x; (4,0) and (0,4) 161-162 vs 214 us, 1.32x-1.33x; other mismatched alignments 188-268 us vs 640-641 us, 2.39x-3.41x. The README's '1.3 to 5.2 times' slightly understates the top of the table (528.9% = 5.29x).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; the C library providing the baseline memcpy (newlib, newlib-nano or a vendor libc) is also not stated.
hardware: Cortex-M4 STM32 microcontroller (memcpy_test uses the STM32 Standard Peripheral Library and TIM5 at a 1 MHz tick); part number, clock and memory region not stated.
tradeoffs: Plain C: copies with long long (LDRD/STRD) loops when source and destination share 8-byte alignment and with 32-bit long loops otherwise, relying on the compiler's code generation and on Cortex-M4 unaligned LDR/STR support; casts between integer widths without regard to strict aliasing; GPL-3.0 licence blocks use in permissive code; Cortex-M4 only.
caveats: No compiler, flags, C library or MCU part are given, and the 10240-byte copy is the only size tested (no small copies, where the dispatch overhead matters). The baseline memcpy takes 640 us for any mismatched or odd alignment but 213 us when both pointers are 4-aligned (derived from page data), which looks like a size-optimised byte-loop memcpy such as newlib-nano's; a speed-optimised libc memcpy would narrow the gap. memcpy_unaligned4 dereferences misaligned long pointers, which is undefined behaviour in C and relies on Cortex-M4 tolerating unaligned LDR/STR; a compiler that merges those accesses into LDM/LDRD would fault, and the author works around this with a reverse-indexed loop. The code casts pointers to u32 (32-bit only) and includes a types.h that is not in the repository. GPL-3.0 is copyleft. Eleven commits in August 2020, no later activity.

name: memcpy_threaded / memset_threaded (Carandiru0 mem.h gist)
baseline: MSVC compiler-intrinsic memcpy and memset (the gist declares #pragma intrinsic(memcpy) and #pragma intrinsic(memset), i.e. the compiler/CRT built-ins), single-threaded and also run multithreaded; MSVC version not stated
workload: Large-buffer copy and fill using AVX/SSE intrinsics, Intel TBB parallel_for and PrefetchVirtualMemory; header comments quote GB/s for single-thread intrinsic, multithreaded intrinsic and the threaded routine.
claimed_speedup: Code comments: 'intrinsic memcpy (single threaded) at 22 GB/s', 'intrinsic memcpy (multithreaded) at 29 GB/s', '___memcpy_threaded at 33.3 GB/s (memory bandwidth is saturated)'; ___memset_threaded 'has the same 33.3 GB/s, but in this case it's all write bandwidth'. The 33.3 GB/s for memcpy is a combined figure ('read 10 GB/s + write 23.3 GB/s'). About 1.5x over the single-threaded intrinsic and about 1.15x over the multithreaded intrinsic (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Windows and MSVC specific (__declspec, #pragma loop, PrefetchVirtualMemory) and needs Intel TBB; threads only pay off once a single core cannot saturate memory bandwidth; the NonCommercial-ShareAlike licence is not OSI-approved.
caveats: Numbers are code comments from the author, measured as memory-controller traffic with Intel PCM, with no CPU model, compiler, flags, buffer size or harness. The baseline is MSVC's intrinsic memcpy/memset (#pragma intrinsic), not a custom routine. The 33.3 GB/s memcpy figure is read plus write bus traffic (10 + 23.3 GB/s), so it is not bytes-copied throughput, and it is unclear whether the 22 and 29 GB/s baseline figures were counted the same way; streaming stores also avoid read-for-ownership traffic, which changes what bus GB/s means. Against the fair multithreaded-intrinsic row the gain is only about 1.15x (derived from page data). The '16x faster' line about SSE stores over rep stosb is quoted from a Microsoft MSRC blog post, not measured. The header is not standalone: it includes the author's ..\Math\superfastmath.h, uses TBB parallel_for and PrefetchVirtualMemory without including their headers, and ___prefetch_vmem is never called (a commenter noted this). Windows/MSVC only (__declspec, __vectorcall), AVX2 streaming intrinsics. Four revisions, all June 10-12, 2022; the June 10, 2025 'last active' date is a comment, not a code change. Licence CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial, not OSI) next to an 'All Rights Reserved' copyright line.

name: mmemmove (AJ528): memmove in ARM Cortex-M assembly
language: ARM Thumb assembly (Cortex-M4 and M0+) with a C test harness
baseline: newlib generic memmove.c (byte loop under -Os; newlib ARM ships no assembly memmove)
workload: common/src/main.c (Greatest tests) times one warm call of each function with the DWT cycle counter after a single untimed call. Sizes are 1, 10, 20 and 50 bytes at source offset 0x81 with destinations 0x7E, 0x82 and 0x102. Slide tests use 15, 21, 34, 512 and 513 bytes against overlapping and non-overlapping destinations. An iterate test up to 35 bytes checks correctness only. Cycle counts are printed over UART and none are committed; the README does not say which size or core gave the 7x.
claimed_speedup: 'In my testing, memmove_() is always faster than my standard memmove(). Sometimes it's only a few cycles faster, other times it is 7x faster.' Object size 'under 230 bytes' on arm-none-eabi-gcc.
compiler_and_flags: arm-none-eabi-gcc (version not stated). Committed Makefiles use -mcpu=cortex-m4 (or the cm0plus equivalent) -mthumb -mfloat-abi=soft --specs=nano.specs -fno-builtin -std=gnu17 -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections, with debug = 1 so OPTIMIZE_FLAGS is -O0 -ggdb3 (-O2 when debug = 0). The flags behind the README claim are not stated. The -O0 setting affects the C harness, not the hand-written assembly or the prebuilt libc memmove.
hardware: STM32WLxx (Cortex-M4 core); README says the code is designed for Cortex-M4 and M0+ and probably works on other ARMv6-M and ARMv7-M cores
tradeoffs: Cortex-M (ARMv6-M, ARMv7-M) only. Exposed as a separate symbol memmove_() to be called explicitly, not a link-time replacement for memmove. GPL-3.0 copyleft is awkward for firmware. The same author's sibling mmemcpy README says that implementation is slower than the Cortex-M4 libc memcpy because it avoids unaligned accesses, so the M4 behaviour of mmemmove is not characterised.
caveats: First-party, unqualified range ('a few cycles' to '7x') with no table of cycle counts, sizes or alignments. The baseline is very likely newlib-nano's size-optimised memmove (--specs=nano.specs in both Makefiles), which is a weak incumbent on Cortex-M (byte loop under -Os; inference). The core on which the 7x was measured (M4 versus M0+) is not stated. Committed Makefiles default to debug = 1 (-O0 harness). Each measurement is a single call, so per-call timer overhead matters at 1-50 bytes. A correctness fix ('fixed a bug where we would try to access unaligned memory sometimes', 2025-02-24) landed on the same day as the README update, so the claim may predate it. Very small project (0 stars, 0 forks).

name: nadavrot/memset_benchmark (AVX2 assembly memset and memcpy)
language: Assembly (x86-64 AVX2, AT&T .S) with C/C++ harness
baseline: glibc memset and memcpy (with and without PLT indirection, 'libc@plt' and 'libc'), also musl and folly (memcpy chart)
workload: README charts: (1) random-size batches, 10M calls x 20 samples (median), size and destination offset each drawn from a pre-computed random u8 sequence (0 to 255 bytes), nop-function call overhead subtracted; memset compares libc@plt, libc and asm_memset, memcpy compares libc@plt, libc, folly and asm_memcpy. (2) Hot-loop fixed-size sweeps for sizes 0 to 511 bytes (16-byte aligned buffer, 10M calls per size), memset against musl, libc@plt and libc-direct, memcpy against libc@plt, libc-direct and folly. memset always writes value 0.
claimed_speedup: README text: 'These implementations outperform the folly and glibc implementations.' Random-size chart values (README image, time units not stated, lower is better): memset libc@plt 24344, libc 20172, asm_memset 14295 (about 1.41x faster than libc, derived from chart data); memcpy libc@plt 28285, libc 25263, folly 23969, asm_memcpy 21547 (about 1.17x faster than libc, derived from chart data).
compiler_and_flags: Harness built with CMake: add_compile_options(-Wall -g3 -O3 -march=native) (CMakeLists.txt); the assembly files are not compiler-dependent; glibc version not stated.
hardware: Not stated (x86-64 with AVX2 required by impl.S; CPU model not given)
stars_or_usage: 344 stars, 18 forks; the memset was upstreamed into Folly as folly/memset.S (commit 0ec02d4, 2022-01-05, 'asm memset implementation' by Ilya Albrecht, citing this repo and Nadav Rotem), with folly/test/MemsetBenchmark.cpp comparing std memset and __folly_memset (no published numbers)
tradeoffs: x86-64 with AVX2 only (vmovdqu/ymm; Apple and Linux symbol variants); tuned for the short-buffer size distribution seen in Chrome, Python and server workloads rather than for large copies; includes exhaustive correctness tester, histogram LD_PRELOAD tool and a proxy tool that swaps builtin memset/memcpy with the local code.
caveats: Results exist only as README chart images from the author's own run (values read from the images; time units not stated). CPU model, compiler and glibc version are not stated (charts date from November 2021, so glibc of that era); CMakeLists.txt uses -O3 -march=native. The random-size benchmark uses one fixed pseudo-random sequence replayed every sample. The charts predate the final memset change (2021-11-29, removal of a second exit block). Last commit 2022-01-10.

name: rte_memcpy (DPDK): SSE/AVX2/AVX-512 memcpy for small, cache-resident copies
baseline: glibc memcpy()
workload: DPDK's app/test/test_memcpy_perf.c (memcpy_perf_autotest) times rte_memcpy and then libc memcpy on the same random source/destination offsets, in TSC ticks per copy averaged over 1,000,000 iterations, printing both tick counts and the percent difference. Variable sizes run from 1 to 8192 bytes (63 sizes, including 1518/1522/1536 packet sizes) and compile-time-constant sizes are 6, 64, 128, 192, 256, 512, 768, 1024 and 1536 bytes, each aligned (16/32/64-byte unit depending on SSE/AVX2/AVX-512 build) and unaligned, cache-to-cache, cache-to-memory, memory-to-cache and memory-to-memory (100 MB buffer). For the constant-size rows the 'memcpy' baseline is normally expanded inline by the compiler, so it is a GCC/Clang builtin rather than glibc. The system-level claim (snippet only) is a vhost Rx/Tx copy path in OvS-DPDK.
claimed_speedup: No rte_memcpy-versus-glibc results are checked into the repo (the test prints a tick pair and a percent difference per size). Intel's article 'Performance Optimization of memcpy in DPDK' (search-result snippet only, page could not be opened): replacing glibc memcpy with rte_memcpy in the DPDK vhost Rx/Tx path gave 22 percent more total bandwidth in a physical-VM-physical OvS-DPDK setup. The 2026 commit d0ab5a7 'eal/x86: optimize memcpy of small sizes' reports only rte_memcpy before/after cycle counts (8 bytes: 4 vs 7 cycles; 16 bytes: 2 vs 4; 64 bytes: 4 vs 7).
stars_or_usage: 4.5k stars (GitHub mirror of dpdk.org); core of the DPDK data plane
tradeoffs: Not a libc drop-in: callers use the rte_memcpy() header function. ISA is chosen at compile time from -march macros (SSE, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512); the header forces SSE instead of AVX on GCC older than 11. Tuned for small copies whose source and destination are in cache; large streaming copies are not its target. x86 header plus separate arm/ppc variants.
caveats: The only glibc comparison number (22 percent) is a system-level bandwidth figure from a search snippet of Intel's article 'Performance Optimization of memcpy in DPDK' (intel.com fails with getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND here); Intel originated DPDK, so it is first-party vendor evidence with no stated CPU, glibc, compiler or OvS/DPDK versions, and not a memcpy microbenchmark. The in-repo harness compares against libc memcpy but no results are checked in. Commit d0ab5a7 (2026, 'eal/x86: optimize memcpy of small sizes') reports only rte_memcpy before/after cycles (8 bytes 4 vs 7, 16 bytes 2 vs 4, 64 bytes 4 vs 7, up to 15 bytes about 4.5 vs 6.5), with no CPU or compiler named. Counter-evidence from the DPDK list (search snippets only, mails.dpdk.org unreachable): Stephen Hemminger wrote in 2022 that rte_memcpy was added because gcc/glibc then used poor x86 instructions and that for small copies plain moves are as fast or faster; Mattias Ronnblom's 2024 series 'Optionally have rte_memcpy delegate to compiler memcpy' argued the benefit 'has been diminishing with every compiler release' (its use_cc_memcpy option is not in meson_options.txt on main, so it was not merged); a 61-patch series 'reduce use of rte_memcpy' was under review in August 2026, with reviewers asking for data-path performance tests and noting sanitizer/bounds tooling understands memcpy but not rte_memcpy. A DPDK mailing-list report (snippet only) found the AVX-512 path slower than AVX2 in an OvS-DPDK test. The 2015 RFC that motivated the AVX path said results depend on the glibc version. last_commit is the repository head; rte_memcpy.h (lib/eal/x86/include) was last touched 2026-09-23 (commit 4f795dd).
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'DPDK rte_memcpy AVX512 faster than glibc memcpy small sizes benchmark blog' (Intel developer article, DPDK mailing-list threads); then github.com/DPDK/dpdk, raw test_memcpy_perf.c and rte_memcpy.h, and the commits page of rte_memcpy.h.

The 2026 commit d0ab5a7 compares rte_memcpy only with its own previous version.

Shortcomings to record: no published microbenchmark results, vendor snippet-only evidence, constant-size baseline is compiler-inlined, upstream doubts about the benefit on current compilers. name: simstr
baseline: std::string and std::string_view idioms: concatenation, std::to_string, std::format hex formatting, find, replace and split code written with the C++ standard library
workload: Google Benchmark microbenchmarks (bench/bench_str.cpp) of string concatenation, number and hex formatting, literal search, replace-while-copying and split/parse, each against a plain std version of the same task.
claimed_speedup: README headline 'Speed up your work with strings by 2-10 times!'. v2.0.0 result files, six toolchains on Xeon E5-2682 v4 (derived from page data): string + number + literal into std::string 1.55-2.46x vs std::to_string concatenation (3.0-5.0x into simstr::stringa), README says 1.6-2x; hex formatting into std::string 4.3-9.2x vs s1 + std::format("{:#x}") + literal (5.9-11.0x into stringa), README says 9-14x, but only 1.3-2.4x vs the std::to_chars version in the same suite; find of three concatenated strings 1.7-3.3x with strexpr into std::string and 3.7-9.7x with stack-buffer lstringa, README says 1.5-9x; conditional concatenation (prec 10) 1.85-3.1x into std::string and 2.1-5.4x into stringa, README says 1.5-2.2x; replace-while-copying 1.4-2.2x, README says 1.5x and higher; split and parse 1.4-3.25x (1.4-1.8x on Linux, 1.8-3.25x on Windows and WASM), README says 2-3x.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 22.0.0 (libstdc++ and, via -stdlib=libc++, libc++) and GCC 15.2.0 on Ubuntu 22 under WSL; clang-cl 22.1.0 and MSVC 19.44.35213 on Windows 10; Emscripten Clang 22 (libc++, 32-bit WASM, -msimd128 -msse4.2 -msse3) run in Chrome 143. CMake Release presets from CMakePresets.json (CMake defaults -O3 -DNDEBUG for GCC/Clang, /O2 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG plus /utf-8 /Zc:strictStrings for MSVC), C++23, no -march; Google Benchmark 1.9.4, 4 repetitions, ASLR enabled. The result files do not name the preset used.
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2682 v4 (32 threads at about 2.5 GHz, 40 MiB L3), Windows 10 and Ubuntu 22 under WSL; WASM build in Chrome 143 on the same machine
tradeoffs: Own string types and 'string expressions' API rather than a drop-in std::string; version 2.0.0 needs C++20 (concepts, std::format); the full library adds UTF conversion and shared/mutable string types.
caveats: Speedups are against the author's own std idioms (std::to_string or std::format concatenation with temporaries, find + substr + strtol, a hand-written std replace loop), not the fastest std alternatives: with std::to_chars the hex-formatting gap shrinks from 4.3-9.2x to 1.3-2.4x, and in decimal int parsing std::from_chars trails simstr's to_int by only 1.3-1.8x on Linux and beats it under MSVC (11.9 ns vs 15.5 ns). The README's 9-14x hex and 2-3x split figures overstate the v2.0.0 result files (4.3-9.2x and 1.4-3.25x). Not every row wins: hashStrMapA is slightly slower than std::unordered_map<std::string> on Linux (3.73 ms vs 3.64 ms for Clang/libstdc++) and faster only on Windows, and ssa::find ties std::string_view::find on Linux. All runs are on one CPU (Xeon E5-2682 v4), the Linux rows ran under WSL, ASLR was on and only 4 repetitions were taken. The result files do not name the CMake preset (Release inferred). The optional CHECK_RESULT answer checks are compiled out by default, though the split benchmark's std and simstr versions compute the same total by design. bench_str.cpp also compares StringZilla and fmt, which are not baselines here.

name: strstr.c (Ron Charlton)
baseline: The compiler's C library strstr (rows 0, 9 and 17 of Competitors/strstrFunctions.c are labelled 'Compiler library strstr'; rows 9 and 17 replaced the SunOS and Boyer-Moore-Horspool versions). The library is not named; comments in the competitor file mention macOS clang (2023-05-01), so it was probably Apple's libc, not glibc or musl.
workload: Finding English words in English text with a 15-line strchr-style strstr, compared with 18 other strstr implementations (BSD, GNU coreutils 5.3.0, Plauger, Moore, Visual C, compiler libraries).
claimed_speedup: README: 'tied for speed with its nearest competitor among 18 diverse strstr implementations' when finding English words in English text; 'Its other competitors are between 10.5% and 348% slower.' The README also says it 'is faster in many cases' than the C Standard Library's strstr.
tradeoffs: Plain C, no SIMD or table setup; 15 executable lines, public domain (CC0, no patent grant). Its inner loop is an unrolled strchr-like scan, so it relies on nothing platform specific.
caveats: Repo holds only strstr.c and the competitor sources (Competitors/strstrFunctions.c); there is no timing harness, test corpus list, per-competitor table, CPU model, compiler or flags, so the result is not reproducible and the library strstr's own margin is never stated separately. The competitor-file header says that when the first pattern character is rare, versions that call the library's SIMD strchr (strstr7, 8, 15, 16) are about 6.5 times faster than the others (strstr1 included), so the claim holds for English-word searches and may lose to a SIMD libc strstr elsewhere. The algorithm is a naive first-character scan plus compare, O(n*m) in the worst case, unlike the linear two-way strstr in glibc and musl. The nearest competitor is GNU coreutils 5.3.0 strstr (Stephen R. van den Berg, GPL-2.0+), not current glibc. Licence: LICENSE.md says CC0 1.0 for strstr.c (no patent grant), but the file header links the Public Domain Mark URL; the Competitors file contains GPL-2.0+ and unlicensed USENET code and is not covered.
