workload: test64 times libc strstr, std::string::find and the 64-bit SWAR first/last-byte filter (10 iterations each, gettimeofday) for every unique word extracted from i386.txt by make_words.sh, so each search succeeds at the word's first occurrence in the same text; analyze.py then prints a histogram of per-word speed-ratio buckets (slower, same, 2-2.99x, 3-3.99x, ... faster) against std::string::find and against libc strstr.

The harness also times libc strstr (analyze.py and the README mislabel it 'strlen'), but no margin over strstr is claimed; strstr must also scan for the terminator while the SWAR routine gets the length. Timing is 10 iterations with microsecond gettimeofday and no warm-up, and words are taken from the searched text, so many searches end early and are timer-resolution noise. By code reading (not run), strstr64.cpp has correctness bugs: the SWAR zero-byte test can flag the byte above a real candidate through borrow, and memcmp checks only needle[1..k-1], so needle 'abb' in text 'a`bb' returns 1 instead of not-found; the loop 'i < n - k' with step 8 skips the last start position when n-k is a multiple of 8; and the 8-byte loads read up to 5 bytes past the string terminator. verify.cpp checks only words from the same text, so these cases are not exercised. The linked article 0x80.pl/articles/simd-friendly-karp-rabin.html was unreachable (DNS ENOTFOUND). last_commit is the last commit touching strstr/ (2016-01-17); the toys repo itself was last pushed 2026-04-08. name: Vectorized std::search and std::find in the MSVC STL (SSE4.2/AVX2 runtime dispatch)
baseline: MSVC STL's own scalar std::search before vectorization (the same PR also times C strstr as an unchanged control)
workload: benchmarks/src/search.cpp: std::search, ranges::search and default_searcher over a lorem-ipsum haystack with small and large needles near the beginning and end, plus adversarial 'evil' patterns, for uint8_t, uint16_t, uint32_t and uint64_t elements, timed in ns per search.

Lavavej's run on an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, merged 2024-09-09): classic_search<uint8_t>/0 1976 to 160 ns (12.35x) and /1 2153 to 175 ns (12.30x); classic_search<uint16_t>/0 and /1 4.62x and 4.53x; ranges_search<uint8_t>/0 9.76x; search_default_searcher<uint8_t> 10.38x and 10.32x. The unchanged C strstr control took 142-143 ns (/0) and 157-162 ns (/1), so strstr stayed faster than the vectorized 1-byte std::search (160 and 175 ns). In that PR 4- and 8-byte rows were unchanged (0.98x-1.04x) and search_default_searcher<uint64_t> moved to 0.74x though its code was not changed (loop alignment suspected). PR #5484 (32- and 64-bit elements plus reworked 8/16-bit paths; 5950X run posted 2025-05-16, merged 2025-05-17): classic_search<uint32_t> /0 to /3 6.95x, 6.23x, 7.61x, 4.23x (1967 to 283 ns for /0); classic_search<uint64_t> /0 to /3 2.91x, 2.88x, 3.03x, 2.37x; uint16_t 1.38x to 1.98x. These were measured on ncruces's go-sqlite3 libc (sqlite3/libc/string.h), not on a wasi-libc build. wasi-libc main has opt-in SIMD versions only of strlen (#586), memchr (#592), strchrnul and hence strchr (#594), memrchr and hence strrchr (#598), memcmp (#603) and strspn/strcspn (#597); strcmp, strncmp and strstr are still the scalar musl code, so the 12.8x, 16.3x and 5.6x figures do not apply to wasi-libc. tradeoffs: Opt-in at build time (-DSIMD=ON) and needs a runtime with wasm simd128; functions landed one by one: strlen (#586), memchr (#592), strchrnul (#594), strspn/strcspn (#597), memrchr (#598), memcmp (#603); memchr was switched to inline assembly after an undefined-behaviour concern about pointer arithmetic (#593).
caveats: Numbers are one rough comment in a tracking issue, measured on the contributor's go-sqlite3 implementations rather than the code later merged into wasi-libc, with no CPU, runtime version, compiler, flags or string sizes; a reviewer asked whether the table used a 4 MB string and the reply gave no size, only saying small calls are hard to measure from the host and that 'there are too many variables (Wasm runtime, CPU architecture, string length), to give any hard guarantees'. The SIMD routines are off by default (-DSIMD=ON, __wasilibc_simd_string), and strspn/strcspn SIMD is skipped on Clang 19 and 20 (llvm/llvm-project#146574 ICE). The baseline is wasm-to-wasm (scalar vs SIMD in the same libc), not native glibc. The go-sqlite3 libc README with updated numbers linked from the issue now returns 404.

name: WebAssembly memory.copy (bulk-memory-operations proposal)
baseline: Emscripten-generated wasm memcpy loop (aligned i32.load/i32.store) used in the Unity demo, plus manually unrolled i32 and i64 load/store loop variants
workload: Each row copies 1 GiB in total with a V8 prototype where memcpy/memmove exports are replaced by memory.copy, versus the wasm loops; copy sizes 32 B to 1 MiB within a 1 MiB working set.
claimed_speedup: At 128 KiB: memory.copy 29.728 Gib/s vs i64 load/store x4 10.032, i64 x2 7.934, i32 x2 3.975, plain i32 loop 2.782 Gib/s. At 1.0 KiB: 17.902 vs 7.010, 6.112, 3.568, 2.614 Gib/s. Loses at 32 B: intrinsic 1.382 vs i64 x4 1.565 Gib/s. At 1 MiB: 11.760 vs 10.091 Gib/s.
license: Per-directory (repo LICENSE): document/ W3C Software and Document Notice and License; interpreter/ and test/ Apache-2.0; papers/ CC-BY-4.0
stars_or_usage: 82 stars, 21 forks; archived Nov 3 2021; finished proposal merged into WebAssembly core spec 2.0 per WebAssembly/proposals finished-proposals.md
tradeoffs: A proposal text plus a hacked V8 prototype, not a library. The repo's LICENSE file points to per-directory licences (document/ under the W3C Software and Document Notice and License). The instruction itself is a runtime feature, so the benefit applies only to engines that call native MemMove for memory.copy.
caveats: Baseline is a 2017-era Emscripten wasm memcpy (gist c57dc945, memcpy.wast: byte prologue to 4-byte alignment, i32.load/i32.store word loop, byte tail; byte path when src and dst alignments differ) plus hand-unrolled variants, not a native libc memcpy; the prototype memory.copy simply called V8's native MemMove, so this is native memmove versus wasm-compiled loops. The benchmark gist (b8e8bc0c, memcpy.js, created 2017-10-26) is public, but its data initialisation and verification block is commented out, and the 'intrinsic' module's exported _memcpy body is a stub returning 0 that only the author's hacked V8 replaced with memory.copy, so the intrinsic column cannot be reproduced on a stock engine from the gist; the size-dependent curve (1.382 Gib/s at 32 B rising to 29.994 at 512 KiB, falling to 11.760 at 1 MiB) is consistent with real copying, not a no-op. Engine version, CPU model and flags are not given, and the stated 'L3 256k' looks mis-stated. Single first-party run. The repository is archived (2021-11-03); WebAssembly/proposals finished-proposals.md lists Bulk memory operations as finished and merged into core spec 2.0 (WG 2021-02-10), so memory.copy is now a standard instruction implemented by engines rather than a library.

name: Apex memmove (Trevor Herselman): SSE2 memcpy and memmove for x86 and x64
baseline: C library memcpy and memmove (the README names no baseline; the repo's source has no comparison)
workload: No benchmark in the repository. README only says 'The fastest memcpy/memmove on x86/x64 ... EVER, written in C (according to the author)' and links the original CodeProject article, which could not be opened.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on the pages opened ('fastest memcpy/memmove on x86/x64 ... EVER').
stars_or_usage: 14 stars, 1 fork; code by Trevor Herselman (2014), mirrored by rukkal in 2016. Discussed on Hacker News as 'Apex memmove', on the PostgreSQL mailing list in July 2016 (Alvaro Herrera raised licence compatibility and asked for real-workload gains; snippet only) and in a 2020 Ultimate++ forum thread (snippet only).
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 only (SSE2 intrinsics from emmintrin.h, cpuid dispatch via __cpuid or __get_cpuid, several variants named tiberium, kryptonite and mithril); falls back to the library functions elsewhere. No license text anywhere in the repository or file headers, so the code is reference only. Handles overlapping moves like memmove.
caveats: Tier D: a self-description with no numbers in the repository. A search-result snippet of a 2020 Ultimate++ forum post reports one user's single MSVC run on a Core i7: apex_memcpy averaged 3.55 ms against 4.37 ms for the CRT memcpy, with clang similar. Neither the block size nor the flags appear in the snippet. The page could not be opened, so none of it is claimed here. The same snippet notes that the code has no licensing information. The CodeProject article is the only methodology source, and codeproject.com does not resolve from here. A CodeProject message titled 'Bug' exists on the article (codeproject.com/Messages/5374685/Bug), but its content could not be read. The mirror has three commits, all dated 2016-09-22, and no tests or benchmark code, so the claim cannot be reproduced from the repository. The dispatcher points apex_memcpy and apex_memmove at the same routine, so memcpy pays the overlap handling. It selects a variant by CPUID: SSE4.2 is taken as a proxy for fast unaligned access (kryptonite), SSSE3 selects tiberium and SSE2 alone selects mithril (32-bit only); every other target falls back to the C library. The code targets 2014-era CPUs, long before ERMS and FSRM made rep movsb competitive in glibc and the MSVC CRT. The .c and .cpp files are near-identical copies.

name: arm-mem (bavison): ARM-accelerated memcpy, memmove, memset, memcmp and strlen
baseline: generic glibc memcpy, memmove, memset, memcmp and strlen on 32-bit ARM (baseline implied by the description, not named in the README)
workload: No benchmark numbers published. test.c (built by the 'test' make target, CFLAGS -std=gnu99 -O2 -fno-inline) runs correctness checks and then times a single CANDIDATE routine (memcpy, memset or memcmp chosen by #if) over L1-, L2- and memory-sized buffers, subtracting a no-op control function, so a glibc comparison needs two runs with and without LD_PRELOAD of libarmmem.
claimed_speedup: No numbers against glibc in the README, the test harness or the commit history. The only figures are self-relative commit titles from the memcpy tuning in 2013 and 2015 ('Improve L1 and L2 results by around 5% and 2% respectively', 'Extra 3-5% speed boost for Cortex-A7 memcpy'). The description claims only 'ARM-accelerated versions of selected functions from string.h'.
hardware: ARMv6 (-v6l) and ARMv7 (-v7l) builds; NEON strlen and memcmp tuned for Cortex-A53; Raspberry Pi class targets
license: BSD-3-Clause (per-file headers: Copyright 2013 Raspberry Pi Foundation and RISC OS Open Ltd, later files 2015-2019 RISC OS Open Ltd; no LICENSE file; test.c and test-strlen.c carry no header)
stars_or_usage: 57 stars, 13 forks (including RPi-Distro/arm-mem and kobolabs/arm-mem); built into Raspberry Pi OS / Raspbian's raspi-copies-and-fills package (RPi-Distro/arm-mem debian/changelog: 0.5-1 initial release June 2015 through 0.13 April 2019) and enabled through /etc/ld.so.preload; Arch Linux ARM replaced libcofi with it (forum snippet only)

caveats: No evidence of speed against glibc: no published numbers, and the harness measures one routine at a time against a no-op control. Correctness history: the NEON strlen tuned for Cortex-A53 shipped in raspi-copies-and-fills 0.8 (January 2019) and needed 'ARMv7 strlen: fix stupid bug' (March 2019, package 0.12), memcmp return values were then limited and later forced to -1/0/+1 (package 0.13), and the April 2019 'Rewrite memcpy / memmove to tune for Cortex-A53' was reverted eleven days later; CNX Software reported (snippet only) that a March 2019 package update broke programs including SSH logins on some boards. name: bddisasm
baseline: Capstone (decode+format throughput); Intel XED, diStorm, iced, yaxpeax-x86, Sleigh and the other listed decoders are measured in the same harness
workload: Decoding (and decoding plus formatting) the code section of a 64-bit x86 binary repeatedly in the disas-bench harness, reported as MB/s of machine code.
claimed_speedup: disas-bench charts (bar lengths measured against axis ticks, approximate): Ryzen 9 9950X: bddisasm decode+format 46.8 MB/s, bddisasm mini decode+format 48.8 MB/s, Capstone decode+format 27.5 MB/s; decode-only bddisasm 105.7 MB/s, bddisasm mini 179.3 MB/s. i9-13900K: bddisasm decode+format 35.6 MB/s, mini 39.0 MB/s, Capstone 25.9 MB/s; decode-only 102.7 MB/s, mini 179.5 MB/s. Decode+format ratio to Capstone 1.70x (AMD) and 1.37x (Intel), mini 1.77x and 1.51x (derived from page data, chart readings). README alone: legacy decoder around 240 CPU clocks per decoded instruction (~12M instructions/s) and mini decoder around 150 clocks (~17M instructions/s) on an Intel Core Ultra 7 165H with BDDISASM v3.0, no baseline.
compiler_and_flags: Harness binaries are built with cc -O3 (bench/cs/Makefile, bench/xed/Makefile, bench/bddisasm/Makefile; bench/zydis via CMake Release), GCC 13.3 on the AMD run and GCC 14.2 on the Intel run. Libraries: Capstone 5.0.6 (submodule accf4df) built with its own Makefile, default CFLAGS -O3, CAPSTONE_ARCHS=x86; bddisasm v3.0.0 via CMake Release with BDD_LTO=ON; Zydis via CMake Release (bench/zydis/CMakeLists.txt, submodule 569320a); XED via mfile.py --opt=3 (make-all.sh).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.8.0) and Intel Core i9-13900K (Debian trixie, Linux 6.12.48)
tradeoffs: C library with Python and Rust bindings, directly usable from C++. Includes a 'mini' decoder with reduced detail and a shellcode-detection emulator (not benchmarked). Decode+format advantage over Capstone is modest.
caveats: Smaller win than iced, yaxpeax-x86 and diStorm in the same charts (iced and yaxpeax decode+format are about 3.4-5.4x faster than bddisasm); the README's own throughput numbers carry no baseline. Each tool is timed in a single run (clock() CPU time over 20 passes of the 0x2460400-byte code section of a checked-in Firefox xul.dll), with no repetitions or variance reported. disas-bench is maintained by Joel Hoener (athre0z), a Zydis copyright holder; the AMD chart was produced by iximeow (yaxpeax-x86 author, 2025-10-24) and the Intel chart by athre0z (2025-10-26). Chart values are bar lengths read off PNGs against the axis ticks (approximate, about +/-1 MB/s), not a text table. Capstone appears only as a decode+format row (cs_disasm_iter, detail off), so decode+format rows are the like-for-like comparison; formatted text differs in detail between libraries. The bddisasm v3.0.0 update and the mini-decoder rows were contributed to disas-bench by ianichitei (2025-10-10), who also authored earlier bddisasm updates there.

name: diStorm3
baseline: Capstone, Zydis, Intel XED, bddisasm, udis86, BeaEngine (x86/AMD64 disassembler libraries); no GNU as, NASM or MASM comparison
workload: Decoding only, and decoding plus formatting, of the 77 MB .text section of Firefox 86.0.1's 64-bit xul.dll, throughput in MB/s (computed as bytes/1024/1024 per second). The README does not state the loop count: bench.py's built-in default is 20 passes over the 36.4 MiB section of the older 63 MB input/xul.dll checked into the repo, and with a custom file and no loop-count argument it scales the count to keep the same total bytes (about 9 passes over a 77 MB section, derived from bench.py). The Firefox 86 xul.dll itself is not in the repo.
claimed_speedup: Decode only: 92.17 MB/s vs Zydis 34.19, XED 55.39, bddisasm 35.48, udis86 80.72 (about 2.7x Zydis, 1.7x XED, derived from page data). Decode+format: 58.85 MB/s vs Capstone 14.02, Zydis 22.24, XED 15.67, bddisasm 16.00 (about 4.2x Capstone, 2.6x Zydis, derived from page data). README: 'ultra fast', and quotes a 2014 thesis that benchmarked five open-source disassembly libraries and chose diStorm3 for best performance.
compiler_and_flags: Kubuntu 21.04, gcc 10.3.0, Rust 1.52.1 (disas-bench README). make-all.sh builds the C libraries with gcc and LTO: Capstone and bddisasm as CMake Release builds with CFLAGS=-flto, XED via mfile.py --opt=3 --extra-flags=-flto, diStorm via its own make/linux Makefile (current version: -fPIC -O2 -std=c99) with -flto prepended, BeaEngine patched to -O3 -flto, udis86 without LTO (it got slower). The C bench drivers (bench/*/Makefile) are built with -flto -O3; the Zydis driver is a CMake Release build with CFLAGS=-flto. The Rust drivers (bench/iced-x86/Cargo.toml, bench/yaxpeax/Cargo.toml) use a release profile with opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1 and no target-cpu setting. C libraries and yaxpeax-x86 are pinned git submodules (last updated March 2021); iced is pulled unpinned from its git master at build time.
hardware: Intel Core i5-6600K, Kubuntu 21.04 (README); test file xul.dll from Firefox 86.0.1.7739, 77 MB code section
tradeoffs: C library with a single decompose API (returns a structured description, optional text formatting), about 45 KB, x86/AMD64 only; Python bindings (distorm3). No commits since 2021 (date read from the GitHub commits page), so recent instruction-set extensions are unlikely to decode.
caveats: Numbers are from the iced author's disas-bench fork (June 2021, i5-6600K) with the diStorm submodule of March 2021; diStorm's last commit is 2021-12-18 (v3.5.3), so it is abandoned and instruction-set coverage added since then by other decoders was not checked. The diStorm README itself gives no numbers, only 'ultra fast' and a 2014 thesis quote ('chose diStorm3, which had the best performance'). The benchmark loop count is not stated (see workload). Each driver runs once per configuration (no repetitions or variance); the C drivers time CPU time with clock(), the Rust drivers wall time with millisecond resolution. The decode+format driver discards distorm_format64's output, but its time is well above decode-only (58.85 vs 92.17 MB/s), so formatting work is being timed. Formatters differ in output syntax between libraries. The yaxpeax author's later fork (i7-12700K, GCC 11, rustc 1.67 nightly, bar chart without numbers) shows diStorm at roughly 138 MB/s decode and 86 MB/s decode+format, still ahead of Capstone, XED, Zydis and bddisasm but behind iced and yaxpeax (values read off the bars, approximate). The comparison is decode/disassembly throughput against other disassembler libraries, not assembly speed against GNU as, NASM or MASM (the category's spec baseline); objdump/libopcodes was not tested.

tradeoffs: Rust library with an x86/x64 decoder, encoder, formatter and assembler; there is no official C or C++ API (bindings exist for .NET, Java, Python, JavaScript/WebAssembly and Lua), so use from C++ needs FFI or a wrapper. Decoded instruction is a 40-byte struct and the decoder does not allocate. x86/x64 only.
caveats: First-party run: disas-bench is a fork of athre0z/disas-bench (MIT, Joel Höner 2017) hosted in iced's own organisation, and the June 2021 results were committed by the iced author; the iced driver's Cargo.toml was written by the yaxpeax author. iced is pulled unpinned from git master at build time, so the measured version is whatever master was in June 2021. The benchmark loop count is not stated (see workload). Each driver runs once per configuration (no repetitions or variance); the C drivers time CPU time with clock(), the Rust drivers wall time with millisecond resolution. The decode-only driver never reads the decoded Instruction (only the decoder position advances), so LTO could drop some operand stores. The decode+format driver uses iced's SpecializedFormatter from the fast_fmt feature with db/dw/dd/dq output disabled and the output-buffer check turned off, the cheapest formatter iced offers, while the C libraries use their general formatters; formatted text differs between libraries. Capstone and BeaEngine have no decode-only mode. The five newest commits (2026-07-14) are dependabot dependency bumps. Decode/disassembly throughput against other disassemblers, not assembly speed against GNU as, NASM or MASM (the category's spec baseline); objdump was not tested.

Each driver runs once per configuration (no repetitions or variance); the C drivers time CPU time with clock(), the Rust drivers wall time with millisecond resolution. A C/C++ interface exists in the repo's ffi/ directory (repackaging for non-Rust callers). name: z88dk (Z80 development kit: C compilers, z80asm assembler and assembly libraries)
baseline: SDCC 4.6.0 (also HI-TECH C 3.09 and 7.80 and IAR Z80 V4.06A in the same tables)
workload: Z80 cycle counts and code size for Dhrystone 2.1, Whetstone 1.2, n-Body, Fasta, Pi, Sieve, Fannkuch and Binary-Trees compiled by each toolchain and run on the z88dk-ticks Z80 emulator (wall clock derived at 4 MHz).
claimed_speedup: From the wiki Benchmarks tables, Z80 cycles for SDCC 4.6.0 against z88dk's zsdcc 4.6.0 #16639 builds: n-Body 4,361,393,645 vs 2,243,368,504 for Z88DK/SDCC_CLASSIC (math48), 1.94x fewer (derived from page data), and vs 860,188,405 for Z88DK/SDCC_CLASSIC/MATH32, 5.07x (derived); the fastest z88dk n-Body row, Z88DK/SCCZ80_NEW/MATH32 at 807,783,742, is 5.40x (derived). Whetstone 1,850,296,726 vs 916,750,272 for Z88DK/SDCC_CLASSIC, 2.02x (derived), and vs 360,608,050 for Z88DK/SDCC/MATH32, 5.13x (derived). Fasta 414,019,207 vs 241,418,675 for Z88DK/SDCC_CLASSIC, 1.71x (derived). Pi without ldiv 7,218,092,827 vs 4,010,854,332 for Z88DK/SDCC_NEW, 1.80x (derived), and vs 1,696,878,309 for Z88DK/SCCZ80_NEW_FAST, 4.25x (derived). Dhrystone 2.1 274,542,684 vs 242,442,688 for Z88DK/SDCC_NEW, 1.13x (derived). Binary-Trees 193,466,493 vs 149,280,700 for Z88DK/SDCC_CLASSIC, 1.30x (derived). The Pi and Dhrystone comparison rows are the NEW library, not the classic library as the record said.
compiler_and_flags: Baseline SDCC 4.6.0 #16608 (Linux), e.g. n-Body: 'sdcc -mz80 -DSTATIC -DTIMER --max-allocs-per-node200000 n-body.c' then makebin, timed with 'z88dk-ticks n-body.bin -start 0d7a -end 0dc0' (support/benchmarks/n-body/sdcc/readme.txt); Pi and Dhrystone use the same sdcc flags (Dhrystone adds -DNOSTRUCTASSIGN). z88dk classic zsdcc 4.6.0 #16639: 'zcc +test -vn -DSTATIC -DTIMER -D__Z88DK -compiler=sdcc -SO3 --max-allocs-per-node200000 n-body.c -o n-body.bin -lmath48 -m -lndos' (math32 rows use --math32); sccz80 classic math32: 'zcc +test -vn -DSTATIC -DTIMER -D__Z88DK -O2 n-body.c -o n-body.bin --math32 -m -lndos' (support/benchmarks/n-body/z88dk-classic/readme.txt). The __Z88DK define only enables intrinsic.h and printf/scanf options; it does not change the computation.
hardware: z88dk-ticks Z80 emulator (cycle-exact count; wall time assumes a 4 MHz Z80), not a physical CPU
license: Clarified Artistic License (SPDX ClArtistic: FSF-libre and GPL-compatible but not OSI-approved per the SPDX license list), 'unless otherwise stated in the appropriate file'
tradeoffs: Z80-family targets only; the speed comes from hand-written assembly libraries and a cheaper calling convention, with larger code in several rows (SDCC is smaller on Sieve, Fannkuch and Dhrystone sizes).
caveats: The win is not uniform. With the NEW library Binary-Trees takes 6,570,984,020 cycles against 193,466,493 for plain SDCC (about 34x slower; the wiki blames the fast-realloc free-block search, issue #113), while the classic library is 1.30x faster. On Sieve the sccz80 builds (4.77M to 4.96M cycles) are slower than SDCC (4,218,689) and only Z88DK/SDCC_NEW (3,679,114) wins, by 1.15x and barely ahead of IAR (3,714,152); on Fannkuch HI-TECH C 7.80 is fastest and smallest (51,982,515 cycles, 868 bytes), sccz80 is slower than SDCC and SDCC_NEW wins by only 1.06x. The large n-Body, Whetstone, Fasta and Pi gains come mostly from z88dk's assembly-language float and 32-bit integer libraries replacing SDCC's C-implemented ones (the wiki says so), since zsdcc is z88dk's patched build of the same SDCC 4.6.0. Rows without a MATH32 label use pre-v2.5 genmath or math48 (48-bit) libraries and are not comparable to MATH32 rows; rows come from different dates (sccz80 NEW April 2021, sccz80 classic January 2022, zsdcc and SDCC August-September 2026). All results, including the HI-TECH C and IAR runs, were measured by the z88dk project itself. HI-TECH C 7.80 gives wrong Fasta output (DISQ). The baseline is a C compiler, not GNU as, NASM or MASM, and the z80asm assembler itself is not benchmarked, so the fit to assemblers-and-asm-tooling is weak. name: KeplerAs and SGEMM assembly (PPoPP 2017 artifact)
language: SASS assembly kernels plus an assembler (implementation language not confirmed; README says KeplerAs is based on MaxAs)
baseline: NVIDIA cuBLAS 7.0 SGEMM (and cuDNN v4.0 for the convolution kernel), i.e. NVIDIA's library kernels built by NVIDIA's own toolchain
workload: Single-precision GEMM on an NVIDIA Tesla K20m, square matrices 384 to 12288 (step 384) and rectangular shapes, plus a convolution kernel on the same GPU (batch size 128).
claimed_speedup: Paper (sgemm.pdf in the repo): at 12288 x 12288 the hand-assembled SGEMM reaches 3.1 Tflop/s (88% of peak) versus cuBLAS 7.0 at 2.7 Tflop/s (76%), a 1.15x speedup; convolution kernel 39%, 46% and 62% faster than cuDNN v4.0 for three CNN configurations.
compiler_and_flags: cuBLAS from CUDA 7.0 as the baseline; the optimized kernels are written directly in SASS and assembled with KeplerAs, so no nvcc flags apply. Compiler flags for any host harness are not stated on the pages opened.
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla K20m (Kepler, 13 SMs); host CPU model not stated in the paper text read
license: No repository-wide licence. KeplerAs/LICENSE is MIT (Copyright 2014 Scott Gray, 2015~2016 Xiuxia Zhang); the SGEMM .sass kernels carry 'Copyright 2015~2017 Xiuxia Zhang ... All rights reserved' lines (commit 'Added licence information', 2017-05-24), and one kernel file carries an Apache-2.0 header.
tradeoffs: Kepler-only SASS (the ISA encoding was cracked for Kepler and differs from Maxwell); kernels and the assembler do not carry over to newer GPUs. The same research line produced MaxAs (Maxwell/Pascal) and TuringAs (Volta/Turing/Ampere).
caveats: This is a peer-reviewed PPoPP 2017 paper ('Understanding the GPU Microarchitecture to Achieve Bare-Metal Performance Tuning', originally 'Demystifying GPU Microarchitecture to Tune SGEMM'), but the repo has no benchmark harness, timing code or run scripts, and the convolution kernels behind the cuDNN claim are not in the repo at all (only KeplerAs, SGEMM and Solver directories). The paper says the 12x12 and 8x8 kernels beat cuBLAS 'in most cases' (8x8 is better at small sizes, the gain grows with matrix size), so 1.15x is the best large-matrix figure, not a uniform one. cuBLAS 7.0 and cuDNN 4.0 (2015-2016) and the Kepler-only ISA encoding are long obsolete. KeplerAs is a Perl assembler (Makefile.PL, lib/KeplerAs) derived from Scott Gray's MaxAs, which is listed separately in wave 13; the measured artifact is hand-written SASS against a vendor library, not an assembler-versus-assembler test. The kernels are 'All rights reserved' and only the assembler is MIT.
found_via: GitHub: daadaada/turingas README 'Related projects' links KeplerAs to this artifact repo; opened github.com/PAA-NCIC/PPoPP2017_artifact and fetched sgemm.pdf from raw.githubusercontent.com

verification.tier_reason: The PPoPP 2017 paper (sgemm.pdf in the repo, ACM ISBN 978-1-4503-4493-7) states on a Tesla K20m that the SGEMM reaches 3.1 Tflop/s (88%) against cuBLAS 7.0's 2.7 Tflop/s (76%) at 12288 x 12288, a 1.15x speedup, and that the convolution is 39%, 46% and 62% faster than cuDNN v4.0. It is peer-reviewed, but the repo holds only the .sass kernels, the assembler and the solver, with no timing harness or run scripts, so it is not A.
verification.notes: Numbers verified in the repo's sgemm.pdf (pdftotext): 3.1 vs 2.7 Tflop/s, 88% vs 76%, 1.15x, and 39%/46%/62% over cuDNN v4.0. Not a duplicate of MaxAs (NervanaSystems/maxas): KeplerAs targets a different ISA (Kepler) using encodings from the authors' solver and has its own paper claim. Usability moved to mixed: MIT assembler, all-rights-reserved kernels.

name: Minotaur
baseline: clang/LLVM -O3 without the Minotaur pass (per search snippets of the paper)
workload: Runtime of code compiled with and without the Minotaur LLVM pass: SPEC CPU 2017, the GMP benchmark suite and LibYUV.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract, seen via search snippets only (paper not opened): on an Intel Cascade Lake processor, GMP benchmark suite mean speedup 7.3% (max 13%) and SPEC CPU 2017 mean speedup 1.5% (max 4.5% on 638.imagick) over clang -O3. Single snippets also give a 1.2% SPEC mean on AMD and a LibYUV geomean of 1.029x on AMD Zen 3; a summary of an older paper version gives different LibYUV figures, so those two are unconfirmed.
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake (GMP and SPEC headline numbers); AMD Zen 3 for LibYUV and the compile-time tables per snippets; exact CPU models not seen
tradeoffs: Runs as an LLVM opt pass or via minotaur-cc / minotaur-c++ wrappers; needs a patched, RTTI- and EH-enabled LLVM build, Alive2, Z3 and Redis (offline cache mode), which makes the build heavy. Synthesis time adds to compile time.
caveats: All numbers come from search-result text of the paper (arXiv 2306.00229 v3, OOPSLA 2024); the paper, the NSF PAR copy, the deepai mirror and the 2022 LLVM Dev Meeting slides were all blocked, so methodology, flags and exact CPU models were not checked. The repo README has no performance numbers and no evaluation scripts (scripts/ holds only cache and compiler-wrapper tools). Gains on SPEC are small (1.2-1.5% mean). Per snippets, cold-cache builds can be hundreds of times slower than plain -O3 and warm-cache SPEC builds about 3% slower. Using it needs a patched LLVM (llvm-main-minotaur.patch) built with RTTI and exceptions, Alive2, Z3 and a redis server. It is an LLVM IR superoptimizer, so only loosely 'assembly tooling'.

name: STOKE
baseline: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 compiled x86-64 code (output quality); expert hand-written assembly for some kernels; Google Native Client's shipped libc string functions in the 2017 paper
workload: Runtime of superoptimized loop-free x86-64 kernels (OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication, Hacker's Delight, SAXPY, linked-list traversal) starting from llvm -O0 code, and 13 libc string functions from NaCl newlib.
claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2013 paper, Figure 1 caption and Section 1: the OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication kernel rewritten by STOKE is '16 lines shorter, 1.6x faster' than the gcc -O3 code 'and slightly faster than expert handwritten assembly'. Abstract: STOKE's programs 'either match or outperform the code produced by gcc -O3, icc -O3, and in some cases, expert handwritten assembly'. Figure 11 plots speedups over llvm -O0 for Hacker's Delight p01-p25, saxpy, mont and list; per-kernel values appear only in the chart. The README's popcount tutorial times a loop at 1.046 s for g++ -O3 -fno-inline versus 0.133 s after STOKE patches popcnt() (about 7.9x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 baselines (versions not stated in the extracted paper text); gcc-4.9 used in the 2017 paper's translation mode; README tutorial uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline
hardware: ASPLOS 2013: synthesis and optimization on a cluster of 40 dual-core 1.8 GHz AMD Opterons (machine used for the runtime speedups not identified in the extracted text); ASPLOS 2017: machines with two Intel Xeon E5-2667v2 3.3 GHz processors and 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and Intel-microarchitecture oriented. Needs test cases plus bounded or SMT-based equivalence checking, search budgets of tens of minutes per kernel on a cluster, and works best on short loop-free sequences. README: 'STOKE isn't production ready' and 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it says it is 'not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code'.
caveats: The paper is from 2013 and the speedups are on a small set of hand-picked loop-free kernels, plotted relative to llvm -O0 starting points in Figure 11; per-kernel numbers are chart-only, and the paper states no gcc/icc versions and does not name the timing machine. The README says 'We're not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code', calls STOKE a research prototype that 'isn't production ready', and says 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it needs gcc 4.9 to build. The README popcount tutorial's ~8x win compares against g++ -O3 without -march, so gcc cannot emit the popcnt instruction that STOKE uses; it shows the tool working, not a fair compiler comparison. The category fit (assembly tooling) is a judgement call: STOKE is a superoptimizer, and its baselines are compilers, not GNU as, NASM or MASM. The last commit (2020-12-04) only added a CodeQL workflow; the last code change is from 2019-10-03.

name: Unison
baseline: LLVM's register allocator and instruction scheduler (output quality, Hexagon, ARM and MIPS back ends)
workload: Estimated speedup and code size of functions from MediaBench and SPEC CPU2006 compiled with Unison's integrated combinatorial register allocation and instruction scheduling versus LLVM.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (arXiv 1804.02452 abstract via WebSearch; paper not opened): mean estimated speedup over LLVM from 1.1% to 10% and mean code size reduction from 1.3% to 3.8% depending on the architecture (code size: MIPS 3.8%, ARM 2.5%, Hexagon 1.3%, where LLVM's heuristics are already near-optimal for size), on functions from MediaBench and SPEC CPU2006. The authors report that running the generated code on Hexagon confirms that the estimated speedup becomes actual speedup.
hardware: Hexagon (execution check); estimates for ARM and MIPS
tradeoffs: Haskell tool driving constraint solvers, used through a Unison-enabled LLVM fork (github.com/unison-code/llvm); solving time is far higher than LLVM's heuristics; targets Hexagon, ARM and MIPS rather than x86.
caveats: Numbers are 'estimated' speedups from a static cost model, not measured runtimes, except for the Hexagon execution check. The metric is the quality of the generated code: Unison's constraint solving is far slower than LLVM's heuristic register allocator and scheduler, and the paper describes scaling to medium-sized functions of up to about 1,000 instructions, so compile time is a cost, not a win. The repo README and project site (unison-code.github.io index.md, checked via raw.githubusercontent.com) make no performance claims and link no results; the paper (arXiv 1804.02452, TOPLAS doi 10.1145/3332373), the project site's publication pages and the Ericsson research blog 'Outperforming state-of-the-art compilers with Unison' were unreachable here, so all numbers are from search-result text. Needs an LLVM fork (unison-code/llvm) as a driver. Last commit 2023-01-15 (abandoned). Filed under assemblers-and-asm-tooling, though it is really a compiler back-end component (register allocation and instruction scheduling).

Mean wall times read from the bar heights of benchmark-time.svg (derived from page data: bar geometry measured against the chart's 0.5 s axis ticks): libxul.so (162MB, 500 queries) gimli 0.10 s vs binutils addr2line 1.15 s (about 11x), llvm-addr2line 0.48 s (about 4.7x), eu-addr2line 3.25 s (about 32x); clangd-18 (360MB, 500 queries) 0.18 s vs binutils 2.92 s (about 16x), llvm 0.39 s (about 2.1x), eu 2.17 s (about 12x); mold (314MB, 1000 queries) 0.14 s vs binutils 1.19 s (about 8.5x), llvm 0.36 s (about 2.6x), eu 0.82 s (about 5.9x); postgres (38MB, 10000 queries) 0.067 s vs binutils 0.176 s (about 2.6x), llvm 0.079 s (about 1.2x), eu 1.91 s (about 28x). name: ai-kernel-optimizer
baseline: GCC -O3 compiled C reference kernels (scalar 256-byte-LUT base64 decode, LZ4 1.10.0 fast-path decode, Redis 7.x SipHash 1-2)
workload: Differential-fuzzed x86-64 assembly replacements, written by an AI model with optimize.py as scaffolding, for three extracted kernels: base64 decode (valid-input-only, no padding, length multiple of 4) timed at 64 B, 1 KiB and 16 KiB inputs; LZ4 1.10.0 fast-path decode loop on 4096-byte blocks (10M iterations); Redis 7.x SipHash 1-2 on 8-, 32- and 128-byte keys. Each benchmark is one back-to-back run (GCC then AI) of the same input with CLOCK_MONOTONIC.
claimed_speedup: Base64 decode 4.80x (64 B, 50M iters: 1.81 s vs 0.38 s, 1,767 to 8,479 MB/s), 6.23x (1 KiB, 5M iters: 1,825 to 11,365 MB/s), 6.26x (16 KiB, 200K iters: 1,857 to 11,635 MB/s) over the GCC -O3 scalar LUT decoder; LZ4 fast-path decode three runs 1.07x, 0.98x, 1.02x (author: within noise); Redis SipHash 1-2 0.96x (8 B keys), 0.97x (32 B), 0.99x tie (128 B), i.e. GCC 3-4% faster on short keys.
compiler_and_flags: Reference kernels: gcc -O3 -march=native (stated in case_studies/SUMMARY.md methodology, the blog post and optimize.py); AI .S assembled with gcc; generic harness built with gcc -O2. GCC version not stated.
tradeoffs: x86-64 only, SSSE3 for the base64 kernel (BMI2 rorx in the SipHash attempt). The base64 kernel assumes valid input, no padding characters and a length that is a multiple of 4, so it skips the error handling a production decoder needs. Base64 code is about twice the size of GCC's (293 vs 145 bytes). The tool only handles pure kernels with no I/O, allocation or global state; the full LZ4_decompress_safe (856 instructions) was too large, so only its fast path was replaced.
caveats: All numbers are self-reported in case_studies/*/REPORT.md, case_studies/SUMMARY.md and blog/ai-assembly-vs-gcc-o3.md. The reports list the C reference, the .S assembly, harness.c and build_and_test.sh, and the blog says each case study is 'a single ./build_and_test.sh away from reproducing', but none of those files are in the repo (raw.githubusercontent.com returns 404 for case_studies/base64/b64_decode_kern.c, harness.c, build_and_test.sh, lz4/harness.c, redis/harness.c; the initial commit was 'optimize.py + 3 case study reports'), so nothing can be rerun and the faster assembly itself cannot be copied: only the optimize.py driver (scanner, prompt generator, fuzz/bench harness generator) is published. CPU model and GCC version are not stated; optimize.py's generated benchmark is a single back-to-back run on one fixed input with no warmup or repeats. The baseline is a naive scalar 256-byte-LUT decoder of unstated origin; the AI kernel is the known SSSE3 pshufb nibble-lookup technique (Mula/Lemire style) without input validation (it assumes valid base64 and no padding), and existing SIMD base64 libraries (aklomp/base64, fastbase64, simdutf) were not compared. The LZ4 timings (0.024-0.027 s for 10M iterations, about 2.5 ns per call, derived from page data) are impossible for decoding a 4096-byte block, so the LZ4 row did not measure the stated workload and is not valid evidence; it is a tie anyway (runs 1.07x, 0.98x, 1.02x). SipHash is slower than GCC. The README's 'provably outperforms GCC -O3' is overstated: verification is 100K differential-fuzz iterations per kernel, and two of three kernels are a loss or a tie. MIT is stated only in the README; there is no LICENSE file or copyright notice and GitHub shows no license. No independent coverage found; the Hacker News thread could not be opened (egress blocked).

name: B2R2 (binary analysis framework, disassembler front-end)
baseline: Capstone (Capstone.NET and Capstone Python bindings), plus SharpDisasm; compared with iced (C#), which is faster
workload: Seconds (in-process Stopwatch) to linearly disassemble three raw x86/x86-64 blobs from the BAR19-Artifact repo (blob_x86, blob_x86_64, libc_x86) and print every instruction to stdout with Console.WriteLine/print inside the timed loop; each number is the mean of 10 runs, lower is better.
claimed_speedup: B2R2 28.298 s on blob_x86, 24.317 s on blob_x86_64, 0.63 s on libc_x86 (average 17.748 s) vs Capstone.NET 127.847 / 106.414 / 2.245 s (average 78.835 s) and Capstone Python 132.693 / 111.604 / 2.22 s (average 82.172 s): about 4.4x faster than Capstone.NET on average (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: dotnet run -c release for each .NET project, TargetFramework net5.0 (from b2r2_test.fsproj and Capstone.NET_test.csproj; SDK version not stated); B2R2.FrontEnd.BinInterface 0.5.0 from NuGet; Capstone.NET is Gee.External.Capstone 2.0.2 with the CapstoneCoreLin4/CapstoneCoreWin4 1.0.0 native packages (Capstone 4.x era); Capstone Python run as 'python capstone_test_python.py' (capstone package version not stated)
tradeoffs: Fully managed F# binary analysis framework (also lifts to IR and recovers CFGs, not measured here); needs .NET, no C or C++ API, so use from C++ requires interop or a separate process.
caveats: Comparison repo is run by the B2R2 authors; no CPU, OS or .NET SDK version is given, and the repo has no license. Every harness prints each instruction to the console inside the timed region, so the times (25-130 s per blob) are dominated by string formatting and console output, and the output destination is not stated. Work is not equal: the Capstone harnesses enable skipdata (undecodable bytes are emitted as .byte pseudo-instructions and printed), while the B2R2 harness silently advances one byte on a parse error without printing; the Python harness prints only address and operands, not the mnemonic. The baseline is Capstone 4.x through managed (Gee.External.Capstone 2.0.2) or Python bindings, so per-instruction marshalling overhead is included and the ratio overstates the gap to native Capstone; current Capstone 5/6 is not measured. Numbers are for B2R2 v0.5.0 (comparison repo last updated 2021-10-23); the framework has changed a lot since. B2R2 is slower than Iced (15.737 s average) and only slightly faster than SharpDisasm (18.321 s) in the same table. B2R2 is an F#/.NET library, not callable from C++ without hosting the CLR. The README's run command names b2r2_test.csproj but the project file is b2r2_test.fsproj. The peer-reviewed BAR'19 paper (artifact repo B2R2-org/BAR19-Artifact) compares lifting front-ends (BAP, BINSEC, Miasm, PyVEX, radare2 docker images), not Capstone, and its PDF was unreachable here.

name: SuperCoder
baseline: gcc -O3 compiled assembly (output quality)
workload: Runtime speedup of LLM-rewritten x86 assembly versus the gcc -O3 assembly on a benchmark of 8,072 real-world programs averaging 130 lines (CodeNet-derived), with test-based correctness checks.
claimed_speedup: Per WebSearch result text of arXiv 2505.11480 only (paper not opened): the RL-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct model reaches a 95.0% test pass rate and a 1.46x average speedup over gcc -O3; the strongest baseline LLM (Claude-opus-4) reaches 51.5% pass rate and 1.43x average speedup.
compiler_and_flags: Per the paper (snippet only): baseline assembly from gcc -O3. Released scripts: src/create_data/convert_to_hf_raw.py emits gcc -O0 -S (stored as 'unoptimized_assembly', the prompt input and the timing baseline) and gcc -O3 -S (stored as the reference answer); all assembly is linked with plain 'gcc file.s -o bin -lm'; gcc version not stated. Timing: hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 10, mean whole-process wall time per test input, up to 10 inputs per program.
stars_or_usage: 2 stars, 0 forks; model weights published as LLM4Code/Superoptimizer_Qwen7B on HuggingFace
tradeoffs: Probabilistic output: correctness is test-based (95.0% pass rate, not formal equivalence), so rewrites need independent verification. Needs a GPU-capable RL setup (verl) to retrain; model weights and dataset are listed on Hugging Face in the README.
caveats: Headline numbers come from WebSearch snippets of arXiv 2505.11480 (paper not opened; arXiv and alphaXiv blocked); the README has no results section and states no hardware or gcc version. The released harness (src/test_benchmark.py) floors every per-input speedup at 1.0 ('If generated code is slower, set speedup to 1.0'), gives failed, non-compiling or benchmark-failing cases a speedup of 1.0 (they are averaged in as 1.0, not excluded), and treats output identical to the baseline assembly as correct at 1.0 without running it, so the reported average can never fall below 1.0 and is biased upward. In the released dataset-building scripts (src/create_data/convert_to_hf_raw.py, create_top_speedup.py) the 'unoptimized_assembly' that test_benchmark.py times against is gcc -O0 output, while the paper says the baseline is gcc -O3; the published HuggingFace dataset (LLM4Code/llm_superoptimizer_ds) could not be opened to check which variant the reported numbers used, so the repo as released does not demonstrably reproduce the -O3 comparison. Correctness is checked on at most 10 CodeNet test inputs per program, and timings are whole-process (startup included) on small competitive-programming programs, run concurrently in a thread pool. The output is a fine-tuned model (HuggingFace LLM4Code/Superoptimizer_Qwen7B, licence not checked), not a library; the repo is a 2-commit code drop. Preprint status.

name: svc-hook (ARM64 system call hook by binary rewriting)
baseline: ptrace-based system call interception (README headline, no numbers); ASC-Hook, another ARM64 binary-rewriting syscall hook (Documentation/README.md, with numbers)
workload: System call interception on ARM64 Linux, Android, FreeBSD and NetBSD by rewriting every svc instruction in the loaded target to a b instruction that branches to a per-instruction trampoline; the README compares hook cost with ptrace.
claimed_speedup: README Key Features: '1,000 times faster than `ptrace`', with no ptrace timing anywhere in the repository. Documentation/README.md 'Overhead Comparision with ASC-Hook': time to hook getpid is 14 ns for svc-hook, 39 ns for ASC-Hook and 3 ns for plain LD_PRELOAD, so the trampoline overhead is 11 ns against 36 ns (about 3.3x, derived from page data); initial setup takes 25 ms against 1890 ms for ASC-Hook ('75 times faster'). The same page reports the cost of hooking against unhooked runs: SQLite per-operation time up 0.01% to 2.6%, PostgreSQL 17.6 pgbench 10790 TPS hooked against 10923 TPS unhooked (1.2% reduction), Samba 4.15 throughput down 0.9% (download, 647 to 641 MB/s) and 0.1% (upload, 858 to 857 MB/s).
hardware: Documentation experiments: HoneyComb LX2 board, NXP LX2160A 16-core Arm Cortex-A72 up to 2.2 GHz, 64 GB DRAM, Linux 5.10 (the ptrace claim itself states no hardware).
tradeoffs: ARM64 only (Linux, Android, FreeBSD, NetBSD). Needs no kernel support but rewrites code in memory: svc to b has a +-128 MiB branch range, so one trampoline of 28 bytes per svc instruction is instantiated (20812 bytes for 728 svc instructions in the test setup). FreeBSD and NetBSD need procfs mounted at /proc and NetBSD needs PaX mprotect restrictions disabled.
caveats: Category fit is weak: syscall-interception tooling built on instruction rewriting, not an assembler or disassembler, and neither ptrace nor ASC-Hook is GNU as, NASM or MASM. The 1,000x ptrace figure is one README bullet with no method, hardware, kernel or command and no ptrace number exists on any repo page. The ASC-Hook numbers are first-party and say only that the setup is 'exactly same with the experiment mentioned in the section 4.1 in our paper'; the getpid microbenchmark is not in the repository and no compiler or flags are stated (hardware for the Documentation experiments: HoneyComb LX2, NXP LX2160A 16-core Cortex-A72 up to 2.2 GHz, 64 GB, Linux 5.10, glibc 2.31). Results 'reflect the implementation state at the time this document was committed' (Dec 2025); NetBSD support and trampoline-allocation changes landed in Aug 2026. The Middleware 2025 paper (Moroo, Tazaki, Yasukata, pages 195-201) was not opened (dl.acm.org blocked). Same research group as zpoline (ARM64 counterpart, separate code base, not a duplicate). Needs GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.rtld.seal=0 on glibc with memory sealing, procfs on FreeBSD/NetBSD and PaX mprotect disabled on NetBSD. Language inferred from main.c and the Makefile because the repo page shows no language bar.

name: zpoline (x86-64 system call hook by binary rewriting)
baseline: ptrace-based system call interception (README headline); Intel Pin System Call API (reviewer Q&A in Documentation/README.md)
workload: Per-system-call hook overhead on Linux x86-64 with an empty hook function, measured with the getpid benchmark of Section 3.2 of the USENIX ATC 2023 paper (the benchmark program is not in the repository; apps/basic only prints syscall numbers).
claimed_speedup: README: '100 times faster than ptrace.' (no numbers on the page). Documentation/README.md (USENIX ATC 2023 reviews Q&A, May 2023): zpoline hook overhead 41 ns (paper Table 1) against 2629 ns for the Intel Pin 3.27 System Call API (2703 ns per getpid minus 74 ns for the kernel getpid), about 64x (derived from page data); the reviewer-suggested short-jump variant gave 31 ns; the later 0xeb 0x6a 0x90 trampoline (May 2023) gave 10 ns, '4 times faster than the previous version'. Paper abstract (WebSearch snippet only, paper not opened): '28.1~761.0 times lower overhead compared to existing mechanisms which ensure exhaustive hooking'.
tradeoffs: Linux on x86-64 only. Replaces the two-byte syscall/sysenter instructions in loaded code with callq *%rax and plants a nop-sled trampoline at virtual address 0, so /proc/sys/vm/mmap_min_addr must be set to 0 (the README also reports mmap failures under SELinux). Uses the libopcodes disassembler from binutils to find the instructions. Rewritten code pages can no longer be shared between processes (glibc-2.35 has 544 syscall/sysenter instructions across 62 pages). Hook functions must avoid issuing rewritten syscalls or they loop forever. NULL-pointer writes no longer fault by default (mitigations exist).
caveats: Category fit is weak: this is syscall-interception tooling built on instruction rewriting, not an assembler or disassembler, and the baselines (ptrace, Intel Pin) are not GNU as, NASM or MASM. The 100x headline has no table, hardware, kernel version or compiler flags on the README page. The 41 ns, 2629 ns and 10 ns figures come from the repo's Documentation page and quote the paper's Table 1 (paper not opened: usenix.org is not reachable here); the CPU is only called 'our hardware'. The 64x ratio mixes the paper's zpoline run with a Pin run done later for the reviews, possibly on different days. The getpid benchmark program is not in the repository; the author posted it and a PTRACE_SYSCALL-based tracer (compiled with gcc -O3, run with 1000 iterations against 100000 for the zpoline run) in issue #10 in November 2023, and the hook returns a dummy value without entering the kernel; setup time (trampoline, rewriting, dlmopen) is excluded from the overhead. Requires /proc/sys/vm/mmap_min_addr set to 0 (trampoline at virtual address 0, which weakens NULL-dereference protection; SELinux may also need disabling). The code is Apache-2.0 but links binutils libopcodes (GPL-3.0) for disassembly. The last commit is from January 2025.

name: Fadec
baseline: libopcodes, Capstone and Zydis (x86 decoding libraries)
workload: Decoding x86-32 and x86-64 instructions with a lookup-table decoder; a separate x86-64 encoder is included.
claimed_speedup: 'Fadec is significantly faster than libopcodes, Capstone, or Zydis due to the absence of high-level abstractions and the small lookup table' (no numbers); encoder API v2 'about 3x faster than v1' (internal comparison).
stars_or_usage: 235 stars, 33 forks, 432 commits (github.com page, 2026-10-11). Used as a git submodule (deps/fadec) by the TPDE compiler back-end framework (tpde2/tpde .gitmodules, opened). Search results also show copies at android.googlesource.com platform/external/lfi/fadec (tagged android-17.0.0_r1) and a Chromium mirror chromium.googlesource.com/external/github.com/aengelke/fadec, plus forks oleavr/fadec and GenKyoko/fadec (snippet only; googlesource host did not resolve here).
tradeoffs: C library with no dependencies, about 95 KiB with decoder and encoder, usable in freestanding environments. Targets Intel 64 behaviour; AMD-specific differences are not handled. Decoded operand sizes are not always exact for speed.
caveats: No benchmark numbers or comparison harness anywhere: the speed claim over libopcodes, Capstone and Zydis is qualitative, and the only timing tool in the repo (decode-profile.c, added 2026-06-01) measures Fadec alone. Fadec is absent from the public disas-bench candidate lists (athre0z and iximeow forks). The encoder v2 '3x faster than v1' figure is an internal comparison with no baseline and comes at ~3 MiB code size (off by default, -Dwith_encode2=true). README lists known issues: low test coverage, register-uniqueness constraints not enforced (VSIB, AMX, AVX-512 FP16 complex multiply), decoded operand sizes not always exact, AMD64-specific behaviour not handled (Intel 64 semantics only), MPX, HLE, XOP, FMA4 and Xeon Phi unsupported. Baselines are disassembler libraries, not GNU as, NASM or MASM. Notability rests on reuse (TPDE, Android LFI, Chromium mirror) rather than stars. Canonical CI pulls from git.sr.ht/~aengelke/fadec.

baseline: GNU as and the clang (LLVM integrated) assembler
workload: Assembling AT&T x86-64 assembly emitted by GCC, Clang, cproc/QBE and chibicc into relocatable ELF objects (no specific workload given)

compiler_and_flags: Builds with cc -O2 (README build commands); no benchmark flags

Roadmap items still open: simple immediate expressions, self-hosting with chibicc, and testing every opcode with all variants. Hobby project ('written for fun and learning'), 231 stars, not widely referenced.

name: SLOTHY
baseline: unscheduled 'clean' hand-written assembly and prior hand-optimized implementations of the same kernels (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs, FFT, X25519); no compiler baseline stated on the pages opened
workload: Instruction scheduling, register allocation and software pipelining of hand-written Arm AArch64, Armv8.1-M and RISC-V assembly for cryptographic and DSP kernels.
claimed_speedup: README: SLOTHY has been used 'to provide the fastest known implementations of various cryptographic and DSP primitives' (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs for Cortex-A55/A72/M55/M85, FFT for Cortex-M55/M85, X25519 for Cortex-A55); no speedup numbers on any page opened. Related adoption number: the AWS-LC pull request that imported the s2n-bignum X25519 rewrite (partly SLOTHY-generated) reports 12867.1 to 22361.9 ops/sec ('74% speedup') on Graviton 2, but that gain is not attributable to SLOTHY alone.
hardware: Targets Cortex-M55, M85, A55 (supported), A72, Cortex-X/Neoverse-V, Apple M1 (experimental) and XuanTie C908
stars_or_usage: 352 stars; adopted in AWS-LC / s2n-bignum, Arm EndpointAI CMSIS DSP and mlkem-native
tradeoffs: Microarchitecture-specific by design: each output is scheduled for one core model (portability note: code tuned for Cortex-A55 is not tuned for other cores). Solver time is seconds to minutes for under 50 instructions and minutes to hours for up to 150 instructions; larger kernels need heuristics. Python tool using Google OR-Tools.
caveats: The TCHES 2024 paper 'Fast and Clean: Auditable high-performance assembly via constraint solving' (issue 1, pp. 87-132, artifact at artifacts.iacr.org/tches/2024/a6; eprint 2022/1303) is peer-reviewed but could not be opened (tches.iacr.org and eprint unreachable); WebSearch snippets only say the SLOTHY-optimized code matches or beats prior art in all cases, with no cycle counts. The repo ships clean and optimized sources (paper/clean, paper/opt), optimization scripts (paper/scripts) and a Docker artifact; cycle benchmarks live in pqax/pqmx and need Cortex-A55/A72 devices or an MPS3 FPGA board (AN547/AN555), and builds without CYCLES=PMU/PERF stub out cycle counts. The only number in the repo is the tutorial's LLVM-MCA model estimate for a toy Cortex-A55 loop (31 to 21 cycles per iteration), a model output against its own unscheduled input, not a measurement. Adoption is real: s2n-bignum PR #108 (merged 2024-02-15) imported the SLOTHY-generated Lenngren-based X25519 without benchmark numbers; the AWS-LC PR #1469 that reports 12867.1 to 22361.9 ops/sec ('74% speedup', Graviton 2) was closed without merge on 2024-03-06 (the README calls it merged) and mixes the algorithm change with SLOTHY scheduling. CP-SAT is non-deterministic, so re-optimization results vary, especially for the heuristic Cortex-A72 model. SLOTHY is a Python tool that produces assembly; it is not linked into the user's program.

name: Almide
language: Almide (statically typed language compiling to Rust and WebAssembly)
baseline: Ordinary hand-written Rust (Box-linked recursive enum, no arena, rustc 1.96.1 opt-level=3, LTO, 1 codegen unit)
workload: Benchmarks-Game-style programs (binarytrees, treealloc, n-body, spectral-norm, fasta, FFT) on native output; wasm output measured as a ratio to native
claimed_speedup: Native output vs ordinary hand-written Rust on Apple M4 Pro (almide 0.62.0, 2026-09-08, median of 9 interleaved runs): binarytrees d17 134 ms vs 382 ms (0.35x time), d19 581 vs 1826 ms (0.32x); treealloc d20 112 vs 375 ms (0.30x), d21 221 vs 748 ms (0.30x). With the region window turned off (ALMIDE_REGION_OFF=1) the same Almide source is 1.10-1.26x slower than the Rust reference. ubuntu-latest CI runner (2026-10-03, almide 0.66.0 dev): binarytrees 0.581 (d17), treealloc 0.365 (d20). Arithmetic kernels (2026-07-30, rustc 1.96.1): n-body and spectral-norm 1.00x, fasta 1.16x and FFT 1.18x slower than Rust. Wasm leg: README ledger (2026-09-29, embedded wasm host vs native binary, min of 2x5 interleaved) gives wasm/native ratios of 0.67x (mapbuild) to 1.96x (listbuild_append), e.g. treealloc 1.04x, binarytrees 1.07x, nbody 1.10x, fft 1.53x; these ratios are on the README, not on BENCHMARKS.md, whose older dated wasm paragraph still describes FFT (~3,500x) and mandelbrot (~130x) cliffs.
compiler_and_flags: almide --release (emits Rust, cargo release profile opt-level=3 + LTO) vs handwritten Rust built by bench.py with rustc -C opt-level=3 -C lto=yes -C codegen-units=1; median of 9 interleaved runs after warmup; byte-identical stdout verified before timing. rustc 1.96.1 is stated for the 2026-07-30 scoreboard; the 2026-09-08 victory JSON records almide 0.62.0 but no rustc version (README says CI builds with 1.96.0).
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (arm64), almide 0.62.0, 2026-09-08; also an ubuntu-latest CI runner
tradeoffs: Young language optimised for LLM code generation; wins on allocation-heavy rows come from a compiler-proven region (bump-arena) window the ordinary Rust program does not have. Loses on fasta and FFT.
caveats: Off the category baseline: the comparison is native Rust output, not TypeScript/JS in V8 or C++ via Emscripten, and the wasm output is only compared with Almide's own native binary, never with JS/V8 or an Emscripten build. The whole win is one optimization (the region window, a thread-local bump arena rewound once per check(make(d)) tree) against a Rust reference that deliberately pays malloc/free per Box node; a Rust program using an arena (bumpalo/typed-arena, as Benchmarks Game Rust entries do) would close most of the gap (the same document shows a Zig arena at 88 ms vs Almide 72 ms at d16). Two workloads, one mechanism. The ratio is allocator-dependent (0.581 and 0.365 on the ubuntu-latest runner vs 0.35 and 0.30 on macOS). The M4 Pro columns were measured on 0.62.0 and not re-measured. The README's third victory row (fannkuchredux 0.21/0.12 via parallel fan) compares a threaded Almide run with a one-thread Rust reference and should not be cited. Self-reported by the project. [retier] Baseline Rust pays malloc/free per node; a hand-written Rust arena beats Almide (issue #3586); victory JSON hand-assembled without per-run data or rustc version; fannkuchredux README row unsupported by raw files; region arena never returns memory and a wrong region-pure verdict is a silent use-after-rewind
found_via: GitHub: topic webassembly filtered to Rust (updated); README performance section and docs/project/BENCHMARKS.md

verification.notes: Numbers on docs/project/BENCHMARKS.md match the raw JSON in the repo and the harness and Rust references are public, so A stands for the native-vs-Rust claim. Shortcomings to record: off-category baseline (no JS/V8 or Emscripten comparison), win comes only from an arena vs a malloc-per-node Rust reference, allocator-dependent ratio, unequal threaded fannkuchredux row on the README.

name: json-as
baseline: JavaScript built-in JSON.parse / JSON.stringify in V8 (also fast-json-parse and assemblyscript-json)
workload: End-to-end JSON deserialize (including allocating the destination object) and serialize throughput in MB/s on small payloads (19 B to 5.5 kB) and nine standard payloads from the yyjson and nativejson-benchmark corpora, with json-as compiled to Wasm by the AssemblyScript compiler (asc) and run in V8.
claimed_speedup: Deserialize, SWAR mode vs built-in JSON in V8: 1,321 vs 568 MB/s (1.1 kB payload), 5,734 vs 1,295 MB/s (5.5 kB payload), 2,196 vs 168 MB/s (108 B payload), 1,056 vs 401 MB/s (52 B alphabet string). Serialize, SIMD mode vs built-in JSON: 7,775 vs 1,062 MB/s (5.5 kB payload), 3,818 vs 696 MB/s (1.1 kB payload). Library comparison on a 5 KiB GitHub-repo payload (deserialize): json-as struct 5,636 MB/s, native JSON 547 MB/s, fast-json-parse 547 MB/s, assemblyscript-json 32 MB/s. Smallest-gain row: 3D Vector (19 B) deserialize, 356-444 vs 83 MB/s across the three typed modes, while the dynamic JSON.Obj path ties built-in JSON on that row (82 vs 83 MB/s). Numbers read from the chart images overview-deserialize.png, overview-serialize.png and library-deserialize.png on the docs branch (v1.5.0).
tradeoffs: Typed, schema-driven (struct) API: the build-time transform generates a specialised serializer per @json class, so it only competes with JSON.parse when the schema is known up front; dynamic JSON.Obj path is slower. Needs AssemblyScript toolchain and a Wasm host; builds use --noAssert and --uncheckedBehavior always, which removes bounds and assert checks. SIMD mode needs Wasm SIMD support.
caveats: First-party: the benchmark author is the library author. Chart values exist only in images (SVG and PNG on the docs branch, charts/v1.5.0), not in a text table. The JS baseline parses into generic JavaScript objects while json-as parses into typed structs generated at build time, so the work differs. Harness asymmetry: the JS blackbox() in bench/lib/bench.js runs an indirect eval of '%PerformMicrotaskCheckpoint();' on every timed op, while the AS blackbox is a single store/load, which inflates JS per-op time most on the 19-108 byte rows (JS ops there take only about 125-640 ns); the 5.5 kB rows are least affected. Benchmark builds use --noAssert, --uncheckedBehavior always and wasm-opt -tnh/-iit, which drop assertion and trap checks. The JSON.Obj path is lazy by default since v1.5.0 (values parsed on first access, untouched values re-serialized by copying source bytes), so its deserialize and serialize bars (up to 19,968 MB/s) defer work and are not like-for-like; on the 3D Vector row JSON.Obj ties built-in JSON (82 vs 83 MB/s), and the 0 values on the Alphabet and UUIDv4 rows mean no JSON.Obj run, not a loss. In the library chart fast-json-parse wraps JSON.parse, which is why it equals native JSON (547 MB/s). The SIMD mode is slower than SWAR on several deserialize rows (Small Payload 1,089 vs 2,196 MB/s). A key-matching correctness bug (final UTF-16 unit of odd-length keys longer than 4 units not compared) was fixed on 2026-10-04 (PR #223), after the charted run; the fix is in toMemCCheck/toMemCDecl, which only the generated __DESERIALIZE_SLOW fallback uses, and the AS large bench asserts a byte-exact round trip, so the charted fast-path numbers are not capped by it. Charts dated Jul 17 2026 (commit 0bb47d4); main has moved to 1.6.1 since.

name: markdown_yo (Yo-language Markdown renderer, WASM build)
language: Yo (new systems language) compiled to WebAssembly via Emscripten and to native
baseline: markdown-it (JavaScript Markdown parser on Node.js/V8)
workload: Markdown-to-HTML conversion of one synthetic ~1.2 KB block (headings, nested lists, blockquote, code fence, table, links, an image and entities, no raw HTML), repeated to 64 KB, 256 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB (benchmark/generate_samples.js). markdown-it is timed in-process on render() only: median of 10 runs after 3 warmups. Native and WASM are timed as the wall time of a whole child process (startup, file read, then 20 conversions with output discarded under --repeat 20) divided by 20.
claimed_speedup: WASM vs markdown-it: 64 KB 12.9 vs 1.6 ms (0.1x, slower), 256 KB 13.1 vs 6.7 ms (0.5x), 1 MB 13.5 vs 28.8 ms (2.1x), 5 MB 32.6 vs 158.9 ms (4.9x), 20 MB 121.5 vs 722.8 ms (6.0x); native build 4.5x to 7.6x

The Yo compiler version used then was not recorded; .yo-version did not exist, and the pin to Yo 0.2.58 was added on 2026-10-10. name: wasm-i128-div-bench (reciprocal 128-bit division for the Wasm wide-arithmetic proposal)
baseline: Rust u128/i128 division operators lowering to compiler-builtins __udivti3/__umodti3 (compiler-rt libcall) on wasm32
workload: criterion microbenchmarks of 128-bit unsigned/signed divide, remainder and divrem, including a loop-invariant-divisor case, native vs V8 (d8) vs wasmtime (Cranelift), reciprocal (Moeller-Granlund) path vs the builtin operators.
claimed_speedup: Loop-invariant divisor (reciprocal hoisted, 5,000 divrems per call): V8 d8 29.67 us -> 18.24 us (-38.5%), wasmtime 52.51 us -> 13.97 us (-73.4%), native 134.44 us -> 9.73 us (-92.8%). Single divisions: native reciprocal is faster (udivrem128 27.86 ns -> 17.18 ns, -38.3%; -28.5% to -38.3% across the six ops), but on Wasm it is not: V8 +19.6% to +33.4% slower (udivrem128 18.27 ns builtin vs 24.38 ns reciprocal), wasmtime -0.7% to +10.3% (udivrem128 +0.2%).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98.0-nightly (61d7280f3 2026-06-06), release profile opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, profile rustflags -Z mir-opt-level=5 -Z inline-mir=yes -Z cross-crate-inline-threshold=always; native x86_64 built with -C target-cpu=native; wasm32 target features +bulk-memory,+multivalue,+reference-types,+wide-arithmetic with build-std (compiler-builtins rebuilt with the same features); criterion 0.8.2 (300 samples, 3 s measurement); d8 15.1.52; wasmtime 45.0.1
hardware: Intel Core i9-9880H @ 2.30GHz, macOS 15.7.7 x86_64
tradeoffs: Requires the wide-arithmetic Wasm proposal (V8 nightly, wasmtime 45 or later) and Rust nightly with build-std. Repo has no LICENSE file, so the code is reference-only. The README also sketches proposed i64.recip128 / i64.divrem_recip128 instructions.
caveats: Mixed result by design: the reciprocal path wins on Wasm only when the divisor is loop-invariant and the reciprocal is hoisted by hand (the bench calls recip128 once before the loop; the builtin libcall cannot be hoisted); for one-off divisions the builtin is faster on V8 and about equal on wasmtime. Each single-op bench times one fixed seeded operand pair, so it measures one kernel path with warm branch predictors. The loop-invariant workload is narrow: one seeded divisor in (0, 2^127) whose high word equals the dividend's high word up to the low 13 bits and the top bit, so quotients are 0 or small and the reciprocal path's Y > X shortcut can fire. The native -92.8% probably reflects a slow native __udivti3 (likely the hardware 128/64 DIV path on this Coffee Lake laptop CPU; verifier inference): the same builtin compiled to Wasm takes 77.9% less time on the loop under d8 than natively (134.44 us native vs 29.67 us d8). Baseline is Rust's compiler-builtins (__udivti3/__umodti3), not TypeScript/JS or Emscripten C++. Single macOS laptop; research micro-benchmark and proposal sketch (extended wide-arithmetic i64.recip128/i64.divrem_recip128), not a library; no license file, 0 stars. Correctness of the reciprocal loop is checked against native division by a unit test (divrem_with_loop_invariant_divisor_matches_native).

name: wasm-perf (Emscripten Wasm SIMD intrinsics vs JavaScript matrix multiply)
baseline: JavaScript (mul_mats.js) running in Node.js v16.16.0 (V8)
workload: Time to complete 10,000 multiplications of two 64 x 64 matrices, JavaScript vs C compiled to WebAssembly by Emscripten with and without -O3 and -msimd128 and with SIMD intrinsics, plus native GCC rows.
claimed_speedup: README table (first-party, Node.js v16.16.0): mul_mats_intrin-wasm-simd-O3 0.245s vs mul_mats.js 5.768s (-95.8%, about 23.5x, derived from page data); -O3 -msimd128 auto-vectorised 0.278s (-95.2%); -O3 without SIMD 2.012s (-65%); Wasm built without -O3 (emcc default -O0) is slower than JS (6.865s, +19%). The JS baseline computes NaN on uninitialised arrays; in a verifier rerun on Node 22.22.0 (different machine, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz) the repo's JS took 10.342s while an Int32Array version with a local accumulator and Math.imul took 4.583s (2.26x faster), so against idiomatic JS the headline would be roughly 10x, not 23.5x (estimate, cross-machine).
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten 3.1.18 with -O3 and -msimd128 (hand-written SIMD intrinsics in mul_mats_intrin.c); GCC 12.2.0 for the native rows (-O3, -O3 -mavx2); Node.js v16.16.0
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i5-1135G7 @ 2.40GHz, 16 GB RAM, Manjaro Linux kernel 5.19.1
tradeoffs: Needs the WebAssembly SIMD proposal (browser or Node support) and an Emscripten toolchain. The win comes from -O3 plus SIMD, not from Wasm alone.
caveats: Baseline defect: mul_mats.js allocates in_a.arr and in_b.arr with new Array(size) and never fills them (its transpose loop writes to the wrapper objects, not .arr), so the timed loop multiplies undefined*undefined = NaN in holey arrays and the output is never checked; the C/Wasm versions fill inputs with 1 and verify the sum. JS uses doubles while C/Wasm use int32 (wasm_i32x4_mul). Verifier rerun on Node 22.22.0: original 10.342s (sum NaN), filled plain arrays 9.876s, Int32Array 6.660s, Int32Array with local accumulator 4.583s; the uninitialised arrays cost little, but the untyped, store-every-iteration JS understates JS by about 2.3x. The intrinsics kernel had an indexing bug fixed on 2022-09-01 (fa08bf6, loads from &in_a[i] instead of &in_a[i*n+k]); that commit re-measured the two -O3 SIMD rows (0.062s became 0.245s) but not the non-O3 intrinsics row (4.718s), which predates the fix. Non-O3 Wasm rows are emcc -O0 debug builds. Native GCC -O3 is baseline x86-64 (SSE2, no pmulld), so Wasm SIMD beating it is a flags artifact; native -O3 -mavx2 (0.119s) is about 2x faster than the best Wasm row. Single 64x64 int32 matrix-multiply microbenchmark from a 2022 Node 16 / Emscripten 3.1.18 setup; demo repo for a blog post, not a library.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'written in AssemblyScript "times faster" than pure JavaScript implementation benchmark' (github.com result jeromewu/wasm-perf)

name: Kobold

caveats: The headline 1.87x over React is a cross-mode comparison: Kobold is a NON-KEYED implementation (reuses DOM nodes) measured against keyed React 19.2 hooks; the suite keeps keyed and non-keyed results in separate tables and has no non-keyed React entry. Non-keyed DOM reuse explains the 0.31x replace-all-rows ratio; remove-one-row is 1.41x slower than React. Like-for-like, Kobold is only 0.967x Inferno non-keyed's time and 1.033x vanillajs-non-keyed's time (derived from page data), i.e. not faster than hand-written JavaScript. Independent public suite but the CPU model and Chrome flags for the Chrome 154 snapshot are not stated (releases.json labels Chrome 144-146 'macOS' and gives no note for 148-154; the README says the runner was switched to /snap/bin/chromium on Linux in July 2026), so tier B not A. The Wasm bundle is checked in prebuilt ('build-prod is a no-op, the generated javascript is already provided'); it was last rebuilt on 2023-05-26 ('Update kobold to 0.9.1', 'Built'), which is the latest crates.io release, but the repo's master has commits after it (to 2024-05-05). The suite's build-prod-force script calls 'dep:rs' while the script is named 'deps:rs', so the documented rebuild-from-source path is broken. Carries suite note #1139 (does not pass strict CSP). name: @gmod/inflate (wasm libdeflate batch inflate)
language: Rust (libdeflater compiled to WebAssembly) with TypeScript
baseline: pako 3.x inflateRaw (pure JavaScript inflate in V8), called once per block with a chunkSize hint. Both arms skip the 2-byte zlib header and leave adler32 unchecked.
workload: Inflate of the real zlib blocks of four BigWig fixtures (49 to 489 blocks per file), whole block run per call, timed in Node against pako and the platform DecompressionStream; the wasm module was extracted from the bbi-js genome-file parser
claimed_speedup: bbi-js docs/wasm.md (benchmarks/inflate.bench.ts, best of three runs, mean ms): wasm 1.9 ms vs pako 6.0 ms on volvox.bw (49 blocks), 5.4 vs 16.6 ms on cow.bw (125), 31 vs 86 ms on ENCFF826FLP.bw (436), 29 vs 62 ms on variable_step_large.bw (489), i.e. 2.1-3.2x (derived from page data). The doc's own speedup table gives per-fixture ranges of 2.3-3.8x across three runs and summarizes them as '~2.5-3x faster'. The platform DecompressionStream, called once per block, is 4-11x slower than wasm. The inflate-js README's 'roughly 4x faster than pako' is not backed by any table and exceeds the doc's own summary.
compiler_and_flags: Rust crate (libdeflater 1.x with the freestanding feature, so libdeflate's C is built through cc-rs by a wasm-capable clang) built with cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown. The release profile in crate/Cargo.toml sets opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1 and panic=abort. wasm-bindgen runs at the Cargo.lock version, webpack base64-inlines the result, and there is no wasm-opt pass. The Node version is not stated. Baseline pako is ^3.0.1 per bbi-js package.json.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (extracted August 2026 from bbi-js, 9 stars, 567 commits, used in GMOD genome-browser parsers)
tradeoffs: Decompression only (inflateRaw and inflateRawBatch), no compression; wasm inlined as base64 in one bundle (about 65 KB) and instantiated lazily; the speedup depends on batching many blocks in one JS-wasm crossing.
caveats: The benchmark lives in the sibling repo bbi-js (benchmarks/inflate.bench.ts, MIT, same author) and runs bbi-js's copy of the crate. Its inflate_raw_batch matches inflate-js's except for the bounds and length checks inflate-js added. inflate-js has no benchmark of its own; it is a 5-commit extraction (v1.0.0, August 2026). The harness asserts byte-identical output before timing, and both arms skip the zlib header and the adler32 check, so the comparison does equal work. CPU, Node version and run count beyond 'three runs on one machine' are not stated, and the doc asks readers to 'treat them as an order of magnitude'. The README's '4x' overstates the doc's 2.5-3x summary. The win is inflate in isolation: an older end-to-end whole-genome parseBigWig comparison was only about 5% apart. Raw deflate has no checksum, so corrupt but legal streams decode silently.
found_via: npm registry search 'keywords:wasm fast' (@gmod/inflate: 'Fast DEFLATE decompression via wasm libdeflate'), then the GitHub README and GMOD/bbi-js docs/wasm.md

verification.tier_reason: bbi-js docs/wasm.md prints wasm-vs-pako timings from the public harness benchmarks/inflate.bench.ts, and the Rust release profile is public in crate/Cargo.toml, but neither the CPU model nor the Node version is stated, and the numbers are first-party (same author), so the tier stays C.
verification.notes: Real entry with a fair, byte-checked harness. Shortcomings to record: the README's 4x claim exceeds the bbi-js doc's 2.5-3x (derived 2.1-3.2x); CPU and Node version are unstated; the benchmark is in bbi-js, not in inflate-js; and the end-to-end gain is about 5%. name: as-proto
baseline: protobuf.js (reflect and static) and google-protobuf in Node.js/V8; also JSON string/buffer
workload: ts-proto's encode/decode/combined benchmark (bench/index.cjs, benchmark.js suite) on one small Test message (string, uint32, nested int32/int64/enum/sint32, repeated bool, double, float), with an as-proto case added that runs inside the wasm module
claimed_speedup: Encoding: as-proto 1,295,297 ops/sec vs protobuf.js (static) 589,866 and (reflect) 589,073 (about 2.2x); combined encode+decode: 548,291 vs 439,242 and 421,963 ops/sec (about 1.3x); decoding is slower: 889,283 vs protobuf.js 1,375,425 and 1,308,310 ops/sec
compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript asc ^0.24.1 with optimizeLevel 3, shrinkLevel 0, converge, noAssert, incremental runtime, ESM bindings (bench/data/assembly/asconfig.json); protobufjs ^6.11.2 and benchmark ^2.1.4 (package.json); Node.js version not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7 2.2 GHz (MacBook Pro 2015); Node.js version not stated
tradeoffs: Generates AssemblyScript message classes from .proto files; no gRPC definitions. Decoding is slower than protobuf.js on the author's run. AssemblyScript's small GC is the usual limit on allocation-heavy paths.
caveats: Mixed result: wins encoding (about 2.2x) and the combined case (about 1.3x), loses decoding by about 1.5x (889,283 vs 1,375,425 ops/sec for protobuf.js static); the README blames AssemblyScript's simple GC. The as-proto cases encode and decode a message pre-built inside wasm and discard the result, so they include no JS-to-wasm marshalling, while protobuf.js and google-protobuf encode a JS object; this matches as-proto's use from AssemblyScript code but is not a like-for-like JS API comparison. The payloads differ slightly: the AS message uses Enum.ONE (0, a proto3 default that is not written to the wire) and int64 682671883329470464, while bench.json uses enum 1 and int64 649545084044315. The README table has separate protobuf.js reflect and static rows, but the current bench/index.cjs runs only one protobuf.js (static) case, so the published numbers come from an earlier version of the script. Hardware is a 2015 laptop with no CPU model and no Node.js version; first-party only.
