name: as-string-sink
baseline: JavaScript string concatenation (String += in V8, which uses ropes) and naive String += in AssemblyScript
workload: Append n alternating 4-character literals ('foo|', '|boo') for n = 100, 50,000 and 200,000 and return the final length; one timed call per size with performance.now after 150 warm-up calls at n = 100 (benchmark/run.js, benchmark/index.ts)
claimed_speedup: 200,000 strings: JS String += 11.93 ms, AS String += 7622.72 ms, StringSink AS 2.88 ms (about 4.1x over JS, derived from page data; README prints ~2600x over AS +=); 50,000 strings: JS 3.34 ms, AS 509.54 ms, StringSink 0.73 ms (about 4.6x over JS, derived from page data); 100 strings: JS 0.013 ms, AS 0.014 ms, StringSink 0.0042 ms (README prints 3x). The README headline 'up to 6 times faster than JS concat' and 'up to 4000 times faster than naive concatenation' exceed every row of its own table.
compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript asc (devDependency ^0.27.0) -O3 --noAssert (package.json build:bench); Node.js version not stated
tradeoffs: Buffer-based string builder with its own write/toString API; only helps accumulation patterns.
caveats: Tiny first-party microbenchmark: no hardware, CPU model or Node.js version stated, and each figure is a single timed call (warm-up only at n = 100), so noise is unquantified. At 100 strings StringSink is about 3x faster than both plain concatenations (0.0042 vs 0.013 and 0.014 ms), but at that size all three are microseconds. The JS baseline returns res.length without flattening V8's rope while StringSink's toString() builds a flat string, which if anything favours JS. The headline 4000x is against AssemblyScript's own naive String +=, which copies the whole string on every append (quadratic), not against JS; the table's best is about 2,650x, and the 'up to 6x over JS' headline is not shown (best row about 4.6x, derived from page data).

baseline: JavaScript image filter in the browser; also Rust compiled to WASM ('Rust Native' row)
workload: Browser demo (examples/wasm_filter/www/index.html): one call of an RGBA filter (invert, grayscale or brightness; the README table does not say which) on a user-uploaded 2.1 MB image, timed with performance.now around a single call with no warm-up or repetition; the wasm rows include wasm-bindgen copy-in and copy-out of the Vec<u8>, the JS row allocates a new Uint8Array
claimed_speedup: README table (2.1 MB image, filter not named): AutoZig (Zig SIMD) 0.80 ms (2631.84 MB/s), Rust 2.50 ms (842.19 MB/s, '3.13x slower'), JavaScript 3.80 ms (554.07 MB/s, '4.75x slower'); headline '3-5x faster than pure JavaScript, 3x faster than Rust native'. Each figure is one click timed with performance.now, quantized to 0.1 ms. The example README (examples/wasm_filter/README.md) carries a different table for a 1920x1080 8.3 MB image (Zig WASM ~5 ms, pure JS ~25 ms, 'Canvas API' ~15 ms for invert) with a Canvas API row that has no implementation in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: Zig -O ReleaseFast -mcpu=mvp+simd128 -fno-stack-protector, target wasm32-freestanding (engine/src/zig_compiler.rs; the example README still says ReleaseSmall); Rust wasm32-unknown-unknown with opt-level "s", lto = true and -C target-feature=+simd128 (examples/wasm_filter/Cargo.toml, .cargo/config.toml), built with wasm-pack --target web; browser and JS engine not stated
tradeoffs: Combines Rust (memory and wasm-bindgen glue) with Zig compute kernels in one .wasm; needs the Zig toolchain at build time.
caveats: Single-sample browser timings (one click, no warm-up, 0.1 ms timer granularity); browser, hardware and which filter was timed are not stated. The Zig SIMD invert_colors_raw subtracts every byte from 255, including alpha, while the Rust and JS versions and the example README ('Alpha channel unchanged') leave alpha intact, so the timed fast path produces different output (opaque pixels become transparent); the SIMD brightness path likewise changes alpha for negative deltas. A correct masked SIMD version would cost about the same, so the bug does not obviously create the speedup, but the row does not time the specified filter. The 'Rust native' baseline is a bounds-checked scalar step_by(4) loop built at opt-level "s" (size), so the 3x over Rust measures hand-written SIMD128 against a size-optimized scalar loop, not Zig against Rust; the grayscale filter is scalar in Zig too. The example README's second table (8.3 MB, ~5 vs ~25 ms, Canvas API row) has no matching code and looks unmeasured. Trivially vectorizable byte filter; crate autozig 0.1.2 with 80 downloads (crates.io, 14 recent); 5 stars; first-party only.

name: BoltFFI
baseline: wasm-bindgen (Rust-to-JavaScript glue); on native targets UniFFI
workload: Benchmark.js microbenchmarks in benchmarks/harnesses/wasm-bench/bench.mjs over the same examples/demo Rust crate exported by BoltFFI and by wasm-bindgen (Node.js): scalar calls, strings, primitive vectors, generating 100/1k/10k records (locations, trades, particles; wasm-bindgen returns arrays of opaque #[wasm_bindgen] class handles that the loop never frees, BoltFFI returns plain JS objects decoded from a wire buffer), passing records from JS to Rust, classes, enums, callbacks and async.
claimed_speedup: README static snapshot (v0.24.0, Apple M3, Benchmark.js mean): 1k particles 29,886 vs 13,532,530 ns (453x); 100 particles 3,117 vs 748,287 ns (240x); 1k locations 21,931 vs 4,037,879 ns (184x); 1k trades 42,015 vs 5,781,767 ns (138x); 100 locations 2,199 vs 283,753 ns (129x); same snapshot shows ties at 2 ns on scalar calls, ties on primitive vectors, 1.6-3.6x on strings. Dashboard (stated source of truth, boltffi/benchmarks-dashboard public/data/archive, five wasm runs 2026-04-16 to 2026-06-25) shows much smaller wins: generate_*_1k/10k means 18-115x, medians 5.9-35x (e.g. generate_particles_1k on Apple M3 Max 2026-06-05: median 29,245 vs 276,455 ns, 9.5x, derived from page data; mean 76x); host-to-Rust record passing 1.1-1.9x; echo_string_1k 1.2-2.7x; and BoltFFI slower on scalar calls in every run (noop 112-247 ns vs 2-8 ns, about 20-50x slower), on primitive vectors (0.27-1.0x), classes (counter_increment_single_threaded 0.51-0.59x in May-June runs), find_even_100 (0.09x) and sum_user_scores (0.71x). README headline also claims up to 1,000x vs UniFFI on Swift (noop <1 ns vs 1,416 ns).
compiler_and_flags: benchmarks/harnesses/wasm-bench/run-bench.sh: BoltFFI side 'boltffi pack wasm --release' with the benchmark overlay; wasm-bindgen side 'cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --features wasm-bench' then 'wasm-bindgen --target nodejs' (CLI version from cargo metadata); Benchmark.js 2.1.4 means. README snapshot states no versions; dashboard runs record rustc 1.95.0 (2026-04-14) or 1.94.0-nightly, Node v20.2.0 to v24.17.0, wasm-bindgen 0.2.108 (2026-04-16 run), no wasm-opt.
hardware: README snapshot: Apple M3 (WASM and Swift), Apple M4 Max (JVM); dashboard runs: Apple M3 Max (14 cores, macOS 15.7.3, local) and Apple M1 (Virtual) GitHub Actions macOS runners (3 cores)
stars_or_usage: 895 stars, 54 forks, 2,244 commits; no GitHub releases listed on the repo page
tradeoffs: Own code generator and annotations (#[data], #[export]); WASM uses a wire buffer format that avoids per-field allocation; also targets Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, Python and C. wasm-bindgen is more general (documented by BoltFFI itself as materialising every struct as a JS object).
caveats: First-party microbenchmarks of trivial constructors and sums that isolate FFI overhead, so the ratios are boundary cost, not application speed. The 453x headline is a mean from a static README snapshot; the dashboard named as source of truth never reproduces it: wasm-bindgen generate_* samples are few (7-29) with maxima up to 327 ms against medians of 0.23-6.0 ms, consistent with GC/FinalizationRegistry pauses from never-freed class handles, so mean ratios overstate the median gap (5.9-35x). BoltFFI is about 20-50x slower than wasm-bindgen on scalar calls in every dashboard run (noop 112-247 ns vs 2-8 ns), contradicting the README snapshot's 2 ns tie, and slower on primitive vectors, stateful classes and find_even. JVM snapshot shows uniffi-bindgen-java (FFM) faster than BoltFFI on inc_u64, echo_string_small and find_even. Baseline is wasm-bindgen's default class-handle representation, not serde-wasm-bindgen or tsify.

name: calaminejs (calamine spreadsheet reader in WebAssembly)
language: Rust (calamine compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-pack) with TypeScript
baseline: SheetJS xlsx 0.18.5 (pure JavaScript spreadsheet parser in V8)
workload: Reading synthetic .xlsx fixtures generated by bench/make-fixtures.mjs, which writes them with SheetJS: a type mix of strings, numbers, dates, booleans and holes. Sizes are small 500x10 (5k cells), medium 20,000x20 (400k cells) and large 150,000x12 (1.8M cells, 23 MB). Each run converts the first sheet to CSV or cell arrays and reports the median of 20, 5 and 3 iterations respectively, on Node 22.18.
claimed_speedup: README table (bench/bench.mjs; every ratio is against SheetJS read + sheet_to_json). Large 1.8M-cell 23 MB sheet: toCsv 865 ms (5.3x), readCells values 981 ms (4.7x) and readCells tagged 1.53 s (3.0x) vs SheetJS sheet_to_json 4.61 s (sheet_to_csv 4.57 s). Medium 400k cells: toCsv 188 ms and readCells values 190 ms vs sheet_to_json 786 ms (4.2x and 4.1x, derived from page data). Small 5k cells: toCsv 2 ms vs sheet_to_csv 8 ms (4x, derived from page data) and readCells values 3 ms vs sheet_to_json 8 ms (2.7x, derived from page data). docs/comparison.md (one subprocess per library, bench/compare/run.mjs) gives readCellsParsed ~1.0 s vs SheetJS read + sheet_to_json ~4.0 s on the large file, about 4x.
compiler_and_flags: wasm-pack build --release --target web (scripts/build.mjs). The Cargo release profile sets opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1 and panic=abort. Rust is pinned in rust-toolchain.toml, and wasm-opt comes from binaryen 131+. Runs used Node 22.18, with Bun 1.3.5 also run. The README table comes from bench/bench.mjs (bun run bench), the comparison.md cost table from bench/compare/run.mjs.
hardware: macOS arm64 (CPU model not stated); comparison.md run dated 2026-08-10
tradeoffs: Read-only (no writing, styling or formula evaluation); no CSV input; 370 KB gzipped (720 KB raw) wasm artifact; the JS-wasm boundary adds 35-55% on top of the 634 ms parse for the large file; async wasm load needed in browsers (await ready()).
caveats: Author-run benchmark. The scripts are public, but the fixtures are generated (not committed) by bench/make-fixtures.mjs, and the CPU model is not stated. bench/bench.mjs runs every strategy in one process in sequence, wasm first. The large file gets only 3 iterations (median, first iteration included), and every speedup divides by SheetJS sheet_to_json, even for the CSV rows. The README says 'up to 5x' while the large-file tables show 3.0-5.3x, and comparison.md itself says 'about 4x'. The SheetJS baseline is the npm-frozen xlsx 0.18.5, not the maintained CDN releases. comparison.md is candid that SheetJS has wider format coverage and maturity, and that the speed comes partly from doing less (read-only, four formats). This is an unofficial binding of tafia/calamine, so the parsing speed is calamine's. The repo has 27 commits, at version 0.1.0 with one maintainer, and wasm32 caps it at 4 GB.

name: cjs-module-lexer (C lexer compiled to WebAssembly)
language: C compiled to WebAssembly (wasi-sdk and Binaryen), with a JavaScript build
baseline: the same lexer's pure JavaScript build (lexer.js) running in V8/Node.js
workload: Lexing 3,635 KiB of real-world JavaScript samples (angular, d3, magic-string, rollup and their minified forms) to detect CommonJS named exports: cold run over all samples and warm runs averaged over 25
claimed_speedup: Cold run, all samples: JS build 299 ms vs Wasm build 43 ms (6.95x, derived from page data); warm run, all samples: 40.28 ms vs 27.76 ms (1.45x, README says about 1.5x faster); angular.js warm 13.96 vs 9.32 ms; module load time 4 ms (JS) vs 10 ms (Wasm)
compiler_and_flags: wasi-sdk 21.0 clang -target wasm32-unknown-wasi -Oz (build/Makefile), then binaryen 116 wasm-opt -Oz; versions are pinned in build/wasm.js and built via docker or npm run build-wasm-local. The build optimises for size, not speed. The JS build is lexer.js. The Node version is not stated; the README numbers date from November 2020, the Node 14 era.
stars_or_usage: 262 stars; used by Node.js ESM-CommonJS interop
tradeoffs: Wasm build needs initSync() or await init() (ESM only; browsers should await init()); wasm instantiation adds about 6 ms of module load; detection patterns are frozen by design; both builds are lexers, not parsers, so the work per byte is small.
caveats: First-party README numbers with no CPU or Node version, run with npm run bench (bench/index.mjs). git blame dates the benchmark block to the 2020-11-02 commit d38263b and the '1.5x faster' line to 2020-09-27. They predate the wasi-sdk/binaryen builder change (2024) and the September-October 2026 perf commits (#122, #123, #124, #131), so they are about six years stale. The harness rounds every timed parse to whole milliseconds (Math.round per call) before averaging, so per-file warm figures under a few ms (magic-string 0.64/0.16/0 ms) are rounding artifacts and the all-samples sums carry up to about 4 ms of rounding per run. The baseline is the project's own JavaScript build, not a third-party package. The warm-run advantage is only 1.45x; the 6.95x cold-run gap reflects JIT warm-up of the JS build that the Wasm build skips. Wasm module load is slower (10 ms vs 4 ms).

name: JavaScript-vs-WebAssembly-Comparative-Analysis (Rust wasm matrix multiply)
baseline: JavaScript matrix multiplication (same naive i-k-j loop over Float32Array, TypeScript served by the Vite dev server) in Chromium via Playwright; the matrix sweeps were run only in Chromium (npm scripts exist only for sweep:*-matrix:chromium); Firefox scripts exist only for the particle demo
workload: n x n matrix multiplication (64 to 512) and a particle-physics rendering demo, written in parallel in JavaScript and Rust (wasm-pack, wasm-bindgen, web target), automated with Playwright.
claimed_speedup: Matrix multiply, median of 20 reps per size, Chromium, JS vs WASM in ms: 64x64 0.50 vs 0.50 (1.00x), 128x128 3.45 vs 2.20 (1.57x), 256x256 28.85 vs 15.65 (1.84x), 512x512 218.05 vs 136.10 (1.60x). On means (matrix_js_vs_wasm.csv) the speedups are 1.49x, 1.69x, 1.46x and 1.50x. P95 in WASM is 57-61% lower at n<=128 but 28-31% higher at n>=256. Particle physics step 1.7-2.8x faster in WASM, but frame rate is equal (about 60 FPS, GPU bound; frame-time ratio 1.01-1.10x).
compiler_and_flags: wasm-pack build --target web --release (QUICKSTART asks for Rust >= 1.90.0, wasm-pack >= 0.13.1); no [profile.release] overrides in wasm-kernels/Cargo.toml or kernels/matrix/Cargo.toml, so Cargo release defaults (opt-level 3) plus wasm-pack's default wasm-opt pass; no simd128 target feature. JS side is TypeScript served unminified by the Vite 5 dev server; Playwright ^1.56 bundled Chromium, version not stated.
tradeoffs: Needs a Rust toolchain and wasm-pack build step; large-matrix tail latency was worse in WASM (cache pressure per the author); GPU-bound workloads show no gain.
caveats: Harness bug: apps/wasm-matrix/src/wasm-bridge.ts passes the JS Float32Array to the Rust set_a/set_b(ptr: *const f32, len) exports via a 'buf as any as number' cast, so the pointer coerces to 0 and Rust copies len floats from linear-memory address 0 (UB on a null pointer in Rust) instead of the seeded matrices; the WASM side therefore multiplies different (probably mostly zero) data and its result is never compared with the JS result (only C[0] is read as a 'checksum'). The loop does the same n^3 scalar f32 multiply-adds, so timing is probably still representative, but the 'identical computation' claim does not hold. Other caveats: academic single-commit repo (master's thesis, Nov 2025); no licence (README says code is for academic and educational purposes), so reference only; CPU, OS and browser versions not given and docs/ENV.md is linked but missing; raw per-run results are gitignored, only aggregated CSV/MD are committed; each page load times 20 reps with no warm-up separation (JIT tier-up included); the 64x64 row sits at the 0.1 ms timer granularity; README figures are medians, means give 1.46-1.69x; naive O(n^3) kernel only, no SIMD on either side.

name: md5-wasm (hand-written WebAssembly MD5)
language: WebAssembly text format (.wat) with JavaScript wrapper
baseline: md5 npm package (pure JavaScript MD5, 'the most popular md5 utility')
workload: MD5 of files from 0.2 MB to 37 MB on a low-powered Ubuntu production server with NodeJS v10.18.1, elapsed ms and MB/s per size
claimed_speedup: README: '30x faster than the most popular md5 utility' (md5 npm). Table (Node v10.18.1, Ubuntu): 37 MB 38,500 ms vs 990 ms (0.96 vs 37 MB/s), about 39x (derived from page data); 24 MB 23,600 vs 700 ms; 12 MB 12,400 vs 490 ms; 8 MB 7,600 vs 400 ms; 4 MB 4,000 vs 330 ms; 2 MB 2,000 vs 240 ms; 1 MB 1,000 vs 170 ms; 0.5 MB 520 vs 360 ms; 0.3 MB 390 vs 300 ms; 0.2 MB 260 vs 90 ms
compiler_and_flags: hand-written WAT (four-logics-syntax.wat) assembled to wasm; NodeJS v10.18.1 on Ubuntu; no benchmark script found in the visible file list
tradeoffs: Asynchronous (Promise) API only, no synchronous version; about 150 ms WebAssembly instantiation cost on the author's server; takes bytes not strings, so strings must be converted first; wasm is used only above a size threshold.
caveats: First-party table from an unnamed 'slow production server', Node v10.18.1 (2019-era V8), no CPU model and no public benchmark script. The baseline md5 npm package runs at about 1 MB/s and is not a tuned JavaScript MD5; Node's built-in crypto.createHash('md5') (native OpenSSL), the obvious server-side incumbent, is not compared. In the current md5-wasm.js only inputs larger than 1,048,576 bytes (bounder) go to WebAssembly; smaller inputs use the bundled pure-JS MD5, so the 0.2-1 MB rows compare two JavaScript implementations, and the WASM path instantiates a new module on every call (about 150 ms per the README) and finishes the tail in JS. The README itself expected 3-5x and attributes the larger gap to number-format conversions in the md5 package. Code dates from 2020-2021; the 2026-04-23 commit ('Fighting with git') is housekeeping. [retier] Byte/word threshold mismatch means the 0.2-2 MB rows ran no WebAssembly and larger inputs finish in JS; synchronous despite the 'non-blocking' claim; module recompiled per call

name: MoonBit
baseline: Plain JavaScript in Node v22.0.0 (V8): an idiomatic Array flatMap/filter/map/reduce chain and the same chain on JS Iterator Helpers, plus the json5 npm library's parse; vendor snippets also compare wasm output against Rust and Go compiled to WebAssembly
workload: MoonBit JS-backend output vs plain JS in Node v22.0.0 (tinybench, warmup then run): bench_iter runs a flat_map/filter/map/map/filter/fold pipeline over a JSON class/member dataset; bench_json5 parses data/data.json5 with MoonBit core's json5 package (compiled to JS) versus json5.parse from npm. Precompiled MoonBit JS is committed in the repo (April 2024).
claimed_speedup: benchmark-202404 README (Node v22.0.0, MBP 2023 Apple M2 Max): iter 2,953,032 ops/s MoonBit vs 383,701 Plain JS (7.7x, derived from page data), 117,733 JS Iterator Helpers (25.1x, derived from page data; the source of the vendor's 'up to 25x faster than native JS' headline) and 155,935 Kotlin/JS; json5 22,908 ops/s MoonbitJson5.parse vs 2,887 json5.parse (7.9x, derived from page data). Snippet only, not checked: fib(46) run ten million times as wasm, MoonBit 177.9 ms vs Rust 160.8 ms vs Go 6357.8 ms (slower than Rust); 626 packages compiled in 1.06 s.
compiler_and_flags: moon build --target js (release output under target/js/release, per bench_iter/package.json and bench_json5/package.json); MoonBit compiler version not stated; JS baselines run as-is on Node v22.0.0
hardware: MacBook Pro 2023, Apple M2 Max
tradeoffs: Wasm-first language with its own toolchain (moon build system); the core library is Apache-2.0 and the repo page does not state whether the compiler source is open. Young ecosystem.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (moonbit-community, April 2024, MoonBit pre-1.0) and runs MoonBit's JS backend, not its wasm backend. The iter baseline is an eager Array chain that allocates an intermediate array per stage while MoonBit's Iter is a fused push-style pipeline; no hand-written JS loop baseline is included, so the 7.7x/25x figures measure iteration strategy more than language. The json5 row compares two different parser implementations (MoonBit's port returns MoonBit JsonValue with a persistent map, json5 builds JS objects), and the harness discards the return value without checking that parse returned Ok; a zenn.dev reviewer (snippet only) attributes the json5 gain to char-code handling that hand-written JS could copy. MoonBit compiler version not stated. The fib(46) and compile-time numbers are snippet-only relays of vendor posts (moonbitlang.com and thenewstack.io unreachable) and show MoonBit slower than Rust. Licensing: moonbitlang/core is Apache-2.0, but the compiler (moonbitlang/moonbit-compiler) is under the MoonBit Public License, a non-OSI 'relaxed SSPL' that allows modification only for non-commercial use, and its wasm backend is not open-sourced; compiled artifacts may be licensed freely.

name: Pyodide (NumPy inv in WebAssembly vs math.js)
baseline: math.js (JavaScript) in Chrome and Safari
workload: Matrix inverse inv(rand(200,200)): numpy running in Pyodide (CPython and NumPy compiled to WebAssembly) in the browser vs math.js in Chrome and Safari, with native Python 3.10 numpy and Octave as references.
claimed_speedup: numpy in Pyodide 0.024 s vs math.js in Chrome 0.475 s (about 20x faster, derived from page data) and Safari 2.403 s; native numpy 0.009 s, Octave 0.005 s.
tradeoffs: Large download and startup cost for the Python runtime and NumPy (not measured in this comparison); results depend on browser Wasm engine.
caveats: There is one informal timing table from a math.js collaborator (dvd101x, 2023-02-11) in mathjs discussion #2744. It states no machine, OS, browser version, Pyodide version or run count. The poster calls it 'only a quick comparison' and notes that math.js's flexibility adds overhead. Each timed expression includes random-matrix generation (math.random / np.random.rand) as well as the inverse. The win comes from NumPy's compiled LAPACK routines running as WebAssembly against math.js's generic pure-JS matrix code, so it compares implementations more than languages. Native numpy is still about 2.7x faster than numpy in Pyodide (derived from page data). Load and warm-up time are not included. Pyodide publishes no such benchmark; its repo has a benchmark/ directory but no README figures. Fit with assemblyscript-and-wasm-langs is loose: Pyodide is CPython plus scientific packages compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): josdejong/mathjs discussion #2744 (surfaced by WebSearch for AssemblyScript pure-JS speedup claims)

name: TensorFlow.js WebAssembly backend (tfjs-backend-wasm)
baseline: TensorFlow.js plain JavaScript CPU backend in V8 (Chrome); also compared with the WebGL backend
workload: MobileNet V2 (3.48M params, ~300M multiply-adds) and Face Detector (0.1M params, ~20M multiply-adds) inference time in ms, averaged over 200 runs, on the tfjs-benchmarks.web.app local-benchmark page (Chrome 79.0) plus one Node v14 row; backends Plain JS (CPU), WebGL, WASM, WASM + SIMD, WASM + SIMD + threads
claimed_speedup: README prose: WASM is ~3X-11.5X faster than the plain-JS CPU backend on MobileNet V2 and ~8.2-19.8X faster on Face Detector. Table rows: MobileNet V2 on a ThinkPad X1 Gen6 (Linux) 122.7 ms WASM vs 1489.4 ms plain JS (12.1x, derived from page data, slightly above the prose's 11.5x), WASM + SIMD 34.6 ms and WASM + SIMD + threads 12.4 ms (120x vs plain JS, derived from page data); iPhone XS 140 vs 426.4 ms (3.0x, derived). Face Detector on desktop Linux 12.6 ms vs 249.5 ms (19.8x, derived); iPhone XS 21.4 vs 176.9 ms (8.3x, derived). WebGL is faster than WASM on MobileNet V2 on every device (for example ThinkPad 44.8 ms vs 122.7 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README beyond: built with the Bazel Emscripten toolchain; wraps the XNNPACK library; separate plain, simd, and threaded-simd binaries
hardware: iPhone X, iPhone XS, Pixel 4, ThinkPad X1 Gen6 (Linux), desktop Windows, desktop Linux, MacBook Pro 15 2019, plus a Node v14 on MacBook Pro row; CPU models not stated; Chrome 79.0

WebAssembly SIMD was not on by default in Chrome 79 (it shipped by default in Chrome 91), and the README does not say how the SIMD columns were run. The baseline is the project's own plain-JS CPU backend, a reference backend rather than a tuned JS implementation. The WebGL backend beats WASM on MobileNet V2 on every listed device, and the README's 5.3-7.7X 'slower than WebGL' range does not match all rows (Pixel 4 2.4x, ThinkPad 2.7x, derived). The speed comes from XNNPACK kernels compiled with Emscripten; XNNPACK is a wave-8 incumbent baseline. Threads need cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP) since Chrome 92, or the backend falls back to SIMD-only. The last commit to tfjs-backend-wasm is 2024-04-12; the monorepo's last commit is 2026-04-06 (a CI chore). The benchmark harness is public in e2e/benchmarks/local-benchmark.

name: tinymt-wasm-typescript-benchmark (minimal AssemblyScript TinyMT32)
baseline: TypeScript TinyMT32 running in V8 (Node 24.18.0) and C++ TinyMT32 compiled with Emscripten and embind
workload: TinyMT 32-bit pseudo random generator producing 10 to 10,000 integers or floats per call, four implementations (minimal AssemblyScript, AssemblyScript with arrays, C++ via Emscripten, TypeScript), run with vitest bench on Node 24.18.0; also output size.
claimed_speedup: Ints x10: AssemblyScript 15,295,751 hz vs C++/Emscripten 14,218,306 vs TypeScript 12,235,627 (1.25x TypeScript, 1.08x C++, derived from page data). Ints x10,000: 21,602 vs 19,316 vs 15,175 hz (1.42x TypeScript, 1.12x C++, derived). Floats x10,000: AssemblyScript 20,544 hz vs C++ 17,688 vs TypeScript 235 hz (about 87x TypeScript, per the README). Size: minimal AssemblyScript 1,260 bytes (wasm plus JS glue) vs C++ 36,445 vs TypeScript 3,568.
compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript via asc ^0.28.20 with --optimizeLevel 3 --shrinkLevel 2 -b esm --enable simd --enable stringref --enable relaxed-simd --noAssert --converge (the Makefile's separate wasm-opt -O3 rule applies only to hand-written .wat files such as the unused main.wat demo, not to the asc output); C++ via em++ -O3 -Oz -lembind -std=c++20 (the later -Oz wins, so a size-optimised build); vitest bench on Node 24.18.0, TypeScript ~6.0.2; native comparison rows from clang++ -O3 -Oz -flto=thin with nanobench
tradeoffs: Fastest build uses only i32/u32 locals (the 128-bit state is unrolled into four variables, no arrays or strings); the same AssemblyScript with Array or StaticArray is 4-5x slower than TypeScript (2.7M hz vs 12.2M hz for ints x10) and 3.5-6x larger, so the win needs hand-restricted code. Native C++ is 2-4x faster than every Wasm build.
caveats: Single-author benchmark repo with no stated CPU or OS; no licence file, so code is reference only. Float comparison is inflated because the TypeScript temperConv allocates an ArrayBuffer, a Uint8Array and a DataView on every call (the author says so; a shared typed-array view would remove the allocation), where Wasm has a single reinterpret instruction. The C++ contender is size-optimised (-Oz overrides -O3) and every call goes through an embind-generated JS invoker, while the AssemblyScript exports are called directly, so the 1.08-1.12x AssemblyScript-over-C++ margin probably includes call-boundary overhead rather than codegen. The integer comparison is the fairer one (1.25-1.42x over TypeScript). Native x86 C++ is 2.4-3.4x faster than the best Wasm row on the same page. The README's native table at x10,000 lists 19,315.69 hz for AssemblyScript, which is the C++/Emscripten number (copy error). Evidence for AssemblyScript (already catalogued) rather than a library of its own.

name: ultrachess (Rust chess library compiled to WebAssembly)
baseline: chess.js (pure JavaScript chess library in V8/Node)
workload: Startpos perft depth 6 (119,060,324 nodes) through the WASM boundary via Chess.create() and chess.perft(6), plus geomean over six standard perft positions
claimed_speedup: WASM startpos d6 on Node 25.7.0: 353.7 ms, 336.7 Mnps; on Bun 1.3.10: 204.9 ms, 581.0 Mnps. chess.js is listed at 5-7 Mnps (cited from upstream, Node 22), so the README claims about 55x chess.js on Node and about 95x on Bun (about 48-67x on Node and 83-116x on Bun if computed from the 5-7 Mnps range, derived from page data); native Rust is about 140x chess.js
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.95.0, cargo --release with LTO fat and codegen-units 1, no SIMD intrinsics; WASM perft via node rust/bench/wasm-perft.mjs --deep --trials 3 (Node 25.7.0, Bun 1.3.10)
hardware: Apple M4 Max (arm64, macOS 26.4.1), single-threaded, min of N trials
tradeoffs: WASM path reaches only 0.40x (Node) to 0.70x (Bun) of native Rust speed; 45 KB brotli WASM plus about 10 KB TypeScript shim; async Chess.create() initialisation; no SIMD movegen because std::simd is not portable to WASM.
caveats: The chess.js (5-7 Mnps, 'Node 22') and chessops (2-3 Mnps) figures are cited without a source link and were never run in the project's harness, although chess.js is already a devDependency (used for differential fuzzing); the chess.js README has no perft numbers. The 55x/95x ratios are therefore cross-run comparisons on unknown hardware. BENCH.md caveat 6: ultrachess perft bulk-counts at depth 1 (popcount of target bitboards instead of materialising moves), while chess.js perft makes and unmakes every leaf move, so perft overstates the gap for real move-by-move use. Perft is a move-generation microbenchmark and says nothing about PGN/SAN parsing or full-library workloads. Single machine (Apple M4 Max), min of 3 trials. Young repo (43 commits, all in April 2026; latest 2026-04-18).

name: VectorJSON
language: Zig (simdjson port compiled to WebAssembly SIMD) with TypeScript
baseline: Stock streaming/partial JSON parsers in the Vercel AI SDK, Anthropic SDK, TanStack AI and OpenClaw (JavaScript, run under Bun); JSON.parse for one-shot parsing
workload: Streaming an LLM tool_use JSON block in ~12-character chunks, materialising a partial object on every chunk, payloads of 1 KB to 100 KB.
claimed_speedup: 1 KB: Vercel AI SDK 3.9 ms vs 283 µs (14x); Anthropic SDK 3.3 ms vs 283 µs (12x). 5 KB: Vercel AI SDK 23.1 ms vs 739 µs (31x); Anthropic SDK 34.7 ms vs 739 µs (47x). 50 KB: Anthropic SDK 3.39 s vs 2.7 ms (1255x). 100 KB: Vercel AI SDK 6.1 s vs 6.6 ms (920x); Anthropic SDK 13.4 s vs 6.6 ms (2028x). One-shot: JSON.parse is faster (1 KB 2.16M ops/s vs 1.37K ops/s).
compiler_and_flags: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall for wasm32 with simd128 (Zig 0.15.2 in CI), then wasm-opt -Oz --enable-simd --enable-bulk-memory and others, JS bundled with bun build --minify; benchmarks run as 'cd bench/ai-parsers && bun --expose-gc bench.mjs' and 'bun --expose-gc bench/parse-stream.mjs' in the CI benchmark job with Bun 'latest' (unpinned); baselines pinned in bench/ai-parsers/package.json: @anthropic-ai/sdk 0.74.0, ai ^6.0.86, @tanstack/ai ^0.5.0, partial-json ^0.1.7
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu x86_64 runner (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Not a JSON.parse replacement: README says JSON.parse wins on one-shot parses of small payloads and is roughly equal at 500 KB+. Wins come from incremental O(n) streaming with a live object versus re-parsing the whole buffer per chunk. WASM SIMD required.
caveats: The 14x-2028x streaming figures come from an algorithmic difference, not raw parse speed: the stock loop does buffer += chunk and re-parses the whole buffer into a fresh object graph on every 12-character chunk (O(n^2)), while VectorJSON's createParser().getValue() returns the same live object that a JavaScript byte-by-byte scanner (spScan in src/js/index.ts) extends in place, so per-chunk work and allocation differ by design; the bench comment saying getValue() re-parses the accumulated buffer with SIMD does not match the code, and no WebAssembly or SIMD contribution is isolated. Where a stock run is slow (warmup x 4 > 30 s, e.g. Anthropic SDK and OpenClaw at 100 KB) the stock time is a single cold warmup run, while VectorJSON is the median of 3 runs after 2 warmups. One-shot JSON.parse is much faster on small inputs (1 KB: 2.16M vs 1.37K ops/s) and still slightly faster at 500 KB-2 MB. Runtime is Bun (JavaScriptCore), not V8; first-party CI numbers, CPU not named, Bun version unpinned. The streaming engine is zimdjson (a Zig port of simdjson) vendored in deps/zimdjson. Fits a JSON-parsing category better than assemblyscript-and-wasm-langs.

name: wasm-and-ffi-performance-comparison-in-node (Rust WASM Collatz)
baseline: JavaScript Number-based Collatz loop in Node (V8), and the same Rust function built as a native cdylib (cargo build --release, no LTO) called through ffi-napi 4.0.3
workload: Collatz step count for input 670617279 in Node, benchmark.js, comparing a JS function, a Rust FFI addon and Rust compiled with wasm-pack.
claimed_speedup: JS 32,172 ops/sec, FFI 225,918 ops/sec, WASM 1,465,898 ops/sec; WASM is 45.6x JS and 6.5x FFI (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: WASM: wasm-pack build --target nodejs --release, Cargo release profile lto = true, wasm-bindgen 0.2.92; FFI: cargo build --release (default profile, no LTO) loaded with ffi-napi ^4.0.3 and ref-napi ^3.0.3; benchmark ^2.1.4; Node version not stated
tradeoffs: Needs a Rust toolchain and wasm-pack; each call crosses the JS/Wasm boundary with a u64 (BigInt) argument; result only holds for a tight integer loop.
caveats: Single-commit toy benchmark; no CPU, OS or Node version stated. The Collatz sequence for 670617279 takes 986 steps and peaks near 9.7e11, above the int32 range, so the JS version runs float64 % and / on heap numbers while the Rust version uses u64 integer ops, which probably explains much of the 45x gap. The 6.5x WASM-over-FFI result measures ffi-napi's per-call marshalling overhead (about 4.4 us per call versus about 0.7 us for the whole WASM call), not native versus WASM code quality; a N-API addon or an in-process native loop would be expected to beat WASM. The wasm wrapper converts the Number argument to BigInt on every call and returns a BigInt. Results are checked for equal step counts before timing. README gives speculative reasons for the win without profiling.

name: wasm-runtime-performance (boost::graph Floyd-Warshall via Emscripten)
language: C++ (Boost.Graph, std::priority_queue) compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten
baseline: graphlib.js alg.floydWarshall (JavaScript, in the browser JS engine)
workload: JS side: graphlib graph of 111 vertices (newline-polluted ids) with one-way edge traversal; wasm side: Boost undirected graph of 100 vertices; outputs never compared
claimed_speedup: With emcc -O3: JS graphlib 61.1135 ms vs WASM boost::graph 10.1569 ms per Floyd-Warshall run (V=100, E=500), about 6.0x faster (derived from page data); unoptimised wasm: JS 62.16 ms vs WASM 1235.41 ms (about 20x slower, derived from page data). Priority-queue test at -O3 (300,000 elements, wasm slower throughout): inserts WASM 58.44 ms (bulk 51.99 ms) vs FastPriorityQueue.js 9.86 ms and Heap.js 13.42 ms (wasm 4-6x slower, derived from page data); peek+pop WASM 39.93 ms (bulk 33.07 ms) vs FastPriorityQueue.js 27.37 ms and Heap.js 32.31 ms.
compiler_and_flags: emcc from a 2017 emsdk (version not stated) with Boost headers (README links Boost 1.64 docs; include path /home/azeem/temp/include). generate_output.sh: unoptimised build `emcc main.cpp -o output/data.html -D COMPILING_TO_WASM -s WASM=1 --shell-file shell_call.html -std=c++11`; optimised build adds -O3 (output/data_O3.html). Browser and JS engine not stated.
tradeoffs: Needs boost and emsdk to rebuild; wasm in 2017-era browsers; wasm module startup excluded (the README says it only times execution after loading).
caveats: 2017 repo (10 commits, April 22 to May 7 2017), single representative run pasted into the README, no CPU, browser or emsdk version, no licence file. Mixed result: the Floyd-Warshall win appears only at -O3, and the std::priority_queue test shows wasm slower than both JS heaps even when the loop runs entirely inside wasm (bulkInsert/bulkPops). The -O0 to -O3 gap is about 122x (1235.41 ms to 10.16 ms, derived from page data), roughly two orders of magnitude; the README's 'improved by 3 orders of magnitude' overstates it. Both timed regions include graph construction (graphlib setNode/setEdge in JS, 500 cwrap addEdge calls into wasm) and a result scan, so the harness is symmetric, but the JS baseline is a generic string-keyed object graph library, not an equivalent data layout to Boost's adjacency_list plus multi_array distance matrix. main.cpp also has a native C++ timing path (non-wasm) with no published numbers. The live benchmark pages are on azeemba.github.io (not opened; host blocked here).

baseline: TypeScript skeletal-animation implementation running in the browser JavaScript engine
workload: CPU-bound skeletal animation of 15 characters on screen, nearly identical logic in TypeScript and C++ compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten, WebGL rendering.

name: webgpu-shaders-study (AssemblyScript SIMD particle loop vs JavaScript)
language: AssemblyScript (WebAssembly SIMD), Rust (WebAssembly SIMD), JavaScript, WGSL
baseline: plain JavaScript loop on the CPU in the browser (V8 assumed, browser not stated)
workload: Particle simulation pulled toward the mouse, Heavy mode (16 attractors per particle), frames per second at 1M, 4M and 16M particles, same data copied to the GPU every frame in the JS and wasm demos
claimed_speedup: Heavy mode on an Apple Silicon Mac: JavaScript 33 fps at 1M and 8 fps at 4M (no 16M figure); WASM AssemblyScript 40, 37 and 6 fps (about 1.2x at 1M and 4.6x at 4M, derived from page data); WASM Rust 60, 41 and 11 fps; WebGPU 60, 60 and ~48 fps. README: Rust's step is about 15% faster than AssemblyScript's in Light mode, more in Heavy
compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript ^0.28.20 (package.json devDependency): `asc 2-wasm/assembly/index.ts --outFile 2-wasm/build/sim.wasm --optimize --runtime stub --noAssert --enable simd`. Rust: cargo --release for wasm32-unknown-unknown with opt-level 3, lto, codegen-units 1, panic abort (2-wasm-rust/sim/Cargo.toml) and -C target-feature=+simd128 (.cargo/config.toml). Compiled .wasm files are checked in. Browser and JS engine not stated.
hardware: Apple Silicon Mac (chip model not stated)
tradeoffs: WASM path needs a full CPU copy to the GPU each frame; only the WebGPU demo keeps particles on the GPU; 16M particles draw 1M points only.
caveats: One-commit repository (2026-10-09) with a results table pasted into the README and no licence file; readings are requestAnimationFrame frame rates (capped at 60) averaged over the last 30 frames, not controlled timings, and include a WebGL upload and draw of up to 1M points shared by all CPU variants (the HUD also shows per-step sim ms, but those are not reported). The kernels are equivalent (same attractor maths over Float32Array data), but JS runs scalar f64 arithmetic while AssemblyScript runs 4-wide f32x4 SIMD, so the gap is mostly SIMD. The AssemblyScript row is internally inconsistent: 40 fps at 1M and 37 fps at 4M for four times the work, then 6 fps at 16M, so the 1M reading looks limited by something other than the simulation step. Browser, chip model and asc patch version are not stated (on a Mac the browser could be Safari's JavaScriptCore rather than V8); the JS 16M cell is blank. Counter-evidence from the same table: at 1M particles the AssemblyScript build is only 1.2x the JS loop, and Rust's wasm beats AssemblyScript at every size. No benchmark harness beyond the interactive pages; the overview page only stores each viewer's own readings in localStorage.

name: xoroshiro128starstar (AssemblyScript WebAssembly seeded PRNG)
baseline: Math.random (V8) and the seedrandom npm package
workload: Generating random integers 0 <= n < 10, 'wasmrandom' vs Math.random vs seedrandom, via do-you-even-bench in Node.js.
claimed_speedup: wasmrandom 81,321,598.18 op/s vs Math.random 73,658,101.35 op/s (about 1.10x, derived from page data) vs seedrandom 24,057,933.98 op/s (about 3.4x, derived); the 262-byte module keeps its state in two u64 globals.
compiler_and_flags: README numbers were measured on the August 2018 build: asc --baseDir assembly -Oz -b index.wasm -t index.wat index.ts --sourceMap --noDebug (package.json at commits c7cf3b3 and e5e290b), with AssemblyScript from GitHub master, unpinned. The current -O3 --validate build and the 52-bit next() float conversion came in commit bc56b66 (2019-01-02) and were never re-benchmarked. Run with Node.js v10.3.0, node --expose-gc bench.js (do-you-even-bench).
tradeoffs: Small 262-byte module with no memory pages; seeded and reproducible unlike Math.random. Includes the JS/Wasm call overhead per number.
caveats: Node 10.3 era numbers (V8 6.7), no CPU stated; the margin over Math.random is only about 10% (derived from page data), and the seeded JS competitor is seedrandom's default ARC4 generator (a slower algorithm). The README numbers predate the 2019-01-02 commit that switched the build from -Oz to -O3 and changed next() from a 53-bit multiply to a 52-bit mantissa trick; that commit fixed no correctness bug (the 2018 xoroshiro128** update is equivalent to the reference), but the published numbers are for the older build. Each call crosses the JS-to-WASM boundary; there is no batch API. Abandoned since 2019.

name: ademakov/bzero
language: Assembly (x86 SSE/AVX, GNU as) with C test harness
baseline: libc memset (bzero_0 in the harness) and the author's trivial and unrolled C versions compiled with gcc -O2
workload: Time to clear buffers of 0 to 2048+ bytes by size, comparing libc memset, trivial/unrolled C, SSE intrinsics, rep stosb, and hand-written SSE/AVX assembly versions.
claimed_speedup: Core i7-4850HQ (total microseconds for 10,000 calls): 32 B bzero_6 26 / bzero_7 23 vs memset 86 (3.3x / 3.7x, derived from page data); 64 B 26 vs 70 (2.7x, derived from page data); 256 B 51 vs 82 (1.6x, derived from page data); 1024 B 189 vs 149 and 2048 B 393 vs 241 (memset faster). Xeon E5520 (no AVX): 64 B 47 vs 71, 256 B 79 vs 127, 1024 B 265 vs 317, 2048 B bzero_6 655 / bzero_7 552 vs memset 664. The README Update says newer AVX versions (bzero_9..bzero_H, added 2019) are 'faster than memset() for any memory size', but no tables or numbers are given for them.
compiler_and_flags: gcc at default -O0 (Makefile sets CC=gcc, no CFLAGS) for the C baselines and the bzero_0 memset wrapper; GNU as for the assembly variants
hardware: Intel Xeon E5520 @ 2.27 GHz (no AVX) and Intel Core i7-4850HQ @ 2.30 GHz (AVX)
tradeoffs: Strong only for small sizes and the SSE versions; the author concludes stock memset is better for large buffers when it can use AVX/AVX2. Public-domain dedication gives no patent grant.
caveats: Units derived from main.c: each figure is the total gettimeofday time in microseconds for 10,000 calls on the same buffer (so 23 vs 26 is within 1 us timer noise; about 2.3-2.6 ns per call); one run per size, hot cache, same size every call (branch-friendly). Published tables come from the 2017 harness (the current main.c prints a different size list) on 2009/2013 CPUs with an unstated glibc; author notes stock memset is 'sometimes unreasonably bad for small buffer sizes' there, which modern glibc ERMS/AVX2/EVEX memset paths likely fixed. Memset wins at 1024 B and 2048 B on the AVX laptop. The 2019 AVX versions have no published numbers; AVX-512 untested. Unlicense (public-domain dedication, no patent grant). [retier] C baselines built at -O0; memset reached through an unoptimised wrapper plus PLT while the assembly routines are called directly; single run, no warm-up, aligned hot-L1 buffers up to 8 KiB only; AVX variants lack vzeroupper; .S files lack .note.GNU-stack; laptop rows may have used macOS libc

name: Boost.Context
baseline: glibc ucontext_t user-space context switch (::swapcontext/makecontext), as wrapped by Boost.Context's own continuation_ucontext.hpp backend (b2 context-impl=ucontext), run through the same callcc()/continuation benchmark
workload: Round-trip context switch through callcc()/continuation, reported as the average per jump (two jumps per round trip) in nanoseconds and CPU cycles, release build.
claimed_speedup: fcontext_t (hand-written per-platform jump_fcontext/make_fcontext assembly): 9 ns / 19 CPU cycles per switch; ucontext_t: 547 ns / 1130 CPU cycles; Windows Fiber: 49 ns / 98 CPU cycles. Roughly 61x lower latency and 59x fewer cycles than ucontext_t (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-6.3.1; b2 properties variant=release, optimization=speed (performance/callcc/Jamfile.v2 also sets link=static, threading=multi and -DBOOST_DISABLE_ASSERTS)
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
tradeoffs: Hand-written assembly per ABI and OS: src/asm holds jump_, make_ and ontop_ files for x86_64, i386, arm, arm64, mips32/64, ppc32/64, riscv64, s390x, sparc64, loongarch64 and alpha across ELF, Mach-O, PE and XCOFF. Stackful switch only; the caller supplies or allocates stacks. ucontext and Windows Fiber backends remain selectable as portable fallbacks (context-impl feature).
caveats: Numbers come from the project's own doc table (about 2017, gcc-6.3.1, Broadwell-era Xeon) and were not re-run; the callcc()/continuation API they measure is now the older of Boost.Context's two APIs (fiber is the newer one). Compiler flags are given as b2 build properties (variant=release, optimization=speed, plus link=static, threading=multi, -DBOOST_DISABLE_ASSERTS in performance/callcc/Jamfile.v2), not literal -O flags. The page does not say how the ucontext_t column was built; the context-impl=ucontext recipe is inferred from build/Jamfile.v2. The Windows-Fiber column cannot have been measured on the Linux machine the page names, so the table mixes at least two setups without saying so. The ucontext baseline is Boost's wrapper around glibc ::swapcontext, which makes a signal-mask system call per swap on x86-64 Linux, so the ~61x gap mostly measures avoiding that call rather than hand-written assembly versus compiled code; a context switch cannot be written in portable C, so no -O3 C comparison exists. Other user-space switchers (libco, minicoro) are not compared. Per-switch figures are a round trip divided by two after subtracting measured clock overhead. The assembly is only part of the repo (src/asm/jump_*/make_*/ontop_* per platform).
found_via: Hacker News: 10 WebSearch queries restricted to news.ycombinator.com (e.g. 'Show HN hand-written assembly faster than compiler -O3 memcpy strlen kernel', 'FFmpeg devs boast of another 100x leap thanks to handwritten assembly code') surfaced only projects already catalogued or without repos. name: crc32-vpmsum (POWER8 vpmsum CRC32 and CRC32C in hand-written assembly)
baseline: slice-by-8 table-driven CRC32 in C (based on Linux kernel lib/crc32.c, shipped in the repo as slice_by_8_bench.c, linked into the same crc32_bench.c driver); it computes the big-endian, non-reflected 0x04C11DB7 CRC rather than the reflected CRC32C (0x1EDC6F41) the default vpmsum build computes
workload: CRC32C (polynomial 0x11EDC6F41) over a 32 kB buffer, 5 000 000 iterations, L1-resident, timed with the shell time command; separate kernel test of btrfs writes to a ramdisk.
claimed_speedup: The vpmsum accelerated CRC is 'just over 41x faster' than slice-by-8: 2.937 seconds (crc32_bench) vs 122.220 seconds (slice_by_8_bench) for 5 000 000 x 32 kB. About 52 GiB/s or 13.6 bytes/cycle on a 4.1 GHz POWER8 (theoretical limit 16 bytes/cycle). The kernel btrfs write test is 3.8x faster.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile CFLAGS: -m64 -g -O2 -mcpu=power8 -mcrypto -mpower8-vector -maltivec -mvsx (assembly built with -m64 -g); gcc is implied by the README but no compiler version is stated
hardware: 4.1 GHz POWER8 (exact model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 33 stars; its crc32c-vpmsum code (Copyright 2015 Anton Blanchard, IBM) is in mainline Linux as lib/crc/powerpc/crc32c-vpmsum_asm.S
tradeoffs: POWER8 and later only (needs the vpmsum vector crypto instructions). Constants are generated by make for a chosen CRC polynomial (CRC32C or Ethernet CRC32 shown), so each polynomial needs its own constants header and renamed symbols. Two variants ship: pure assembly (crc32.S plus crc32_wrapper.c) and a gcc vector-intrinsics version (vec_crc32.c).
caveats: First-party numbers from a loop of 5,000,000 calls on a 32 kB L1-resident buffer timed with shell 'time'; compiler version and exact POWER8 model unstated, so tier C although the benchmark source is public. The baseline is a table-driven C slice-by-8 for a different polynomial and bit order (big-endian 0x04C11DB7 versus reflected CRC32C), equivalent work per byte but not the same checksum; it runs at about 1.34 GB/s, roughly 0.33 bytes/cycle at 4.1 GHz (derived from page data), so it is a modest baseline. No compiler auto-vectorized or carry-less-multiply C version is timed against the assembly: the repo's own vec_crc32.c intrinsics version of the same algorithm has a vec_crc32_bench target but no published figure, so the win is not attributable to hand-written assembly versus C. The btrfs 3.8x figure is a kernel-side ramdisk test with no details. Hardware is old and the repo has not been updated since 2020-03-26.

name: CryptOpt
baseline: GCC 12.1.0 and Clang 15.0.6 compiling Fiat Cryptography's generated C at -O3 -march=native -mtune=native; also hand-optimized assembly (OpenSSL fe-51/fe-64, libsecp256k1 asm, HACL* fe-64)
metric: latency (CPU cycles per finite-field multiply and square)
workload: Multiply and square in nine prime fields (Curve25519, NIST P-224/P-256/P-384/P-521, secp256k1, Curve448, SIKEp434 field, Poly1305) on ten x86-64 CPUs, plus scalar multiplication through SUPERCOP.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: mean speedup 1.74 over GCC 12.1.0 and 1.40 over Clang 15.0.6 across ten x86-64 platforms; the 1.04x over libsecp256k1's hand-optimized assembly is the verified Fiat path (Table 5: 527k vs 547k cycles; Opt 528k), under 1% over libsecp256k1's C and slower than that C on all four AMD machines (Table 7); Table 6 'Final' multiply vs the better compiler: 1.00x P-521, 1.01x Curve448, 2.26x SIKEp434
compiler_and_flags: Baseline C built with GCC 12.1.0 and Clang 15.0.6, highest optimization level with -march=native -mtune=native -O3; CPU frequency fixed, boosting disabled, performance governor; Ubuntu Server 22.04.1.
hardware: Ten x86-64 machines: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 1900X (Zen 1), Ryzen 7 5800X and Ryzen 9 5950X (Zen 3), Ryzen 9 7950X (Zen 4); Intel Core i7-6770HQ, i7-10710U, i9-10900K, i7-11700KF, i9-12900KF, i9-13900KF (performance cores only).
stars_or_usage: 73 stars, 14 forks; PLDI 2023 Distinguished Paper Award and GECCO 2023 Humies Gold award (university news pages, snippet only); verified assembly published in fiat-crypto's fiat-amd64 directory and Curve25519 code integrated into BoringSSL (per the repo README)
tradeoffs: x86-64 only; the assembly is found by randomized search per microarchitecture (20 to 40 wall-clock hours per machine for the 18 primitives) and must be regenerated for new CPUs; correctness is checked by an equivalence checker only when the input is Fiat IR, the libsecp256k1 variant is unverified; fixed-size field arithmetic, not a general library.
caveats: The assembly is machine-generated by random program search, not hand-written; it sits here because it is compared against both compilers and hand-written assembly. Each platform's numbers come from code optimized on and for that same platform (best of three optimization runs per primitive per machine), against generic compiler output. Gains vary: Curve448 and P-521 multiply are slightly slower than GCC (0.98 and 0.97); gains are modest for Curve25519 and Poly1305. The baseline is Fiat Cryptography's generated C, not each library's own C. In whole scalar multiplication through SUPERCOP (Table 5, geometric-mean cycles) CryptOpt-enhanced code is on par with OpenSSL fe-51 (524k vs 530k) and fe-64 (461k vs 455k) assembly and slower than HACL* fe-64 (452k); for secp256k1, libsecp256k1's hand asm (547k) is itself slower than its portable C (530k), so CryptOpt's 527k (Fiat, verified) and 528k (Opt) are under 1 percent faster than libsecp256k1's C (derived from page data), and the 1.04 speedup over hand asm comes from the libsecp256k1-derived path that the equivalence checker cannot verify. The Zenodo artifact was not opened (blocked here); the repo README repeats the Table 4 means. Last commit 2023-11-16. [retier] Generated assembly needs ADX/BMI2, System V ABI only, uses the red zone, clobbers rbp, no .cfi directives; HACL* fe-64 is faster than CryptOpt Curve25519 on 11th-13th gen Intel in Table 7 despite the prose

name: FP-ASM (FP_ASM_LIB_DEV)
language: Assembly (NASM x86-64 AVX2) with a C API
baseline: Scalar C reference loops compiled with gcc 13 -O3 -march=native
workload: 100k-element f32 arrays, best of 200 runs: reduce sum, dot product, axpy, scale and a mat4 x vec3 batch transform; plus a 1M-star simulation (swarm_bench) FP-ASM versus plain C.
claimed_speedup: reduce sum (f32) 85.0 us scalar -O3 vs 9.9 us (8.6x); dot product (f32) 96.0 vs 18.9 us (5.1x); mat4 x vec3 batch 189 vs 122 us (1.5x); axpy 34.4 vs 34.2 us and scale 25.8 vs 25.7 us (parity). swarm_bench 1 thread on Emerald Rapids: total 7.01 vs 14.48 ms/frame (2.1x).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13; benchmarks/bench_math.c is built by the Makefile bench target at -O3 -march=native (scalar reference and library caller alike); swarm_bench is built with the library CFLAGS -O3 -std=c11 -march=<ISA, default native>; reproduce with make bench and make run-swarm-bench
hardware: Intel Core i7-4600M (Haswell, AVX2) for the kernel table; Intel Xeon Emerald Rapids (AVX-512), 4 vCPUs for swarm_bench
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX2 only (NASM required); float reductions use several SIMD accumulators so results differ in rounding from a strict scalar sum. Memory-bound element-wise kernels gain nothing.
caveats: The reduction wins come from multiple SIMD accumulators: the scalar reference (benchmarks/bench_math.c) is a single-accumulator strict-order loop that gcc cannot vectorize without -ffast-math or -fassociative-math, so a hand-unrolled or -ffast-math C loop would close much of the 8.6x/5.1x gap; outputs are not bit-identical to the strict-order loop. bench_math.c times only (best of 200, volatile sink) and does not compare results; swarm_bench does check FP-ASM vs plain C within float reassociation. Memory-bound kernels (axpy, scale) are at parity. Kernel table is one older laptop CPU (i7-4600M); the Emerald Rapids swarm numbers ran with the 100 MB working set in a large L3, and the demo rows under rendering drop to 1.4x total. Young project (1 star, 0 forks).

name: go-and (bwesterb)
language: Go (AVX2 and NEON assembly, generated with avo)
baseline: naive one-byte-at-a-time Go for loop (and a uint64-wise pure-Go version, build tag purego), both compiled by the Go gc compiler
workload: bitwise and/or/xor/andnot, any-bit-set (masked and unmasked) and popcount (masked and unmasked) over []byte slices, Go benchmarks with -count=10 compared with benchstat
claimed_speedup: Intel i9-13900: geomean time 16.14us naive -> 1.046us asm (-93.52%, about 15x derived from page data); And-32 6942.5ns -> 360.8ns (-94.80%); Xor-32 6996.5ns -> 361.9ns; Popcnt-32 177.46us -> 22.49us (-87.33%); throughput And 4.293GiB/s naive -> 82.618GiB/s asm. Apple M2 Pro (NEON): geomean 30.52us naive -> 1.455us asm (-95.23%).
compiler_and_flags: Go gc toolchain with default go test flags; exact commands in benchmark.sh (go test -run=^# -count=10 -bench='^Benchmark(And|Or|Xor|AndNot|Any|AnyMasked|Popcnt|PopcntMasked)$', the same with -tags purego, and the *Naive benchmarks), compared with benchstat@latest. Go version not printed in the README output; go.mod and internal/asm/go.mod require go 1.24.0 (the Popcnt benchmarks use b.Loop, which needs Go 1.24+).
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i9-13900 (AVX2) and Apple M2 Pro (arm64 NEON)
tradeoffs: AVX2 required on amd64 (runtime dispatch, AVX variants also generated) and NEON on arm64; pure-Go fallback via purego tag; amd64 and arm64 only; function-call overhead dominates tiny slices (Go never inlines asm).
caveats: Baseline is a deliberately naive byte loop; the stronger comparison is the uint64-wise purego column (derived from page data: asm about 7.8x faster than purego on And-32 2825.5ns vs 360.8ns, about 2.95x on Popcnt-32 66.45us vs 22.49us, geomean about 5.1x on the i9-13900 and about 4.6x on the M2 Pro). The amd64 AVX2 assembly is generated by avo programs in internal/asm (and_amd64.s carries a 'Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT' header); the arm64 NEON code in and_arm64.s is hand-written Go assembly. The and/or/xor/andnot/any benchmarks run on 32,000-byte buffers (a commit of 2024-08-04 moved to 32K buffers 'so we're less memory constrained'), so the 80+ GiB/s rows are cache-resident; popcount rows use 1,000,000-byte buffers; Any benchmarks use an all-zero buffer (full scan, worst case). The Apple M2 Pro table comes from an older run: it has a Memset row that the current benchmark.sh no longer runs and lacks the Any, AnyMasked and PopcntMasked rows. The baseline is Go gc output, not a C/C++ -O3 compiler, and the library is a Go package (not directly callable from C++). Very small repo (2 stars, 2 forks).

name: memcpy_benchmark (AVX-256, AVX-512 and rep movsb NASM memcpy)
baseline: libc built-in memcpy (glibc version not stated)
workload: Single-threaded copy of one large buffer per run (512 MiB when result.txt was recorded on 2020-09-20; the current code uses 128 MiB), 11 runs per routine; each run mallocs a fresh source (memset before timing) and a fresh, untouched destination, times one copy with gettimeofday, then checks it with memcmp. Routines: libc memcpy, NASM AVX-256 and AVX-512 unrolled copies with prefetcht1, and a three-instruction rep movsb. The multithreaded mode (option 5, libs/memcpy_multithread.c) was added later and is not in result.txt.
claimed_speedup: result.txt, seconds per copy of one 512 MiB buffer (MEM_ALLOC at the result commit; units from memcpy_bench.c's printf), lower is better. Xeon Platinum 8269CY: libc memcpy min 0.3494 / avg 0.3853 vs AVX-256 asm min 0.2711 / avg 0.2987 (about 1.29x), AVX-512 asm min 0.2854 / avg 0.3150 (about 1.22x), rep movsb min 0.3020 / avg 0.3333 (about 1.16x). AMD A8-6410: libc min 0.5464 / avg 0.6221 vs AVX asm min 0.4471 / avg 0.4967 (about 1.22-1.25x) and plain rep movsb min 0.4450 / avg 0.4970 (about 1.23-1.25x); AVX-512 not supported. Ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Harness built with gcc at default -O0 at the result commits (Makefile sets no optimisation flag); NASM for the assembly routines
hardware: AMD A8-6410 APU (2 GHz, no AVX-512) and Intel Xeon Platinum 8269CY (2.5 GHz; cpuinfo flags include 'hypervisor', so a cloud VM); README tells users to set the performance governor, not confirmed for these runs
tradeoffs: x86-64 only; AVX-512 variant needs AVX-512 (reported 'CPU is not supported' on the AMD A8); rep movsb performance depends on ERMS/FSRM support; routines are plain memcpy without small-size dispatch.
caveats: Author's own runs; the README makes no speed claim. Harness flaws: the loop runs TEST_COUNT+1 = 11 copies but divides the total by 10, so every reported Avg exceeds its Max (Xeon libc Avg 0.3853 vs Max 0.3533); ratios survive because all routines share the bug. The destination is a fresh 512 MiB malloc (mmap) never touched before timing, so each timed copy includes about 131,072 first-touch page faults; derived copy rates of about 0.9-2.0 GB/s are well below memory bandwidth, so the numbers mix fault cost with copy speed and may reflect how each store pattern interacts with faulting rather than kernel efficiency. On the A8 the plain rep movsb routine matches the AVX routine, so the gain there is not from the AVX kernel. AVX-512 is slower than AVX-256 on the Xeon. glibc version (which selects the memcpy variant and its non-temporal threshold), compiler and NASM versions are unknown; one result set per machine. The current code uses a 128 MiB buffer, so rerunning it does not reproduce the recorded configuration. The asm measured equals today's libs/memcpy_avx256.asm (only a comment changed).

name: neon-ntt (hand-written Armv8-A Neon assembly NTTs for Dilithium, Kyber and Saber)
baseline: Dilithium reference C implementation (pq-crystals ref code compiled with gcc 10.3.0 -O3 on Cortex-A72 and Apple clang 12.0.5 -O3 on Apple M1); for Kyber and Saber the baseline is the previous Neon implementation by Nguyen and Gaj (re-benchmarked in SUPERCOP)
workload: Median or mean cycle counts for NTT, inverse NTT, base multiplication, matrix-vector multiplication, inner product and full key generation, encapsulation/signing and decapsulation/verification of Dilithium2/3/5, Kyber512/768/1024 and Saber on a Raspberry Pi 4 (Cortex-A72) and an Apple M1.
claimed_speedup: Paper Table 4 (dilithium3, Cortex-A72): NTT 2 241 cycles vs 9 302 for the reference code (4.15x, derived from page data), inverse NTT 2 821 vs 11 633 (4.12x, derived); Apple M1 NTT 479 vs 2 865 (5.98x, derived). Table 5: dilithium2 MatrixVectorMul 26 268 vs 135 182 cycles on Cortex-A72 (5.15x, derived) and 5 316 vs 45 742 on M1 (8.6x, derived). Table 6 (dilithium3, Cortex-A72): key generation 515 776 vs 743 166 cycles (1.44x, derived), signing 1 089 387 vs 2 308 598 (2.12x, derived), verification 447 460 vs 728 866 (1.63x, derived). Against prior Neon work the paper states kyber768 MatrixVectorMul is 1.7x faster on Cortex-A72 and 2.1x on M1, full Kyber 9-14% faster on Cortex-A72 and 26-41% on M1, Saber MatrixVectorMul 2.0x on Cortex-A72.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.3.0 -O3 on Cortex-A72 (full schemes through SUPERCOP 20210604); Apple clang 12.0.5 -O3 on Apple M1
hardware: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (Broadcom BCM2711, Arm Cortex-A72 at 1.5 GHz); Apple M1 Mac mini
stars_or_usage: 34 stars; artifact of a TCHES 2022 paper
tradeoffs: Armv8-A (aarch64) only, tuned for Cortex-A72 and Apple M1. The benchmark harness is only tested on Cortex-A72; user-mode cycle-counter access needs a kernel module there and root on the M1. The speedups combine new algorithms (Barrett multiplication, asymmetric multiplication, interleaved butterflies) with hand-written assembly, so they are not a pure assembly-versus-compiler comparison. Bundled third-party code is CC0, Apache-2.0, MIT or public domain.
caveats: The Dilithium baseline is the unoptimised portable reference code, so the 4-8x kernel gains largely measure hand vectorisation against scalar C; the Kyber and Saber comparisons are against another Neon implementation (Nguyen-Gaj, intrinsics), where gains are roughly 1.1-2.1x. The paper notes the Nguyen-Gaj NTT cycle counts omit the final reduction. Cortex-A72 numbers are medians (10 000 runs; 100 000 for full Dilithium), Apple M1 numbers are averages (10 000 runs; 1 000 000 for full Dilithium). Full-scheme ratios mix NTT and hashing gains: the optimised builds use a two-way Neon SHA-3/SHAKE (Nguyen et al.) on Cortex-A72 and Westerbaan's Keccak with the M1's SHA-3 instructions, and the paper does not separate the two effects. The repository's microbenchmarks and m1_benchmarks harnesses time only the optimised code; the reference rows of Tables 4-5 have no harness in the repo, while Table 6 reference rows can be reproduced through SUPERCOP 20210604 (README steps, first okcompilers line only). The microbenchmark Makefile builds with gcc -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -march=native -mcpu=native. The repository was updated after publication (last commit 2024-11-10, PQClean namespacing and new compressions); the README says to use commit a96c17dbe74ac7675c785a728396e216555c432b to reproduce the paper. The LICENSE file offers MIT or CC0 1.0, and files without a header are CC0; vendored third-party files keep their own licences (Kyber and Dilithium reference code CC0 or Apache-2.0, Nguyen-Gaj Neon Kyber Apache-2.0 or public domain, feat.S MIT). CC0 has no patent grant. Cycle counts were read from the paper PDF (copy on the author's github.io repository), not re-run. The hand-written files are the __asm_NTT.S, __asm_iNTT.S, __asm_base_mul.S and __asm_poly.S sources in each scheme's ntt directory.

name: pospop (positional population count, Go assembly + C)
language: Go (assembly kernels), with a C version in src.c
baseline: the repo's own portable pure-Go kernels (generic8/16/32/64 positional popcount), compiled by Go 1.16
workload: positional population count (per-bit-position counts) over a 100 kB buffer, GB/s per kernel
claimed_speedup: README table (100 kB buffer, GB/s): amd64 avx512 82.1, avx2 34.8, sse2 16.0 versus generic8 1.02, generic16 1.71, generic32 2.66, generic64 3.43 (avx512 is 24x the best generic64 and 80x generic8; avx2 10x and 34x; derived from page data); arm64 neon 36.9 versus generic8 1.68 and generic64 6.56 (5.6x to 22x derived); 386 avx2 31.6 versus generic8 0.297.
compiler_and_flags: README says 'all using Go 1.16', but the amd64 rows (avx512, avx2, sse2, generic8-64) and the arm64 NEON row were re-measured for v1.4.0 (commit 18a8661, 2024-11-26) when the code needed Go 1.20 or newer (go.mod 'go 1.20', unsafe.StringData in dispatch.go), so the toolchain for those rows is unstated; the 386, arm and arm64 generic rows are unchanged since October 2021 and plausibly Go 1.16. Go has no optimisation flags; all amd64 kernels are compiled in regardless of GOAMD64.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6138 @ 2.00 GHz (amd64 and 386); Apple M1 (arm64); ARM Cortex-A72 r0p3 on Raspberry Pi 4B (arm)
tradeoffs: AVX2/AVX-512/NEON/SSE2 kernels written as Go assembly (countavx2_amd64.s, countavx512_amd64.s, countneon_arm64.s); the arm32 build has no SIMD kernel. Specialised operation, not a general-purpose replacement for any standard library routine.
caveats: The baseline is the repository's own portable Go code (generic8 to generic64), not an external incumbent; the README does not compare against the earlier Klarqvist-Mula-Lemire positional popcount (mklarqvist/positional-popcount, already in this wave's list), which the peer-reviewed paper by Clausecker, Lemire and Schintke (Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience 37(27-28), 2025, DOI 10.1002/cpe.70435, arXiv 2412.16370) benchmarks against according to search snippets; the paper itself was not opened (blocked). The README's 'Go 1.16' toolchain line is stale for the amd64 and NEON rows re-measured in November 2024 (the earlier 2021 table had avx512 90.2 GB/s, avx2 35.9 GB/s, generic64 3.59 GB/s). The 100 kB buffer fits in L2, so figures are cache-resident kernel throughput. A C/C++ port with the same kernels lives in src.c (ELF SysV/AAPCS only); the README gives no numbers for it.

claimed_speedup: 'The speed improvement on finite field arithmetic is up 60% with MULX, ADCX, ADOX on BLS12-381 (6 limbs)'; '2.4x perf ratio between using plain GCC vs GCC with inline assembly'; Clang/MSVC/ICC generate code 'up to 20~25% faster than GCC' for add-with-carry code

name: FastMemcpy
language: C (header-only FastMemcpy.h using SSE2/AVX intrinsics, no assembly)
baseline: System memcpy of gcc 4.9 and MSVC 2012
workload: Total milliseconds for many copies per size from 32 B to 8 MiB across aligned/unaligned source and destination combinations, plus a random-access run.
claimed_speedup: 32 B (16,777,216 copies, both aligned) memcpy_fast 81 ms vs memcpy 281 ms (3.5x, derived); 64 B 91 vs 364 ms (4.0x, derived); 512 B 124 vs 242 ms; 8 KiB 55 vs 70 ms; 8 MiB 287 vs 421 ms (1.5x, derived); random access 487 vs 1000 ms. Title claim: speed-up over 50% on average. At 1 MiB with both aligned memcpy_fast 181 ms is slower than memcpy 165 ms.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.9: gcc -O3 -msse2 FastMemcpy.c (AVX: -O3 -mavx FastMemcpy_Avx.c); msvc 2012: cl -arch:SSE2 -O2
tradeoffs: SSE2 or AVX only; jump table for small sizes, non-temporal stores and prefetch for huge sizes.
caveats: Implementation is SSE2/AVX intrinsics (85 _mm_ calls in FastMemcpy.h, 91 in FastMemcpy_Avx.h, no inline asm), so it is a memcpy-baseline entry rather than hand-written assembly. CPU model and glibc version not stated; the README results are from 2015 (gcc 4.9 / MSVC 2012); the 2017 AVX version has no published numbers. Only one README row is slower (1 MiB, both aligned: 181 vs 165 ms); the others show gains. Harness flaws (FastMemcpy.c): same src/dst and size every call (hot cache, perfectly predicted branches), millisecond gettimeofday timer, memcpy always runs first on freshly malloc'd buffers, benchmark() not marked noinline so sizes may be constant-propagated; alexey-milovidov (issue #6) called the benchmark 'nonsense' for these reasons and saw glibc slightly faster in a ClickHouse perf test. Independent runs on newer toolchains show it slower than glibc memcpy: issue #4 (gcc 7.5.0, glibc 2.27: 32 B 230 vs 63 ms, random 1953 vs 635 ms; gcc 5.4: 512 B 77 vs 56 ms) and issue #6 (gcc 10.2.1, Clear Linux: 32 B 48 vs 35 ms, 1024 B 85 vs 41 ms, random 802 vs 662 ms). Issue #5 (gcc 4.4.7, 278 vs 85 ms at 32 B) was a build-flag mistake per the reporter.

name: fastxor (lukechampine)
baseline: naive byte-wise Go for loop and a word-wise (uint64) Go loop, compiled by the Go gc compiler
workload: xor of byte slices of 16 B, 1024 B and 65536 B, run in place on one zeroed buffer (Bytes(buf, buf, buf)) with SetBytes counting one stream; plus a specialised 16-byte Block function
claimed_speedup: README BenchmarkBytes table (committed 2018-07-06 in 000cb37; unknown AVX2-capable CPU, GOMAXPROCS 4, Go version unstated): AVX 65k 67217.99 MB/s vs byte-wise loop 1684.45 MB/s (39.9x, derived from page data) and word-wise loop 13203.25 MB/s (5.09x, derived); 1024 B AVX 66089.39 vs byte-wise 1677.18 (39.4x, derived) and word-wise 11455.33 MB/s (5.77x, derived); 16 B AVX 2579.65 vs byte-wise 1263.77 (2.04x, derived) and word-wise 2170.17 MB/s (1.19x, derived); SSE 65k 32619.21 MB/s (2.47x over word-wise, derived). README conclusion: '2-40 times faster than a naive for loop'. The Block row (13546.30 MB/s for 16 bytes, committed 2018-10-11) is the library's own word-wise Go function compared with its Bytes/16 (2579.65 MB/s, 5.25x derived; README says 'about 6 times'), not a baseline comparison.
hardware: not stated (the AVX2 path ran, so an AVX2-capable x86-64 CPU; GOMAXPROCS 4 from the -4 suffix)
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX/SSE assembly with generic Go fallback (xor_unaligned.go); Go never inlines assembly, so tiny slices lose most of the gain.
caveats: No CPU model, Go version or flags; GOMAXPROCS 4 is the only setup detail. The README's AVX/SSE/word-wise/byte-wise numbers were committed on 2018-07-06 (000cb37). The SSE row predates commit 62a404d ('fix SSE segfault', same day), which rewrote the SSE loops: the measured code XORed from memory operands that fault on unaligned input (the benchmark's buffers happened to be aligned). The AVX path was dispatched on cpu.X86.HasAVX while using 256-bit integer VPXOR, which needs AVX2. It crashed with an illegal instruction on AVX-only CPUs such as the i7-3770 (issue #2) until PR #3 on 2021-03-22. That bug did not affect the measured path. The 40x headline is against a byte-wise loop that, in 2018, still had per-iteration bounds checks (BCE hints were added in 43ff724, 2020). Against the word-wise loop the gain is 1.2-5.8x. The benchmark aliases dst, a and b to one zeroed buffer, so the working set is a third of a real three-buffer xor. The modern Go incumbent, crypto/subtle.XORBytes (exported in Go 1.20; its amd64 assembly is a 16-byte SSE2 loop), was not benchmarked. fastxor's own SSE row is the closer analogue, so the AVX2 gain over today's stdlib is plausibly about 2x, not 5-40x (inference, not measured). There is no VZEROUPPER after the AVX2 loop. The author calls it a first try at Go assembly. amd64 only; other architectures use plain Go loops. 12 commits, last change 2021-03-22.

name: go-byte-test (tmthrgd)
baseline: Go gc compiler output for the loop that checks every byte equals a value (BenchmarkGoTest)
workload: test whether every byte of a slice equals a given value, sizes 32 B to 512 MiB
claimed_speedup: README speedup table (committed 2017-02-23 in 2eb5216; unknown CPU, GOMAXPROCS 8, Go version unstated), naive Go byte loop to go-byte-test: 32 B 893.80 to 4488.67 MB/s (5.02x), 128 B 15.45x, 1K 1177.11 to 40050.28 MB/s (34.02x), 16K 42.28x, 128K 36.34x, 1M 24.66x, 16M 14.67x, 128M 14.71x, 512M 1172.27 to 17316.31 MB/s (14.77x).
hardware: not stated (GOMAXPROCS 8 from the -8 suffix)
tradeoffs: x86-64 assembly only, generic fallback elsewhere; README describes it as SSE accelerated (128-bit vectors, no AVX2).
caveats: No CPU model, Go version or flags; only GOMAXPROCS 8 can be read from the -8 suffix. The README table was committed on 2017-02-23. The assembly was touched on 2018-04-22 only to replace hand-encoded PTEST bytes with the mnemonic (48837c9) and to drop the tmthrgd/asm generator; neither is a correctness fix. The baseline is a naive byte-at-a-time range loop written inline in the benchmark. A uint64-wise Go loop, or a stdlib SIMD route such as bytes.Count(data, []byte{value}) == len(data) through internal/bytealg, was not compared and would narrow the gap. The 34-42x peaks are at L1/L2-resident sizes; from 16M up it is memory-bound at about 17 GB/s (14.7x). The benchmark data is all equal to the value, so it measures the full-scan case only. The assembly uses PSHUFB (SSSE3) and PINSRB/PTEST (SSE4.1) with no CPUID check: amd64 CPUs without SSE4.1 (pre-Penryn Intel, AMD K10) will fault. It also uses R15, which Go's assembler reserves under -dynlink. amd64 only; other targets get the plain Go loop. Repository archived, 1 star, 12 commits.

name: go-popcount (tmthrgd)
language: Go (x86-64 POPCNT assembly, popcnt_amd64.s and popcount_amd64.s)
baseline: Go loop over math/bits.OnesCount64 (BenchmarkCountBytesGo and BenchmarkCountSlice64Go)
workload: population count over byte slices and []uint64 slices, 32 B to 512 MiB
claimed_speedup: README benchmarks (refreshed 2018-01-11 in 3918361; unknown CPU, GOMAXPROCS 8, Go version unstated). CountBytes vs Go math/bits.OnesCount64 loop: 32 B 5854.04 vs 2883.25 MB/s (2.03x, derived from page data); 1K 20804.48 vs 8896.25 MB/s (2.34x, derived); 16K 28642.76 vs 9986.94 MB/s (2.87x, derived); 512M 11912.45 vs 7855.21 MB/s (1.52x, derived). CountSlice64 vs Go loop: 32 B 5804.87 vs 4840.05 MB/s (1.20x, derived); 1K 19932.68 vs 9184.79 MB/s (2.17x, derived); 16K 27414.74 vs 10012.94 MB/s (2.74x, derived); 512M 11874.91 vs 7813.19 MB/s (1.52x, derived).
hardware: 'an AMD64 CPU with POPCOUNT support' (model not stated; GOMAXPROCS 8 from the -8 suffix)
license: BSD-3-Clause AND MIT (portions copyright 2015 Hideaki Ohno under MIT, per the LICENSE file and the headers of popcount.go, popcount_test.go and popcnt_amd64.s)
tradeoffs: x86-64 only; requires POPCNT; pure-Go fallbacks (popcount_generic.go, safe and unsafe variants).
caveats: CPU model, Go version and flags are not stated. The README numbers were refreshed on 2018-01-11, alongside the switch of the Go path to math/bits and of Travis to go1.9. The later 2018 assembly commits are formatting and generator removal, not correctness fixes. The baseline already uses the POPCNT-backed math/bits.OnesCount64 intrinsic over an unsafe []uint64 view. The 1.5-2.9x gain comes from 4x unrolling into separate destination registers, which the asm comments say is meant to dodge Intel's POPCNT false output dependency, an erratum of older Intel cores. Gc's per-call POPCNT feature check also costs the baseline time (removable with GOAMD64=v2 on Go 1.18+); this is an inference, not measured. So the gap is likely smaller on newer CPUs and compilers. At 512 MiB both sides are memory-bound (1.5x). For []uint64 input of 32 B the gain is only 1.2x. The package is derived in part from Hideaki Ohno's MIT-licensed go-popcount (Count64, hasPOPCNT, tests), though it is not a GitHub fork. amd64 only, with a CPUID check for POPCNT; other targets use the Go loop. Repository archived.

name: gocrack (wa7nt)
baseline: Go standard library crypto/md5 and crypto/sha1 (single-stream hashing)
workload: hashing short candidates (up to 55 bytes, one padded block) for brute-force and wordlist password recovery, 8 candidates per AVX2 register (multi-buffer), 1 core
claimed_speedup: md5x8 kernel alone 48 MH/s vs crypto/md5 5.7 MH/s (about 8.4x, derived from page data); sha1x8 compare path 22 MH/s vs crypto/sha1 4.1 MH/s (about 5.4x, derived); whole MD5 brute-force pipeline 38 MH/s on 1 core and 151 MH/s on 4 threads; kernels at 88-90% of a measured ALU-op ceiling
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 darwin/amd64; no flags stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-7360U (Skylake, 2 physical cores, AVX2, no AVX-512, no SHA-NI)
tradeoffs: AVX2-only, Skylake-tuned 8-lane kernels; only single-block messages (55 bytes or less); multi-buffer design raises throughput over many independent candidates but does not speed up one hash; x86-64 only.
caveats: A stdlib comparison harness does exist for MD5: internal/md5x8/bench_test.go TestBenchmarkReport times md5x8 on a pre-built transposed buffer (the same 8 candidates every iteration, compression only) against md5.Sum([]byte("cand-0000")), which also pays digest init, padding and finalization, so the 48 vs 5.7 MH/s kernel ratio overstates the per-compression gain; the end-to-end brute-force pipeline (38 MH/s, generator included) is the fairer 1-core figure, about 6.7x (derived from page data). No harness for the crypto/sha1 4.1 MH/s row was found (internal/sha1x8/bench_test.go benchmarks only the sha1x8 digest and match kernels). The README does not say which command produced the table. Go's crypto/md5 and crypto/sha1 on amd64 are themselves scalar assembly, so this is 8-lane multi-buffer AVX2 against single-stream scalar code, not like-for-like latency. Single 2-core laptop, single run, no repeat statistics. No LICENSE file (usability reference). Two commits (both 2026-09-28), one star. Password-cracking tool; README says it is for authorised testing and recovery of credentials you own. Candidates limited to 55 bytes (one block).
