name: libco (higan-emu)
language: C (hand-assembled machine-code context switch per CPU)
baseline: POSIX ucontext context switch (libco's own ucontext.c backend), plus its setjmp/longjmp and Windows-fiber backends, each expressed as a multiple of an ordinary C function call; the README also contrasts kernel-scheduled preemptive threads
workload: Cost of one co_switch between cooperative threads relative to an ordinary C function call, per backend (doc/targets.md); README asserts 10,000,000+ user-space switches per second versus kernel thread switching becoming the bottleneck above 100,000 per second.
claimed_speedup: doc/targets.md switch overhead versus an ordinary C function call: libco.amd64 ~6x (~10x on Windows), libco.x86 ~5x, libco.ppc ~20x, versus libco.fiber (Windows fibers) ~15x, libco.sjlj (setjmp/longjmp) ~30x and libco.ucontext (POSIX ucontext) ~300x; about 50x lower switch overhead for the hand-assembled amd64 backend than the ucontext backend (derived from page data). README: 'libco can easily scale to 10,000,000 or more context switches per second' while applications needing '100,000 or more context switches per second' hit kernel overhead with preemptive threads (assertion, no measurement).
stars_or_usage: 183 stars; README names servers and emulators as ideal use cases
tradeoffs: Four-function C89 API (co_active, co_create, co_delete, co_switch); backends for x86, amd64, PowerPC, PowerPC64 ELFv1/ELFv2, ARM, AArch64, plus setjmp, ucontext and Windows fiber fallbacks. No safety checks by design. Single-core cooperative scheduling only. The amd64 backend writes the switch routine as a byte array of machine code (co_swap_function) made executable at runtime.
caveats: The overhead figures are rough first-party multiples ('~6x', '~300x') with no benchmark code, methodology, compiler, hardware or date in the repo; the 10,000,000 switches per second README figure is an assertion. The ucontext backend's cost is dominated by the signal-mask system call glibc swapcontext makes, so the gap mostly reflects avoiding that call. Not compared against Boost.Context fcontext, minicoro or other user-space switchers. The amd64/x86 backends store the switch routine as hand-assembled machine-code bytes in a const array placed in the text section (or made executable with mprotect/VirtualProtect under LIBCO_MPROTECT), which hardened toolchains or W^X policies may object to. valgrind.h is under a BSD-style license; the rest is ISC. Last commit 2024-09-10.

name: md5-optimisation (animetosho)
language: C++ (inline x86, ARM and ARM64 assembly headers)
baseline: OpenSSL v1.1.1h MD5 (itself hand-tuned x86 assembly), reading from `openssl speed md5` at 16 KB
workload: Single-buffer MD5 of long inputs, bytes per cycle normalised across seven x86 microarchitectures at locked frequency; the repo's hand-written x86 assembly variants versus a 'Standard' control schedule that the author says roughly equals OpenSSL.
claimed_speedup: README: 'beat OpenSSL's implementation by roughly 5% in the general case, and 23% for processors with AVX512 support'; the % table is relative to the repo's 'Standard' control, e.g. Skylake-X GOpt +5.35%, NoLEA-G +9.70%, AVX512 +23.11% (4.734, 4.546 and 4.051 cpb vs ~4.99 cpb). The chart's data table (images/bench.png) also prints OpenSSL's absolute bytes/cycle: Skylake-X OSSL 0.196 vs Standard 0.201, GOpt 0.211, NoLEA+G 0.220 (about +12% over OpenSSL, derived from page data); Haswell OSSL 0.200 vs NoLEA+G 0.220 (+10%, derived); Piledriver OSSL 0.180 vs GHOpt 0.210 (+17%, derived); Merom OSSL 0.184 vs GHOpt 0.194 (+5%, derived); Airmont OSSL 0.157 vs NoLEA+GH 0.170 (+8%, derived); K10 OSSL 0.204 vs NoLEA+G 0.217 (+6%, derived); Jaguar OSSL 0.199 vs Cache8+G 0.207 (+4%, derived); AVX512 on Skylake-X about +26% over OSSL (derived from 4.051 cpb vs 0.196 B/cycle).
compiler_and_flags: Clang 11.0.0 x86-64; Makefile at the benchmark commit e42661105: -O3 -static -std=c++11 -fno-rtti -fno-exceptions -ggdb (plus -mavx512vl for the AVX512 build; current Makefile adds a -mbmi build); OpenSSL v1.1.1h built statically, fastest of 3 `openssl speed md5` runs at 16 KB
hardware: Merom, Haswell, Skylake-X, Airmont, K10, Piledriver, Jaguar (named by microarchitecture only, locked frequency); AVX512 variant measured on Skylake-X only
tradeoffs: x86 variants are microarchitecture sensitive: plain NoLEA is slower than the control on Merom, Piledriver and Jaguar, and the AVX512 variant needs AVX512 (the author says AMD Zen4's 2-cycle vector bit-rotate latency makes AVX512 undesirable there, so only Intel AVX512 benefits). Single-buffer MD5 only; ARM and ARM64 headers exist but no ARM numbers are published. MD5 is cryptographically broken.
caveats: The README's headline percentages are relative to the author's 'Standard' control, not to OpenSSL; OpenSSL's own readings are only in the chart image's data table, where Standard is sometimes faster than OpenSSL (Skylake-X, Piledriver, Jaguar) and sometimes slightly slower (K10, Airmont). OpenSSL was timed with its own `openssl speed` harness while the repo's variants were timed with md5.cpp (16 KB calloc'd zero buffer, 16384 rounds, best of 5, known-answer tests run first), so the two harnesses differ. CPUs are named by microarchitecture only, at locked frequency. No single variant wins everywhere: NoLEA is slower than Standard on Merom, Piledriver and Jaguar, and on Jaguar the best gain over OpenSSL is about 4%. The AVX512 variant was measured on Skylake-X only; the README says AMD Zen4's 2-cycle vector rotate makes it undesirable there. OpenSSL 1.1.1h dates from 2020 and is itself hand-written assembly, so there is no -O3 C reference comparison. The repo is a technique write-up with inline-asm headers (md5-x86-asm.h, md5-arm-asm.h, md5-arm64-asm.h) rather than a packaged library.

Not a drop-in replacement for IEEE libm: NaNs become infinities, denormals are flushed to zero, single-precision trig needs arguments in -128..+128 and double-precision trig in -1024..+1024, and the scientific functions are about 1 ulp, so part of the speed gap against a full-range libm comes from reduced range and accuracy. name: rt_memcpy_cm
language: Assembly (ARM Cortex-M, GCC/IAR/Keil sources) with a C interface
baseline: RT-Thread's C rt_memcpy and the Keil C library memcpy
workload: Copying 10,000 bytes 10,000 times under Keil.
claimed_speedup: rt_memcpy 1261 ms; this assembly version 883 ms (1.43x, derived from page data); C library memcpy 906 ms (assembly 1.03x faster, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Keil (version and flags not stated)
hardware: Cortex-M3/M4/M7 (MCU and clock not stated)
stars_or_usage: 12 stars; distributed as an RT-Thread online package
tradeoffs: Cortex-M3/4/7 only; handles non-word-aligned addresses; uses LDMIA/STMIA multi-register transfers (up to 40 bytes per operation).
caveats: Single undocumented Keil run: no benchmark code in the repo, no MCU, clock, Keil version, optimisation level or buffer alignment. The win over the Keil C library memcpy is about 2.6% (906 vs 883 ms, derived from page data), essentially parity; the 1.43x headline is against RT-Thread's own C rt_memcpy. The code is Silicon Labs uC/LIB assembly (Copyright 2004-2020 Silicon Laboratories, SPDX Apache-2.0 headers, ported to RT-Thread in 2020), and the README credits the LDMIA/STMIA load/store-multiple instructions (40 bytes per instruction pair), not assembly as such. Each call pushes R3-R12, which costs on short copies; buffers are not checked for overlap (memcpy semantics only). README is in Chinese. Last commit 2022-06-09.

name: seelabs/nasm (AVX2 hex encoder and decoder for 256-bit values in NASM)
baseline: reference C++ hex encode and decode routines taken from rippled (compiled with g++ -O3 according to build.sh)
workload: Encode a 32-byte binary value into 64 hex characters (encode_hex256) and decode 64 hex characters into 32 bytes (decode_hex256), 100 million iterations each, test driver src/main.cpp.
claimed_speedup: README table: encoder 1790 ms (C reference) vs 319 ms (assembly), 5.6x (derived from page data); decoder 4694 ms vs 561 ms, 8.4x (derived from page data). README prose says 'about 10x faster than the reference C++ implementation'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README and no compiler version anywhere. build.sh uses nasm -felf64 and g++ -std=c++14 -O3 (no -march or -mavx2, so the C reference is scalar); CMakeLists.txt instead defaults to clang with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Debug plus -ggdb -fno-omit-frame-pointer. Which build produced the table is unknown.
hardware: Intel Xeon E3-1505M v6 at 3.00 GHz
tradeoffs: x86-64 with AVX2 only, Linux System V calling convention only, fixed 32-byte (64 hex digit) inputs. No LICENSE file in the repository root, so the code must not be copied. Author states it is for learning and not well tested.
caveats: The kernels are specialised to one fixed size (32 bytes, 64 hex digits) while the rippled baseline handles any length, so part of the gain comes from specialisation rather than assembly itself. The README's 'about 10x faster' is not matched by its own table (5.6x encode, 8.4x decode). Single machine, single run, the same constant input every iteration, no compiler version. The table cannot be reproduced from the committed code without edits: in the repository's only commit (2018-05-22) src/main.cpp returns right after test_base58(), so the hex benchmarks are unreachable, and build.sh does not assemble decode58.asm although codec_base58.h declares base58_8_coeff, while CMakeLists.txt defaults to a clang Debug build. The reference loops write to a local buffer that is never read, so an optimising compiler could shrink the C side (this would understate, not inflate, the assembly gain). The driver does random-test both kernels against the reference (1 million inputs, including invalid digits for the decoder), but the author calls the code a learning exercise that is 'not well tested'. No licence file, so reference only. The README also reports an AVX base58 coefficient routine gave only about 6% overall, and its 10x base58 gain over rippled (2199 ms versus 231 ms, 1 million iterations) is plain C++, not assembly.
found_via: WebSearch 'hand-written assembly vs C reference benchmark ... NASM AVX2 README' surfaced the seelabs/nasm hex codec; repo page, readme.md, build.sh and CMakeLists.txt opened

name: tmthrgd/go-hex (SSE/AVX assembly hex)
baseline: Go standard library encoding/hex
workload: Hex encode and decode of 14 or 15 bytes up to 128 MB buffers.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark table (committed 2016-11-11; unknown CPU, GOMAXPROCS 8, Go version unstated) with its own speedup column: Encode/1k 11572.80 vs encoding/hex 451.49 MB/s (25.63x); Decode/1k 6093.43 vs 245.43 MB/s (24.83x); encode ranges from 2.08x (15 B) to 31.17x (16k), decode from 4.26x (14 B) to 44.70x (128k); Encode/128M 4793.16 vs 457.13 MB/s (10.49x); Decode/128M 5397.68 vs 143.72 MB/s (37.56x). An independent re-measurement in the go-simd/hex README (1 MiB random buffer, GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest AMD EPYC, GOAMD64=v1, median of 6, recent Go) gives encode 18785 vs 980 MB/s (19.2x) and decode 9566 vs 2095 MB/s (4.57x) for tmthrgd/go-hex against current encoding/hex.
stars_or_usage: 26 stars, 2 forks; archived 2025-09-11 (repo description says '[Abandoned]'); a pinned dependency of go-simd/hex (go.mod), and search results show it vendored in GoToSocial's tree (snippet only)
tradeoffs: amd64 only with SSE4.1/AVX paths and Go fallback; repository is marked abandoned and read-only.
caveats: The README numbers were committed on 2016-11-11 (Go 1.7 era), not about 2017. CPU model, Go version and flags are not given; only GOMAXPROCS 8 can be read from the -8 suffix. The asm was regenerated afterwards without re-running the table (go1.8/go1.10 updates, PEXTRB workaround 77b1f74, AVX/SSE split, pre-SSE4.1 fallback). None of those commits is a correctness fix of the measured path. Current golang/go encoding/hex Decode uses a reverseHexTable lookup, and stdlib throughput has risen since then. The independent go-simd/hex CI run (competitor package, 1 star, CPU model not given) measures only 4.57x for decode and 19.2x for encode at 1 MiB against current stdlib, so the README's 25-45x decode ratios are stale. Only amd64 builds get SIMD: dispatch is on AVX or SSE4.1, not AVX2, so the kernels are 128-bit. Non-amd64, gccgo and appengine builds use hex_other.go, the old Go-Authors scalar code. go-simd/hex reports that path's arm64 decode as about 9.7x slower than its own fallback, which tracks encoding/hex, so it is slower than the stdlib there. The decode benchmark input is built by an overlapping in-place Encode; it is still valid hex and identical for both rows. The repo is archived and called abandoned by its author, so no fixes will come. Licence is BSD-3-Clause. asm_gen.go also carries Wojciech Mula's Simplified BSD (BSD-2) notice, and hex.go/hex_other.go carry the Go Authors' BSD notice, all OSI.

name: vectorcmp (hexon)
baseline: pure-Go scalar loop that sets one bit per matching element (build tag purego), compiled by the Go gc compiler
workload: comparison of one search value against 65,536 + rand(0..2047) elements of uint8/16/32/64 or float32/64 (Equals, NotEquals, GreaterThan, LessThan, GreaterEquals, LesserEquals, IsNaN) producing a bit-packed result mask with AVX2 VPCMP (AVX1 fallback); test data is drawn from three values ('a', 'b', 'c'; search 'b') plus 20 max-value or NaN entries
claimed_speedup: README benchstat table (i9-14900, n=10, re-measured in the 2025-10-03 bugfix commit cb1b7b5), purego vs avx2 sec/op: VectorEquals8 145594.5ns -> 628.0ns (-99.57%, about 232x derived from page data); VectorEquals16 151.078us -> 1.325us (-99.12%); VectorEquals32 146.441us -> 2.626us (-98.21%); VectorEquals64 146.577us -> 4.468us (-96.95%); VectorGreaterThan8 146456.5ns -> 856.9ns (-99.41%); geomean over all 38 rows 133.0us -> 2.492us (-98.13%, about 53x derived from page data). The IsNaN rows, where the scalar branch is predictable, show only 23.555us -> 2.228us (float32, about 10.6x derived from page data) and 23.687us -> 4.410us (float64, about 5.4x derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench compared with benchstat (n=10, p=0.000); purego column is the scalar Go fallback (purego build tag), avx2 column the default amd64 build with runtime AVX2+BMI2 dispatch; GOMAXPROCS 32 (-32 suffix); Go toolchain version not stated (go.mod says go 1.18)
hardware: 14th Gen Intel Core i9-14900
tradeoffs: amd64 AVX2 only, with runtime detection and a pure-Go fallback; result is a packed bitmask, so callers must consume bitmaps; array sizes fixed by the benchmark.
caveats: The baseline is the library's own naive scalar Go loop (gc compiler, no auto-vectorisation) with a data-dependent branch and a read-modify-write of the output byte per element. The test data matches the search value about one time in three at random, so that branch mispredicts heavily: the scalar Equals8 row costs about 2.2 ns per element, while the IsNaN rows (20 NaNs, predictable branch) cost about 0.35 ns per element and give only 10.6x (float32) and 5.4x (float64) (derived from page data). The 97-99.6% reductions therefore mostly measure branch mispredictions, not SIMD versus good (branchless or SWAR) scalar code, and there is no C/C++ -O3 baseline. The assembly is generated by internal/avo (asm_amd64.s and dispatch_amd64.go say 'Code generated by avo.go. DO NOT EDIT.'), with instructions chosen by hand in the avo DSL. The README table was re-measured in commit cb1b7b5 (2025-10-03, 'Bugfix: we accidentally did signed comparisons instead of unsigned'), so it postdates that correctness fix; two later optimisation commits (2025-10-04/05) are not reflected. README row names (VectorEquals8-32) do not match the current benchmark functions (BenchmarkAsmVectorEquals8 and BenchmarkGoVectorEquals8), so the table came from renamed or restructured runs. Buffer length is random per run (up to 3% different between columns). The Go Reference badge points at github.com/Jille/vectorcmp, a 0-star fork of this repo; the module path in go.mod is github.com/hexon/vectorcmp. amd64 only; other architectures use the scalar loop.

name: zeebo/blake3 (Go BLAKE3 with avo-generated AVX-512, AVX2, SSE4.1, NEON assembly)
baseline: The same library built without its assembly (pure Go, compiled by the Go toolchain), plus the upstream Rust blake3 crate (single-threaded) shown in charts
workload: BLAKE3 hashing of 64 B to 1024 KiB inputs, full-buffer, incremental and reset modes; x86 on an i7-6700K (AVX2) and arm64 on an Apple M4 (NEON).
claimed_speedup: README timing tables, asm vs the same library without assembly. x86 (i7-6700K, AVX2, tables written Feb 2020): 64 B full buffer 205ns vs 254ns (about 1.24x, derived from page data); 1 KiB 1.01us vs 1.77us (about 1.75x, derived); 1024 KiB 262us (4.00GB/s) vs 883us (595MB/s). The 1024 KiB no-ASM row is internally inconsistent: from timings the ratio is about 3.4x, from the rate column about 6.7x (both derived from page data). The rate column matches the author's note that no-ASM speed caps out at about 1 KiB (580MB/s at 1 KiB), so the 883us cell is the more likely error and the real large-input gain is probably nearer 6.7x, but the page does not settle it. Apple M4 NEON (table added Jul 2026): 1024 KiB 459us (2.29GB/s) vs 1.00ms pure Go (1.05GB/s), about 2.2x (derived); 4 KiB 2.11us vs 4.03us (about 1.9x); 1 KiB 1.10us vs 1.08us (no gain; inputs of two chunks or fewer use the pure path). Versus the upstream Rust crate (single-threaded, SVG charts only, numbers not read): README says large full-buffer inputs perform similarly and small inputs are 3-4x slower in rate (about 100ns absolute) because of internal buffering. No AVX-512 or SVE2 numbers are published.
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain, version not stated (the x86 tables were committed on 2020-02-12, so a Go release of that era; the NEON table on 2026-07-23); go test -bench with default flags; the README does not say how the 'No ASM' build was made (the repo has a purego build tag)
hardware: Intel i7-6700K (x86 tables; no AVX-512, so the AVX-512 kernels were never measured) and Apple M4 (NEON table); the author says CPU throttling and noise were not controlled
tradeoffs: Go only (not callable from C++ without cgo). Assembly is emitted by Go programs written with avo (the _asm directory), not hand-typed .s files. x86-64 with AVX2/AVX-512/SSE4.1 plus arm64 NEON/SVE2 variants; other targets fall back to pure Go. Does its own internal buffering and is single-threaded, so very small inputs are slower than the Rust crate. LICENSE file is CC0 and LICENSE-MIT is also present.
caveats: First-party numbers with an unstated Go version; the author states no attempt at precise measurement. The x86 tables (Small, Large, No ASM) date from 2020-02-12 (git blame) and the code has since been rewritten (AVX-512 backends and a two-chunk ymm layout for the AVX2 path in Aug 2026), and the NEON table (2026-07-23) predates the 2026-08-19 NEON critical-path change, so all published numbers are stale relative to current code (performance work, not correctness fixes). The 1024 KiB no-ASM row is internally inconsistent (883us at 595MB/s implies about 0.5 MiB). The Rust comparison appears only as SVG charts whose numbers were not read; Rust was limited to AVX2 and one thread. The baseline is the same Go code without assembly, not a C or C++ implementation. Go-only library: a C++ project cannot use it without cgo, so its value to the catalog is as a reference for avo-generated BLAKE3 kernels. The README also lists an SVE2 backend not named in the record.

name: Raspberry Pi Pico SDK hand-coded RP2040 float and memory routines (pico_float, pico_mem_ops)
baseline: the compiler's soft-float library (libgcc) and C library memcpy/memset on the Cortex-M0+ cores of the RP2040
workload: Single-precision floating point arithmetic and math functions, and memcpy/memset, on RP2040. The SDK ships a cycle-level harness, test/pico_float_test/float_benchmark.c (and double_benchmark.c), built once per float implementation (compiler, pico, pico_vfp, pico_dcp) and timed with SysTick, but publishes no results. The third-party numbers come from tana/pico_float_bench float_bench.c: generate 4000 Gaussian floats with Box-Muller (rand, logf, sqrtf, cosf, sinf, plus one double multiply by M_PI), then compute a running mean and variance with float multiply, add and divide.

name: argminmax

name: CAFS (cache-aware frequency sort)
baseline: vqsort (Google Highway), std::sort, pdqsort, IPS4o, ska_sort
workload: Sorting integer arrays with N elements and K distinct values over a 1600-point (N, K) grid, 592,770 measurements, AVX2 hot loop (one cmpeq per element on 64-byte buckets).
claimed_speedup: Bin-mean speedup 1.7-3.1x vs pdqsort, 1.97-3.52x vs IPS4o, 1.27-2.34x vs vqsort, 4-17x vs ska_sort and 8-17x vs std::sort across the K << N band (README table, K = 4 to 8 distinct values: std::sort 17.10x, ska_sort 16.96x, IPS4o 3.50x, pdqsort 3.10x, vqsort 1.32x). It loses where K approaches N: bin-mean 0.60 vs vqsort and 0.66 vs ska_sort for K of 8.4e6 to 1.7e7, and the README says vqsort wins by 1.5 to 2 times beyond K = 6.7e5.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 13.2 -O3 -mavx2 -mbmi -DNDEBUG (Windows 11); benchmark/main_bigdata.cpp in the repo
hardware: Intel Core i5-12400F, 32 GB DDR4-3200
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, x86-64 with AVX2 and BMI only; targets integer columns with few distinct values; an adaptive dispatcher falls back to pdqsort for high-entropy input (worst case observed about 5x pdqsort time). Primarily a sorting algorithm that uses SIMD, so it may belong with the sorting lists.
caveats: Very new single-author repo (7 commits, 2026-05-09 to 2026-08-07, 32 stars); all numbers from one Windows 11 desktop (i5-12400F, AVX2 path only, no AVX-512 run of vqsort). std::sort is libstdc++ (inferred from the g++ 13.2 toolchain; the README does not name the library). Timings are best of 2 runs per (N, K) point with high_resolution_clock, on uint64 keys drawn from a K-value palette spread over the 64-bit range; only the u64 path is benchmarked although int32/int64 specializations exist. The raw CSV is not in the repo (README says it ships with the preprint artifact); arXiv 2605.25040 exists (seen via a search snippet only, arXiv blocked) and is not peer reviewed. The README is internally inconsistent about std::sort: its crossover line says std::sort reaches parity at K = 1.7e7, while the table shows 3.47x for that bin and the operational table says CAFS still wins at K = N. CAFS loses to vqsort (0.60x) and ska_sort (0.66x) near K = N, and the dispatcher's worst case is about 5x pdqsort time. A 'signed-radix fix' landed on 2026-05-09 but does not touch the u64 path measured. This is a sorting library; it fits the existing 'sorting' category better than simd-intrinsics-libraries.

name: camellia-simd-aesni
baseline: Camellia reference implementation (NTT camellia-BSD-1.2.0 camellia.c, table-based scalar C, built at -O2 in the same harness)
workload: Camellia-128 encryption/decryption throughput in MiB/s from the repo's own test harness main.c, SIMD implementations processing 16 or 32 blocks in parallel versus the reference doing one block at a time.
claimed_speedup: README bullets, versus the table-based reference camellia.c in the same harness: SIMD256 32-block intrinsics, AVX512+GFNI ~18.7x on Ryzen 9 7900X, ~17.8x on Core i3-1115G4 (gcc-14), ~14.1x on Ryzen 9 9950X3D (gcc-15); AVX512+VAES 7.4x to 8.9x; AVX2+AES-NI ~5.4x on Core i5-6500. SIMD256 assembly: AVX2+GFNI ~18.2x on 7900X (~0.92 cycles/byte), ~14.1x on 9950X3D; AES-NI AVX2 ~5.8x on i5-6500. SIMD128 16-block: ~3.1x to 4.5x on x86, ~2.2x to 3.0x on ARM (ThunderX2, Cortex-A53) and ~2.4x on POWER9. The 1-block SIMD128 (constant-time) variants are 1.2x to 2.9x slower than the reference except AVX512+GFNI on the i3-1115G4 (~1.2x faster). README sample outputs on the 7900X: test_simd256_asm_x86_64 reference 372.041 MiB/s vs SIMD256 5159.460 MiB/s (about 13.9x, derived from page data); test_simd256_intrinsics_x86_64_gfni_avx512 reference 313.426 vs SIMD256 5977.907 MiB/s (about 19.1x, derived). Cortex-A53 sample: 29.027 vs 36.700 MiB/s for 16 blocks (about 1.26x, derived), below the ~2.2x bullet.
compiler_and_flags: GCC -O2 with per-target -march flags given in the README build log (sandybridge/haswell/znver4 plus -maes -mvaes -mgfni -mavx512*); individual rows cite gcc-13, gcc-14 or gcc-15; harness is main.c and the reference is camellia-BSD-1.2.0/camellia.c in the repo
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7900X (Zen 4), Ryzen 9 9950X3D (Zen 5), Intel Core i3-1115G4, Core i5-6500, ARM ThunderX2, Cortex-A53 (648 MHz), POWER9
tradeoffs: Only pays when 16 or 32 blocks are available in parallel (CTR, CBC decrypt, CFB decrypt, XTS, OCB); not useful for CBC encryption or single blocks. Needs AES-NI/VAES/GFNI with AVX2 or AVX-512 on x86, ARMv8 Crypto Extension on AArch64, VSX plus AES on POWER, or RVA23 Zvkb+Zvkned on RISC-V. Hand-written GAS assembly files and C intrinsics; targets one cipher, not a general SIMD library. The README presents a constant-time alternative to table lookups.
caveats: First-party numbers. The baseline is the NTT table-based reference camellia.c (which the README calls the OpenSSL reference) compiled at -O2 without -march, one block at a time; OpenSSL's Camellia x86-64 assembly, libgcrypt and the Linux kernel's AES-NI/AVX2 Camellia were not measured, so the gain over an optimised incumbent is unknown. Best-case ratios (14-19x) need GFNI on AVX-512 hardware; the 1-block SIMD128 variants are 1.2x to 2.9x slower than the reference on most listed CPUs (one 1.2x faster case), as the README admits. The README sample outputs do not match its own bullets: the plain AES-NI AVX2 assembly sample shows 13.9x on the 7900X while the bullet for the faster VAES build on the same CPU says ~9.2x, the reference itself reads 372 vs 313 MiB/s in two samples on the same machine, and the Cortex-A53 sample shows 1.26x against a ~2.2x bullet, so the samples come from older builds or compilers than the bullets. Only a 16-32 block parallel workload benefits (CTR, CBC/CFB decryption, XTS, OCB). Better filed under a cipher category than simd-intrinsics-libraries. Last commit date taken from the commits page.

name: corvus
baseline: scalar vendor libm called through std::cos/std::sin/std::exp/std::lgamma (UCRT on Windows, Apple libSystem on macOS); also compared against corvus's own element-at-a-time calls
workload: Element throughput (ns per element) of SIMD-vectorised double-precision erf, lgamma, exp, log, log1p, cos, sin over n = 10^6 seeded inputs, median of repeated timings after warm-up, on a quiet machine gated at 5% ambient CPU.
claimed_speedup: docs/PERFORMANCE.md section 11.1 (n = 10^6, tier-asserted) and raw outputs in docs/bench-evidence: cos/sin 5.50x/5.58x vs UCRT on Zen 4 (1.6 ns/el), 4.87x/4.98x vs Apple x86 libm on Kaby Lake (4.4 ns/el), 3.27x/3.21x vs Apple arm64 libm on M1 (single gated run, 'reported, not published'). The trig gain is size dependent: at n <= 10^4 it is 2.2x to 2.4x on Zen 4 and 2.7x to 3.0x at n = 1000 on Kaby, and at n = 1000 on M1 sin is 0.28x and cos 1.35x (raw evidence files). exp: 1.20x vs UCRT and 1.28x vs Apple arm64, but 0.65x (slower) vs Apple x86 libm on Kaby. erf: 6.33x vs UCRT at n = 10^6 (3.71x at n = 1000), 3.56x vs Apple x86 libm; erfc 3.12x to 9.34x vs UCRT by band, 1.27x to 3.46x vs Apple x86 libm. lgamma 1.5x to 5.2x vs UCRT but 0.2x to 0.93x vs Apple libm (Kaby and M1). log 0.64x, 0.27x, 0.21x and log1p 0.92x, 0.40x, 0.32x (slower than every libm, by design for correct rounding). Other families (gamma_p, beta, digamma, inverses, Bessel) are timed only against corvus called one element at a time ('upper bnd', 4-140x), not against any library, and those batching tables overstate today's gain by up to about 2.5x after the 2026-09-30 baseline change (#42).
compiler_and_flags: clang-cl Release via the windows-clang-cl CMake preset with Ninja (version not stated in PERFORMANCE.md; PLAN.md cites clang-cl 22.1.3 for a later 2026-09-30 build) on Zen 4; Apple Clang 15 Release ('release' preset, Ninja) on Kaby Lake; project-wide -ffp-contract=off (CORVUS_FP_FLAGS); harness tools/quiet_bench.ps1 / tools/quiet_bench.sh, bench sources tests/bench_*.cpp, raw evidence under docs/bench-evidence/2026-08-30-zen4-quiet, 2026-08-30-kaby-quiet and 2026-08-31-m1-indicative
hardware: Ryzen 7 (Zen 4, AVX3_ZEN4 tier; exact model not stated) on Windows 11, Intel i7-7820HQ (Kaby Lake, AVX2) on macOS 13.7, Mac Mini M1 (NEON) on macOS Tahoe
stars_or_usage: 1 star; built on Highway for dispatch
tradeoffs: Accuracy-first double-precision kernels (about 1 ULP bounds, validated against an mpmath oracle) that carry double-double intermediates, so the README states that throughput is not the claim. Needs array-style batch calls; advantage is close to none at two lanes. Highway (Apache-2.0) is distributed with binaries. Covers statistical special functions (erf/erfc, lgamma, incomplete gamma and beta and inverses, Bessel I0/I1) plus an elementary family.
caveats: Wins are function specific: sin, cos and erf/erfc win against every libm measured, exp is slower than Apple's x86 libm (0.65x), log and log1p are slower than every vendor libm by design (correctly rounded), and lgamma is faster than UCRT but slower than Apple's libm in all stable bands. The libm baseline matters more than the kernel (the document says so). Only Windows UCRT and Apple libms were measured; glibc/libstdc++ and MSVC-compiled builds were not. The baseline is a scalar std:: libm loop; vectorised peers the README itself names (SLEEF, Highway contrib math) were not compared, so the result shows the gain of SIMD batching over scalar libm, not over the SIMD incumbent. Ratios depend on array size: the 5.5x trig headline is the streaming n >= 10^5 figure, n <= 10^4 gives 2.2-2.4x on Zen 4, and M1 at n = 1000 is slower for sin (0.28x). Trig inputs are uniform in [-1e6, 1e6], so the huge-argument reduction path is not timed. The M1 elementary column is a single run (indicative only), the Zen 4 CPU model is not named, erfinv and Bessel families are flagged not reproducible, and the batching-gain tables predate the 2026-09-30 per-element baseline change (#42). A 1-star repository maintained by one author; depends on Google Highway (Apache-2.0).

name: libhat
baseline: std::search (MSVC STL) called by libhat's own scan_mode::Search path: std::search(begin, end, sig.begin(), sig.end()) over a std::byte haystack with a std::span<const hat::signature_element> needle, each comparison doing (byte & mask) == value; a wildcard-capable scalar baseline, not a plain-byte std::search
workload: Single-threaded search for a 9-byte pattern (01 02 .. 09) that never matches in a seeded random buffer of 4 MiB to 256 MiB, Google Benchmark, real time, 4 s minimum per run, libhat AVX2 scanner without scan hints.
claimed_speedup: libhat+AVX2 55.1129 GiB/s at 4 MiB and 23.3351 GiB/s at 256 MiB versus std::search 2.89578 GiB/s and 2.89598 GiB/s (about 19x and about 8.1x, derived from page data); the two other pattern scanners in the table reach 2.29 GiB/s (csgosimple) and about 0.96 GiB/s (learn_more).
compiler_and_flags: clang-cl 22.1.1 with the MSVC 14.51.36231 toolchain on Windows, default release flags /GR /EHsc /MD /O2 /Ob2 (README); benchmark source test/benchmark/Compare.cpp read via raw.githubusercontent.com
stars_or_usage: 148 stars; vcpkg port 'libhat' in the vcpkg ports list
tradeoffs: Scanner needs SSE4.1 or AVX2 (x86), AVX-512 (x86-64) or NEON (ARM) for the vector paths, with runtime cpuid validation; patterns are IDA-style byte signatures with wildcards, not general string search. Optional x86_64/aarch64 scan hints trade a small data table for faster scans of machine code. C++20; bindings for C, Java, Python and C#. Aimed at game hacking in user space (signature scanning, memory protection helpers).
caveats: First-party benchmark on one CPU and one compiler. The std::search row is libhat's scan_mode::Search fallback (include/libhat/scanner.hpp, find_pattern_search<X1>): std::search with a heterogeneous needle type (hat::signature_element with a bitmask, compared to std::byte via a masked operator==), so no memcmp-style or vectorised STL search path can apply; its flat 2.9 GiB/s is a scalar search, and a plain-byte search (memmem, a vectorised std::search or std::boyer_moore_horspool_searcher on bytes) without wildcard support would narrow the 8x to 19x gap. The README row labels (libhat+AVX2, std::search) differ from the names the current Compare.cpp prints (libhat+AVX2+X1, libhat+Search+X1), so the table was relabelled by hand; both files were last changed in the same commit (Adaptive anchors, #46, 2026-10-10). 4 MiB to 16 MiB buffers fit in the i7-14700K's L3 and run at 50-55 GiB/s; 32 MiB and above drop to 23-31 GiB/s. The needle has no wildcards and never matches (full-buffer scan). On real machine code (chrome.dll, test/benchmark/Chromium.cpp) unhinted, unaligned libhat falls to 6.09 GiB/s, and that table has no std::search row. AVX2 is selected at runtime; the build uses default release flags without /arch:AVX2.

name: marcelcases/simd (std::experimental::simd kernels)
baseline: scalar C++ version of each kernel built with compiler auto-vectorization disabled (-fno-tree-vectorize)
workload: Seven exercises (nine kernel rows: element-wise add, memory-bound FMA, sum reduction, dot product, upper-bound clamp, count above threshold, stable softmax, horizontal blur, 1D convolution) written with libstdc++ std::experimental::simd versus scalar versions; 16,777,216 floats for the first four, 4,194,304 for softmax, a 1920x1080 grayscale image for blur, 1,048,576 floats for convolution; median of 9 samples.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+, one pinned core, GCC 14.1: sum reduction 5.37x, 1D convolution 5.89x, upper-bound clamp 6.81x, count above threshold 4.85x, horizontal blur 2.12x, dot product 1.78x, element-wise add 1.62x, softmax 1.57x, memory-bound FMA 1.04x. icpx 2025.2 on the same CPU: clamp 10.29x, dot product 4.45x, sum reduction 5.32x. Apple M1 Pro, GCC 15.2.0: count above threshold 24.51x, clamp 20.00x, sum reduction 4.00x, 1D convolution 4.02x, element-wise add 2.60x. Banana Pi F3 (RVV 1.0, VL=8): sum reduction 4.51x, 1D convolution 2.15x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.1 (MareNostrum 5), icpx 2025.2, Homebrew GCC 15.2.0 (M1), conda-forge GCC 16.2 cross-compiler (RISC-V). Makefile: Linux -std=c++2b -O3 -march=native -mavx512f -mavx512vl -mavx512dq -mavx512bw -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math; macOS arm64 -std=c++2b -O3 -mcpu=apple-m1 -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math; RISC-V (README) -std=c++23 -O3 -march=rv64gcv_zvl256b -mrvv-vector-bits=zvl -static -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math. Scalar builds add -fno-tree-vectorize -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns (GCC) or -fno-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize (icpx/clang). RISC-V VL=4 and VL=8 variants used separate builds with temporary SIMD aliases not in the repo.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ (MareNostrum 5 GPP, one pinned core, exclusive node); Banana Pi F3 (RISC-V RVV 1.0, 256-bit VLEN); Apple M1 Pro (4-lane NEON, not pinned)
tradeoffs: Needs a C++23 compiler with libstdc++ <experimental/simd> (GCC); does not use C++26 <simd>. Makefile defaults target MareNostrum 5 AVX-512 and Apple M1, not generic hosts. Portable across x86-64, AArch64 and RISC-V RVV, but the RISC-V toolchain reports one lane for native_simd<float>, so fixed widths 4 and 8 were used.
caveats: Teaching study, not a reusable library; the SIMD side is libstdc++'s std::experimental::simd itself (std::simd is one of the category's listed baselines), so the entry measures std::simd code against scalar loops, not a library beating an incumbent. The baseline is deliberately de-vectorized scalar code, so the speedups say little about beating a normally compiled -O3 build; the exception is sum reduction and dot product, which GCC cannot auto-vectorize at -O3 without -ffast-math anyway, so those rows (5.37x and 1.78x on the Xeon with GCC) are the ones that would hold against a plain -O3 build. Element-wise add and memory-bound FMA are memory-traffic-limited (1.01x to 1.65x on x86 and RISC-V). The README itself notes that count_above on RISC-V contained no RVV instructions (gain is scalar unrolling), that icpx vectorizes softmax's exp loop through SVML, and that the large M1 clamp/count gains come from replacing branches with masks. x86 exercises 1-5 used three initial warm-ups instead of per-sample warm-ups and have not been refreshed. The RISC-V VL=4/VL=8 variants cannot be rebuilt from the repo (temporary aliases), and no result CSVs are committed (results/ is absent). M1 run had no core pinning. name: positional-popcount
baseline: pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive (portable scalar C, auto-vectorized by GCC) and pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive_nosimd
workload: Positional population count (set-bit counts at each of 16 bit positions) over arrays of 16-bit values; the speedup tables cover arrays of 128 to 65536 values on one core, while the cycles-per-integer and MB/s tables use 1 million uniformly random simulated FLAG fields over 1,000 repetitions.
claimed_speedup: pospopcnt_u16_avx512_harley_seal is 16.28x faster than the auto-vectorized scalar naive version at 65536 values (6.43x at 4096, 9.41x at 8192) and 138.71x faster than the no-SIMD naive version at 65536 values; AVX-512 adder forest 4.96x at 2048; at 128 values the Harley-Seal version is 0.52x (slower). README also states about 50 GB/s (about 0.120 cycles per 16-bit integer) with AVX-512.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 7.3.1 20180303 (Red Hat 7.3.1-5); Makefile OPTFLAGS -O3 -march=native, CFLAGS -std=c99, bench built with -std=c++11
hardware: Cannon Lake Core i3-8121U for the speedup table; cycles and MB/s tables also give Sky Lake Xeon W-2104 and Haswell Xeon E5-2697 v3
stars_or_usage: 57 stars; code of the paper 'Efficient Computation of Positional Population Counts Using SIMD Instructions' (Klarqvist, Muła, Lemire), Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience 33(17), 2021, DOI 10.1002/cpe.6304 (venue from search snippet; arXiv 1911.02696); README points production users to libalgebra
tradeoffs: Fastest variants need AVX-512 (Cannon Lake / Skylake-X class); SSE and AVX2 fallbacks are included; experimental repo, the README points production users to libalgebra.h; small arrays (under about 512 values) can be slower than the scalar path.
caveats: Speedup-table baseline is the compiler auto-vectorized scalar version at -O3 -march=native, a fair baseline; the 138.71x figure is against a deliberately non-vectorized baseline. Speedup table comes from one 2019-era laptop-class Cannon Lake CPU; the AVX-512 paths do not run on most AMD or client Intel parts of that era. The README tables predate the final code: the cycles and MB/s tables list methods (pospopcnt_u16_avx512_csa, avx2_csa, mula3) that no longer exist under those names in pospopcnt.c, and the speedup table's avx512_adder_forest/blend names are now avx512bw_*. Timing uses CPUID/RDTSC serialization per call and the input is regenerated and pre-touched by the reference function before each timed call, so small-array (128-512 values) ratios include fixed overhead and warm-cache effects. Peer-reviewed in CCPE 2021 (venue from search snippet only; arXiv not reachable). libalgebra (same author) reuses these kernels, so the two entries overlap; a follow-up paper (arXiv 2412.16370, Clausecker, Lemire, Schintke) extends the method to AVX2, AVX-512 and ASIMD.

name: Pure SIMD (pure_simd)
baseline: scalar_shader, the same per-pixel shader written as a plain scalar C++ loop in the repo's benchmark directory
workload: Per-pixel integer shader over a 512x512 int screen buffer (99 iterations of multiply and modulo-by-constant integer arithmetic per pixel), pure_simd_shader instantiated with vector sizes 1 to 128, against the same loop written in plain scalar C++.
claimed_speedup: Scalar 103 ms vs pure_simd width 64 10.9 ms (about 9.4x, derived from page data); width 32 12.5 ms, width 16 16.2 ms, width 8 28.0 ms; width 128 regresses to 158 ms (slower than scalar).
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 9.0 -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel Core i7-9750H, Ubuntu 18.04
tradeoffs: No intrinsics: variadic-template unrolled vector types that rely on the compiler's SLP vectorizer (gcc or clang needed). Vector width must be tuned (too wide hurts the instruction cache). Header-only C++17; Conan is needed to build the tests and benchmarks.
caveats: A single toy workload (one shader adapted from the 'Practical SIMD Programming' tutorial) on one laptop CPU; the scalar baseline is the author's own loop with the same flags. Its inner loop is a serial 99-step dependency chain per pixel, so the gain comes from the compiler SLP-vectorizing the unrolled independent pixels, while the scalar loop as written evidently was not vectorized (it ties vector size 1 at 103 ms) and size 128 is 1.5x slower (158 ms). The shader relies on signed 32-bit overflow (px*py terms exceed INT_MAX), which is undefined behaviour in both versions; outputs match in the repo's test. The second benchmark (benchmark/sum.cpp) has no published results. Numbers are aggregate means of 10 repetitions. No comparison with Highway, xsimd, Eigen or std::simd; the README calls the library experimental with unstable interfaces.

name: qAverageColor
baseline: serial (scalar C++) average-colour routine in the same repo
workload: Average colour of RGBA8 pixels: tests/BigBench.cpp times one call each of the serial AverageColorRGBA8 and qAverageColorRGBA8 over 10,000,000 pixels all set to 0xBEEFFEEB (table); tests/AverageColor.cpp does the same on a loaded 3840x2160 image (write-up). Paths: psadbw byte sums (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512F) and vpdpbusd (AVX-512 VNNI).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.2.1 (README footnote, one footnote for rows added 2019-2021); CMakeLists.txt: CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG) with -march=native -Wall -Wextra, C++17 with GNU extensions; the serial baseline and SIMD paths are compiled with the same flags
tradeoffs: x86 only (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512 paths plus serial fallback); RGBA8 input only; 64-bit accumulators so no overflow below about 69 billion megapixels; a snippet-sized library, not a general image toolkit.
caveats: The baseline is the author's own plain serial loop (shifts and uint8 casts into 64-bit sums; _bextr_u64 appears only in the SIMD routine's scalar tail, not in the baseline), not a library such as OpenCV. Each function is timed once with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock, serial first, with no warm-up or repetition, so run-order and frequency effects are not controlled. The 10-megapixel test image is one repeated pixel value (the work is data-independent, so this matters little). Write-up numbers on the i7-7500U (2.63x SSE, 4.13x AVX2 on 3840x2160) differ from the table (2.85x and 4.41x on 10 megapixels). The README credits all rows to GCC 8.2.1 although rows were added from 2019 to 2021 (i9-11900K row 2021-04-17). Code-reading finding: the AVX-512 VNNI path's outer loop increments i by 16 after the inner loop exits, so it drops the last Count%16 pixels (and skips a 16-pixel block each time the 4,210,752-iteration 32-bit span fills, about 67 megapixels) while still dividing by Count; both benchmark sizes (10,000,000 and 8,294,400 pixels) are multiples of 16 and below the span, so the measured numbers are unaffected. Speedup depends heavily on the CPU (AVX2 2.61x on i9-7900X to 5.35x on i9-11900K). Results 2019-2021.

name: qReverse
baseline: std::reverse (serial element-swapping reversal)
workload: Reversing arrays of 1-byte elements (ELEMENTSIZE=1 struct of one uint8_t) of 8 to 1,000,000 elements; each size gets 10,000 back-to-back reversals of the same in-cache array, each call timed individually with high_resolution_clock and averaged, std::reverse vs qReverse<1>.
claimed_speedup: i3-6100, g++ -m64 -Ofast -march=native, 1-byte elements, bswap variant vs std::reverse: 1000 elements 290 ns vs 36 ns (8.056x); 10000: 2740 vs 191 ns (14.346x); 100000: 27511 vs 1739 ns (15.820x); 1,000,000: 279525 vs 24710 ns (11.312x); 8 elements 19 vs 19 ns (1.000x). SSSE3 variant peaks at 10.510x (10000 elements) and the AVX2 variant at 16.053x (100000 elements: 27515 vs 1714 ns). AVX512 on i9-7900x, built with Visual Studio 2017 x64-Release: peak 22.357x at 10000 elements (2504 vs 112 ns), 11.153x at 1,000,000. The top-of-README speedup table (AVX2 x22.032 and AVX512 x22.357 on i9-7900x, AVX2 x16.053 on i3-6100) lists peak speedups over std::reverse (the 'Serial' x1 column); the i3-6100 and i9-7900x AVX512 values equal the peaks of the std::reverse tables (derived from page data), while the i5-8600K, E5-2697 v4 and BCM2837 rows have no table or flags behind them.
compiler_and_flags: i3-6100 run: g++ -m64 -Ofast -march=native; i9-7900X AVX-512 run: Visual Studio 2017 x64 Release
hardware: Intel Core i3-6100 (8 GB DDR4), Core i9-7900X, Core i5-8600K, Xeon E5-2697 v4, Broadcom BCM2837 (Raspberry Pi)
tradeoffs: Per-architecture intrinsic kernels (SSSE3, AVX2, AVX-512BW, NEON) plus a bswap-based path; treats elements as raw bytes, so only suitable for trivially copyable element types. Headers only (include/), CMake build.
caveats: Numbers are from 2017-2018 (last README benchmark update 2018-10-30) with an unstated g++ version; newer GCC/Clang may vectorize std::reverse better. Per-call timing with high_resolution_clock means rows under about 30 ns are dominated by clock overhead (8 elements: 19 ns vs 19 ns). The benchmark does not check the reversed output (correctness is covered by the separate tests/verify.cpp). The AVX512 table on i9-7900x was built with Visual Studio 2017 x64-Release (MSVC STL baseline, exact flags not given); the i5-8600K, E5-2697 v4 and Raspberry Pi BCM2837 speedups are listed without tables or flags. Only 1-byte elements are tabulated, although the harness supports 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16-byte elements. Abandoned since 2018-12-19.

name: Quickenshtein
baseline: naive baseline Levenshtein implementation in the repo, and Fastenshtein (other fast .NET Levenshtein library)
workload: Levenshtein edit distance of 10, 400 and 8000 character strings in BenchmarkDotNet, with AVX2/SSE4.1 intrinsics, optional threading, on .NET Framework 4.7.2 and .NET Core 5.0.
claimed_speedup: docs/OverallComparison.md (BenchmarkDotNet, i7-6700HQ), 8000 characters on .NET Core 5.0: Baseline 356,315,300.0 ns, Quickenshtein 17,253,112.5 ns, Quickenshtein_Threaded 16,973,617.7 ns, Fastenshtein 82,207,344.4 ns. The table's 20.92x Speedup column is relative to the .NET 4.7.2 Baseline job (360,927,200.0 ns); against the same-runtime .NET Core 5.0 Baseline it is about 20.65x (derived from page data), and Quickenshtein is about 4.76x faster than Fastenshtein (derived from page data). 400 characters on .NET Core 5.0: Quickenshtein 64,781.7 ns vs Fastenshtein 342,278.1 ns, about 5.28x (derived from page data). 10 characters on .NET Core 5.0: Quickenshtein 317.7 ns vs Fastenshtein 181.4 ns (slower). docs/IntrinsicsPerformance.md (8000-character run): all intrinsics 17.31 ms, without AVX2 (COMPlus_EnableAVX2=0) 28.94 ms, no intrinsics (COMPlus_EnableHWIntrinsic=0) 100.04 ms, so the SIMD path is about 5.78x faster than the library's own scalar path (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet v0.12.1, .NET Core SDK 5.0.201, .NET Core 5.0.4 and .NET Framework 4.8 (4.7.2 target), ShortRun job IterationCount=3 LaunchCount=1 WarmupCount=3
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700HQ 2.60GHz (Skylake), 4 cores, Windows 10 2004
tradeoffs: Uses hardware intrinsics with scalar fallback; optional multi-threading allocates a little; the benchmark shows large gains only with SSE4.1 and AVX2 enabled (disabling SSE4.1 gives the no-intrinsics time).
caveats: Slower than Fastenshtein on 10-character strings on .NET Core 5.0 (317.7 ns vs 181.4 ns). On .NET Framework 4.7.2 (no hardware intrinsics) Quickenshtein loses to Fastenshtein at 400 characters (625,731.9 ns vs 346,120.9 ns) and ties it at 8000 characters single-threaded (99,787,886.7 ns vs 101,566,466.7 ns); it wins there only in threaded mode (30,820,936.5 ns), which compares multi-threaded against single-threaded Fastenshtein. The 'Baseline' is a deliberately naive jagged-matrix implementation built with LINQ that allocates the full (n+1)x(m+1) matrix (256 MB at 8000 characters), so the 20x figure is against a strawman; Fastenshtein (about 4.8x) and the library's own no-intrinsics path (about 5.8x) are the meaningful comparisons. The table's Ratio/Speedup columns are relative to the .NET 4.7.2 Baseline job, not the same-runtime baseline. ShortRun job with 3 iterations and 1 launch, so error bars are wide (Quickenshtein 8000 chars: error 3,559,513.67 ns). One synthetic string pair built by repeating 'aabcdecbaabcadbab' and 'babdacbaabcedcbaa'. Published numbers come from an older revision (.NET Core 5.0, BenchmarkDotNet 0.12.1); the current benchmark project targets net6.0 and net472 with BenchmarkDotNet 0.13.4 and Fastenshtein 1.0.0.8, so HEAD reproduces a different configuration. C# library, not C++.

name: simd-radix-sort (SIMD MSB radix sort with separate key and payload streams)
baseline: std::sort (STLSort in the thesis); thesis also compares Intel IPP Radix Sort, Bramas AVX-512 quicksort, Blacher AVX2 quicksort and Moeller's SIMD radix sort
workload: Sorting 2^18 elements, time per element, int32 keys with uniform distribution (also int32 key plus int32 payload, and double keys with Gaussian distribution), AVX-512 build.
claimed_speedup: Thesis Figure 8.16 (int32, Uniform): RadixSIMD 10.16 ns/element vs STLSort 41.87 ns/element (about 4.1x, derived from page data). Figure 8.17 (int32-int32): 11.19 vs 41.94 ns/element (about 3.7x, derived). Figure 8.18 (double, Gaussian): 16.33 vs 44.71 ns/element (about 2.7x, derived). Not the fastest: on int32 Uniform IPPRadix 5.55, BramasSort 3.62 and BlacherSort 2.45 ns/element are all faster than RadixSIMD.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 12.1.0 (thesis section 7.4); Makefile: -std=c++20 -O3 -mavx512f -mavx512bw -mavx512dq -mavx512vl -mavx512vbmi -mavx512vbmi2
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700K at 5 GHz, 32 GB RAM, Manjaro Linux kernel 5.17.15 (AVX-512 enabled; thesis notes Intel does not officially support AVX-512 on Alder Lake)
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and needs AVX-512 F/BW/DQ/VL/VBMI/VBMI2 (the single header must be compiled with those flags); C++20; generic over key and payload types; sorts keys and payload streams separately.
caveats: Bachelor's thesis benchmark (not peer reviewed) with the author's own harness (src/perf-thesis.cpp with src/sort_methods.hpp; results written to /tmp). STLSort is std::sort over DataElement structs with std::less; libstdc++ is implied by gcc 12.1.0 on Manjaro, not stated. The Makefile was edited after the thesis (commit 'Add warnings in Makefile', 2023-12-15), so the thesis-time flags are inferred from the current file. Timing uses CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID, averaged over max(1, 2^18/n) runs after warmup runs. The perf harness only checks sortedness (a separate test program checks keys and payloads). The cross-algorithm comparison covers only 2^18 elements. Not faster everywhere: in appendix B RadixSIMD is slower than std::sort in 19 of 56 key/distribution cases, including sorted, reverse-sorted and almost-sorted inputs for int32, int32-int32, float, float-int32 and double, and Zero/ZeroOne inputs with payloads or double keys (for example double Zero 14.37 vs 4.77 ns/element and int32 ReverseSorted 5.56 vs 3.02 ns/element). It is also slower than IPPRadix, BramasSort and BlacherSort on the headline cases; the thesis says most of its time is spent in the comparison sorter. The README says a quicksort variant performed about the same and was not published as a paper, and points to Intel x86-simd-sort as an equally generic alternative. AVX-512 is required (the i7-12700K had it enabled in the BIOS). The IPP rows need the proprietary Intel IPP library.

name: simd-sort (AVX2 and AVX-512F quicksort, Wojciech Mula)
baseline: std::sort (GCC toolchain; version not stated for the valid issue #8 run)
workload: Sorting uint32_t arrays of 10k to 20M elements (random() keys, ascending, descending); speed.cpp reports the minimum of N iterations. Valid random-input numbers come only from the issue #8 run with the in-place sorting bug fixed.
claimed_speedup: The repo's results/ files (GCC 5.3.0, 2016) print AVX2 quicksort 1.91x vs std::sort at 1M 'random' uint32 on i7-6700, but those runs sorted already-sorted data (harness bug, issues #7 and #8). With the harness fixed, a third party (issue #8 comment by bbqz007, 2022-01-22, Tiger Lake, CentOS 8, RDTSC cycles) measured on random input: the repo's qs::avx2::quicksort 0.84x of std::sort at 1M, 0.91x at 10M and 0.92x at 20M (slower); Daniel Lemire's 'AVX2 alt quicksort' in the same repo (avx2-altquicksort.h, wrapped_avx2_pivotonlast_sort) 1.61x at 1M, 1.82x at 10M and 1.85x at 20M; 'AVX2 nate nodutch' 1.23x at 1M and 1.36x at 10M; the repo's scalar quicksort about 0.68x to 0.71x. Ratios as printed in the comment. No valid AVX-512 random-input numbers exist.
compiler_and_flags: Repo results files: GCC 5.3.0, Makefile -std=c++11 -mbmi2 -mavx2 (or -mavx512f) -O3 -DNDEBUG, but those runs are invalid (presorted data). Issue #8 fixed-harness run: compiler and flags not stated.
hardware: Issue #8 valid run: Intel Tiger Lake (model not stated), CentOS 8. Invalid repo results: i7-6700, i7-4770, Xeon Phi 7210.
tradeoffs: x86 only; needs AVX2 or AVX-512F (and BMI2 for some variants); uint32_t keys only; no runtime dispatch; not stable; README calls the code unfinished.
caveats: Harness bug: PerformanceTest::run copies the input to tmp and then sorts input.pointer() in place, and all algorithms share one InputData, so after std::sort's first iteration every timed run sorted presorted data; the results/ 'random' and 'ascending' rows are the same within 1% for every algorithm on Skylake, Haswell and Knights Landing (std::sort 12.3 ms for 1M 'random' keys on an i7-6700 is a presorted-data time). Reported in issue #7 (2021) and issue #8 (2022), both still open; the 2017 fix for issue #5 only corrected a t1/t2 typo in the gettimeofday branch. Once fixed, the headline AVX2 quicksort is slower than std::sort on random data; only Lemire's alternative AVX2 quicksort (a file in this repo that its own comment calls 'not meant to be fast as such') and the nodutch variant win. The AVX-512 implementation was fixed on 2017-01-28, after the September 2016 Knights Landing results. Open issue #10 (2025) reports a never-ending loop and access violation in avx2-nate-quicksort.cpp; open issue #2 reports the AVX512+BMI2 variant failing on large inputs. Research code (README: 'still unfinished'), last commit 2017-11-22; superseded by x86-simd-sort and Highway vqsort, which are already catalogued.

The float32 table mixes runs (Variance/StdDev re-measured after fix #214 under a median-of-9 protocol, other rows from one earlier run) and its Variance/StdDev Go figures come from SIMD_DISABLE=all because those benchmarks have no Go sub-benchmark. name: Vectis
baseline: scalar C++ loop (and the same loop with four independent accumulators, and the same loop built with -ffast-math), as the reference for an AVX2 intrinsics/assembly dot-product kernel
workload: dot_f32 over n = 1024 floats, L1-resident, min of 21 runs, comparing scalar, scalar-4acc, intrinsics and hand-written GAS assembly twins with the same shape.
claimed_speedup: README 'The assembly verdict' table, dot_f32 at n = 1024 floats, L1-resident, min of 21 runs: scalar 1491 ns (4.92 cycles/element, 1.00x), scalar-4acc 679 ns (1.73 cycles/element, 2.05x), intrinsics 107 ns (0.338 cycles/element, 13.93x), asm 107 ns (0.333 cycles/element, 13.93x); against the four-accumulator scalar loop the vector kernels are about 6.3x faster (derived from page data). The README also states that the naive loop compiled with -ffast-math reaches 6.9x, but no benchmark in the repo measures that row (README text only). saxpy at n = 1024: asm 100 ns versus intrinsics 132 ns (1.28x), a small-n effect that disappears at DRAM sizes where asm sometimes loses (0.92x). SoA table (bench_soa.cpp): SoA vectorised 1.61x (n=8) and 1.37x (n=16) over AoS scalar at 28 KiB, 1.41x/1.28x at 448 KiB, 0.95x-0.96x at 7 MiB, 0.95x/0.87x at 112 MiB.

name: PQ Fast Scan
baseline: PQ Scan (product quantization distance scan with lookup tables in L1 cache; the project's own reference implementation, also with SSE, AVX and AVX gather variants)
workload: Nearest-neighbour scan of 8x8-bit product-quantized codes (ANN_SIFT100M1 split into 8 partitions of about 25M codes, ANN_SIFT1B queries): the distance lookup tables are kept in SIMD registers instead of the L1 cache and the results are exactly the same as PQ Scan.
claimed_speedup: README: 'PQ Fast Scan to perform 4-6x faster than PQ Scan, while returning the exact same results' (chart image not readable here). The README's sample pqfastscan output gives pq_us 75392 vs fast_pq_us 12272 (about 6.1x) and 74754 vs 17480 (about 4.3x) for two queries on a partition of 25,159,451 codes (derived from page data). PVLDB paper: 4-6x lower scan latency (search snippet only; the paper could not be opened).
compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.9.x ('we benchmarked it with this version only'); CMakeLists.txt: -std=c++11 -g -ggdb -O3 -m64 -march=native -ffast-math -Wall -Werror, AVX option ON, AVX2 option OFF
tradeoffs: Needs SSE2/SSE3/SSSE3 and POPCNT; relies on reorganising code lists, which prevents combining it with inverted indexes (README); Linux with libpfm4; best results only with g++ 4.9.
caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed PVLDB 9(4) paper (Andre, Kermarrec, Le Scouarnec; presented at VLDB 2016). The paper could not be opened (vldb.org blocked), so the 4-6x figure comes from the README and a search snippet. No reachable page gives a CPU model. The baseline is the authors' own scalar PQ Scan. In the README's pqscan output the SSE+prefetch (91214) and AVX+vgather+prefetch (97841) variants are slower than the scalar scan (74758), while AVX+prefetch (68490) is about 9% faster, so most of the gain comes from the register-resident lookup tables, not from vectorizing the plain scan. Builds use -march=native -ffast-math. The technique requires reorganizing the code lists (grouping), which the Quick ADC README says prevents combining it with inverted indexes, and it was tuned for 8x8-bit PQ codes on ANN_SIFT100M1 partitions. The datasets were generated with a commercially licensed libpq. Clear BSD has no patent grant and is not OSI-listed (permissive, treated as copyable).

name: Quick ADC
baseline: ADC (asymmetric distance computation in product quantization, lookup tables in L1 cache; the authors' scalar implementation)
workload: Nearest-neighbour search over product-quantized codes using 4-bit quantizers so lookup tables fit SIMD registers (AVX/AVX2 scan_avx_4), batches of 32 queries, with inverted-index support.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Quick ADC achieves 4-6x better performance than ADC by storing lookup tables in SIMD registers'. The README example on SIFT1M with an IVF index of 256 cells and ma=24 gives scan_us 86 for db_query_4 (16x4 OPQ, Recall@100 0.9426) vs 323 for db_query ADC (8x8 OPQ, Recall@100 0.9646), about 3.8x (derived from page data). Paper abstract (arXiv 1704.07355): a 3 to 6 times speedup over ADC (search snippet only).
compiler_and_flags: g++ 5.4 or newer; CMakeLists.txt: -std=c++14 -g -O3 -m64 -march=native -ffast-math -fopenmp -Wall -Werror; sequential (single-threaded) BLAS, OpenCV core, Cereal 1.2.2
hardware: Tested on Intel Haswell, Broadwell and Skylake processors (README); exact CPU model for the speedup chart not stated
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 (Haswell or newer); 4-bit quantizers cause 'a slight decrease in accuracy' (README says often negligible); builds on the same idea as PQ Fast Scan.
caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed ICMR 2017 paper cited in the README; the paper (ACM and arXiv) could not be opened here, so the figures come from the README and a search snippet (the abstract says 3-6x, the README 4-6x). The README example compares different quantizers (16x4 OPQ for Quick ADC vs 8x8 OPQ for ADC) at lower recall (0.9426 vs 0.9646), and Quick ADC scans a 'keep' fraction of codes without SIMD first, so the 3.8x example is not like for like. 4-bit quantizers cost some accuracy (the README calls it slight and often negligible). The baseline ADC is the authors' own scalar implementation. Tested on Intel Haswell, Broadwell and Skylake, but no CPU model is given for the published numbers. Builds use -march=native -ffast-math. Clear BSD has no patent grant and is not OSI-listed (permissive, treated as copyable).

name: ARM NEON Compositor
baseline: the same alpha-overlay routine without NEON intrinsics, compiled with GCC -O3
workload: overlay_alpha_stride (div255_round) on random square BGRA images, sides 1-200 px in steps of 1 (small) and 50-5000 px in 100 steps (large), called through Python ctypes by examples/perf_test/perf_test.py. Time per call is averaged over max_size*10/size iterations, one run per size. The NEON build is compared with the same library built with DISABLE_NEON (scalar fallback with GCC unroll/ivdep pragmas, left to GCC -O3 auto-vectorization).
claimed_speedup: README text: up to 3.5x faster than the same routine without NEON intrinsics for small images, and around 1.4x for very large images. From the committed CSVs (examples/perf_test/output, derived from page data): for square images of 1-200 px per side, 0.93x at 1 px (NEON slower), 1.40x at 33 px, 2.53x at 97 px and 3.47x at 200 px, with a maximum of 3.58x at 186 px; for 50-5000 px, 1.37-1.40x from 450 to 1650 px, rising to 1.54-1.59x from 2450 to 5000 px.
compiler_and_flags: GCC -O3 (version not stated)
hardware: Raspberry Pi 3B+, Ubuntu 20.04 64-bit
tradeoffs: ARM NEON only (AArch64 Raspberry Pi class); GPL-3.0 licence. Narrow function (alpha overlay), not a general SIMD library.
caveats: The baseline is the library's own non-NEON fallback (overlay_alpha_1 looped 8x under '#pragma GCC unroll 8' and 'ivdep'), not an external incumbent such as OpenCV. GCC version unstated, and the gain depends on how well that version auto-vectorizes the fallback. Timing runs from Python via ctypes, and both paths use '#pragma omp parallel for', so a fixed per-call overhead of about 20 us deflates the ratios below about 30 px (NEON is 0.93x at 1 px). It is not documented whether the committed .so files were built with OpenMP. Each size was run once with no variance reported. Raw data is public in examples/perf_test/output, and the prebuilt aarch64 and x86_64 .so files are committed.

name: fast-bernoulli (AVX Bernoulli sampler with LLVM JIT)
baseline: std::bernoulli_distribution<> drawing from std::mt19937_64, one draw per output bit packed into bytes (TStdSampler in fast-bernoulli/cc/sampler.cc)
workload: Google Benchmark BM_*Sampler/128 at p = 0.6 (tolerance 1e-3 for the fast samplers): fast samplers fill NoSrcBlocks x 128 blocks with mt19937_64 output and combine them with and/not into 128 blocks of 256 Bernoulli bits; the Std sampler fills 16x as many bits (524,288) one std::bernoulli_distribution draw per bit.
claimed_speedup: README Google Benchmark table (parameter 128, p = 0.6): BM_StdSampler 72,260,140 ns, BM_GenericSampler 104,076 ns, BM_AvxSampler 71,017 ns, BM_JitAvxSampler 55,667 ns. The raw time ratios (1017x AVX, 1298x JIT AVX) compare unequal work: BM_StdSampler allocates and fills 16 * 128 * 32 bytes = 524,288 bits per iteration while the other samplers produce 128 blocks of 256 bits = 32,768 bits. Per output bit: Std about 138 ns, AVX about 2.17 ns, JIT AVX about 1.70 ns, i.e. about 64x (AVX), 81x (JIT AVX) and 43x (generic, no SIMD) faster than std::bernoulli_distribution (derived from page data and sampler_bench.cc). The throughput column is bytes/s in both rows (55.4 KiB/s vs 55.0 MiB/s), computed from the same 4096 bytes per iteration, so it repeats the 16x error.
compiler_and_flags: README build: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, C++17, library objects compiled with -mavx -mavx2, optional LLVM 8/9 JIT; compiler and version not stated
hardware: 4 x 3400 MHz CPUs, L1d 32K, L2 256K, L3 4096K (Google Benchmark header); model not stated
tradeoffs: Returns bit-packed blocks rather than bools; probability is quantised into a sequence of AND and NOT operations; uses AVX vectors and optional LLVM JIT; Python bindings.
caveats: The benchmark gives BM_StdSampler 16x more bits per iteration than the fast samplers (size = 16 * noblocks * GetBufferSize()), so the README's raw ~1000x time gap is about 64x per bit (43x for the non-SIMD generic sampler, so most of the win is the algorithm's fewer RNG draws per bit, not AVX). The fast samplers are approximate: the probability is quantised to within the 1e-3 tolerance. The Std baseline ORs bits into a buffer that is never cleared (*it |= ...), so its output is wrong after the first call (timing barely affected). BM_JitGenericSampler calls the non-JIT BM_Sampler, so that row is not JIT (its time matches the generic row). In the current tree the JIT benchmarks sit under a misspelled #ifdef USE_JIT_EXCUTOR while CMake defines USE_JIT_EXECUTOR, so HEAD cannot reproduce the JIT rows; the README table came from the October 2019 src/ layout, which had the same 16x factor. name: faster (Rust SIMD iterators)
baseline: scalar Rust iterators
workload: cargo bench over a 1024-element f32 array filled with -123.456 (benches/usage.rs). map_scalar computes 9*sqrt(ceil(recip(sqrt(sqrt(abs(v))))))-4-2 per element and collects into a Vec; map_simd computes 9*sqrt(ceil(rsqrt(sqrt(abs(v)))))-4-2 with faster's rsqrt, which on x86 is the approximate _mm256_rsqrt_ps/_mm_rsqrt_ps instruction, then scalar_collect. Built for ivybridge (AVX), x86-64 (SSE2) and pentium (polyfill only) targets on an Ivy Bridge host.
claimed_speedup: README (author's 'extremely unscientific' cargo bench runs on an Ivy Bridge host): target-cpu=ivybridge (AVX): map_scalar 6,963 ns/iter vs map_simd 879 ns/iter (about 7.9x, derived from page data); reduce_scalar 6,905 vs reduce_simd 839 ns/iter (about 8.2x, derived from page data); target-cpu=x86-64 (SSE2): map 7,237 vs 1,879 ns/iter (about 3.9x, derived from page data); target-cpu=pentium (polyfills only): map 7,195 vs 6,271 ns/iter (about 1.15x, derived from page data). Some rows are slower with SIMD: zip_simd 1,128 vs zip_scalar 901 ns/iter on the AVX target; bench_determinant3_simd 593 vs 354 ns/iter and bench_nop_simd 69 vs 38 ns/iter on the pentium target.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench (Cargo.toml profile.release opt-level = 3) with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=ivybridge' / 'x86-64' / 'pentium'; requires a nightly rustc (src/lib.rs uses #![feature(stdsimd)] and #![feature(test)]), version not stated
hardware: host is ivybridge (only stated in README comments); exact CPU model not given
tradeoffs: Iterator-style SIMD abstraction for Rust with polyfills for CPUs lacking the target feature; depends on packed_simd_2 (nightly-era API). Not usable from C++ without FFI.
caveats: The README calls its own benchmarks 'extremely unscientific'; single host named only as Ivy Bridge, rustc nightly version unstated. Unequal kernels: the SIMD map and reduce benchmarks call faster's rsqrt, which on x86 is the approximate _mm256_rsqrt_ps/_mm_rsqrt_ps (the trait documents significant error past 1e-3), while the scalar baseline does an exact sqrt().recip(), i.e. one extra sqrt and a division per element; the ceil() in the chain hides the approximation for the constant input -123.456, so results match, but part of the 7.9x comes from cheaper math rather than SIMD width alone. The input is a constant-filled 1024-element array. Some SIMD rows are slower than scalar (zip_simd on AVX, determinant3 and nop on the pentium polyfill target). The crate never built on stable Rust: it needs nightly with #![feature(stdsimd)] and packed_simd_2; the stdsimd feature gate was later removed from nightly, so it likely does not build on current toolchains (not built here). Last commit 2021-03-25; abandoned.

name: intel-intrinsics (inteli, SIMD library for D)
baseline: Phobos std.digest.sha sha256Of (scalar D standard-library SHA-256)
workload: SHA-256 of a 1,024,000-byte buffer (512 * 2000 bytes of 'a'), repeated 1000 times, comparing std.digest.sha sha256Of against a SHA-NI implementation written with inteli intrinsics (examples/sha256/source/main.d); both print elapsed microseconds and the digest.
claimed_speedup: README: '18x faster SHA-256 vs Phobos' with intel-intrinsics; separately cites a 3.5x speed-up for some particular loops in a DConf 2019 talk and dg2d renderer 'twice as fast as Cairo' (unmeasured on the page).
compiler_and_flags: LDC; examples/sha256/dub.json sets dflags-ldc ["-mattr=+sha,+sse4.2,+popcnt"] and no build type (dub builds in debug mode unless --build=release is passed); LDC version and the build command used for the 18x figure are not stated.
stars_or_usage: 73 stars; used by Auburn Sounds and Cut Through Recordings audio products, dg2d and PixelPerfectEngine
tradeoffs: D language only (usable from C++ only by calling D code through a C ABI). Provides the Intel intrinsics API (MMX to AVX2, F16C, BMI2) with one syntax across LDC, DMD and GDC and emulates it on AArch64 and 32-bit ARM. Project states semantics are preserved even at the cost of speed. SHA-NI benchmark needs a CPU with SHA extensions. ARM differences: MXCSR emulated through FPCR, masked loads and stores need padded buffers.
caveats: The 18x figure is a README claim without hardware, compiler version, build type or timing output; the benchmark source prints times but the repo does not record results. dub.json sets no buildType, so a plain 'dub run' builds debug; both sides are templates compiled with the same flags, but the ratio depends on the unstated build mode. Baseline is Phobos' portable SHA-256 (std/digest/sha.d uses transformSHA2 for SHA-256; its SSSE3 assembly path covers SHA-1 only), not an optimised library such as OpenSSL, and the fast path relies on dedicated SHA-NI instructions rather than generic SIMD, so the ratio reflects hardware offload as much as the library. On Windows the example's getTickUs defaults to QueryThreadCycleTime scaled by the QPC frequency, which its own comment calls unreliable; both rows use the same timer, so the ratio is unaffected but the printed microseconds may be wrong. Example code is derived from the Crypto++ SHA-SIMD reference (Walton, Blumenthal, Raad) by Johan Engelen (public domain). Claims for dg2d versus Cairo and the 3.5x DConf 2019 talk figure have no numbers on the page and are not part of this entry's tier. Licence file is named COPYING (BSL-1.0, also declared in dub.json). D language, not C++.

name: IntrinsicML (hand-vectorized SIMD microkernels for ML)
baseline: plain triple-loop scalar C++ reference (GCC -O3 -ffast-math); also OpenBLAS sgemm single thread (where it is slower)
workload: Single-precision GEMM (packed AVX2/AVX-512 kernel) at 64x64 to 512x512, and GeLU on 1M elements, single core.
claimed_speedup: README table (approximate, 'this environment', no backing table): packed SGEMM vs a plain triple-loop scalar reference about 0.7x at 64x64 (slower), about 10x at 128, about 26x at 256; vs single-thread OpenBLAS about 4%, 29%, 55%, 59% of its speed at 64-512. docs/BENCHMARKS.md CI run (main_bench, avx_matmul kernel vs scalar): 0.069 vs 0.017 ms at 64 (4.1x), 1.114 vs 0.162 ms at 128 (6.9x), 20.88 vs 2.006 ms at 256 (10.4x) (derived from page data); OpenBLAS table 6.4 vs 165.0 GFLOPS at 64 up to 73.8 vs 124.0 at 1024. GeLU: the README's 6-10x is the author's expected speedup on platforms without SVML; the measured CI run shows AVX2 tanh GeLU and the erff reference within 2% of each other (1,908,062 vs 1,939,830 cycles at n = 1M).
compiler_and_flags: docs/BENCHMARKS.md: GCC-12, -O3 -march=native -mfma -ffast-math -DNDEBUG, Ubuntu 22.04 (CMakeLists.txt PERF_FLAGS); README states both kernel and scalar reference built with -O3 -ffast-math
hardware: Virtualised x86-64 CI runner with AVX2+FMA, about 2.1 GHz calibrated TSC, exact model varies (docs/BENCHMARKS.md)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 + FMA (AVX-512 kernel auto-dispatched); educational middle ground between textbook loops and production BLAS; Python bindings via pybind11.
caveats: Slower than OpenBLAS at every size (4% to 60% of its single-thread throughput) and, per the README, slower than the scalar loop at 64x64. The baseline is a textbook i-j-p triple loop that walks B with stride N (naive_gemm.hpp), whose throughput falls from 7.6 to 1.6 GFLOPS between 64 and 256, so the 10x-26x figures are against a straw-man scalar loop. The README speedups are rounded figures not traceable to any committed table; docs/BENCHMARKS.md shows 4x-10x for the avx_matmul path, and the bench_stat harness that times the packed kernel has no scalar row. The GeLU 6-10x is an expectation for non-SVML platforms; measured, the AVX2 tanh approximation equals glibc's SVML-vectorised erff (1.02x), and the two compute different formulas. The main_bench 'GElems/s' column is a FLOP proxy (15 ops per element), about 15x the true element rate. Numbers come from noisy shared CI VMs with no CPU model, and OpenBLAS's 165 GFLOPS at N=64 exceeds the stated 2.1 GHz peak, so the utilisation percentages are unreliable. The Zenodo preprint was not opened (zenodo blocked).

name: ISPC (Intel SPMD Program Compiler)
baseline: reference serial C++ implementations of the examples/ workloads (gcc 4.2.1 on OS X 10.7.2; MSVC 2010 on Windows Server 2008 for the 40-core table)
workload: The example programs in the repo's examples/ directory (aobench, binomial and Black-Scholes options pricing, Mandelbrot, ray tracer, 3D stencil, volume rendering; perf page adds deferred shading and Perlin noise), each timed against its included serial C++ reference (minimum of several runs; the examples print '(N.NNx speedup from ISPC)').
claimed_speedup: InPar 2012 paper Table 2 (4-core 3.4 GHz Core i7 iMac, 8-wide AVX), versus serial non-SIMD C++: 1 core / 1 thread aobench 5.58x, Binomial Options 4.39x, Black-Scholes 7.43x, Mandelbrot 5.85x, Ray Tracer 6.85x, Stencil 3.37x, Volume Rendering 3.24x (geomean about 5.0x, derived from page data); 4 cores / 8 threads 12.03x-34.82x. Table 3 (40-core Xeon E7-8870, SSE4, 80 threads, MSVC 2010 serial baseline): 9.40x-243.18x. SSE to AVX geomean 1.42x. README: 'frequently provides a 3x or more speedup on architectures with 4-wide vector SSE units and 5x-6x on architectures with 8-wide AVX vector units'. ispc.github.io/perf.html (gcc 4.2.1 serial baseline on the same iMac): 1 core 3.60x-8.45x, 4 cores 15.53x-33.43x.
compiler_and_flags: ispc of 2011-2012 (built on LLVM); serial C++ baseline compiled with clang built from the same LLVM (paper notes gcc gave essentially the same results); 40-core runs used MSVC 2010; perf page used gcc 4.2.1 (OS X 10.7.2). Optimization flags not stated.
hardware: 4-core 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7 Apple iMac with AVX (exact model not stated; first-generation AVX, Sandy Bridge era) for Table 2 and the perf page; 2-way hyper-threaded 40-core Intel Xeon E7-8870 at 2.40 GHz with SSE4 on Windows Server 2008 for Table 3.
tradeoffs: A separate SPMD language and compiler (outputs object files callable from C/C++) rather than an intrinsics library; targets x86 SSE2/SSE4/AVX/AVX2/AVX-512, ARM NEON and Intel GPUs. Examples are in the repo's examples/ directory.
caveats: Evidence is from ISPC's Intel authors: a peer-reviewed paper (InPar 2012) plus Intel's perf page, both measured around 2011-2012 on first-generation AVX and SSE4 hardware with an unnamed Core i7 model, unstated flags and an unstated ispc version; nothing newer is published. The baseline is serial non-SIMD C++ (both versions 'received equivalent amounts of performance tuning'), not hand-written intrinsics or SIMD libraries (Highway, xsimd); the paper gives only user anecdotes for intrinsics parity (0.99x-1.05x). Multi-core figures combine task parallelism and hyper-threading with SIMD. ispc is a compiler for an SPMD C dialect, not an intrinsics library, so the category fit is loose. The ispc.github.io perf page was read from its source in the ispc/ispc.github.com repo (github.io blocked here).

name: java-fast/quad-search
baseline: java.util.Arrays.binarySearch
workload: Quaternary narrowing over 16-element block boundaries, then a Vector API (jdk.incubator.vector, SPECIES_PREFERRED) block scan, versus Arrays.binarySearch over sorted, strictly increasing int arrays of 4k to 1m elements (array count shrinks from 256k to 1k as size grows, about 4 GB of data per run). Cold-cache runs switch arrays on every query; warm-cache runs reuse each array for 128 consecutive queries (README says 100). Queries are uniform in [0, 8n) while array values average 4.5n, so about 44% of queries lie beyond the last element. JMH sample mode on Oracle JDK and GraalVM.
claimed_speedup: README: 'outperform Arrays.binarySearch by up to 25% on Oracle JDK, up to 16% on GraalVM on Apple M4 ARM64 (Neon 128-bit)' and 'up to 24% on Oracle JDK, up to 29% on GraalVM on x86-64 AMD (AVX2 256-bit)'; 'p99 values are better than default binary search almost in all test cases'. The percentages are reductions in mean ns/op of simdQuadSearch versus binarySearchDefault and match the best single result files: arm64 Oracle 4k warm 32.540 vs 24.496 ns/op (24.7%), arm64 GraalVM 64k cold 240.503 vs 201.196 (16.3%), amd64 Oracle 16k warm 202.130 vs 153.170 (24.2%), amd64 GraalVM 8k cold 659.617 vs 466.574 (29.3%, about 1.41x) (derived from page data). docs/results/amd64 Oracle JDK 1m cold: binarySearchDefault 1192.757 ns/op, quadSearch 1020.096 ns/op, simdQuadSearch 1053.785 ns/op (about 12% less time for the SIMD variant, derived from page data). Typical gains across the 72 files are 5 to 15%.
compiler_and_flags: Java 25 toolchain (Oracle JDK and GraalVM; exact builds not stated), JMH 1.37 via the me.champeau.jmh 0.7.3 Gradle plugin, Mode.SampleTime, 3 forks, 5 x 2 s warmup, 10 x 2 s measurement; JVM args --add-modules=jdk.incubator.vector --enable-preview -Xms12g -Xmx12g -XX:+UseG1GC (build.gradle); run-benchmarks.sh sweeps the nine sizes for both benchmarks
hardware: Apple M4 (arm64, NEON 128-bit) and an unnamed x86-64 AMD CPU with AVX2 (model not stated in the README, the results files or docs/index.html)
tradeoffs: Needs --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector (incubator module); int arrays only; same return semantics as Arrays.binarySearch.
caveats: Gains are modest (about 10 to 29%). In the 1m cold sample file the non-SIMD quadSearch variant beat the SIMD variant, so the win comes mostly from quaternary narrowing and cache behaviour rather than SIMD. Idea credited to a Daniel Lemire blog post. CPU models are not stated, so tier C although JMH files are in the repo.
