name: kelindar/simd
baseline: generic pure-Go implementation inside the same package
workload: Element-wise add/sub/mul/div and sum/min/max reductions on uint8..uint64, int8..int64, float32 and float64 slices of 256, 4096 and 16384 elements filled with the repeating pattern (i % 100) + 1; the baseline is the package's own generic scalar Go loop (selected by setting hardware=false), the fast path is clang auto-vectorized C translated to Plan9 assembly (AVX2 on amd64, NEON on arm64).
claimed_speedup: README tables on an i7-13700K: uint8 sum 16384 elements 52.57x, uint8 min 4096 55.02x, uint16 min 16384 84.12x, uint32 sum 16384 10.07x, uint32 add 16384 5.06x, uint8 div 4096 1.19x, uint16 div 16384 0.79x (slower). An Apple M3 Pro table is also given.
compiler_and_flags: Go version for the README runs not stated (go.mod declares go 1.18; CI uses Go 1.25); assembly generated from C by gocc (clang) with -O3 and --arch avx2 / neon / apple per codegen/generate.sh; default go test -bench settings; the SPEEDUP column is base-mode ns/op divided by simd-mode ns/op from runBenchmark in simd_test.go
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i7-13700K (Windows, amd64) and Apple M3 Pro (darwin, arm64)
tradeoffs: AVX2 on amd64 and NEON on arm64 only; generic Go fallback otherwise; README lists reductions (Sum, Min, Max) and element-wise Add, Sub, Mul, Div; the Div rows show about 1x.
caveats: Many rows exceed 50x (uint16 min 16384 84.12x, int8 min/max 16384 about 68.7x on the i7-13700K; uint8 max 4096 65.16x on the M3 Pro) against a hand-written scalar Go loop, not slices.Min or the min/max builtins; Go's compiler does not auto-vectorize, so the ratio mostly measures clang vectorization versus scalar Go, on L1/L2-resident data. Division gives about 1x and is slower in several rows (uint16 div 16384 0.79x, int8 div 0.69x to 0.71x on the i7-13700K). The SIMD path takes &input[0] without length checks, so an empty slice panics, and Add/Sub/Mul/Div pass len(dst) to the assembly without checking input1/input2, so shorter inputs are read out of bounds. Capped at C because the Go version is not stated.

With the driver's default KFAST_multithread = true this is multi-threaded KFAST against single-threaded OpenCV and Rosten code. No single-threaded measurement is shown for the 60% figure; the main.cpp header instead says '40-60% single-threaded or 500% multi-threaded' over 'the reference implementation'.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: g++ (version not stated) with -Ofast -std=gnu++17 -march=native -mavx2 -mfma -flto -funroll-all-loops -fpeel-loops -ftracer -ftree-vectorize -fomit-frame-pointer; Rosten's C is built with gcc and the same flags; OpenCV is the system library (version and build flags not stated). The screenshot looks like a Windows console, so the measured build may have been MSVC; this is not stated.

caveats: The headline 5.1x ('500%') compares multi-threaded KFAST with single-threaded cv::FAST and single-threaded scalar Rosten code; the single-threaded 60% claim has no published measurement. One image, one threshold, no CPU model, no compiler version, OpenCV version unknown. The screenshot was added on Sep 12, 2016, before the Oct 2016 'horizontal AVX shuffle' performance commit and before PR #2 (Jan 2019), which fixed an off-by-one in the main column loop (j < cols - 35 instead of cols - 34) that let last_cols_mask = (1 << 32) - 1 overflow; the maintainer said this undefined shift fails to catch any corners in the last 32 columns for affected image widths. The measured image passed the driver's equality check, so the shown run was not affected. Requires AVX2 with no fallback. Last code changes 2016 to January 2019; the 2021 commit only adds the MIT LICENSE; the Rosten folder is BSD-3-Clause. It is a computer-vision kernel rather than a general SIMD library.

name: Leftpack (komrad36)
baseline: naive scalar left-pack loop (branchy, 'super naive') and branchless naive scalar loop, both listed in the README
workload: AVX2 left-pack (compress) of one 256-bit vector per call (32 8-bit, 16 16-bit, 8 32-bit or 4 64-bit elements), driven by an integer bitmask or a vector mask; needs AVX2 plus BMI2 (PDEP/PEXT) and POPCNT, with *_Zen2 variants that avoid PDEP/PEXT for AMD Zen1/Zen2.
claimed_speedup: README 'Approx. speedup vs. naive methods': 8-bit 39x versus super naive and 5.3x versus branchless naive; 16-bit 31x and 3.8x; 32-bit 14x and 2.2x; 64-bit 7.8x and 1.6x. README also says it beats the AVX-512 VCOMPRESS instructions for the bitmask case (no number given).
compiler_and_flags: README: supports clang, gcc and MSVC, and its simple correctness tests (test.cpp) were exercised on all three; no compiler versions, flags or CPU are given for the speedup table, and the repo has no benchmark code.
tradeoffs: x86 AVX2 (8-bit and 32-bit versions use BMI2 PDEP/PEXT, very slow on AMD Zen 1 and Zen 2, so alternative slightly slower implementations are provided); header leftpack.h with test.cpp.
caveats: First-party table only. The repo holds leftpack.h and test.cpp, and test.cpp checks every mask exhaustively against the branchless scalar loop for correctness but times nothing, so the speedups cannot be reproduced from public code. No CPU, compiler, flags, input size or mask distribution are stated. The 'super naive' branchy loop mispredicts on random masks, so the 39x end flatters the result; the branchless loop (1.6x to 5.3x) is the fairer scalar baseline. The claim that it beats AVX-512 VCOMPRESS has no numbers. Every call writes a full 32 bytes at pOut whatever the kept count, so the caller must provide slack. The PDEP/PEXT versions are very slow on Zen1/Zen2. Last commit 2023-10-04, three years and one week before the run date.

The README also shows a positional-popcount table (up to 138.71x at 65536 values for pospopcnt_u16_avx512_harvey_seal), but those numbers are identical to the mklarqvist/positional-popcount README (measured there with gcc 7.3.1) and are not produced by libalgebra's benchmark.cpp.

name: math_intrinsics
baseline: C standard library scalar float math functions (acosf, asinf, atanf, cbrtf, cosf, sinf, expf, exp2f, logf, log2f); libc and compiler not stated
workload: tests/benchmark.c (README run matches commit a9e8fe5, NUM_ITERATIONS 1,000,000,000; current code uses 200,000,000): the AVX2 loop evaluates 8 independent lanes starting at 0..0.875 and stepping by FLT_EPSILON (inputs stay in about [0, 2]); the C std loop calls acosf/asinf/atanf/cbrtf/cosf/sinf/expf/exp2f/logf/log2f through a function pointer in a serial dependency chain total += f(total), seeded with the SIMD time in ms.
claimed_speedup: AVX2 vs C std: acos 723.7 ms vs 5408.2 ms (7.47x), asin 7.83x, atan 5.13x, cbrt 12.84x, cos 17.62x, sin 18.14x, exp 5.30x, exp2 2.06x, log 16.51x, log2 7.50x. The __MATH_INTRINSINCS_FAST__ mode adds roughly 1.4x to 1.9x for sin, cos, acos, asin, exp2 and pow.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -mavx2 -mfma for the benchmark targets (tests/CMakeLists.txt, non-MSVC); compiler of the README run not stated (CI builds with clang on ubuntu-latest and the default compiler on macos-latest)
hardware: old Intel Core i7 from 2018 (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Single header; AVX2 (x86) and NEON (checked manually on an M1 Pro, not in CI); float only; max errors around 1e-7 for most functions, up to 6.5e-5 for acos/asin in fast mode. Author states performance is not the focus.
caveats: Baseline harness is not like-for-like: the SIMD side is a throughput loop over 8 independent lanes with inputs in about [0, 2], while the libm side is a latency-bound serial chain total += f(total) seeded with the SIMD time in milliseconds (README run, commit a9e8fe5), so acosf/asinf received |x|>1 and then NaN for the whole run, expf/exp2f overflowed to +inf after the first call and sinf/cosf ran on arguments near 880 (current code seeds with seconds, but log2f still drops to NaN and acosf/asinf still leave the domain after one or two calls). The 2.06x-18.14x ratios are therefore not a valid measure of speed against libm. Compiler, libm (glibc or Apple) and CPU model of the README run are not stated ('old Intel Core i7 from 2018'). The author writes 'Performance is not the focus.' The benchmark source is tests/benchmark.c (not visible in the repo root). Fast-mode gains (~1.4x-1.9x for sin, cos, acos, asin, exp2, pow) are against the library's own precise mode. No comparison with SLEEF or xsimd math (both catalogued).

name: ParallelReductionsBenchmark
baseline: std::accumulate (serial)
workload: Summing a 1 GB array (268,435,456 floats, all set to 1.0f by std::fill_n) with serial std::accumulate, an 8-accumulator unrolled loop, hand-written SSE/AVX2/AVX-512, NEON and SVE kernels, OpenMP, fork_union, Taskflow, std::reduce with execution policies, Thrust, CUB and CUDA kernels, reported in bytes/s with an error% column against the exact sum n.
claimed_speedup: Single thread versus serial std::accumulate (libstdc++, GCC 12), 1 GB array of 1.0f, README tables. AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl: unrolled/f64 14.7387 GB/s vs std::accumulate/f64 5.58465 GB/s (about 2.6x, derived from page data, both exact); unrolled/f32 28.2311 GB/s, neon/f32 22.2544 GB/s and sve/f32 21.4542 GB/s vs std::accumulate/f32 5.58767 GB/s (about 5.1x, 4.0x and 3.8x, derived from page data). AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl: unrolled<f64> 34.0189 GB/s and avx2<f64> 19.3258 GB/s vs std::accumulate<f64> 4.88389 GB/s (about 7.0x and 4.0x, derived from page data, exact); unrolled<f32> 35.1514, avx2<f32> 33.3195 and avx512<f32interleaving> 26.8351 GB/s vs std::accumulate<f32> 4.88655 GB/s (about 7.2x, 6.8x and 5.5x, derived from page data); avx2<f32kahan> 9.73619 GB/s, exact, about 2.0x std::accumulate (derived from page data). Nvidia DGX-H100 host: avx2<f32> 9.69112 vs std::accumulate<f32> 5.5322 GB/s (about 1.75x, derived from page data). Multithreaded std::reduce<par> (368.528 GB/s on Zen4, 550.384 GB/s on Graviton4) is libstdc++'s own parallel algorithm on oneTBB, not this repository's code.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12 (NVCC 12.1 for the CUDA rows); CMakeLists.txt defaults to Release and appends -O2 to CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE (effective -O2) and sets -march=native -fopenmp for GCC; the Apple M2 Pro table names no compiler
hardware: AWS Graviton4 (c8g.metal-24xl, 96 cores), AWS m7a.metal-48xl (AMD Zen4, 192 threads at 3701.95 MHz; CPU model string not printed), Nvidia DGX-H100 node (160 threads at 2100 MHz; CPU model not named), Apple M2 Pro
tradeoffs: Educational benchmark harness rather than a drop-in library. Hand-written AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels are x86 only; NEON and SVE variants exist for Arm. Huge pages, NUMA and Kahan summation are handled by hand.
caveats: This is an educational benchmark collection, not a reusable library, and it has no LICENSE file (raw LICENSE returns 404, no licence in the GitHub sidebar or Cargo.toml), so it is reference only. The baseline is std::accumulate, whose required left-to-right fold is latency-bound on the float add chain at -O2 without -ffast-math; most of the gain comes from reassociation with multiple accumulators, and no single-threaded std::reduce (or unseq) row is measured, which is the standard library's own reassociating alternative. Hand-written intrinsics do not beat the plain unrolled C++ loop in most tables: on Zen4 avx2<f32> 33.32, avx2<f64> 19.33 and avx512<f32interleaving> 26.84 GB/s are all below unrolled<f32> 35.15 / unrolled<f64> 34.02 GB/s, and on Graviton4 neon/f32 22.25 and sve/f32 21.45 GB/s are below unrolled/f32 28.23 GB/s, contradicting the README's statement that hand-written AVX2 beats auto-vectorization (it holds only on the DGX-H100 host). All f32 rows give wrong sums because the input is 2^28 ones and each f32 accumulator saturates at 2^24 (std::accumulate<f32> 93.75% error, unrolled<f32> 50%, neon/sve 75%); only f64 and Kahan rows are exact, and avx2<f32kahan> is about 2x std::accumulate on Zen4. The DGX-H100 table's std::reduce<par, f64> and <par_unseq, f64> rows report 100% error. The Zen4 and DGX tables use older row labels and predate the 2025 code. Single hand-pasted runs with no variance. The README's own conclusion is that multithreaded std::reduce is the CPU winner. [retier] Three kernels in current main return wrong sums on non-uniform data; Zen4 1 GB AVX-512 rows measured by pre-fix kernels that read half the array; no licence file
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/sve (C++ list) surfaced the repo; README result tables for DGX-H100 and AWS Zen4 read directly

name: PTMS (Parallel Tournament Merge Sort)
baseline: std::sort (1 thread) and tbb::parallel_sort
workload: Sorting 4,000,000 uniform random ints in [-1e6, 1e6] (fixed seed) with OpenMP tasks, parallel merging and AVX2/AVX-512 bitonic base cases; median of 600 timed runs after 400 warm-ups, with the input re-copied outside the timer before each run, at 16 threads on the 6900HX (AVX2 path, since that CPU lacks AVX-512).
claimed_speedup: Median seconds: std::sort 0.300 (1.00x), tbb::parallel_sort 0.036 (8.30x), PTMS 0.0163 (about 18.4x versus std::sort; about 2.2x versus tbb::parallel_sort, derived from page data). On a Ryzen 7 7500F with AVX-512: median 0.0162 s at 12 threads.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated (README lists GCC 9+, Clang 10+, MSVC 2019+ via clang-cl). CMakeLists.txt defaults to a Release build and, for GCC/Clang, adds -O3 and -march=native (SIMD=AUTO) plus OpenMP with -std=c++17; MSVC gets /O2 with /arch:AVX2 or /arch:AVX512.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 6900HX (16 threads); AMD Ryzen 7 7500F (AVX-512, 12 threads)
tradeoffs: Int (sort_int) only, needs a caller-supplied scratch buffer, OpenMP tasks (MSVC needs clang-cl), AVX2 or AVX-512 base cases selectable with -DSIMD; benchmark program in the benchmark/ folder.
caveats: The baseline rows cannot be reproduced. benchmark/benchmark.cpp times only PTMS, with no std::sort or tbb::parallel_sort code anywhere and no TBB link in CMakeLists.txt. The PTMS timer wraps ptms::detail::sort_body inside an OpenMP parallel region that is already open, with a preallocated scratch buffer, so it leaves out the parallel-region start-up the public ptms::sort_int pays on each call. The headline 18.4x compares 16 threads with one-thread std::sort; the like-for-like result is about 2.2x over tbb::parallel_sort (CITATION.cff says '~2x on cache-resident data'). The 'cache-resident' label is doubtful: the 16 MB input plus a 16 MB scratch buffer is 32 MB on a CPU with 16 MB of L3. The same input is re-sorted 1000 times. One size, int keys only, compiler unstated; the Ryzen 7 7500F AVX-512 figure (0.0162 s at 12 threads) has no baseline numbers. The repo is brand new with no external verification, and the LICENSE and CITATION.cff say 2025 (author Andrey Afimov) although the first commit is 2026-10-10. It is a parallel sort more than a SIMD library and would fit the wave-1 sorting category, where std::sort is the listed baseline.

name: qHilbert
baseline: Wikipedia d2xy/rot C implementation (in source/qHilbert.cpp), called once per index from tests/benchmark.cpp; the README table does not label it
workload: tests/benchmark.cpp: map all 16,384 indices of an order-7 (128x128) Hilbert curve to 2D points, 10 trials averaged with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock, output checked against d2xy (PASS/FAIL). qHilbert2D uses the Hacker's Delight (Lam-Shapiro/Steele) parallel-prefix method, with pext under BMI2 and SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512 paths.
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt: -Ofast -Wall -Wextra on the GCC branch, plus -mbmi2 / -msse4.2 / -mavx2 / -mavx512f per Benchmark-* executable; compiler and version not stated

caveats: The table's baseline (Wikipedia d2xy, branchy loop with one cross-translation-unit call per point and no LTO) is not labelled on the README; it is identified from tests/benchmark.cpp. Most of the gain is algorithmic (Hacker's Delight parallel-prefix rewrite): the Serial/BMI2 column is already x42.5 on i9-7900x, AVX-512 adds about 1.19x over it (derived from page data), and AVX2 is slower than SSE4.2 on E5-2697 v4. In the public CMakeLists.txt the per-target ISA flags are PRIVATE to the Benchmark-* executables (tests/benchmark.cpp) and do not reach the qHilbert static library (source/qHilbert.cpp) that holds the SIMD paths, so a build as written runs the same generic serial code in every target; the flags actually used for the table's columns are not public. Each trial is only 16,384 points (microsecond-scale timing). Compiler not stated. 2018 numbers; repo abandoned since 2018-12-31.

name: recip_rsqrt_benchmark (fast vectorized reciprocal and rsqrt)
baseline: the repo's own 'ieee' variants in routines_sse.h: _mm_div_ps(1, x) and _mm_div_ps(1, _mm_sqrt_ps(x)) (and the _pd forms), i.e. the divps/sqrtps instructions a compiler emits for 1.0f/x and 1.0f/sqrtf(x)
workload: Vectorized 1/x and 1/sqrt(x) on __m128 (4 floats) or __m128d (2 doubles; the fast double variants convert to float and use rcpps/rsqrtps) over about 33.5M float and 16.8M double test values (an exhaustive 1.0 to 2.0 range plus exp2 of uniform(-20, 20)); each value is passed through the function 4 times in 4 interleaved streams; rdtsc cycles per call and maximal relative error against the div/sqrt variant.
claimed_speedup: README sample results (float4): recip ieee 7.30 cycles vs fast 1.13 (about 6.5x, max error 3.0e-4) vs nr1 3.69 (about 2.0x, error 1.47e-7); rsqrt ieee 14.46 vs fast 1.12 (about 12.9x, error 3.3e-4) vs nr1 5.52 (about 2.6x, error 3.1e-7); double2 rsqrt ieee 28.21 vs fast 3.38 (about 8.3x) (ratios derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2013 C++ compiler, x64 mode (README); optimisation flags not stated and no project or build file in the repo; later commits fixed compilation on GCC (2015) and MSVC 2017 (2018)
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (Ivy Bridge)
stars_or_usage: 11 stars; tied to a Stack Overflow answer
tradeoffs: Approximate results (error trade-off listed per variant); SSE on x86 only; benchmark of approximate rcpps/rsqrtps tricks rather than a packaged library.
caveats: No licence file, so reference only. Results are from July 2015 on Ivy Bridge with MSVC 2013; newer CPUs have much faster divps and sqrtps (general knowledge, not from the page), so the gap is likely smaller today. The README describes the metric as throughput (cycles per call), not latency; the harness chains 4 calls per stream over 4 independent streams, so it mixes latency and throughput, and rdtsc counts reference cycles rather than core cycles. The fast variants trade accuracy (max relative error about 3e-4 without refinement, about 1.5e-7 to 3e-7 with one Newton-Raphson step), so they are not drop-in replacements for exact division; the 'ieee' rsqrt reference is div plus sqrt (two roundings), not a correctly rounded rsqrt. The baseline is the authors' own exact variant in the same harness. Tied to a Stack Overflow question (31555260).

name: SIMD-math-prims (vectorizable approximate sin, cos, log, exp)
baseline: libm sinf, cosf, logf, expf (scalar single-precision functions)
workload: test_fun.cpp: each function is evaluated over a 1024-element array of floats drawn uniformly from [0, 1) (vals_test), repeated 100,000 times for libm and 1,000,000 times for the approximations, single thread, timed with clock() and reported in million evaluations per second. The intervals [-pi, pi], [1e-10, 10] and [-10, 10] are used only for the separate error statistics (bias, mean/RMS/min/max error against libm), not for the throughput loop.
claimed_speedup: README output: sinf 213.3M/s vs sinapprox 6238.5M/s (about 29x); cosf 226.7M/s vs cosapprox 7380.7M/s (about 33x); logf 115.2M/s vs logapprox 4112.9M/s (about 36x); expf 111.3M/s vs expapprox 2366.8M/s (about 21x) (ratios derived from page data). README text: 'speedups from 20x to 40x' with gcc vectorisation.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: g++ test_fun.cpp -o test_fun -Wall -W -O3 -std=c++11 -march=native (auto-vectorisation); gcc version not stated; README says clang also works
tradeoffs: Approximate: sin mean absolute error 3.7e-6, cos 2.6e-5, log 5.6e-6 (README output); header-only and portable but relies on compiler auto-vectorisation, so speedups depend on gcc or clang loop vectorisation.
caveats: Output is 'on my computer' with no CPU or compiler version. The README output dates from 2015 (README last changed 2015-10-22), before commit 5c3caea (2019-01-11, 'Prevents dead code optimizations in test_fun.cpp') added an asm barrier to the benchmark loop; the 2015 figures (about 1.5-2 evaluations per cycle) are too low to reflect an elided loop, but they were not re-measured on the fixed harness. The speedup is a vectorised approximation against scalar, correctly rounded libm (gcc does not vectorise sinf/logf calls without -ffast-math and libmvec), so it trades precision for speed: sinapprox max abs error 5.9e-6, cosapprox 4.0e-5, logapprox 9.1e-6, expapprox max relative error 8.6e-6; glibc libmvec or other vector math libraries (SLEEF, SVML) were not compared. name: Ultra-Sort (SIMD sorting DSL for AVX2 and AVX-512)
baseline: std::sort (also std::stable_sort, ips4o::sort, pdqsort)
workload: gtest cases in test/avx512/simd_sort_test.cpp sort uniform random values from [-10000, 10000] (LO/HI in test/include/test_util.h, so 1M inputs hold heavy duplicates); each algorithm is timed once per case with currentSeconds() on a copy of the same input; the checked-in NNUM is 65536, so the report's 1M (2^20), 1024 and 10M runs required editing it; N must be a power of 2. Settings: 32/64-bit int and float keys and key-value pairs, single core via OMP_NUM_THREADS=1.
claimed_speedup: Project report Table 4 (1M elements, 32-bit int, single core): avx512::sort 0.010364 s vs std::sort 0.080234 s; Table 2 states the speedup as 7.741558x. Same table: ips4o 0.035442 s, pdqsort 0.036089 s, avx256::sort 0.019070 s. Report: 'best-cast speedup of 8x on single-core and 17x on multicore AVX512' (multicore numbers shown only in a figure). Table 7 (1024 elements, 32-bit int): avx512::sort 5.689899x std::sort.
compiler_and_flags: Report: 'compile with flag -O3 -flto'; CMakeLists: -g -O3 -flto -Wall -march=native -fopenmp; compiler vendor and version not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon Silver 4114 at 2.20 GHz, 40 logical CPUs, L3 14080 KB (Skylake-SP, AVX-512)
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX2 or AVX-512 only; element count must be a power of two (README); built for course-project scale, no NUMA support; single-thread SIMD sort, optional OpenMP multicore.
caveats: Course-project report, not peer reviewed; README speedup chart is an image. Compiler name and version missing (CMakeLists: -g -O3 -flto -Wall -march=native -fopenmp), and the std library tested is not named. Single-shot timings with no repetition. The report's tables contain copy errors: Table 1 (1M IPC) and Table 6 (1024 IPC) are identical, Table 4 gives avx256 and avx512 the same 64-bit int time (0.028105 s) while Table 2 gives them 1.48x and 2.93x, and Table 3's 1M 32-bit key-value times (avx512 0.0337 s slower than avx256 0.0201 s) contradict Table 4 (0.0337 vs 0.0681). Gains are uneven: at 1M the 64-bit key-value int sort (0.106933 s) and 64-bit key-value float sort (0.107151 s) are slower than std::sort (0.085000 s, 0.099286 s), and ips4o (sequential) beats avx512::sort on 3 of 8 settings at 1M (64-bit key-value int 0.044091 s, 32-bit key-value float 0.042667 s, 64-bit key-value float 0.049526 s); in the 10M AVX2 table avx256::sort is only 1.5x std::sort while ips4o is 7.4x. The 17x multicore claim has no table. Harness frees posix_memalign buffers (aligned_init in src/common.cpp) with delete, which is undefined behaviour, and seeds inputs from std::random_device, so runs are not repeatable. Fits wave 1's sorting category better than simd-intrinsics-libraries.

name: UltraSIMD
baseline: the benchmark's own scalar reference loops: scalar_dot_product_no_autovec / scalar_dot_{f16,i8,bf16}_no_autovec for dot products (volatile per-element loads, noinline, optnone under Clang), plain inline scalar loops for L2, cosine, Hamming, Jaccard and SAXPY; the whole benchmark target is built with auto-vectorization disabled
workload: Dot product, SAXPY, L2, cosine, Hamming and Jaccard distances over F32, F16, I8, BF16 and U8 vectors of 15 to 16384 elements, 175 benchmark rows, AVX-512 path versus scalar path.
claimed_speedup: Plain-scalar rows 1.7x to 7.6x; F32 dot 0.18x to 1.84x in the fuller CSV; the 18.7x headline rests on a volatile-slowed baseline.
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt Release benchmark targets: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -mavx2 (plus -mavx512f -mavx512bw -mavx512vl when supported), and with SIMD_DISABLE_AUTO_VECTORIZATION ON (the default) also -fno-tree-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize -fno-tree-loop-vectorize and DISABLE_SCALAR_AUTOVEC (which adds a GCC optimize pragma or '#pragma clang optimize off' over the benchmark functions); compiler and version used for the CSVs not stated
hardware: CPU model not stated; CSV lists features AVX512F, FMA, F16C, VNNI

The fair-looking rows (plain scalar loops without auto-vectorization) give 1.7x to 7.6x. No CPU model or compiler stated (CSV lists AVX512F, FMA, F16C, VNNI); three CSVs with different results and no record of which run is current; vectors of 15 to 16384 elements, cache-resident. Tiny repo (2 stars, 2 commits on 2025-06-28); no comparison with Highway, xsimd or Eigen. README mentions AMD enterprise support, but the repo is a personal project. name: utf8lut
baseline: scalar slow path of the same library (-b=0), a scalar UTF-8 to UTF-16 and UTF-16 to UTF-8 converter
workload: Converting about 1 MB buffers from RAM to RAM, UTF-8 to UTF-16 (decode) and UTF-16 to UTF-8 (encode), on a random code-point dataset (33% each of 1, 2 and 3 byte) and the Russian novel 'War and Peace' in fb2 format; CPU cycles per byte.
claimed_speedup: Fast path (-b=3 -m=2) vs scalar slow path, cycles per byte (core conversion by rdtsc): random decode 1.65 vs 15.3 (about 9.3x), random encode 0.74 vs 9.9 (about 13x), fb2 decode 1.00 vs 9.10 (about 9.1x), fb2 encode 0.68 vs 4.89 (about 7.2x); ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the table. The sample benchmark commands run FileConverter_msvc.exe, which scripts/build_msvc_file_conv.cmd builds with cl /O2 /Oi /EHsc /MD /D NDEBUG /D TIMING (MSVC version not given); non-MSVC builds need -mssse3 -std=c++11.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 1600, single core, 3.4 GHz
tradeoffs: x86 with SSSE3 only; a large lookup table that barely fits the CPU cache, so speed depends on the code-point length distribution (uniform random is the worst case); the fast path needs more than 99% of characters handled to pay off; non-BMP characters use the slow path; the iconv-style interface deviates from the spec.
caveats: The comparison is against the library's own scalar slow path (-b=0, which forces validate mode), not against iconv, ICU or another incumbent; the fast-path row uses -m=2, which is cmValidate, so both rows validate. Each run converts one ~1 MB array from RAM to RAM repeatedly, so the large lookup table stays warm; the README warns it barely fits in cache and that performance depends on the code-point length mix. The compiler for the table is only implied (MSVC build of FileConverter, version unstated). The README's blog article with broader comparisons is on dirtyhandscoding.github.io, which is blocked here. Per search snippets only, Lemire and Mula's peer-reviewed 'Transcoding Billions of Unicode Characters per Second with SIMD Instructions' (Software: Practice and Experience 52(2), 2022; arXiv 2109.10433, blocked here) benchmarks utf8lut beside ICU, LLVM, u8u16 and utf8sse4 and reports that u8u16 and utf8sse4 often beat it on European-language text because utf8lut has no ASCII fast path; utf8lut-versus-ICU numbers were not seen. README calls it mainly a proof of concept. Repo migrated from Bitbucket and last changed in 2020.

name: vectorized_find (AVX2 find experiments)
baseline: std::find on a raw array and on std::vector (plus a naive loop)
workload: Worst-case search (target at the end) over 4096 int elements, Google Benchmark, billions of elements per second.
claimed_speedup: README table (4096 int elements, target in the last slot, G-elements/s, rounded): std::find on a raw array ~7.7 and on std::vector ~8.1 vs FIND_IntrinsicFind (AVX2 cmpeq + movemask, 2x unrolled) ~24.9, about 3.2x over raw-array std::find (derived from page data), and FIND_IntrinsicFloatFind ~25.3; naive loop ~4.6. FIND_Intrinsic2Find ~49.7 is not a find: it counts elements below the target over the whole array (lower_bound on sorted input) and its final reduction is wrong, so it is not a valid speedup over std::find.
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists: GCC -mtune=native -march=native -mavx2 -Ofast -funroll-loops -ftree-vectorize; Clang -O3 -ffast-math ...; compiler used for the table not stated
tradeoffs: AVX2 only; fixed 4096-element size in the quoted table; Intrinsic2Find has lower_bound semantics on a sorted array rather than a plain find.
caveats: Personal experiment with no licence file and no hardware stated. The archived docs/perf_results/results.txt is an older run (BM_ names, no CPU header; perf stat files show 24 CPUs only) that has no std::find or Intrinsic2 rows and gives IntrinsicFind/4096 at 21.06 G/s and NaiveFind/4096 at 4.48 G/s, lower than the README's ~24.9; the README's std::find numbers have no raw output in the repo. intrinsic2_find (src/intrinsics/intrinsic_find.cpp) counts elements less than the target with no early exit (a lower_bound on sorted input, not std::find semantics) and its reduction returns _mm256_extract_epi32(sum,0)+_mm256_extract_epi32(sum,1), which is twice the sum of lanes 0-3 and ignores the upper 128-bit half; on the benchmark input (4095 zeros then the target) it returns 4096 instead of 4095. intrinsic_find has no tail loop: it always reads 16 elements per step, so sizes that are not a multiple of 16 read past the buffer (the benchmark rounds sizes 2 and 4 up to 8 and then reads 8 ints beyond the malloc). Both sides are compiled with -Ofast -march=native (GCC) or -O3 -ffast-math (Clang); the std::find side is compiled with the same flags, but which standard library was used is not stated. Numbers are rounded ('~').

name: vek
baseline: pure-Go fallback of the same library (plain Go loops)
workload: In-place float32 and float64 vector operations (Add, Mul, Abs, Sum, Round, Sqrt, Pow, Exp, Log, Max, Find, comparisons, boolean And/All) on 1k and 100k element slices, plus MatMul and 4x4 matrix multiply.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Fast, average speedups of 10x for float32 vectors'. Table at 100k elements: vek32.Sum 65,007 ns Go vs 3,191 ns SIMD (20x), vek32.Exp 1,120,300 vs 49,694 ns (22x), vek32.Log 16x, vek32.Add 6x, vek.Add 2x, vek.MatMul 7x and vek32.MatMul 14x at m=n=p=1k, vek.And 139x.
compiler_and_flags: go test -benchmem -timeout 0 -run=^# -bench=. ./internal/... ; Go version not stated; the AVX2 kernels are assembly generated from C++ (asm/_cpp with Agner Fog's vectorclass/version2 submodule) compiled with -ffast-math according to the README Notes
tradeoffs: AVX2 and FMA on x86-64 only (acceleration disabled by default on macOS, no ARM kernels); behavior undefined on NaN or Inf inputs; minor precision differences from math.Exp, Pow and Log.
caveats: CPU model, Go version and run count are not stated. The speedup column uses the 100k-element sizes; at 1k some gaps are smaller (vek.Add 484 vs 192 ns, vek.Maximum 1,000 vs 517 ns, vek.And 1,172 vs 60 ns, derived from page data). The 139x vek.And row compares against And_Go, a short-circuit loop 'x[i] = x[i] && y[i]' over random 50% booleans: a branchy worst case for a scalar baseline that a branchless Go loop would narrow. BenchmarkLogic clones the input under StopTimer on every iteration. The Go fallback Sum is a single-accumulator serial loop, and the SIMD kernels are built with -ffast-math, which allows reassociation, so results can differ slightly in precision and are undefined for NaN or Inf inputs (README Notes). The MatMul baseline is the library's own pure-Go loop, not gonum or a BLAS. Acceleration needs x86-64 AVX2 and FMA (no ARM path) and is off by default on macOS. An Any() bug (wrong result for len > 256 and len % 32 > 0, stale RAX in the generated assembly) was fixed in August 2025 (commit 0ce8425). It does not touch any benchmarked row. Last commit (2025-09-06) is a README note on fast math.

name: EVE (Expressive Vector Engine)
baseline: scalar C++ / compiler auto-vectorization (no baseline stated; successor of Boost.SIMD)
workload: C++20 SIMD wrapper with a math function library for SSE2 to AVX-512, NEON/ASIMD and fixed-size SVE; the repo has a benchmarks/module harness (nanobench) but no published results.

caveats: No benchmark numbers in the README or repo; benchmarks/ has only the nanobench harness (CMakeLists.txt, experiment.hpp, generators.hpp, nanobench.h, module/ with algorithm, combinatorial, core, math and special subdirectories) and no result tables. name: Vector Class Library (VCL) version 2
baseline: standard scalar math function libraries (libm) and scalar code that the compiler fails to auto-vectorize
workload: No benchmark workload is published. The manual states qualitatively that vector math functions (log, exp, pow, trig, hyperbolic) process whole SIMD vectors and so beat scalar math libraries, and that VCL gives the same optimization level as hand-written intrinsics.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. Manual: 'Both versions are many times faster than standard (scalar) math function libraries' (inline and external SVML-based vector math versions).
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars; used as a dependency by other libraries (for example andyD123/DR3 vendors a VCL2 copy)
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 only (SSE2 up to AVX-512 and AVX512-FP16 types); the README says there are no plans for ARM or other instruction sets. Header-only, C++17 or later. The external vector math library variant needs Intel's SVML (Intel compiler); the inline variant is portable across GCC, Clang and MSVC. Manual rates exp-type math functions as 'poor' efficiency relative to simple operations, though still faster than scalar alternatives.
caveats: Tier D: the speed claims have no benchmark, hardware, compiler or flags. Included under the notable-D allowance (1.5k stars, 156 forks, very widely referenced, named repeatedly in HN threads about SIMD wrappers). The manual itself recommends compiler auto-vectorization where it works and positions VCL as the alternative when it fails. The external math-library variant (vectormath_lib.h) needs Intel's proprietary SVML from an Intel compiler installation; only the inline vectormath_*.h functions are fully Apache-2.0. Inline math functions trade subnormal support for speed (per the author's forum remarks, snippet only). x86/x86-64 only; the README says there are no plans to support ARM. Manual date 2026-09-09 matches the latest commit.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch restricted to news.ycombinator.com for SIMD wrapper libraries surfaced the threads 'It's much better to use any of the numerous SIMD wrappers such as libsimdpp or V...' verification.tier_reason: The manual (dated 2026-09-09) only says the inline and SVML-based vector math versions are 'many times faster than standard (scalar) math function libraries' (section 8.3); it has no benchmark, numbers, hardware or flags, and a WebSearch found no independent VCL-vs-libm/SLEEF timing, so D.
verification.notes: Record accurate: no numbers anywhere in the manual or README; Apache-2.0, 1.5k stars, last commit 2026-09-09 (version 2.02.04) confirmed. Shortcomings: no benchmark at all (tier D), SVML variant depends on proprietary Intel library, x86-only.

name: BlazeDiff core-wasm (@blazediff/core-wasm)
baseline: pixelmatch (JavaScript)
workload: Pixel-by-pixel YIQ perceptual image diff of PNG fixtures (4K, ~1.6 MP and page-sized images, with identical-pair variants), decode excluded, 25 iterations after 5 warmup, Node.js.
claimed_speedup: ~50.8% faster on average than pixelmatch; 4k/1 332.26 ms vs 33.18 ms (90.0% less time, ~10x, derived from page data); 4k/3 423.14 ms vs 44.65 ms; small blazediff/1 1.24 ms vs 0.24 ms; identical-pair rows near parity (4k/2 identical 22.70 ms vs 22.17 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Rust (rustc version not stated), cargo build --release for wasm32-unknown-unknown with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+simd128,+bulk-memory' and the workspace release profile in crates/Cargo.toml (opt-level 3, lto = "fat", codegen-units 1, panic = abort), wasm-bindgen 0.2.100 post-processing, then wasm-opt -O3 only if wasm-opt is installed (crates/blazediff/scripts/build-wasm.sh); harness apps/image-benchmark (tinybench 5, pixelmatch ^7.2.0) under Node.js 22.
hardware: Apple M1 Max, Node.js 22, macOS (BENCHMARKS.md 'Hardware Specifications')
tradeoffs: Needs WebAssembly SIMD (v128). Classifies pixels with the same YIQ delta as pixelmatch but not bit-identically: counts differ by up to ~0.05% (e.g. 22,869 vs 22,883 differing pixels). Part of a larger ecosystem (JS core, native Rust binary, PyPI bindings).
caveats: First-party benchmark, measured in Node.js 22 on an Apple M1 Max, not in a browser. In the wasm run pixelmatch is 1.5-1.9x slower on the large differing fixtures than in the same page's JS run (4k/1 332.26 ms vs 201.60 ms, 4k/3 423.14 vs 253.77, page/2 513.06 vs 267.84) while small and identical rows agree, so the headline 4k/1 ratio of about 10x is about 6.1x against the JS-run pixelmatch time (derived from page data). Whether wasm-opt ran on the measured module is not recorded, and the rustc version is not stated. Results differ slightly from pixelmatch (counts within ~0.05%, e.g. 4k/1 69,932 vs 69,912 pixels). Byte-identical pairs used to be a 60-70% loss; pixel-by-pixel.md says skipping a scalar memcmp shortcut on wasm32 turned them into small wins (4k/2 identical 22.70 ms vs 22.17 ms). On identical pairs the plain JS @blazediff/core (2.50 ms for 4k/1) is far faster than the wasm build (17.47 ms).
found_via: npm registry search (queries 'webassembly faster than javascript', 'wasm faster than js', 'wasm times faster', 'webassembly simd fast') found @blazediff/core-wasm; opened github.com/teimurjan/blazediff README, BENCHMARKS.md and benchmarks/pixel-by-pixel.md

name: kmeans-wasm
language: Rust (WebAssembly SIMD, simd128) with JavaScript wrapper
baseline: skmeans (JavaScript k-means library)
workload: k-means clustering of random RGB pixels, random multi-dimensional points and four real photographs for colour quantisation; median of five runs.
claimed_speedup: 10,000 points x 50 dims x 10 clusters 83.15 ms vs skmeans 1456.35 ms (17.5x); 100,000 random RGB pixels, 32 colours 247.03 vs 1677.87 ms (6.8x); photo blue-marble, 16 colours 109.24 vs 11133.62 ms (101.8x); small input 1,000 pixels, 2 colours 0.47 vs 0.41 ms (0.9x, slower)
compiler_and_flags: Rust (edition 2024, rust-version 1.98 minimum; exact rustc version not stated) built with wasm-pack build --release --target nodejs; Cargo.toml [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = abort, strip; .cargo/config.toml rustflags -C target-feature=+simd128 for wasm32-unknown-unknown; wasm-opt -O4 --enable-simd --enable-bulk-memory --enable-nontrapping-float-to-int. Harness: js_bench/src/vector.ts, rgb.ts, images.ts (TypeScript, Node).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 9600X, Node.js 26.10.0
tradeoffs: Requires wasm SIMD (Chrome 91+, Firefox 89+, Safari 16.4+); small inputs and tiny cluster counts gain little or lose.
caveats: First-party; most of the code and the harness since v3.2.0 were written by AI assistants (README says so). The baseline skmeans is a naive Lloyd k-means in plain JavaScript that scans all n*k distances every round, while kmeans-wasm uses Hamerly bounds and, for the packed RGB/RGBA entry points, collapses the input to its distinct colours with weights; most of the speed-up is algorithmic, not from wasm or SIMD, and the README says the image speed-up falls from 84x to 13x as the distinct-colour share grows. No stronger JS k-means (e.g. a bounds-based one) is compared. Small or k=2 cases are level or slower (1,000 pixels, 2 colours 0.9x; 100,000 pixels, 2 colours 1.1x). Real-image skmeans timings are one measured run after one warm-up. Seeds differ per run on both sides (random distinct input points vs skmeans kmrand), so the two sides can converge to different local minima; kmeans-wasm always runs all 100 iterations (threshold 0) while skmeans may stop early, which favours skmeans. 2 stars.
found_via: npm registry search (queries 'webassembly faster than javascript', 'webassembly simd fast', 'wasm parser') then github.com/vusolapohvistr/kmeans-wasm README Benchmarks section and commits page

verification.tier_reason: README tables compare kmeans_rgb/kmeans against skmeans with the harness public in js_bench/src/vector.ts, rgb.ts and images.ts (same 100-iteration cap, threshold 0 so kmeans-wasm never exits early, skmeans' own kmrand seeding, inputs built outside the timer); build flags are public in Cargo.toml (release: opt-level 3, LTO, codegen-units 1, panic abort; wasm-opt -O4) and .cargo/config.toml (+simd128), and the CPU (AMD Ryzen 5 9600X) and runtime (Node.js 26.10.0) are stated. Only the exact rustc version is unpinned (rust-version 1.98 minimum).
verification.notes: README numbers match the record exactly (10,000 x 50 x 10: 83.15 vs 1456.35 ms, 17.5x; 100,000 RGB px, 32 colours 247.03 vs 1677.87 ms, 6.8x; blue-marble 16 colours 109.24 vs 11133.62 ms, 101.8x; 1,000 px 2 colours 0.47 vs 0.41 ms, 0.9x). Flags are public in the repo's build config, so A stands; record the shortcoming that the win is mostly algorithmic (Hamerly bounds plus distinct-colour dedup) against a naive JS baseline, with single-sample skmeans image runs and a tiny project (2 stars, AI-written). License MIT (LICENSE_MIT), last commit 2026-09-27 (release v3.7.0), not a fork.

name: libxml2-wasm
language: C (libxml2) compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten; TypeScript wrapper
baseline: libxmljs2 0.32.x (native N-API binding of libxml2) and the pure-JavaScript XML parsers @rgrove/parse-xml, fast-xml-parser and xmldoc
workload: DOM-tree parse of three XML fixtures (780 B, 35,562 B and 2,337,522 B) under Node.js, via the benchmark/ suite in the repo (cd benchmark && npm install && npm test).
claimed_speedup: docs/performance.md (ops/s, Apple M3 Max, Node v18.19.0). Like-for-like string input (both bindings parse a JS string): libxml2-wasm String API 120,578 vs libxmljs2 78,688 ops/s on the 780-byte file (1.53x), 6,013 vs 12,414 on 35,562 bytes (0.48x, slower) and 43 vs 50 on 2,337,522 bytes (0.86x, slower). Buffer API rows: 167,479, 17,114 and 62 ops/s, i.e. 2.1x, 1.4x and 1.2x libxmljs2, but the harness gives the Buffer API a pre-read UTF-8 Buffer while libxmljs2 gets the string and pays the UTF-16 to UTF-8 conversion in its timed call even though it also accepts a Buffer. Buffer API vs pure-JS parsers fed strings: 2.1x, 3.4x and 3.3x over @rgrove/parse-xml; 3.2x, 6.3x and 3.9x over fast-xml-parser (ratios derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Measured build (numbers unchanged since commit 9ed22d8, 2023-12-26, package v0.1.0): Emscripten, CI pinned EM_VERSION 3.1.44 but the local Apple M3 Max run does not state its version; libxml2 master 30d22be configured through gulpfile.babel.js (emconfigure autogen.sh --without-python --without-http --without-sax1 --without-modules --without-html --without-threads --without-zlib --without-lzma --disable-shared --enable-static, no explicit CFLAGS) and linked with emcc -s MODULARIZE -s ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH -s SINGLE_FILE and no -O level. Current HEAD differs: CFLAGS='-O2' and link flags -O2 -flto --closure 1 (binding/emcc.txt), EM_VERSION 5.0.2. Baseline libxmljs2 ^0.32.0 is a prebuilt native addon bundling libxml2 2.9.9 (vendor/libxml/include/libxml/xmlversion.h), flags not stated. Node.js v18.19.0.
hardware: Apple M3 Max (Darwin arm64), Node.js v18.19.0
stars_or_usage: 54 stars; published on npm as libxml2-wasm
tradeoffs: ES module only; needs Node.js 18+ or Chrome/Edge 89+, Safari 15+ (README). libxml2 is built without the HTML parser, SAX1, catalogs, threads, modules and debug support. The String API converts UTF-16 to UTF-8 on every call; the docs recommend the Buffer API for speed. Wrapper licence is MIT and the bundled libxml2 keeps its own notice (LICENSE.libxml2).
caveats: First-party benchmark (docs/performance.md, numbers unchanged since 2023-12-26). Harness asymmetry: benchmark/index.mts passes the Buffer API a pre-read UTF-8 Buffer but passes libxmljs2 the JS string, so libxmljs2's timing includes UTF-16 to UTF-8 conversion although its fromXml also takes a Buffer; on like-for-like string input libxml2-wasm is faster only on the 780-byte file and slower than native libxmljs2 on the 35 KB (0.48x) and 2.3 MB (0.86x) files. libxml2-wasm calls dispose() on each document while libxmljs2 documents are freed by GC finalizers inside the timed loop. Version gap: the wasm side was built from libxml2 master 30d22be (late 2023) while libxmljs2 0.32.x bundles libxml2 2.9.9, so part of the gain may come from newer libxml2 rather than the binding. The measured build predates the current -O2/-flto/--closure flags (no -O at link then); the local Emscripten version is not stated and libxmljs2 is a prebuilt binary with unstated flags. Single machine, Node 18, no warm-up or iteration policy stated beyond benny defaults. The bundled libxml2 carries its own license (LICENSE.libxml2).
found_via: Blogs / talks: registry text search (npm search API 'emscripten compiled c library faster', 'wasm port faster than pure js') surfaced libxml2-wasm; README footnote led to docs/performance.md.
WebSearch result app.unpkg.com/libxml2-wasm README (query on wasm libraries faster than JS builtins); then opened github.com/jameslan/libxml2-wasm and docs/performance.md

verification.tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (benchmark/index.mts, benny) and the CPU is stated (Apple M3 Max, Node v18.19.0), but the headline Buffer-API rows hand libxml2-wasm pre-encoded UTF-8 bytes while libxmljs2, which also accepts a Buffer (src/xml_document.cc FromXml), is fed a JS string and converts it inside the timed call; the like-for-like String API rows lose to native on the 35 KB and 2.3 MB files. The numbers have been unchanged since commit 9ed22d8 (2023-12-26, v0.1.0), whose build used no optimisation flag at link and an unstated local Emscripten version, not the HEAD flags the record lists, so these are first-party numbers short of A.

name: Pare
language: C (x264, SVT-AV1, libvmaf) compiled to WebAssembly SIMD128 with Emscripten, TypeScript web app
baseline: ffmpeg.wasm 0.12 (x264 built without its assembly) single-threaded and multithreaded; native x264 as the ceiling
workload: Compress Big Buck Bunny (10 s, 30.7 MB) to at least 50% smaller at matching VMAF NEG in headless Chrome, including the size plan and test encodes, on a 4-core 8-thread cloud VM.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md 'Speed in context' (Big Buck Bunny, 10 s, 30.7 MB): Pare 24.9 s from the click, including the size plan and Auto's test encodes (13.4 MB, VMAF NEG 93.1, worst frame 88.9), vs ffmpeg.wasm 0.12 single-threaded x264 `faster` CRF 19 158.9 s and multithreaded 42.4 s (both 12.2 MB, VMAF NEG 93.0, worst frame 89.8): 6.4x and 1.7x as fast per the page; native ffmpeg x264 with Pare's settings 6.4 s. Pare's encode alone took 12.9 s, about twice native x264 on the same cores. README/RESEARCH.md: about 1,500 lines of WebAssembly SIMD128 kernels make encoding 2.0-2.3x faster per core than the plain C build with byte-identical output, and the single-thread WebAssembly build runs at 54% of native x264 with the same settings (4.25 vs 7.85 fps on park).
compiler_and_flags: emcc -O3 -msimd128 (x264 configured with --extra-cflags=-O3; the threaded build adds -pthread), x264-wasm/build.sh; Emscripten version not pinned; browser is Playwright's Chromium build 1243 (playwright-core 1.63.0, research/benchmark.mjs); baseline ffmpeg.wasm is @ffmpeg/core and @ffmpeg/core-mt 0.12.10 with @ffmpeg/ffmpeg 0.12.15 (research/ffmpeg-wasm/package.json)
hardware: Xeon Platinum 8259CL 2.5 GHz (2019), 4 cores / 8 threads cloud VM shared with other work, no GPU
tradeoffs: GPL because of x264; needs WebAssembly SIMD128 and Web Workers; chunked parallel encoding costs 4-9% more bytes than a single encode; the app picks its own rate factor to hit a size target;
caveats: First-party and very new (94 commits, first in late September 2026, 3 stars). The headline 6.4x/1.7x over ffmpeg.wasm is a whole-pipeline comparison, not a kernel one: Pare adds chunked multi-worker encoding, WebCodecs decoding and its own x264 settings (diamond motion search and no 8x8-and-smaller inter partitions, about two thirds of the CPU time of the `faster`-based setting), while ffmpeg.wasm ran stock `faster` CRF 19; ffmpeg.wasm also produced a smaller file (12.2 MB vs 13.4 MB) at the same VMAF NEG with a better worst frame, and Pare's time includes finding its own rate factor. The cleanest kernel claim (2.0-2.3x per core over scalar C WebAssembly) is a sentence in RESEARCH.md without a per-kernel table. One run per row on a 4-core cloud VM shared with other work (the page reports up to 25 s variation between identical encodes in a busy session). Emscripten version unpinned. ffmpeg/ffmpeg is already catalogued; x264 itself was not in the known list.
found_via: github.com/topics/wasm-simd listed x1xhlol/pare; README and research/BENCHMARKS.md read via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com

name: TurboRes
baseline: FFmpeg 7.1.1 native CLI (single- and multithreaded, plus VideoToolbox hardware decode) and ffmpeg.wasm
workload: Apple ProRes decode (422 HQ 4K, 4444 1080p, 422 HQ 1080p, 422 Proxy 1080p), frames per second averaged over 10 runs of decoding a file.
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded: 42 FPS vs 15 FPS native FFmpeg at ProRes 422 HQ 4K (~2.8x, derived from page data), 128 vs 55 (4444 1080p), 158 vs 57 (422 HQ 1080p), 450 vs 161 (Proxy 1080p). Multithreaded: 250 FPS vs 107 FPS native FFmpeg and 84 FPS ffmpeg.wasm at 4K; 2310 vs 948 FPS at Proxy 1080p. Native hardware-accelerated FFmpeg: 160 FPS at 4K.
compiler_and_flags: TurboRes: Zig 0.16, zig build-exe -target wasm32-freestanding -O ReleaseSmall -mcpu=generic+atomics+bulk_memory+multivalue+nontrapping_fptoint+reference_types+sign_ext+simd128 -fno-single-threaded --shared-memory --import-memory (scripts/build-zig.sh --release, called by scripts/build.sh). Browser/wasm engine and version used for the table not stated. Native FFmpeg 7.1.1 build provenance and flags not stated; ffmpeg.wasm row uses @ffmpeg/ffmpeg 0.11.6 with @ffmpeg/core 0.11.0 from unpkg.
hardware: Apple M4 (4P+6E) MacBook Air; TurboRes 1.2.0, FFmpeg 7.1.1
tradeoffs: Decoder only (no ProRes encoder). Needs WebAssembly SIMD; the multithreaded path uses wasm shared memory and a worker pool option. MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft. Hand-written for ProRes, so no other codecs.
caveats: First-party numbers on one Apple M4 laptop; the browser (and so the wasm JIT) is not named. Baseline weakness: FFmpeg 7.1.1's ProRes IDCT has SIMD only on x86 (libavcodec/proresdsp.c calls ff_proresdsp_init_x86 under ARCH_X86 and nothing for aarch64), so on the M4 native FFmpeg ran its scalar C IDCT while TurboRes uses wasm SIMD128; the 2-3x lead over native FFmpeg may shrink on x86. Harness asymmetry: TurboRes pre-demuxes all packets into memory (Mediabunny) and runs 3 warm-up passes, while the FFmpeg CLI script ((11-loop rtime minus 1-loop rtime)/10 with -f null) includes mov demuxing and file reads; the VideoToolbox row (-hwaccel videotoolbox without a hardware output format) includes copying frames back to system memory. benchmark-turbores.html is the multithreaded variant only and benchmark-ffmpeg-wasm.html hard-codes 10 threads, so the single-threaded rows are not reproducible from committed code; the benchmark hard-codes proresFourCc 'apch' for every file, so the 4444 file is decoded under the 422 HQ profile (10-bit output scale vs FFmpeg's yuva444p12le). Correctness: the README says decoding is bit-exact, but PR #3 (merged 2026-07-09, after the 1.2.0 benchmark update of 2026-07-02) fixed 4444 (ap4h/ap4x) output values that were 4x too small and reported Y/U/V only 84-87% bit-identical to FFmpeg 6.0 (max difference 2) and 97.2-97.7% to VideoToolbox (float AAN IDCT), so outputs are close but not bit-exact; the 'apch' path used by the benchmark was not affected by that bug. Release build uses ReleaseSmall. Test videos are hosted on an external R2 bucket. A second merged record of the same repo exists (paper:turbores-aslang-registry, category assemblyscript-and-wasm-langs).

name: DuckDB-Wasm
language: C++ (DuckDB) compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten, TypeScript API
baseline: Arquero (JavaScript dataframe library) and SQLite WASM; danfo also in the table
workload: Third-party in-browser benchmark on 1,000,000 Bandcamp sales rows (24 columns): analytical SELECTs (overall metrics, group by day, top 5 countries per item and slug type, random rows) plus index, update, insert and delete tests, run on a separate browser thread.
claimed_speedup: Independent repo (timlrx/browser-data-processing-benchmarks README; times in seconds, Date.now() difference / 1000 in index.js), i7-1165G7 with Chrome 116: Test 1 top-level metrics Arquero 0.067 s vs DuckDB-Wasm 0.014 s (4.8x, derived from page data); Test 2 group by day 1.05 s vs 0.163 s (6.4x, derived from page data); Test 3 top 5 countries 4.847 s vs 0.114 s (42x, derived from page data); Test 4 10 random rows 0.517 s vs 0.032 s (16x, derived from page data). Against in-memory SQLite WASM without indexes DuckDB-Wasm also wins Tests 1-4 (e.g. Test 1 0.376 s vs 0.014 s, 27x, derived from page data). On the M2 MacBook Air with Firefox 117 the Arquero gaps are smaller (Test 3 0.852 s vs 0.132 s, 6.5x; Test 2 0.634 s vs 0.169 s, 3.8x; derived from page data). DuckDB-Wasm loses the load step (4.309 s vs Arquero 2.866 s and SQLite 0.893 s on Chrome), loses to indexed SQLite on Tests 2 and 4 (0.005 s and 0.002 s vs 0.163 s and 0.032 s), and loses every transactional test to in-memory SQLite WASM (1000 indexed selects 1.048 s vs 0.054 s, 1000 inserts 1.397 s vs 0.041 s, 1000 deletes 2.376 s vs 0.035 s). VLDB 2022 paper abstract (search snippet only): outperforms previous data processing libraries for the Web on TPC-H at multiple scale factors; no figures seen.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1165G7 @2.80GHz Windows laptop with Chrome 116; Apple M2 MacBook Air with Firefox 117
tradeoffs: Large WASM download; extensions such as Parquet, JSON and ICU are autoloaded lazily; HTTP stack differs from native DuckDB (CORS and HTTPS required); weaker than SQLite WASM on small transactional updates.
caveats: The VLDB PDF (vldb.org), duckdb.org and ir.cwi.nl were not reachable (DNS-blocked here); the paper claim comes from a search snippet, though the repo's packages/benchmarks/src holds TPC-H suites for DuckDB-Wasm, sql.js, Arquero and Lovefield that match the snippet's comparison set. The independent repo (7 stars, 23 commits) is a single run per browser on one machine, timed in seconds with Date.now() around a Comlink call to a web worker (so worker messaging and 1 ms clock resolution are included in the 0.002-0.03 s rows); its README says fetch and load timings are noisy. It pins old packages (@duckdb/duckdb-wasm ^1.27.0, @sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm ^3.43.0-build3, arquero ^5.2.0, 2023), and the workloads are not identical: the Arquero group-by-day test also sorts its output, which the DuckDB query does not. DuckDB-Wasm is slower to load than Arquero and SQLite and far slower than SQLite WASM on point lookups, updates, inserts and deletes; its wins are analytical scans and aggregations. No comparison against native DuckDB (the category's 'same library compiled natively' baseline) was found. Default build is single-threaded; multithreading is experimental.

workload: Building an uncompressed tar archive in memory from 1,001 generated lorem-ipsum text files (3 paragraphs each) in Node.js (examples/nodejs-benchmark/bench.ts); each library runs once, cold, one after the other in the same process, with no warm-up, repetitions or output comparison.
claimed_speedup: README: 'it can be 50-160x faster than existing JavaScript implementations on NPM'. Printed run: @bytedance/tar-wasm 24.63 ms; tar-js 3943.50 ms (160.1x slower); tarts 1251.60 ms (50.8x slower).

caveats: Single cold run of each library on small text files, results from 'my machine' (Xeon Platinum 8269CY), Node and toolchain versions not stated; the README output was printed by an earlier version of bench.ts (labels differ from the current script). Both baselines are quadratic writers: tar-js 0.3.0 (lib/utils.js extend) allocates a buffer just large enough, rounded to 10,240 bytes, zero-fills it with a byte-by-byte JS loop and copies the whole archive, up to twice per appended file; tarts 2.0.1 (tarts.js) builds the archive with reduce, allocating a new Uint8Array of size a+b and copying the whole archive for every file. tar-wasm wraps the Rust tar crate (tar 0.4.38) over a Vec<u8> with amortized growth, so the 50-160x mostly measures the baselines' O(n^2) buffer growth; widely used JS tar writers (tar-stream, node-tar) were not compared. The README asterisk says 'depending on the browser' but only a Node run is shown. Every entry gets mode 0777, uid/gid 0 and mtime 0. set_gzip(true) compresses with yazi Format::Zlib, so the 'gzip' option emits a zlib stream rather than a gzip file (not on the benchmarked path). Repository archived by the owner on 2025-07-21; last commit 2023-01-24.

language: JavaScript backend for SQLite compiled to WebAssembly (sql.js)

Baseline harness (src/examples/bench/queries-raw-idb.js) is the slowest raw-IndexedDB pattern: sumAll walks an openCursor one record per step and populate issues one store.put per row, while absurd-sql packs rows into 4096-byte SQLite blocks; Nolan Lawson's follow-up post 'Speeding up IndexedDB reads and writes' (2021-08-22) argued batched getAll()/getAllKeys() pagination and relaxed durability close much of that gap (search snippet only: in Chrome a 50,000-row cursor read took 1194.2 vs 488.3 with 1,000-item batches, units not shown). Timing is asymmetric: the SQLite sumAll timer starts after db.prepare, the raw-IDB timer includes opening the transaction. The harness's populateLarge inserts 400,000 rows. Requires the author's sql.js fork (@jlongster/sql.js), SharedArrayBuffer with COOP/COEP headers, and a worker; Hackaday's write-up (snippet only) says native SQLite is 2-3x faster than absurd-sql. name: blake3-jit
baseline: @napi-rs/blake-hash (native Rust BLAKE3 Node addon)
workload: BLAKE3 hashing of 96 B, 512 B, 1 KB, 32 KB and 1 MB inputs through blake3-jit (JavaScript with runtime-generated WASM SIMD) versus the native napi addon.
claimed_speedup: 96 B: 362 MB/s vs 149 MB/s (2.4x faster); 512 B: 748 vs 521 MB/s (1.4x); 1 KB: 811 vs 701 MB/s (1.2x); 32 KB: 1.36 vs 1.97 GB/s and 1 MB: 1.38 vs 2.06 GB/s (native wins).
tradeoffs: Faster than the native addon only for small inputs where FFI overhead dominates; native wins from tens of KB up. Generates wasm at runtime so there is no .wasm file to ship.
caveats: First-party; no hardware or Node version stated. Inputs below 4 KB (SIMD_THRESHOLD = 4 * CHUNK_LEN in src/hash.ts) run the pure JavaScript path, so every size where blake3-jit wins (96 B, 512 B, 1 KB) is pure JS beating napi call overhead, not WebAssembly; the runtime-generated WASM SIMD path (4 KB and above) is slower than the native addon (32 KB 1.36 vs 1.97 GB/s, 0.69x; 1 MB 1.38 vs 2.06 GB/s, 0.67x, derived from page data). The baseline @napi-rs/blake-hash is the same author's napi binding of the official blake3 Rust crate (a different implementation, not the same code compiled natively). The harness also times @huggingface/blake3-wasm (a wasm-vs-wasm comparison) and blake3-fast, but the README publishes only the napi column; the blake3-fast build is loaded from ../tmp and is not in the repo. Correctness of the timed paths is checked only on a 5-byte input in the harness.

verification.tier_reason: First-party README table; the harness bench/compare-blake3-fast.ts is public (blake3-jit vs @napi-rs/blake-hash 1.4.0, @huggingface/blake3-wasm and a blake3-fast build loaded from an untracked ../tmp path), but no CPU model, Node version or run command output are stated.
verification.notes: Numbers, MIT licence, 35 stars, 122 commits and last commit 2026-10-07 (renovate bot; active) verified. Shortcoming for this category: the WASM part never beats native; wins are pure-JS small-input FFI-overhead wins. baseline_in_list left false; the napi baseline wraps the listed BLAKE3 crate (wave 7) if the orchestrator wants to treat it as an in-list baseline.

name: brepkit
baseline: occt-wasm 3.8.3 (OCCT compiled to wasm) with a double-build defect in every two-operand boolean, fixed in occt-wasm 5.5.1 (PR #383, 2026-10-03)

claimed_speedup: brepkit (wasm) vs OCCT (wasm): fuse(box,box) x10 0.43 ms vs 44.9 ms (103x); cut(box,cylinder) x10 19.2 vs 64.9 ms (3.4x); box+chamfer 0.10 vs 5.6 ms (55x); box+fillet 0.33 vs 6.1 ms (18x); intersect(box,sphere) x10 0.23 vs 59.1 ms (252x); multi-boolean 4.6 vs 30.3 ms (6.6x); mesh sphere 6.2 vs 49.4 ms (7.9x); volume x100 0.18 vs 9.8 ms (54x); exportSTEP x10 0.85 vs 14.3 ms (17x).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.88+, cargo build -p brepkit-wasm --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release (wasm-opt settings not stated). The current occt-wasm README states its build: emcc -O3 -flto -fwasm-exceptions with WASM SIMD (-msimd128, no relaxed SIMD), then wasm-opt -O4 --converge --gufa; it does not say whether the benchmarked 3.8.3 release (published 2026-08-03) used the same flags. Released npm packages exact-pinned in the brepkit-bench package.json and lockfile: brepkit-wasm 3.0.0, occt-wasm 3.8.3, brepjs 18.120.0, tsx 4.23.1; Node 20+.
hardware: Linux x86_64, CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 32 stars; npm package brepkit-wasm, crate brepkit-operations
tradeoffs: Different kernel, not a port of OCCT: feature coverage is narrower (IGES is experimental, PLY import not exposed in wasm). AGPL-3.0-only with a commercial licence for proprietary embedding and a contributor licence agreement; versions through 2.129.x were MIT OR Apache-2.0. Native Rust build is faster still than the wasm build.

The percentages are time reductions relative to Clipper1, i.e. 1.69x, 1.34x, 1.44x and 1.15x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten em++ (version not stated) with -O3 -s DISABLE_EXCEPTION_CATCHING=1 --bind -s MODULARIZE=1 -s WASM_BIGINT -s ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1 -DUSINGZ (clipper2-wasm/compile-wasm.sh prod); Clipper2 static library built with emcmake cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE=-O3 -DCLIPPER2_HI_PRECISION=OFF (README.dev.md). tradeoffs: Wasm module must be loaded and instantiated before use; objects created on the wasm side need explicit delete().
caveats: Numbers exist only as a PNG screenshot in the README (checked; the four rows match). The comparison is Clipper2 against Clipper1, both as wasm, so the gain is mostly algorithmic, not wasm versus JS or native; the category's baselines (same library native, JS equivalent) are not measured, so the entry is off-baseline. Harness asymmetry in clipper1-vs-clipper2.html and testPolyOperation.js: the Clipper1 timed loop calls clipToPaths with plain JS {x,y} arrays, so every op marshals 2 x 5,000 input points into wasm and converts the result back to JS objects, while the Clipper2 inputs are converted to native Paths64 once before timing and the output stays in a native Paths64; part of the gap is therefore JS-wasm marshalling, not clipping. Single timed run per clip type, no warm-up, Clipper1 always runs first. Browser and Emscripten version not stated. Clipper2 itself (AngusJohnson/Clipper2, C++) is a separate project and is not listed.

name: commp-wasm (@hugomrdias/commp-wasm)
baseline: @web3-storage/data-segment (original JavaScript CommP implementation)
workload: Streaming Filecoin Piece Commitment (CommP) hashing of 1 MiB inputs in Node and in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit via playwright-test.
claimed_speedup: Node 26: 181.2 MiB/s vs 11.8 MiB/s original JS (15.38x), versus 41.4 MiB/s for a faster JS SHA-256 variant (3.52x). Browsers: Chromium 153 185.6 vs 7.5 MiB/s (24.8x), Firefox 155 170.7 vs 5.0 (34.2x), WebKit 187.3 vs 16.5 (11.3x).
compiler_and_flags: Rust release profile opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, strip; wasm-opt -O4 --enable-bulk-memory --enable-simd --strip-producers (rs/commp/Cargo.toml); rustc 1.92.0 pinned per compare/README.md; wasm32 simd128 with a 4-message multi-buffer SHA-256 backend.
hardware: Apple Silicon (chip not stated for the README tables), Node 26, Chromium 153, Firefox 155, WebKit (Safari 26.6). The repo's compare/results/apple-m1-pro-darwin-arm64.md run of 2026-09-30 is on an Apple M1 Pro with node v26.10.0 and shows the same wasm rate (182.8 MiB/s at 1 GiB), so the README bench probably ran on that machine (inference, not stated).
tradeoffs: Inline base64 wasm, streaming with O(log n) memory. Checked against go-fil-commp-hashhash known-answer vectors (rs/commp/tests). Uses wasm SIMD for the 4-message SHA-256 backend.
caveats: Very new (npm package created 2026-09-30), 0 stars, first-party, chip model not stated for the README tables. Harness: tinybench (100 ms, 250 iterations) hashing one constant 1 MiB buffer per iteration with create/write/digest (plus free for wasm) for every implementation; correctness is checked separately by differential tests against data-segment and Lotus vectors (compare results: 1072 checks, 0 failures). The baseline data-segment hashes through sync-multihash-sha2 (npm metadata: a node-specific sha256 export in Node, @noble/hashes in browsers); its per-call cost was not inspected and likely dominates the 11.8 MiB/s figure. The 'Fast JS (@webbuf/sha256)' row may itself run WASM SHA-256 (the README describes webbuf as an inline-base64 WASM pattern). Against the category's native baseline the wasm build is slower: on the M1 Pro, native single-thread Rust reaches 681.2 MiB/s and go-fil-commp-hashhash with GOMAXPROCS=1 343.0 MiB/s vs 182.8 MiB/s for wasm (compare/results/apple-m1-pro-darwin-arm64.md), i.e. wasm about 3.7x slower than native Rust (derived from page data). License: README and npm package say MIT, the Rust crate's Cargo.toml says MIT OR Apache-2.0, and the repo has no LICENSE file.

name: contour-wasm
baseline: MarchingSquares.js isoBands (pure JavaScript, used internally by turf-isobands)
workload: Isoband computation on grids of 5,307 to 1,010,880 points with 14 to 23 intervals; the sizes match the cases in example/index.html (volcano 87x61 = 5,307 points, dem_big 336,960 points, dem_big concatenated three times 1,010,880 points; derived from page data). One cold call per library per case in the browser, timed with performance.now().
claimed_speedup: 5,307 points / 23 intervals: 16 ms vs 12 ms; 17,608 / 15: 25 vs 15 ms; 336,960 / 14: 369 vs 186 ms; 1,010,880 / 14: 832 vs 492 ms (about 1.3x to 2.0x faster, derived from page data).

The two sides run with different options: contour-wasm is called with use_quad_tree: false while MarchingSquaresJS.isoBands runs with its quadtree enabled (noQuadTree: false), and the wasm timed region also includes the Float64Array copy and a console.log of the result, so the comparison is not like for like (both asymmetries handicap contour-wasm). name: crypto-js-wasm (@originjs/crypto-js-wasm)
language: WebAssembly (source language not confirmed; repo has a rust directory)
baseline: crypto-js (JavaScript)
workload: MD5, SHA-x, AES, RC4 and other hash/cipher operations through crypto-js-wasm versus crypto-js in Chrome 102, Firefox 101 and Node.js 16.6.4, plus RSA versus jsencrypt in Chrome.
claimed_speedup: README text: up to 16x faster than crypto-js. Per-algorithm results exist only as bar charts of average time for 10 loops (values read approximately from the PNGs, derived from page data): Chrome 102 SHA-3 ~103 vs ~1775 ms (~17x), SHA-512 ~288 vs ~1410 ms (~4.9x), SHA-384 ~297 vs ~1450 ms, MD5 ~245 vs ~490 ms (~2x), SHA-256 ~318 vs ~340 ms (~1.07x), AES ~275 vs ~248 ms (wasm slower); Firefox 101 SHA-512 ~452 vs ~1700 ms (~3.8x), RIPEMD160 ~422 vs ~1345 ms (~3.2x), SHA-3 ~138 vs ~555 ms (~4x), AES ~240 vs ~215 ms (slower); Node 16.6.4 SHA-512 ~300 vs ~1492 ms (~5x), SHA-3 ~118 vs ~678 ms (~5.7x), AES ~320 vs ~292 ms (slower). RSA vs jsencrypt in Chrome: about 1.8-2x (4096-bit OAEP ~115 vs ~234 ms, 2048-bit ~17 vs ~34 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Rust via wasm-pack build --release; Cargo release profile opt-level 3, lto = true (rust/*/Cargo.toml); rustc and wasm-pack versions not stated; wasm binaries pako-deflated and base64-inlined (rust/build-rust.js).
hardware: Desktop PC with Intel i5-4590, 16 GB RAM, Windows 10 21H2
tradeoffs: Same API as crypto-js but initialisation is async (loadWasm) and the wasm binaries are base64-embedded. Covers 15+ algorithms plus RSA.
caveats: Numbers are bar charts only; the headline 16x rests on crypto-js SHA-3 in Chrome 102 (~1775 ms there vs ~555 ms in Firefox), a Chrome-specific slowdown of the JS baseline; elsewhere SHA-3 gains are 4-6x. AES is slower than crypto-js in all three charts, and SHA-1/SHA-224/SHA-256/Rabbit/RC4 gain only about 1.05-1.15x in Chrome and Node, because the crypto-js-compatible API keeps string-to-WordArray conversion on the JS side. Harness (public in originjs/WASM-benchmark, packages/benchmark_base/src/benchmarkTests): 1 MiB random strings per item, warm-up and benchmark loop counts as parameters, same API calls for both libraries; which crypto-js-wasm version produced the 2022 charts is not stated (benchmark_base depends on ^1.1.0). Mulan PSL v2 is an OSI-approved permissive licence.

name: diamond-types
language: Rust (npm packages diamond-types-node and diamond-types-web via WebAssembly)
baseline: Automerge v0.5.9 (Rust) and Yjs v13.6.10 (JavaScript on Node.js v22.2.0), per the EuroSys 2025 Eg-walker paper; also the authors' own reference CRDT (Yrs, the Rust port of Yjs, was run but omitted from the paper)
workload: Merging each of seven real editing traces (S1-S3 sequential, C1-C2 concurrent, A1-A2 asynchronous) into an empty document as if received from a remote replica, plus reloading the saved document; Yjs is timed on Y.applyUpdateV2 of the pre-encoded document, Automerge and Yrs on loading their encoded documents.
claimed_speedup: Native Rust, CPU time to merge a whole editing trace received from a remote replica, means from egwalker-paper results/timings.json (derived from page data): diamond-types 1.77-82.6 ms vs Automerge 485-24,636 ms, i.e. 22x (A2) to 404x (S3); vs Yjs (55-88 ms) 32.5x on S1, 31.8x on S2, 22.3x on S3, 1.5x on C1, 10.0x on A1, 3.2x on A2, but 0.67x on C2 (diamond-types slower, 82.6 vs 55.2 ms). Cached document reload takes 0.012-0.12 ms against CRDT load times equal to their merge times. Paper text: 160,000x faster than OT on trace A2 and 7-10x faster than the authors' reference CRDT on the sequential traces. The README's link to a '5000x faster' blog post and its 'another 10-80x' claim, and the About text 'The world's fastest CRDT', could not be checked (blog unreachable).
tradeoffs: README marks it WIP; the crates.io package is described as out of date; wasm packages exist for Node and browsers; designed to interoperate with positional updates (operational transform).
caveats: All measured numbers are for the native Rust library; no benchmark of the wasm builds exists, and the npm packages diamond-types-node and diamond-types-web were last published as 1.0.2 on 2023-05-15 (crates.io 1.0.0 on 2022-08-25; the README says the published crate is quite out of date), so the wasm packages predate the benchmarked May-2024 code. Mixed against Yjs: diamond-types is slower on C2 (82.6 vs 55.2 ms) and only 1.5x faster on C1, although the paper text says it is significantly faster than Yjs on C1, C2 and A2. Yrs was omitted from the paper on the grounds that it was slower than Yjs, yet the artifact's committed results/timings.json shows Yrs at 8-13 ms, faster than diamond-types on C1 (4.8x), C2 (9.5x) and A2 (1.8x); Yjs and Yrs times are nearly flat across traces of very different size, which an enricher should check. Diamond-types is also slightly slower than the authors' reference CRDT on C1 and C2. The cached-load advantage comes from storing the final document text, a design difference rather than a like-for-like load. Automerge was measured as its Rust v0.5.9 core, not the JavaScript build. The paper is first-party (diamond-types' author, co-authored with Automerge's creator) but peer-reviewed. The 5000x and 10-80x README figures remain unverified because josephg.com did not resolve. Not part of dmonad/crdt-benchmarks (its README lists Yjs, ywasm, Loro and Automerge only).

For a get directive with one argument, the generator (parser/binder.go) emits a property lookup indexed by the byte slice (TestObject_GetRandom[slice]), so crypto.getRandomValues never runs and nothing is copied back. The syscall/js side invokes the function and calls CopyBytesToGo. The micro-benchmark environment (browser, Go version, hardware) is not stated, the numbers are one first-party run, and the table predates the May 2024 changes (Go 1.21+ compatibility #2, noescape and disabled verifications #5). One listed case (GetLocationHostname) is slower, and the README says results vary with how each API is used. The InkWasm DOM loop frees each object explicitly while syscall/js relies on finalizers. In the real Gio application the gain shrinks to 13-37%, measured on a fork against one upstream commit; the live comparison page (gio-bench.pages.dev) was not checked. name: iswasmfast
language: C++ compiled to WebAssembly and to an N-API addon, JavaScript harness
baseline: Pure JavaScript implementation (labelled 'Native' in the README) and the same C++ code built as a Node.js N-API addon
workload: Levenshtein distance, Fibonacci, Fermat primality test, simple linear regression and SHA256 in Node.js, benchmark.js ops/sec.
claimed_speedup: Fibonacci: WebAssembly 11,508,910 ops/s vs N-API addon 5,204,691 and JS 4,044,156. Fermat primality: WebAssembly 2,402,964 vs addon 1,833,692 and JS 1,678,845. SHA256: addon 67,807, WebAssembly 34,445, JS 13,453. WebAssembly loses on Levenshtein (210,776 vs addon 308,924 and JS 295,433) and on simple linear regression (WebAssembly 37,117 and 42,521 with TypedArrays vs JS 291,985).
compiler_and_flags: WASM: emcc --bind -std=c++14 src/wasm.cpp -s WASM=1 -s SINGLE_FILE=1 -O3 (package.json build:wasm; Emscripten version not stated). Addon: node-gyp rebuild --release with default node-gyp Release flags (binding.gyp sets no extra flags). Node version not stated.
tradeoffs: Mixed result by design: WASM beats the same C++ built as an addon when per-call overhead dominates (Fibonacci, Fermat) but loses where data is copied across the boundary (regression, Levenshtein).
caveats: Toy kernels with +-8-15% reported variance; no CPU, Node version or Emscripten version stated, and the README labels the pure-JS version 'Native'. WebAssembly is fastest on only 2 of 5 tasks (Fibonacci, Fermat); it beats pure JS on 3 of 5 (also SHA256, 34,445 vs 13,453 ops/s, about 2.6x derived from page data) but loses to JS on Levenshtein and linear regression and to the N-API addon on Levenshtein, regression and SHA256. The Fibonacci kernel is tail-recursive, which the C++ compiler turns into a loop while JS has no tail calls, so that row mostly measures tail-call elimination. benchmark.js draws random inputs on every call and its randomInRange helper ignores its min argument (Fibonacci n ranges 0-45, not 30-45); inputs are identically distributed for all three implementations. A benchmark/demo repository rather than a reusable library; last release 0.0.13 (2019-05-06), last commit 2022-04-09. The linked Medium post was not opened (blocked).

name: spow
language: Rust (server crate, browser WASM and JS-only solvers)
baseline: the JS-only browser solver shipped in prebuilt/browser, and optimised native Rust (the wasm build is slower than native)
workload: Time to solve a Hashcash-style proof of work (the README says 'Hashcat'): SHA-256 over challenge plus counter until the hash has `difficulty` leading zero bits (difficulty 10-99, default 20), in the browser with the prebuilt WASM solver vs the prebuilt JS-only solver (prebuilt/browser/js/spowJs.js), and vs native Rust (src/pow.rs, sha2 crate).
claimed_speedup: README: the wasm version 'is up to ~20 times faster than JS only'; 'the JS version is ~20 times slower than wasm'; in the browser the wasm version needs 'roughly 2.5 - 3 times the amount of time' of optimised native Rust ('first tests').
tradeoffs: Solve time grows exponentially with difficulty (10-99); wasm needs a getrandom backend setting in .cargo/config.toml; server-side validation time is independent of difficulty.
caveats: The README gives ratios only ('first tests'), with no table, hardware, browser, difficulty or sample count. benches/main.rs is a native-only Criterion bench (Pow::work on five difficulty-14 challenges, Pow::validate) and the bin target (src/main.rs, 'cargo run --features server --release 20 100') prints native percentiles; neither measures WASM or JS. The JS baseline is weak: spowJs.js awaits crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256') once per candidate and allocates a new TextEncoder each iteration, so the ~20x mostly measures per-hash async WebCrypto/promise overhead rather than JS hashing speed; a synchronous pure-JS SHA-256 loop was not compared. The wasm build is itself 2.5-3x slower than native Rust, so it beats only the JS baseline.

language: Rust FFI over C (Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03) compiled to WebAssembly
baseline: astronomy-engine 2.1.19 (pure-JavaScript astronomy library; version pinned in deno.json and benches/browser_bench.html)
workload: One fixed date (2000-01-01 12:00 UT) repeated every iteration. benches/comparison.ts (deno bench): swe_julday + swe_calc_ut(SE_SUN or SE_MOON, SEFLG_SWIEPH|SEFLG_SPEED) vs astronomy-engine GeoVector(Body, new Date('2000-01-01T12:00:00Z'), aberration=true). benches/deno_throughput.ts and benches/browser_bench.html: 100,000 Sun iterations each, timed with performance.now().
claimed_speedup: Moon position: ~182,000 iter/s vs ~126,000 iter/s for astronomy-engine, '1.44x Faster' (Deno bench). Sun position is slower: ~319,000 vs ~577,000 ops/s in Chrome and ~178,000 vs ~434,000 ops/s in Deno ('the overhead of calling WebAssembly dominates. Pure JS is faster here').
license: MIT for the wrapper (LICENSE, Cargo.toml, deno.json), but the WASM compiles in Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03 C sources (vendor/swisseph submodule of aloistr/swisseph), which are dual-licensed AGPL-3.0 or Swiss Ephemeris Professional License (the README calls it 'GPL/Commercial')

Per source reading (not run): the WASM build stubs fopen to return NULL (src/lib.rs), so no ephemeris files can load and SEFLG_SWIEPH silently falls back to the Moshier analytic ephemeris on every call; the README's 'high-precision'/'more accurate' claim therefore refers to Moshier, not the SE1 files, and swe_calc_ut then repeats the calculation because the returned ephemeris flag differs from the requested one (sweph.c), so the WASM side likely does two computations per call and its save-area cache never hits. In comparison.ts the astronomy-engine loop parses a Date string every iteration while the WASM loop calls swe_julday; deno_throughput.ts warms up only astronomy-engine.
