name: tinyfft (rluts/tinyfft)
baseline: fft.js (pure JavaScript, f64)
workload: 1D complex FFT round trip throughput at N=1024 and N=65536 with persistent plans, SIMD and scalar wasm builds against fft.js.
claimed_speedup: Round trip with persistent plans (bench/README.md sample run, Apple Silicon, Node 25): tinyfft SIMD ~124 vs fft.js ~97 MSamples/s at N=1024 (~1.28x) and ~79 vs ~57 at N=65536 (~1.39x); forward ~250 vs ~207 at N=1024 (~1.21x) and ~159 vs ~115 at N=65536 (~1.38x), but ~262 vs ~258 at N=256 (a tie); ratios derived from page data. The scalar build (~91 and ~43 MSamples/s round trip) is slower than fft.js at both sizes.
compiler_and_flags: Rust (version not stated) for wasm32-unknown-unknown with -C target-feature=+simd128 (.cargo/config.toml); release profile opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic=abort; wasm-opt -O3; scalar variant built with -C target-feature=-simd128 (bench/build-scalar.mjs); bench/run.mjs with 150 ms warmup and 500 ms measurement; Node 25
hardware: Apple Silicon (chip not stated), Node 25
tradeoffs: Single-precision f32 only, in-place, planar real/imag layout (helpers interleave/magnitudes provided); ~16 KB wasm. Unrelated to the older C tinyfft already catalogued.
caveats: First-party sample run on one unnamed Apple Silicon machine; modest gains (about 1.2-1.4x, a tie at N=256 forward). tinyfft is f32 while fft.js is f64 (round-trip error ~1e-7 vs ~1e-14), so precision differs; the bench README says so. Only fft.js is benchmarked although the bench describes 'popular JS/WASM FFT libraries'; no other wasm FFT (for example a pffft or KissFFT wasm build) is compared. The forward loop includes a 2N-float re-seed copy for tinyfft that fft.js does not pay. The scalar wasm build loses to fft.js, so the win depends on wasm SIMD. The live browser benchmark is on rluts.github.io (blocked here, not opened). 1 star, created mid-2026.

name: wa-ulid
language: Rust compiled to WebAssembly (Cargo.toml in repo) with a TypeScript wrapper
baseline: ulid 2.x (ulid/javascript, the reference pure-JavaScript ULID generator; devDependency ^2.3.0)
workload: ULID generation (ulid(), monotonicFactory()) and time encode/decode, ops/sec measured with Benchmark.js in Node (benchmark.js, pnpm benchmark).
tradeoffs: Wasm module adds about 110 KB versus 4.7 KB for ulid; README recommends it mainly for backend use.
caveats: First-party, 4 commits, untouched since May 2024. The 43x ulid() row measures random-number batching, not wasm codegen: ulid 2.3.0 calls Node crypto.randomBytes(1) once per character (16 calls and Buffer allocations per ULID), while wa-ulid fills the 16 characters from rand::thread_rng (a userspace ChaCha12 CSPRNG seeded once through getrandom's js feature). Both are cryptographically secure, so the row is a real API-level win, but a JS implementation that batches getRandomValues would close most of the gap (not measured). The README's statement that randomness does not use browser or Node crypto APIs is only true per call; the seed comes from them through getrandom. The other rows are 1.27x-2.73x. A user-supplied PRNG path calls back into JS once per character and was not benchmarked. Single machine; numbers not reproduced independently.

name: xxhash-wasm
language: WebAssembly with JavaScript wrapper (implementation of xxHash 32-bit and 64-bit)
baseline: xxhashjs (pure JavaScript xxHash, uses cuint for 64-bit math); also Node built-in crypto md5 and sha1 (different, cryptographic algorithms)
workload: XXH64/XXH32 hashing via the public JS API. Third-party: byte-array one-shot (4 B, 8 B), 1 MiB bulk, streaming 1 MiB in 64 B-64 KiB chunks, and ASCII strings (8, 32 chars). First-party README: Benchmark.js ops/sec on random ASCII strings from 1 byte to 100,000,000 bytes, plus Node crypto md5/sha1 for comparison.
claimed_speedup: Third-party (haya32x64 docs/benchmarks.md, snapshot 2026-08-09, xxhash-wasm 1.1.0 vs xxhashjs 0.2.2, public API, medians of nine 150 ms samples): XXH64 one-shot 4-byte input 39.4 ns vs 1939.3 ns on C8a (AMD EPYC 9R45), about 49x (derived from page data), and 63.9 vs 2691.0 ns on C8g (Neoverse V2), about 42x (derived). 1 MiB bulk 15,973 vs 37 MB/s (about 432x, derived) on C8a and 10,738 vs 28 MB/s (about 384x, derived) on C8g. 8-char strings 59.2 vs 2437.8 ns (about 41x, derived). First-party README (Benchmark.js ops/sec): the prose says the 32-bit hash is up to 90x and the 64-bit up to 350x faster than xxhashjs. The table itself shows 32-bit from 11.2x at 1 byte (5,752,446 vs 513,517 ops/sec) up to 140.7x at 1,000,000 bytes, and 64-bit from 373x at 1 byte (4,438,501 vs 11,896 ops/sec) up to 677.8x at 100,000 bytes. At 100,000,000 bytes 64-bit is 34.56 vs 0.13 ops/sec (265.8x). All README ratios are derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Hand-written src/xxhash.wat built with wasm-opt --enable-bulk-memory -O4 (package.json build-wasm script; npm 1.1.0 artifact). Third-party run under Node.js 24.18.0 / V8 13.6.233.17-node.50 via node --expose-gc js.mjs (haya32x64 bench/, calibration plus warmup, then nine 150 ms samples, median). The first-party README table comes from bench/index.js (Benchmark.js, node --max-old-space-size=4096 index.js), with Node 17.3 stated for the Node-crypto table.
hardware: Third-party: AWS EC2 c8a.2xlarge (AMD EPYC 9R45) and c8g.2xlarge (Arm Neoverse V2), Ubuntu 26.04, timed work pinned to CPU 2. First-party README: an x64 MacBook Pro (CPU model not stated) running Node 17.3; the xxhash-wasm 64-bit column is identical in the xxhashjs and Node-crypto tables, so both appear to come from the same run (inference).
tradeoffs: Needs BigInt in WASM, bulk memory and TextEncoder.encodeInto (Chrome >= 85, Firefox >= 79, Safari >= 15, Node >= 15); older xxhash-wasm 0.4.2 is 3-4x slower. WASM instantiation takes about 1 ms in the browser and a little over 2 ms in Node. Small bundle (11.4 kB minified, 2.3 kB gzipped) versus xxhashjs 41.5 kB.
caveats: The baseline xxhashjs is a slow pure-JS port that emulates 64-bit math with cuint, not a tuned JS hash. The Node crypto comparison uses cryptographic md5/sha1. There is no native xxHash C baseline. The README prose (up to 90x/350x) understates its own table (up to ~141x/~678x, derived). In the first-party bench/index.js the xxhashjs calls also run .toString(16) on each result while xxhash-wasm returns raw numbers/BigInt, so the baseline does extra work (small at large inputs). Not the fastest wasm xxHash: hash-wasm 4.10.0's README shows XXHash64 at 101.66 MB/s vs xxhash-wasm 1.0.2's 47.58 MB/s at 32 bytes (2.1x, derived), with a tie at 1 MB (15,989 vs 15,929 MB/s). name: zaw (Zero-Allocation WASM)
language: Zig and Rust (WebAssembly) with TypeScript host
baseline: Plain JavaScript loop and Rust wasm-bindgen
workload: XOR of a scalar into an Int32Array passed in and out of WebAssembly, for 10 to 100,000 elements, measured with vitest bench.
claimed_speedup: XOR Int32Array (copy in, XOR, read out), zaw Rust build vs plain JavaScript loop: 6.03x at 100 elements, 11.39x at 1,000, 12.80x at 10,000, 13.75x at 100,000; vs Rust wasm-bindgen: 6.20x, 6.88x, 3.32x, 4.32x. zaw Zig build vs JavaScript: 6.0x, 9.7x, 9.9x, 10.0x; vs wasm-bindgen 6.2x, 5.9x, 2.6x, 3.1x (derived from page data). At 10 elements plain JS is 1.66x faster than zaw Rust and 1.67x faster than zaw Zig. Transfer Out Float64Array: zaw 4.3x to 10.65x faster than wasm-bindgen; Transfer In Float64Array: wasm-bindgen 1.03x to 1.22x faster than zaw up to 10,000 elements. 4x4 Float32 matrix multiply: zaw 1.23x (batch 1) to 24.35x (batch 1000) faster than JS.
compiler_and_flags: Zig: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, wasm32-freestanding with +simd128, then wasm-opt -O4 --enable-simd --enable-bulk-memory (scripts/build-zig.sh, examples/wasm-zig/build.zig). Rust (zaw): cargo build --release with opt-level 3, LTO, codegen-units 1, panic=abort, RUSTFLAGS +simd128, then wasm-opt -O4 --enable-simd (scripts/build-rust.sh, examples/wasm-rust/Cargo.toml). wasm-bindgen baseline: wasm-pack build --target web with +simd128. Toolchain versions of the benchmark run not stated: docs/benchmarks.md was last updated 2026-02-17, before the 2026-05-24 'Upgrade to zig 16' commit, so the Zig 0.16.0 badge does not describe the measured build; Rust is unpinned 'stable'; Node/V8 version not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-Core Processor (docs/benchmarks.md); Node/browser version not stated
tradeoffs: It is an interop protocol, not an algorithm library; wins only when data is large enough to amortise the call (not at 10 elements) and the author picks the cheapest possible kernel to expose interop cost.
caveats: Micro-benchmarks of interop overhead, first-party. Harness asymmetries: the JS XOR baseline allocates a fresh Int32Array per call, while zaw returns a subarray view into the WASM output buffer (implementations/host-typescript/src/conduit.ts readInt32Elements) that the next call overwrites, so a caller that keeps the result must copy it and the 'zero-allocation' gain partly comes from not materializing output; the JS 4x4 matmul baseline does two slice() copies plus a new Float32Array per matrix, which inflates the 20-24x matmul ratios. The wasm-bindgen comparison is fair on kernel (both call the same shared::xor_array_i32), the difference being Vec allocation and copy-out. In 'Transfer In Float64Array' wasm-bindgen is faster than zaw up to 10,000 elements. Toolchain and Node versions of the run are not stated, and the published numbers predate the Zig 0.16 upgrade.

name: zip.js (@zip.js/zip.js WebAssembly zlib codec)
language: JavaScript with bundled WebAssembly zlib and AES codecs
baseline: zip.js's own pure-JavaScript zlib port, jszip (pako) and fflate; also native CompressionStream and node:zlib shown for reference
workload: Compress/decompress 20 MB of compressible text, 20 MB incompressible data and 5,000 x ~2 KB text files in Node, each (library, operation, workload) in a fresh process, median of 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: Head-to-head (benchmarks/bench.js, fresh Node v26.10.0 process per row, median of 3, level 6): decompress 20 MB text WASM zlib 71 ms vs zip.js pure-JS zlib 155 ms, jszip/pako 140 ms, fflate 116 ms; compress 20 MB incompressible WASM 460 ms vs pure-JS 787 ms, jszip 854 ms (fflate 298 ms is faster); compress 20 MB text WASM 1098 ms vs pure-JS 1229 ms, jszip 1753 ms (fflate 908 ms is faster at 2% larger output); 5,000 x ~2 KB files compress WASM 551 ms vs pure-JS 962 ms, jszip 846 ms (fflate 278 ms is faster). Codec alone (benchmarks/bench-codecs.js, in-process, warm): WASM inflate 41 ms (483.7 MB/s) vs Node DecompressionStream 56 ms, pure-JS 108 ms, fflate 122 ms, i.e. 27% faster than Node's native zlib stream; WASM deflate level 5 493 ms for 6,562,182 bytes vs fflate level 5 534 ms for 6,648,574 bytes; at level 6 WASM 1025 ms is slower than CompressionStream 695 ms. AES-256 WinZip entry, 20 MB stored, write/read (benchmarks/bench-aes.js): WebAssembly 134/135 MB/s vs JavaScript engine 119/108 on Node, 119/121 vs 115/117 on Bun, 124/124 vs 144/133 on Deno (JS faster there); browsers WASM 125/125 vs JS 79/79 (Firefox 156) and 136/138 vs 104/104 (Chrome 153).
tradeoffs: WASM module instantiation costs about 20 ms per fresh process; peak memory is higher than fflate (139 MB vs 68 MB delta on the 20 MB text compress); the codec is used only when native CompressionStream is unavailable or the wasm backend is configured.
caveats: The wasm backend is not the fastest option overall: native CompressionStream and node:zlib beat it on compression (text 678-730 ms vs 1098 ms) and fflate beats it on incompressible data (298 ms) and on small files (278 ms compress, 101 ms decompress); on Node zip.js uses CompressionStream by default at level 6, so the WASM codec runs only for other levels, with useCompressionStream: false, or where no native stream exists. The win is WASM versus the JS port of the same codec and versus pako/fflate, plus a warm inflate 27% faster than Node's DecompressionStream. No decompression row verifies CRC-32 (page says enabling it costs about 7 ms per 20 MB on WASM). Fresh-process rows include about 20 ms of wasm instantiation. Author-run on one Apple M2 machine; levels are not equal work across libraries, which the page handles by printing output sizes. The AES figures in the original record (131 vs 114 MB/s, release 2.15.0 page on jsr.io) are not on BENCHMARKS.md and were replaced with the page's numbers.

name: DTVM (ZetaEngine lazy-JIT Wasm VM)
baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift); also Wasmer Singlepass, Cranelift and LLVM
metric: startup (time to first invocation) and latency (processing time = load+compile+execute)
workload: PolyBench/C 4.2.1 (30 kernels, int data, DUMP_ARRAYS; the package build notes say SMALL_DATASET) run as archived prebuilt wasm, 20 WAPM packages (time to first invocation only), a recursive Fibonacci(30) and an Integer Overflow (Uniswap-like swap) contract with host APIs mocked in memory. DTVM multipass and lazy JIT are compared against Wasmtime (Cranelift) and Wasmer Singlepass, Cranelift and LLVM.
claimed_speedup: Paper (arXiv 2504.16552 preprint, April 2025 copy at resources/DTVM_paper.pdf). Time to first invocation with lazy JIT on: DTVM 0.95-0.96 ms vs Wasmtime (Cranelift) 20.5-20.6 ms on PolyBench. Table 9 averages: 22.21x over Wasmtime (Cranelift), 4.05x over Wasmer Singlepass, 68.01x over Wasmer Cranelift and 234.13x over Wasmer LLVM on 30 PolyBench cases; on WAPM, 18.87x over Wasmtime, 4.35x over Wasmer Singlepass (one case at 0.49x), 18.66x over Wasmer Cranelift and 197.99x over Wasmer LLVM. Figure 9 shows 21.35x and 21.54x (deriche, doitgen) and 24.51x and 23.36x (echo, pi), so 21.54x is the larger of two displayed PolyBench cases, not a per-case maximum. From the appendix tables (derived from page data): per-case Wasmtime ratios run 19.2-26.0x on PolyBench and 3.2-24.2x on the 20 WAPM packages, and the Wasmer Cranelift PolyBench average is about 22.2x rather than Table 9's 68.01x. Processing time (load + compile + execute; section 5.2.2 says lazy compilation was off): DTVM beats Wasmtime (Cranelift) in 20 of 30 PolyBench cases (1.20x average there, best 1.63x on deriche) and loses the other 10 (0.76x average, worst about 0.57x on trisolv, derived from page data); it averages 11.03-12.14x over the three Wasmer backends. Fibonacci(30): 11.73 ms, which is 11.8% less than Wasmtime (Cranelift) and 25.6%, 29.6% and 40.5% less than Wasmer Cranelift, Singlepass and LLVM. Integer Overflow: 5.5 ms, about 20.6% less than Wasmtime (Cranelift) and up to 64.6% less than the Wasmer variants. The abstract also claims up to 2x over evmone on ERC20/721/1155; that was not checked here.
compiler_and_flags: PolyBench wasm: archived prebuilt binaries whose toolchain was inferred from binary traces (WASI clang 11.0.0 for 27 cases, 14.0.3 for 3). benchmarks/paper/benchmarks/polybenchc/build.sh reconstructs them with wasi-sdk clang -O3 -DSMALL_DATASET -DDATA_TYPE_IS_INT -DPOLYBENCH_DUMP_ARRAYS -D_WASI_EMULATED_PROCESS_CLOCKS. Paper-era DTVM: commit 882c83155 with LLVM 15. The package's Release build line (-DZEN_ENABLE_SINGLEPASS_JIT=ON -DZEN_ENABLE_MULTIPASS_JIT=ON -DZEN_ENABLE_CHECKED_ARITHMETIC=ON) and run flags (-m multipass [--enable-multipass-lazy] --disable-multipass-greedyra --disable-multipass-multithread) are reconstructions marked 'inferred from xlsx', and the paper does not record its build type. Baselines in the paper text: Wasmtime 31.0.0 (Cranelift) and Wasmer 5.0.5. The package records Wasmer 5.0.4 with Singlepass from v5.0.5-rc1, and its current pins are Wasmtime 45.0.0, Wasmer 7.1.0 (LLVM 21) and DTVM c3c3fd856.
hardware: Cloud VM, 8 vCPU, 16 GiB, Intel Xeon Platinum 8369B @ 2.70GHz, CentOS 7.9, Linux 3.10.0 (paper section 5). benchmarks/paper/ENVIRONMENT.md records Turbo Boost off only for the contract microbenchmark machine and says the other baselines may have run on a different machine.
tradeoffs: Built for blockchain smart contracts (deterministic execution, gas metering, EVM ABI compatibility, TEE portability), not a general-purpose WASI runtime. Lazy JIT with LLVM 15 requires x86-64; the singlepass JIT and interpreter modes are the portable ones. Small codebase (69.5 KLoC vs 143.6 KLoC for Wasmtime per the paper).
caveats: The paper is a first-party arXiv preprint (arXiv 2504.16552; a v2 exists but arxiv.org is blocked here) by Ant Digital Technologies authors and is not peer reviewed. The reproduction package (benchmarks/paper, added 2026-09) ships cases, version pins and reconstructed scripts but no result data, no per-runtime logs and not the paper's 'Average time' timing script; the contract microbenchmark runner is not included. Its runtimes/dtvm/BUILD.md marks the paper-era DTVM run flags as 'inferred from xlsx'. Its docs/XLSX_FORMAT.md is an issue log: the archived table's cell semantics (compile vs total, ms vs s) are unconfirmed, and the paper's DTVM PolyBench values (2mm 3283.6 ms) match the archived 'dtvm multipass + lazy' total cell (3283.55), although section 5.2.2 says lazy compilation was disabled for that comparison (the eager 'dtvm multipass' cell is 3314.16). The time-to-first-invocation (TTFI) metric is asymmetric. DTVM lazy counts load, lazy precompile, instantiation and the first function's JIT; Wasmtime counts an eager whole-module compile_module(); Wasmer counts Module::new. The package FAQ says DTVM's own eager multipass compile reads about 90 ms on the current build, so the 22x comes from lazy vs eager compilation, not from a faster compiler. Wasmer's three backends post nearly identical processing times about 10x Wasmtime's on compute-heavy kernels (2mm: Cranelift 43.5 s, LLVM 43.9 s, Singlepass 53.0 s vs Wasmtime 3.8 s). LLVM no faster than Cranelift points to a harness or configuration effect in the Wasmer runs, so the 11-12x averages over Wasmer are unexplained. The paper's tables disagree internally. Table 9 lists 30 WAPM cases where appendix Table 12 has 20. Table 9's 68.01x Wasmer Cranelift TTFI average does not match the appendix (about 22.2x, derived from page data). Table 8's Wasmer backend labels are permuted relative to the appendix columns. The build notes say SMALL_DATASET, but the multi-second processing times (2mm 3.3 s) are far above what SMALL_DATASET kernels need, so the dataset size of the archived wasm is unclear. The package's WAPM set replaces the paper's zuk with fortune. zuk was DTVM's worst case: 0.49x vs Wasmer Singlepass and only 3.2x vs Wasmtime. Versions: the paper used Wasmtime 31.0.0 and Wasmer 5.0.x with DTVM 882c83155. The package now pins Wasmtime 45.0.0, Wasmer 7.1.0 and DTVM c3c3fd856 (2026-05-29) for a revised experiment set whose numbers are not in the repo. The package says it is not recorded whether the paper's wall-clock runs cleared the Wasmtime and Wasmer module caches; TTFI runs need WASMTIME_CACHE=0. The README build examples use CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug, which the package warns is far slower than the paper's Release build. Lazy JIT is x86-64 only. The LICENSE is Apache-2.0, with LLVM-derived portions under Apache-2.0 and BSD-3-Clause.

PolyBench processing time (load + compile + execute): faster than Wasmtime (Cranelift) in 20 of 30 cases (1.20x average on those, 0.76x on the 10 it loses) and 11.03x-12.14x on average over the three Wasmer backends. Fibonacci(30): 11.73 ms, which is 11.8% less than Wasmtime (Cranelift), 25.6% less than Wasmer (Cranelift), 29.6% less than Wasmer (Singlepass) and 40.5% less than Wasmer (LLVM).

The reproduction package under benchmarks/paper ships cases, scripts and version pins but no result data, and its own notes say Wasmtime and Wasmer keep an on-disk module cache by default while DTVM recompiles on every launch, so wall-clock runs need the cache disabled; the contract microbenchmark runner is not included. The paper's runs used older Wasmtime and Wasmer versions (31.0.0, 5.0.x) than the package now pins (45.0.0, 7.1.0). Time-to-first-invocation compares DTVM's lazy per-function compile against baselines that compile the whole module eagerly. Wasmtime is faster than DTVM in 10 of 30 PolyBench cases (0.76x average there) and DTVM is slower than Wasmer Singlepass in one WAPM case. Host APIs are mocked in memory. Numbers read from the paper PDF checked into the repo (resources/DTVM_paper.pdf), fetched through the Git LFS media host.

name: wasman
baseline: wazero v1.12 (interpreter mode and compiler mode); also wagon v0.4 and life
workload: Go benchmarks over tiny hand-written .wat modules: Fib(20) recursive, 100k-iteration Sum loop, 64KiB MemRW, module Instantiate (decode+validate+instantiate), plus JIT-mode kernels Sort (10k i32 quicksort), Dispatch (br_table), Hash, Mandel, Indirect (call_indirect).
claimed_speedup: Interpreter vs wazero interpreter (Apple M3, ns/op): Fib 974,787 vs 1,787,663; Sum 3,014,618 vs 3,930,498; MemRW 4,751,546 vs 5,153,545; Instantiate 2,129 vs 14,100; README says 1.1-1.8x faster than wazero's interpreter, 1.5-2.4x faster than wagon, about 2x faster than life, instantiation 3-14x faster. JIT vs wazero compiler: MemRW 39,575 vs 70,643, Sort 367,952 vs 477,368, Sum 27,112 vs 26,850 (level), Fib 41,187 vs 37,832 (slower), Indirect 3,926,713 vs 2,812,512 (1.4x slower); on dual EPYC 7K62 Sum 2.0x and MemRW 1.6x ahead of wazero compiler, Fib 1.6x behind.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.24 (per bench/README.md); go test -bench . -benchmem ./bench with default Go flags; fixtures compiled from .wat with wat2wasm and checked in. bench/go.mod at HEAD declares go 1.25.0 and pins wazero v1.12.0, wagon v0.4.0 (via replace) and life at a 2019 commit. Every timed iteration checks the returned value against a constant.
hardware: Apple M3 (main tables); dual AMD EPYC 7K62 server for the amd64 JIT comparison
tradeoffs: Pure Go with zero dependencies (no cgo), interpreter by default; optional tiered JIT (EnableJIT) only on arm64 and amd64 and per-function interpreter fallback (optimizing tier covers about 86% of spec-suite function bodies). The README claims full official spec-suite conformance, metering and interruption support.
caveats: Self-benchmarked by the author. Each row is a single run with no variance reported, and run-to-run noise is visible: the wasman interpreter's Fib reads 974,787 ns in the main table and 1,120,975 ns in the JIT table, 15% apart, which is larger than the 1.08x MemRW margin over wazero's interpreter. Workloads are very small (Fib(20) is about 13.5k calls). The Instantiate sub-benchmark for wazero creates and closes a whole wazero Runtime on every iteration (NewRuntimeWithConfig + Instantiate + Close, with no CompiledModule reuse), so the 6.6x instantiation win over wazero includes runtime setup and teardown that wasman's row does not pay. The README bolds wasman-jit on Sum even though its 27,112 ns is 1% slower than wazero-compiler's 26,850 ns. The EPYC 7K62 claims (Sum 2.0x, MemRW 1.6x ahead, Fib 1.6x behind) are ratios only, with no table. Only Go engines are compared: cgo runtimes (wasmtime-go, wasmer-go) are excluded, so there is no comparison with wasmtime, wasmer, V8 or WAMR. The JIT result is mixed: ahead of wazero's compiler on memory-bound code (MemRW 1.8x, Sort 1.3x), level on Sum and Dispatch, and behind on Fib (9%), Hash (9%), Mandel (3%) and Indirect (1.4x). LICENSE carries 'Copyright (c) 2020 @mathetake', the author of gasm, which became wazero, so wasman shares ancestry with its main baseline. Interpreter and JIT correctness fixes landed 2026-08-16 to 08-19, after the documented numbers (host-call resolution, toll return sentinel). None of them touches the benchmark workloads, which have no imports and no TollStation. Wazero is the Go incumbent but not one of the listed baselines.

name: Cage (wasmtime-mte, MTE-based memory safety and bounds checking for 64-bit Wasm)
baseline: Plain 64-bit Wasm (wasm64/memory64) run in Wasmtime without MTE, where the sandbox relies on software bounds checks; the paper reports speedups 'over wasm64' (search snippet of arXiv 2408.11456; whether the baseline build is upstream Wasmtime or the fork with MTE off was not confirmed).
workload: PolyBench/C kernels compiled to 64-bit Wasm with Cage's LLVM fork and run in the wasmtime-mte fork on a Google Pixel 8 (per search snippets of the paper); Cage offloads the wasm64 sandbox bounds check to Arm MTE and adds MTE heap/stack safety and PAC pointer protection.
claimed_speedup: cage-meta README abstract: memory-safety runtime overhead <5.8% and memory overhead <5.3% (the BibTeX abstract on the same page says <3.7%), and MTE-based sandboxing 'achieving a speedup of over 5.1%'. Search snippet of arXiv 2408.11456 (snippet only): on a Google Pixel 8 (Tensor G3), PolyBench/C mean speedup of MTE sandboxing over wasm64 of 3.7±6.5%, 5.1±4.0% and 33.9±2.4% on the three core types (33.9% on the in-order Cortex-A510 cores); memory safety plus MTE sandboxing 2.1±5.6%, 4.5±4.1% and 29.2±2.5% versus wasm64.
compiler_and_flags: LLVM fork (TUM-DSE/llvm-memsafe-wasm) and wasi-libc fork; flags not stated on the pages opened
hardware: Google Pixel 8 (Google Tensor G3) with Arm MTE and PAC, per the paper's artifact appendix as quoted in a search snippet; LLVM, wasmtime and benchmarks cross-compiled on an x86 host. Not confirmed from an opened page.
tradeoffs: Needs Arm CPUs with MTE and PAC, 64-bit Wasm (memory64) modules, and the authors' forks of LLVM, wasmtime, wasm-tools and wasi-libc; the wasmtime fork carries the upstream Apache-2.0 LICENSE file but cage-meta has no LICENSE file. Primary purpose is memory safety; the speedup is a side effect of replacing software bounds checks.
caveats: The CGO 2025 paper (doi 10.1145/3696443.3708920, pp. 538-552), arXiv 2408.11456, the CGO slides on dse.in.tum.de and the Zenodo artifact (doi 10.5281/zenodo.13772996) were all unreachable here; per-core numbers come from search snippets only. The 5.1% is a mean with a ±4.0% spread on one core type; on the big cores the mean is 3.7% with a ±6.5% spread (spread larger than the mean), and only the in-order Cortex-A510 shows a large gain (33.9%). The win is against wasm64 software bounds checks, not against 32-bit Wasm with guard pages, which needs no explicit checks. Requires Arm MTE hardware (Pixel 8 class). README abstract (memory overhead <5.3%) and BibTeX abstract (<3.7%) disagree. wasmtime-mte is a research fork of bytecodealliance/wasmtime (12,557 commits, mostly upstream; last MTE commits 2026-01-14), not upstreamed; its README is the stock wasmtime README with no MTE instructions.

name: KinoWASM (KinoRuntime)
baseline: WAMR iwasm fast interpreter (also compared against wasm3)
workload: CoreMark 1.0 compiled to a WASI wasm module (Clang 11.0.0, -O3) and a recursive fibonacci(40) module, each run through the runtime's own CLI; interpreter versus interpreter.
claimed_speedup: CoreMark Iterations/Sec: KinoRuntime 4385.746651, wasm3 3555.555556, iwasm (WAMR fast interpreter) 1734.417344; page states approximately 1.23x wasm3 and 2.53x iwasm. fibonacci(40): KinoRuntime 1838.94 ms, wasm3 2601.12 ms, iwasm 4298.94 ms; page states approximately 1.41x wasm3 and 2.34x iwasm.
compiler_and_flags: Guest CoreMark module: Clang 11.0.0 (LLVM 176249bd6732), -O3. The fibtest.wasm guest is built locally with Emscripten emcc (WASMData/README.md; binary not in Git). Runtime executables: KinoRuntime 'standard Clang build' with compiler version and preset not recorded; wasm3 and iwasm build configurations not recorded. CMakePresets.json also offers MSVC PGO presets (x64-Release-pgo-gen/use) trained on CoreMark, described as lifting CoreMark by about 6.7%; which preset built the measured binary is unrecorded. The public build needs MSVC 14.50+ or clang-cl (guaranteed tail calls via musttail) with AVX2 enabled.
hardware: Intel Core i7-13700F, Windows 11 (user-reported)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks, 6 commits; the README says it is used in several production console titles (console integrations are private, so this cannot be checked)
tradeoffs: Interpreter (register-TOS, direct-threaded, tail calls), so far slower than JIT/AOT engines such as wasmtime or wasmer. Public repo builds only for Windows x64 and needs a compiler with guaranteed tail calls. No SIMD execution, no threads/atomics, no GC; WASI only partial; memory64 and exception handling partial. Host-controlled suspend/resume of guest execution is a feature. Embedding needs a host-provided linear-memory backend.
caveats: benchmark.md calls the numbers 'user-supplied measurements' and a 'preliminary snapshot'. There is one machine (Windows 11), and the runtime versions, runtime compiler flags, KinoRuntime preset/PGO settings, measurement date, workload hashes and per-run spread are all unrecorded. CoreMark is not bundled, and iwasm ran 30,000 iterations while the other two ran 60,000. The final CRC differs between iwasm (0x5275) and wasm3/KinoRuntime (0xbd59). That is consistent with the different iteration counts, since CoreMark's final CRC accumulates over iterations, and all three logs report validation passed. Fibonacci timing uses the in-guest clock through each runtime's WASI clock, and the repeat count is unrecorded. The baselines were Windows builds of unknown configuration. WAMR's core/config.h enables labels-as-values (computed-goto) dispatch only under __GNUC__, so an MSVC or clang-cl build of iwasm falls back to switch dispatch, which may explain much of the 2.5x gap to iwasm. wasm3 on Windows may be similarly disadvantaged. The repo carries CoreMark-trained PGO presets, which is a tuning risk if one built the measured binary. The project is very new (first commit 2026-09-30, 6 commits, single author), and correctness fixes landed 2026-10-08/09 (live register tracking below wide-arithmetic operands; integer overflow in buffer-read bounds checks), possibly after the undated measurements.
